# Reading - typescript/02_functions

The theory behind the five signatures you just wrote, and the four or five
questions an interviewer will ask about them.

## Notes

**Optional vs default is a real distinction, not a style choice.** `level?:
number` makes the parameter `number | undefined` inside the body, so every use
of it must handle the missing case; `level = 1` makes it `number` inside the
body and optional at the call site. Reach for the default whenever there is a
sensible fallback, because it puts the fallback in the signature — the first
place anyone reads — instead of burying it in a `??` three lines down. Reach
for `?` when "absent" is genuinely different from any value you could pick, and
then handle it explicitly. One trap worth knowing: passing `undefined`
explicitly (`heading("x", undefined)`) triggers the default, but passing `null`
does not, because defaults fire on `undefined` only.

**`void` means "ignore my result", not "return undefined".** This is the most
commonly failed question about function types. A function type whose return is
`void` accepts implementations returning anything at all — that is deliberate
special-casing in the assignability rules, and without it
`items.forEach((x) => list.push(x))` would not compile. The consequence to
remember: if you *declare* a variable of type `() => void` and call it, the
result you get back is typed `void`, so you cannot use it even when the
underlying function returned something real. Contrast with a function
*declaration* annotated `: void`, where returning a value is an error.

**`never` is the empty type, and it earns its keep in three places.** As a
return type it marks a function that never finishes normally — it throws or
loops forever — which lets the compiler treat a call to it as the end of a code
path. As a parameter type it makes a function uncallable, which is how the
exhaustiveness check in lesson 04 works. And as an element type, `never[]` is
what you get from `[]` with no context, which is why an unannotated empty array
sometimes refuses every `push` you try. Remember: `void` is "returns, but with
nothing useful"; `never` is "does not return".

**Overloads are a declaration, not a dispatch mechanism.** There is exactly one
function at runtime; the overload list is a compile-time menu, and resolution
picks the *first* signature that matches the arguments. The implementation
signature is not one of the choices, which surprises people — you cannot call
`unwrap(someStringOrNumber)` if the overloads only list `string` and `number`
separately, because no single overload accepts a union. That is the standard
argument for preferring a union parameter (or a generic) over overloads unless
the return type genuinely depends on the argument type. Overloads also do not
check that your implementation actually honours them, so `function f(x:
string): number; function f(x: any): any { return "oops"; }` compiles. They are
a promise you make, and you own it.

## ex1 — a default the caller can override

The runtime half is `Math.round`, and the reason the gate checks both `1/3` and
`2/3` is to separate rounding from truncation: `Math.floor` gives 33 and 66,
rounding gives 33 and 67. Formatting bugs of exactly this kind are what makes a
dashboard show "99%" forever.

The type half is what `expectTypeOf(progressLine).parameters` reports. With
`total = 12` the parameter list is `[done: number, total?: number]` — the
default made it optional at the call site while keeping it `number` inside the
body. That asymmetry is the feature. Writing `total: number = 12` produces the
same type and one redundant annotation; writing `total?: number` and then
`total ?? 12` in the body produces the same behaviour with the fallback moved
somewhere less visible.

The subtle thing to carry forward is that defaults are evaluated *per call*, at
call time, left to right, and may reference earlier parameters:
`function slice(text: string, end = text.length)` is legal and often exactly
what you want.

## ex2 — as many scores as you like

`bestOf(scores: number[])` and `bestOf(...scores: number[])` have identical
bodies and completely different call sites. Which one to write is a genuine API
decision: rest parameters read beautifully for two or three arguments
(`Math.max(a, b)`), and become awkward the moment a caller has an array and has
to remember to spread it — or, worse, has an array of 200,000 elements, where
`Math.max(...values)` overflows the call stack. Node's argument limit is in the
tens of thousands, and "why does this crash only in production" has been traced
to that spread more than once.

The seed value is the other quiet decision. Seeding at `0` makes `bestOf()`
return `0` for free, which the README chose deliberately. Seeding at
`-Infinity` is the mathematically honest answer for "the maximum of nothing",
and returning `undefined` is the honest *API* answer — but that changes the
return type to `number | undefined` and pushes a narrowing step onto every
caller. All three are defensible; what is not defensible is not deciding.

## ex3 — a function that takes a function

Two lessons hide in one small function. The first is that function types are
ordinary types: they can be aliased, unioned, put in arrays, and inferred. When
you pass an inline arrow to `forEachTrack`, TypeScript *contextually types* its
parameters from the declared callback type, which is why you write `(name,
index) => ...` with no annotations and still get full checking inside. Delete
the callback's second parameter from the signature and that same arrow starts
reporting an implicit `any` — which is precisely the failure the stub produces.

The second is the `=> void` assignability rule, which the gate exercises with
`forEachTrack(["a"], (name) => seen.push(name))`. `push` returns a number; the
callback type says `void`; it compiles anyway. Interviewers like this one
because the wrong answer ("that should be an error") sounds so reasonable.

Also worth noticing: a callback may accept *fewer* parameters than the type
declares, never more. That is why `names.forEach(visit)` works when `visit`
takes one argument, and why passing a function that takes four parameters to
`forEach` is an error — the caller only ever supplies three.

## ex4 — one name, two signatures

The reason overloads exist is that `duplicate(value: string | number): string |
number` is a *worse* contract than it looks. Every caller who passes a string
gets back something they must narrow before using, even though you and they
both know it is a string. Overloads move that knowledge into the type system.

Three practical notes. First, order matters: resolution takes the first
matching overload, so put the more specific signature first when two could
match. Second, the implementation signature must be assignable to none of the
overloads' *callers* — it is invisible from outside — but TypeScript only
loosely checks that it is compatible, so a wrong implementation can slip
through. Third, modern TypeScript often has a better answer: generics with
conditional return types (lesson 09), or simply two functions with two names.
"Should this be an overload or two functions?" is a real code-review question,
and the honest default is two functions unless callers benefit from the shared
name.

## challenge — retry

Retry logic is a standard interview exercise because it exposes how carefully
someone reads a spec. Rethrowing the *last* error rather than a fresh one keeps
the stack and message that describe what actually went wrong; throwing
`new Error("all attempts failed")` destroys the evidence. Counting the total
attempts rather than the retries (three attempts means one call plus two
retries, not four calls) is the off-by-one everyone has to think about once.

The type-level detail is `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, on in this course and on
by default under `strict` since TypeScript 4.4. A caught value is `unknown`,
not `any`, because JavaScript can throw literally anything — `throw "nope"` and
`throw 42` are legal. That means `error.message` does not compile until you
narrow, which is exactly what lesson 10's guards are for. Storing it as
`unknown` and rethrowing it untouched is the correct move here and the one that
preserves the most information.

The `never` helper is optional but instructive: `function fail(msg: string):
never { throw new Error(msg); }` lets a guard clause be one call, and the
compiler still believes the surrounding function returns a `string`, because a
call to a `never`-returning function terminates the path. Try annotating `fail`
as `void` instead and watch the surrounding function suddenly claim it might
return `undefined`.

## review1 — padCell

Two defaults, one no-op case, and a `repeat` that throws on a negative count —
the same shape as ex1 with the failure mode moved. If you computed
`filler.repeat(width - text.length)` before checking whether the text was
already wide enough, `padCell("overlong", 4)` threw a `RangeError`, which is a
nice reminder that "the types are fine" and "the function is correct" are
different claims.

The design question worth sitting with: nothing in the signature stops a caller
passing a two-character filler and getting a cell wider than `width`. You could
fix that at runtime (slice the result), in the type system (lesson 05's literal
types can demand a single character, sort of), or in documentation. Knowing
which fixes are available — and that the type system is only one of them — is
most of what "typed thinking" actually means.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: More on Functions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html) — optional and default parameters, rest parameters, overloads, `void` and `never`, in one authoritative page.
- [Handbook: Assignability of functions (`void` return)](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#return-type-void) — the exact rule behind the `forEach`/`push` line in the type gate.
- [`tsconfig` reference: `useUnknownInCatchVariables`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#useUnknownInCatchVariables) — why the challenge's caught value is `unknown`.
- [MDN: rest parameters](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Functions/rest_parameters) — the JavaScript half of ex2, including how rest differs from the old `arguments` object.
- [TypeScript Deep Dive: function overloading](https://basarat.gitbook.io/typescript/type-system/functions) — a blunt walkthrough of when overloads help and when they hide bugs.

## Challenge — retry (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `retry(attempts, action)`:

- it calls `action()` and returns its result the first time it does not throw
- if `action` throws, it tries again, up to `attempts` times in total
- if every attempt throws, it rethrows the error from the **last** attempt
- if `attempts` is less than 1, it throws an `Error` whose message is exactly
  `retry: attempts must be at least 1`

The gate counts calls, so an off-by-one is visible immediately. Honest
difficulty note: the loop is short, but `useUnknownInCatchVariables` is on in
this course, so the caught value is `unknown` — store it and rethrow it as-is
rather than assuming it is an `Error`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 02_functions challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three behaviours, and they are easiest to write in this order: refuse a
nonsense `attempts`, return the first successful call, and - if every call
threw - rethrow the error from the *last* attempt rather than inventing a new
one.

The gate counts how many times your `action` runs, so an off-by-one shows up
immediately.

## Hint 2

A `try`/`catch` inside a loop is the shape:

```ts
for (let i = 0; i < attempts; i++) {
  try {
    return action();
  } catch (error) {
    // remember it and keep going
  }
}
```

`return` inside `try` exits the loop and the function, so no success flag is
needed. Under this course's `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, `error` is `unknown`,
so store it in a variable typed `unknown` and rethrow it untouched.

## Hint 3

Guard `attempts < 1` first and throw an `Error` whose message is exactly
`retry: attempts must be at least 1`. Then loop, returning on success and
remembering the caught value. After the loop, throw the remembered value.

The `never` part: write the guard's throw as a small helper -
`function fail(message: string): never { throw new Error(message); }` - and
notice that TypeScript still accepts your function as returning `string`,
because a call to a `never`-returning function ends that code path. Whether
you use the helper or throw inline is your call; the gate cannot tell, but the
reading explains why one of them scales.

## Exercise 1 — a default the caller can override

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `progressLine(done, total)`, which renders a
one-line progress summary:

- `progressLine(3)` → `"3/12 (25%)"` — twelve is the default lesson count
- `progressLine(1, 3)` → `"1/3 (33%)"`
- `progressLine(2, 3)` → `"2/3 (67%)"`
- `progressLine(0, 5)` → `"0/5 (0%)"`

The percentage is `done / total` as a percentage, rounded to the nearest whole
number. The stub declares `total` as required; the gate calls the function with
one argument, so that has to change. The type gate checks that `total` ends up
*optional*, not that you deleted it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 02_functions ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the gate's first call: `progressLine(3)`. One argument, two parameters.
There are two ways to make that legal in TypeScript and only one of them gives
`total` a value to work with.

The number in the expected output tells you what that value is.

## Hint 2

A default parameter is written in the signature, exactly as in JavaScript:

```ts
function example(label: string, times = 3) { ... }
```

## Exercise 2 — as many scores as you like

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement `bestOf(...scores)`, returning the highest
score it was given:

- `bestOf(4, 9, 2)` → `9`
- `bestOf(5)` → `5`
- `bestOf()` → `0` — no scores yet, so no progress yet
- `bestOf(...[1, 8, 3])` → `8`

Scores in this course are never negative, which is what makes `0` a sensible
answer for the empty call. The stub takes an *array*; the gate passes separate
arguments. One character of syntax stands between those two worlds.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 02_functions ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`bestOf([1, 2, 3])` and `bestOf(1, 2, 3)` are different function signatures,
and the gate calls the second one. Only one character stands between them.

The other decision is what `bestOf()` - no arguments at all - should hand back.
The README states it; it is not `undefined` and it is not `-Infinity`.

## Hint 2

The rest parameter collects every remaining argument into an array:

```ts
function join(separator: string, ...parts: string[]): string { ... }
```

Inside the body, `parts` is an ordinary `string[]`. A rest parameter must be
last, and there can only be one.

For the body: a running maximum, seeded so that the no-arguments case already
gives the answer the README asks for.

## Hint 3

Write `...scores: number[]`, seed the running best at `0`, loop, and keep the
larger value. Because the seed is `0`, an empty call returns `0` without a
special case - which is why the README chose that rule.

The decision left to you: whether the seed doubles as the empty-case answer
(as above) or whether you guard `scores.length === 0` explicitly. One of those
two survives a later change to the rule better than the other.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — one name, two signatures

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement `duplicate(value)` so that:

- `duplicate("ab")` → `"abab"` (a `string`)
- `duplicate("")` → `""`
- `duplicate(2)` → `4` (a `number`)
- `duplicate(0)` → `0`

And so that `duplicate("ab")` is *typed* `string` while `duplicate(2)` is typed
`number`. A single signature returning `string | number` would pass the runtime
gate and fail the type gate, which is the entire point of the exercise: callers
should not have to narrow a result whose type you already know.

Booleans have no `duplicate`, and the type gate proves it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 02_functions ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The gate wants `duplicate("ab")` to be a `string` and `duplicate(2)` to be a
`number` - not `string | number` in both cases. A single signature cannot say
that, because a single signature has exactly one return type.

TypeScript's answer is to let you declare the same function more than once.
The README's Concept section shows the shape.

## Hint 2

Overloads are two or more signatures with no body, followed by one
implementation signature that has a body:

```ts
export function example(value: string): string;
export function example(value: boolean): boolean;
export function example(value: string | boolean): string | boolean {
  ...
}
```

The implementation signature is not visible to callers - only the overloads
above it are - so it can be as loose as it needs to be. Inside the body,
`typeof value === "string"` tells the compiler which branch it is in.

## Hint 3

Write two overload signatures - `(value: string): string` and
`(value: number): number` - then an implementation signature accepting
`string | number` and returning `string | number`. Branch on `typeof` inside,
concatenating for strings and multiplying by two for numbers.

Left to you: the order of the overloads. Swap them and everything still
compiles here, but the resolution rule is "first match wins", which matters a
great deal once two overloads can both accept the same argument.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The gate wants `duplicate("ab")` to be a `string` and `duplicate(2)` to be a
`number` - not `string | number` in both cases. A single signature cannot say
that, because a single signature has exactly one return type.

TypeScript's answer is to let you declare the same function more than once.
The README's Concept section shows the shape.

## Hint 2

Overloads are two or more signatures with no body, followed by one
implementation signature that has a body:

```ts
export function example(value: string): string;
export function example(value: boolean): boolean;
export function example(value: string | boolean): string | boolean {
  ...
}
```

The implementation signature is not visible to callers - only the overloads
above it are - so it can be as loose as it needs to be. Inside the body,
`typeof value === "string"` tells the compiler which branch it is in.

## Hint 3

Write two overload signatures - `(value: string): string` and
`(value: number): number` - then an implementation signature accepting
`string | number` and returning `string | number`. Branch on `typeof` inside,
concatenating for strings and multiplying by two for numbers.

Left to you: the order of the overloads. Swap them and everything still
compiles here, but the resolution rule is "first match wins", which matters a
great deal once two overloads can both accept the same argument.

lessons.briefing:
# 03 — Objects and interfaces

Almost nothing in a real program is a lone `number`. It is a lesson, a draft, a
set of options, a row from an API — an object with named parts, half of which
are optional, most of which nobody should be mutating. Describing those shapes
is what you will spend most of your TypeScript life doing.

Here is the thing that surprises people arriving from C# or Java: TypeScript
does not care what your type is *called*. It cares what it *contains*. Two
types with the same members are the same type, even if they were declared in
different files by different people who never met. This is **structural
typing**, and it is the single largest difference between TypeScript and the
nominal type systems it superficially resembles.

That one rule explains a great deal of day-to-day behaviour: why an object
literal you never annotated satisfies an interface, why "it just worked" when
you passed something from another library, and — the flip side — why a
`UserId` type alias for `string` does not stop you passing a product ID.

## Concept — shapes, not names

An interface names a shape:

```ts
interface Track {
  name: string;
  lessons: number;
}

function describe(track: Track): string {
  return `${track.name} (${track.lessons})`;
}

const anything = { name: "react", lessons: 12, colour: "blue" };
describe(anything);   // fine: it has everything Track asks for
```

That last call is structural typing in one line. `anything` was never declared
as a `Track`; it has the members a `Track` needs, so it is one. The extra
`colour` is ignored — with one important exception:

```ts
describe({ name: "react", lessons: 12, colour: "blue" });
//                                     ^ Object literal may only specify known properties
```

Passing a *fresh object literal* directly triggers **excess property
checking**, a deliberate special case that catches typos where structural
typing would otherwise shrug. Assign the literal to a variable first and the
check goes away, which is a genuinely confusing rule until you know it exists.
Its real value is catching `{ retires: 2 }` when you meant `retries`.

**Optional members.** A `?` means the property may be absent, and reading it
gives you `T | undefined`:

```ts

  slug: string;
  challenge?: boolean;   // boolean | undefined
}
```

**Readonly members.** `readonly` means the property may not be reassigned
*through this type*. It is compile-time only — no `Object.freeze` is involved —
and it does not go deep: `readonly tags: string[]` still lets you `push`. For
that you need `readonly tags: readonly string[]`, which is two different
promises stacked.

**Index signatures.** When the keys come from data rather than from you:

```ts

  [slug: string]: number;
}
```

Every string key now reads as a `number`. TypeScript takes that literally and
will not warn you that `tally.nope` is `undefined` at runtime — an index
signature is a promise you are making, not one the compiler verifies.

**`interface` vs `type`.** This is an interview question in every TypeScript
screen, so learn the honest answer. They are nearly interchangeable for object
shapes. `interface` can be reopened and merged (declare it twice and the
members combine — how libraries let you augment their types) and reads better
in error messages; `type` can express things an interface cannot — unions,
tuples, mapped and conditional types, primitives:


expect to extend, `type` for everything else. What you should never say in an
interview is "interfaces are for classes" — that is Java's answer, not this
language's.

**Spread, and why it matters here.** `{ ...draft, title }` builds a new object
with every own enumerable property of `draft`, then overrides `title`. Later
keys win, which is why order matters, and the copy is *shallow* — nested
objects and arrays are shared, not cloned.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Complete the `Lesson` interface so it describes the
objects the gate passes, then implement `describeLesson(lesson)`:

- `{ slug: "02_functions", title: "Functions", exercises: 4, challenge: true }`
  → `"02_functions: Functions - 4 exercises + challenge"`
- `{ slug: "05_literals_enums", title: "Literals", exercises: 3 }`
  → `"05_literals_enums: Literals - 3 exercises"`
- `{ slug: "09_mapped", title: "Mapped", exercises: 4, challenge: false }`
  → `"09_mapped: Mapped - 4 exercises"`

which is which. Note that a missing `challenge` and `challenge: false` render
identically.


Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Mark every member of `Draft` as read-only — including
the contents of `tags` — and implement `renameDraft(draft, title)`, which
returns a **new** draft with the new title and everything else copied across.

afterwards, and the type gate checks that `draft.id = "d2"` and
`draft.tags.push("late")` both fail to compile.

```

```

members with no holes — and implement `resolveOptions(options)`:

# Reading - typescript/03_objects_interfaces

Structural typing, the `interface`/`type` question you will be asked in an
interview, and the four object features that carry most real code.

## Notes

**Structural typing, properly.** TypeScript compares types by their members,
not their names. A function asking for `{ name: string }` accepts any value
that has a `name: string`, whoever declared it, whatever it is called, however
many extra members it carries. This is why TypeScript integrates so painlessly
with plain JavaScript objects and JSON, and why "duck typing, but checked" is a
fair one-line summary. The cost is that a type alias gives you no protection
against mixing up two things that happen to share a shape: `type UserId =
string` and `type OrderId = string` are the same type, full stop. Teams that
need the distinction reach for *branded types* — `type UserId = string & {
readonly __brand: unique symbol }` — which fake nominal typing by adding a
member no one can produce by accident.

**Excess property checking is a special case, and knowing it is a rite of
passage.** Structural typing says extra properties are fine, so
`const x = { a: 1, b: 2 }` is assignable to `{ a: number }`. But a *fresh
object literal* assigned directly to a typed target gets an extra check that
rejects unknown members, because a literal with a member the target has never
heard of is almost always a typo or a misunderstanding. Assign the literal to a
variable first and the check disappears — the literal is no longer "fresh".
Interviewers love this one because it looks like an inconsistency and is
actually a deliberate usability trade-off.

**`interface` vs `type`, the answer that gets you hired.** For describing an
object shape they are interchangeable, and either is fine. The real
differences: `interface` supports *declaration merging* (declare the same
interface twice and the members combine — that is how you augment `Window` or a
library's types), and it produces slightly friendlier error messages; `type`
can name things interfaces cannot — unions, intersections, tuples, primitives,
mapped and conditional types. `interface X extends Y` and `type X = Y & {...}`
mostly agree, but intersections silently produce impossible members where
`extends` reports a conflict. A good short answer: "interfaces for object
shapes that might be extended or merged, type aliases for everything else, and
never mix the two styles inside one module without a reason."

**`readonly` is shallow, and it is erased.** `readonly title: string` stops
assignment through that type and nothing else — a second reference typed
without `readonly` can still write to it, `Object.assign` still works, and
nothing is frozen at runtime. For arrays, `readonly tags: readonly string[]` is
two separate promises: the property cannot be swapped out, and the array cannot
be mutated. Deep immutability needs a recursive mapped type, which lesson 09
builds from scratch.

**Index signatures describe maps, and they lie a little.** `{ [slug: string]:
number }` says every string key yields a `number`, so `tally.typo` typechecks
and is `undefined` at runtime. That gap is real, and it is why
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` exists (it makes every index read `number |
undefined`) and why `Record<string, number>` — lesson 08 — has exactly the same
hole. When keys really are a known set, a literal union key type is far safer:
`Record<"draft" | "published", number>` forces you to handle both.

## ex1 — finish the interface, then use it

The three test objects were the specification. Two of them carry a `challenge`
member and one does not, which is what forces the `?`; and the `challenge:
false` case forces the *rendering* to be a truthiness check rather than a
presence check. Those are different questions — "does this property exist" and
"is this property true" — and conflating them is a genuine bug class, most
famously with `hasOwnProperty` versus `if (obj.prop)` on a value that is
legitimately `0`, `""` or `false`.

Notice also what you did *not* have to do: the gate passes object literals
directly, and they satisfy `Lesson` without a single `as` or annotation. That is
structural typing paying for itself. Try deleting the `?` from `challenge` and
reading the resulting error — TypeScript points at the *literal*, tells you
which member is missing, and names the type it was checking against. Error
messages of that quality are the whole reason to describe your shapes.

## ex2 — a draft nobody can vandalise

`{ ...draft, title }` is the copy-on-write idiom, and it is everywhere in modern
JavaScript: Redux reducers, React state updates, immutable domain objects. The
ordering rule — later properties win — is worth burning in, because
`{ title, ...draft }` compiles perfectly and silently does nothing.

The type gate's two probes correspond to the two levels of `readonly`. Marking
`tags: readonly string[]` rather than `tags: string[]` is the deeper of the two
and the one people forget; without it, `draft.tags.push("late")` mutates an
object your type promised nobody would touch. And the honest caveat: spread is
shallow, so the renamed draft *shares* the tags array with the original. With
`readonly string[]` that sharing is safe, because neither side can mutate it
through the type — which is a neat demonstration of how an immutability
annotation can buy you a performance decision (no defensive copy) rather than
just a safety one.

## ex3 — keys you do not know in advance

The `(tally[slug] ?? 0) + 1` line is the whole exercise, and it is worth
knowing why `||` would also have worked here: the only falsy `number` is `0`,
and adding 1 to a fallback of `0` produces the same answer as adding 1 to `0`
itself. That coincidence is exactly what makes `||` such a durable source of
bugs — it works until the day a legitimate `0`, `""` or `false` is the answer
you needed to keep, and then it fails somewhere far from where it was written.

The type-level lesson is that an index signature is a *claim*. `tally["anything
at all"]` is a `number` according to the compiler and `undefined` according to
the runtime, and TypeScript accepts that gap for ergonomics. Whenever you write
one, ask whether the key set is genuinely open. If it is closed — statuses,
levels, track names — a union key type turns every missing case into a compile
error instead of an `undefined` at 3am.

## ex4 — optional in, required out

Two types for one concept is not duplication; it is the difference between what
callers may say and what your code may assume. Library authors write this pair
constantly (`Options` and `ResolvedOptions`, `Props` and `NormalizedProps`), and
lesson 08's `Partial<T>` and `Required<T>` will let you derive one from the
other in a single line instead of writing both by hand.

The `??` versus `||` distinction is the most frequently-cited "modern
JavaScript" interview question, and this exercise is its canonical shape.
`options.retries || 1` turns an explicit `0` into `1`; `options.retries ?? 1`
does not, because `??` only falls back on `null` and `undefined`. The same trap
with `verbose: false` is even nastier, because a boolean option that cannot be
turned off looks like a bug in something else entirely.

The hint's aside about `{ ...defaults, ...options }` is worth chasing. That
spelling is shorter and it is what most libraries do — but if a caller passes
`{ label: undefined }` explicitly, the spread copies that `undefined` over your
default, while the `??` version does not. Both behaviours are defensible; only
one of them is what you probably meant.

## challenge — summarise a curriculum

Nesting interfaces is unremarkable, which is the point — the type system scales
by composition, and `readonly Lesson[]` inside `Part` reads exactly like
`readonly string[]` did in lesson 01. The two counts come from two different
operations on the same array, and the empty part checks that both of them are
written to survive it: `[].length` is `0`, and `[].reduce((a, b) => a + b)`
*throws* unless you pass an initial value. That initial value is the single
most common `reduce` bug, and it is the reason many teams prefer an explicit
loop.

The arrow-returning-an-object trap deserves its own line, because everyone hits
it once: `(part) => { title: part.title }` is a function with a *labelled
statement*, not an object literal, and it returns `undefined`. The parentheses
in `(part) => ({ ... })` are not style, they are syntax.

## review1 — greetLearner

The nickname fallback is `??` for the third time in this lesson, deliberately.
Spaced review is not about remembering that this exercise used `??`; it is
about the reflex that "absent" and "falsy" are different questions, so that in
two months, when a real options object with a `0` in it crosses your desk, the
right operator is already in your fingers.

The zero-streak branch is the same shape as lesson 00's pluralisation: a
rendering decision the type system has no opinion about. Types will tell you
that `streak` is a `number`; they will never tell you that `0` deserves
different words. That division of labour — types for shape, tests for
behaviour — is the whole reason this course grades both.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Object Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html) — optional and readonly members, index signatures, extending interfaces, and the excess property check.
- [Handbook: Everyday Types — `interface` vs type alias](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#differences-between-type-aliases-and-interfaces) — the official side-by-side, including declaration merging.
- [Handbook: Type Compatibility (structural typing)](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/type-compatibility.html) — how assignability is actually decided, with the surprising cases.
- [MDN: spread syntax](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Spread_syntax) — object and array spread, and exactly how shallow it is.
- [MDN: nullish coalescing (`??`)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Nullish_coalescing) — the operator ex4 is built on, with the `||` comparison spelled out.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — summarise a curriculum (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Finish the `Part` and `PartSummary` interfaces
and implement `summarise(parts)`, which produces one summary per part, in
order:

```ts
summarise([
  { title: "Part 1", lessons: [{ slug: "01_types", exercises: 4 },
                               { slug: "02_functions", exercises: 4 }] },
  { title: "Part 2", lessons: [{ slug: "06_generics_1", exercises: 3 }] },
  { title: "Part 3", lessons: [] },
]);
// [ { title: "Part 1", lessonCount: 2, exerciseCount: 8 },
//   { title: "Part 2", lessonCount: 1, exerciseCount: 3 },
//   { title: "Part 3", lessonCount: 0, exerciseCount: 0 } ]
```

Honest difficulty note: the nesting is the only new thing, and the empty part
is the case that decides whether your `reduce` was written carefully.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 03_objects_interfaces challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three shapes and one transformation. Start by finishing the two unfinished
interfaces from the gate's data: a `Part` has a title and the lessons inside
it, and a `PartSummary` has a title and two counts.

An interface member may be typed with another interface. That is the whole
trick to nesting.

## Hint 2

`readonly Lesson[]` as a member type says "a list of lessons this code will not
modify". The summary is one output object per input part, in the same order,
which is `map`'s job description.

Watch the arrow-function-returning-an-object trap: `(part) => { title: ... }`
parses the braces as a function body, not an object. Wrap the object in
parentheses.

## Hint 3

`Part` gains `lessons: readonly Lesson[]`; `PartSummary` gains
`lessonCount: number` and `exerciseCount: number`. Then `parts.map(...)` with
`lessons.length` for the first count and a `reduce` over `exercises` for the
second.

Left to you: whether the empty part - a part with no lessons at all - needs a
special case. Write the `reduce` with an explicit initial value and see whether
it does.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The gate asserts that the object you were handed is unchanged afterwards, and
the type gate asserts that assigning to a property of a `Draft` does not
compile. Those are the same idea enforced at two different times.

Start by marking the members, then write a function that cannot mutate even if
it wanted to.

## Hint 2

`readonly` goes in front of a member name; for the array member you need it in
two places, because a `readonly string[]` property and a `readonly` property
holding a `string[]` are different promises:

```ts
interface Example {
  readonly id: string;          // cannot reassign the property
  readonly tags: readonly string[];   // ...and cannot push into it either
}
```

For the body, object spread copies every own property into a fresh object, and
later properties win over earlier ones.

## Hint 3

Mark all three members `readonly`, make `tags` a `readonly string[]`, and
return `{ ...draft, title }` - spread first, override second. Reverse those two
and the new title is immediately overwritten by the old one, which is a fun
five minutes to lose.

The decision left to you: whether `renameDraft` should also copy the `tags`
array. Spread is shallow, so both objects share one array; think about whether
that matters given how `tags` is now typed.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The gate asserts that the object you were handed is unchanged afterwards, and
the type gate asserts that assigning to a property of a `Draft` does not
compile. Those are the same idea enforced at two different times.

Start by marking the members, then write a function that cannot mutate even if
it wanted to.

## Hint 2

`readonly` goes in front of a member name; for the array member you need it in
two places, because a `readonly string[]` property and a `readonly` property
holding a `string[]` are different promises:

```ts
interface Example {
  readonly id: string;          // cannot reassign the property
  readonly tags: readonly string[];   // ...and cannot push into it either
}
```

For the body, object spread copies every own property into a fresh object, and
later properties win over earlier ones.

## Hint 3

Mark all three members `readonly`, make `tags` a `readonly string[]`, and
return `{ ...draft, title }` - spread first, override second. Reverse those two
and the new title is immediately overwritten by the old one, which is a fun
five minutes to lose.

The decision left to you: whether `renameDraft` should also copy the `tags`
array. Spread is shallow, so both objects share one array; think about whether
that matters given how `tags` is now typed.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Change `Tally` into a lookup from lesson slug to count,
then implement `countAttempts(slugs)`:

  → `{ "01_types": 2, "02_functions": 1 }`

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The keys of this object are lesson slugs, and no one can list them in advance -
they come from the data. An interface that names its members cannot describe
that. TypeScript has a member form whose "name" is a type rather than an
identifier.

## Hint 2

An index signature declares the type of the key and the type of every value:

```ts
interface Scores {
  [name: string]: number;
}
```

`name` there is documentation - it could be `key` or `slug` and nothing
changes. What matters is that reading *any* string property now gives you
`number`, and that is a promise TypeScript takes at face value: `scores.nope`
typechecks and is `undefined` at runtime.

For the body, the first sighting of a slug has no entry yet, so treat a missing
count as zero. `??` is the operator that does that without also swallowing a
real `0`.

## Hint 3

Give `Tally` the member `[slug: string]: number`, start with an empty object
annotated as `Tally`, and for each slug write
`tally[slug] = (tally[slug] ?? 0) + 1`.

Left to you: whether to use `??` or `||` there. For counting they behave
identically - work out why, and then work out the case where they would not.

## Hint 1

The keys of this object are lesson slugs, and no one can list them in advance -
they come from the data. An interface that names its members cannot describe
that. TypeScript has a member form whose "name" is a type rather than an
identifier.

## Hint 2

An index signature declares the type of the key and the type of every value:

```ts
interface Scores {
  [name: string]: number;
}
```

`name` there is documentation - it could be `key` or `slug` and nothing
changes. What matters is that reading *any* string property now gives you
`number`, and that is a promise TypeScript takes at face value: `scores.nope`
typechecks and is `undefined` at runtime.

For the body, the first sighting of a slug has no entry yet, so treat a missing
count as zero. `??` is the operator that does that without also swallowing a
real `0`.

## Hint 3

Give `Tally` the member `[slug: string]: number`, start with an empty object
annotated as `Tally`, and for each slug write
`tally[slug] = (tally[slug] ?? 0) + 1`.

Left to you: whether to use `??` or `||` there. For counting they behave
identically - work out why, and then work out the case where they would not.

lessons.briefing:
# 04 — Unions and narrowing

Up to now every value you have typed has been exactly one thing. Real values
are not so tidy. A cell in a report is a string, a number or a boolean. A
failure is an `Error`, or an HTTP response, or a timeout. A lesson event is a
pass, a fail or a hint, and each one carries different data.

TypeScript's answer is the **union type**, `A | B | C`: a value that is one of
these, and the compiler does not yet know which. What makes unions more than
notation is what happens next — until you *prove* which member you have,
TypeScript only lets you touch what all members share. Proving it is called
**narrowing**, and it is done with the JavaScript you already write: `typeof`,
`instanceof`, `in`, `===`, truthiness, and a plain `switch`.

If you have worked through the SQL track, you have met the shape of this idea
already. `NULL` there is a third possibility that infects every expression
until you handle it explicitly with `IS NULL` or `COALESCE`; `string | null`
here is the same bargain, made by a compiler instead of a query planner. Both
languages are telling you the same thing: the case you did not think about is
the one in production.

## Concept — the compiler follows your control flow

Start with what a union offers before you narrow it:

```ts
function shout(value: string | number) {
  value.toUpperCase();   // Property 'toUpperCase' does not exist on type 'string | number'
  value.toString();      // fine - every member has toString
}
```

That error is not obstruction, it is arithmetic: the union's members are
`string` and `number`, and only their *common* members are available. Prove
which one you have and the whole type opens up:

```ts
function shout(value: string | number) {
  if (typeof value === "string") {
    return value.toUpperCase();   // value: string
  }
  return value.toFixed(2);        // value: number - the only member left
}
```

Notice the second line. After the `if` returns, TypeScript knows the `string`
case is gone and narrows the rest of the function to `number` on its own. This
is **control flow analysis**, and it is the reason TypeScript feels less like
casting and more like reading.

The narrowing tools, and what each is for:

| you write | it narrows | use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `typeof x === "string"` | primitives | `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `bigint`, `symbol`, `undefined`, `function` |
| `x instanceof Error` | class instances | anything built by a constructor |
| `"code" in x` | object shapes | plain objects that differ by property |
| `x.kind === "circle"` | discriminated unions | the workhorse — see below |
| `if (x)` / `x != null` | nullability | dropping `null` and `undefined` |

**The discriminated union** is the pattern worth building a habit around.
Several object types, each with the same property name pinned to a different
*literal* type:

```ts
type Answer =
  | { kind: "yes"; because: string }
  | { kind: "no" };

function render(answer: Answer): string {
  switch (answer.kind) {
    case "yes":
      return `yes, ${answer.because}`;   // narrowed: because is available
    case "no":
      return "no";                       // narrowed: because is not
  }
}
```

The discriminant does not have to be called `kind` and does not have to be a
string — a literal `true`/`false` works just as well, which is how the
`Result` type in this lesson's challenge is built. What matters is that each
member pins it to one literal value, so comparing it tells the compiler which
member it is looking at.

**Exhaustiveness, and why `never` is the hero.** Add a fourth member to
`Answer` and the `switch` above silently starts returning `undefined` for it.
You can make that a compile error instead:

```ts
function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new Error(`unhandled variant: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}
```

In a `default` branch of an exhaustive `switch`, the value has been narrowed to
`never` — every member handled, nothing left — so `assertNever(answer)`
compiles. Miss a case, and the value is not `never` any more, so the call fails
with an error naming the type you forgot. That is a compile-time to-do list you
get for free, and it is the single most valuable habit in this lesson.

## Exercise 1 — one parameter, three types

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Widen `formatCell` to accept a `string`, a `number` or
a `boolean`, and render each:

- `formatCell("ada")` → `"ada"`
- `formatCell(3)` → `"3.0"` — one decimal place
- `formatCell(9.96)` → `"10.0"`
- `formatCell(true)` → `"yes"`, `formatCell(false)` → `"no"`

`null` is not a member, and the type gate proves it still is not.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 04_unions_narrowing ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — a discriminated union

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Finish the `DojoEvent` union — one variant is written
for you, two are missing — and implement `describeEvent(event)`:

- `{ kind: "pass", exercise: "ex2", attempts: 3 }` → `"ex2 passed after 3 attempts"`
- `{ kind: "fail", exercise: "ex2", message: "wrong shape" }` → `"ex2 failed: wrong shape"`
- `{ kind: "hint", exercise: "ex1", tier: 2 }` → `"ex1 revealed hint 2"`

Every variant carries `kind` and `exercise`; each one carries exactly one
member of its own. The type gate checks that `event.tier` exists only in the
`hint` branch and that `{ kind: "skipped" }` is rejected outright.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 04_unions_narrowing ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — narrowing without a discriminant

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Widen `Failure` to cover the three things that go wrong
in this program, and implement `explainFailure(failure)`:

- `new Error("boom")` → `"caught: boom"`
- `{ code: 404, detail: "not found" }` → `"http 404: not found"`
- `{ timeoutMs: 250 }` → `"timed out after 250ms"`

None of these has a `kind`, so `switch` has nothing to switch on. Use
`instanceof` for the class and `in` for the plain objects — and think about the
order, because the checks are tried top to bottom.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 04_unions_narrowing ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — make the compiler check your cases

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. The `Shape` union is complete. Two things are not:

1. `assertNever` currently takes `unknown`, which accepts anything and proves
   nothing. Change its parameter type to `never`.
2. Implement `area(shape)` — `Math.PI * r * r`, `side * side`,
   `width * height` — with a `default` branch that calls `assertNever`.

The gate then smuggles a `{ kind: "triangle" }` past the type system with a
cast and checks that your code throws `unhandled variant: ...` rather than
returning `undefined`. Types are erased at runtime; the assertion is what
survives.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 04_unions_narrowing ex4
```

## Challenge — Result, by hand (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Finish the `Result` union and the `Partitioned`
interface, then implement both functions:

- `unwrapOr({ ok: true, value: "green" }, "fallback")` → `"green"`
- `unwrapOr({ ok: false, error: "boom" }, "fallback")` → `"fallback"`
- `partition([{ ok: true, value: "a" }, { ok: false, error: "x" }, { ok: true, value: "b" }])`
  → `{ values: ["a", "b"], errors: ["x"] }`
- `partition([])` → `{ values: [], errors: [] }`

This is the type half of the JavaScript world's alternative to exceptions, and
you will meet it again in Rust, Go, and every `neverthrow`-shaped library.
Honest difficulty note: the code is short; the thing to get right is that the
discriminant is a *literal* `true` and a *literal* `false`, not `boolean` in
both variants. Write it the wrong way once and read the error — it is
instructive.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 04_unions_narrowing challenge
```

## Review — describePayment

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Finish the `Payment` union and implement
`describePayment(payment)`:

- `{ method: "cash" }` → `"cash"`
- `{ method: "card", last4: "4242" }` → `"card ending 4242"`
- `{ method: "transfer", iban: "DE89 3704 0044" }` → `"transfer to DE89 3704 0044"`

```
uv run dojo test typescript 04_unions_narrowing review1
```

# Reading - typescript/04_unions_narrowing

Unions are the feature that makes TypeScript feel like a different language
from the one whose syntax it borrows. This page is the theory, the interview
answers, and the traps.

## Notes

**A union is a set, and the members you can touch are the intersection.** For
`string | number`, the available members are the ones both types have — which
is why `toString()` works and `toUpperCase()` does not. This surprises people
who expect a union to behave like a base class. It is the opposite: a union
gets *narrower* in capability as it gets *wider* in possible values, and an
intersection (`A & B`) gets wider in capability as it gets narrower in values.
Saying that sentence out loud in an interview does you no harm at all.

**Control flow analysis is the machinery behind narrowing.** TypeScript
simulates the paths through your function and tracks what each check told it. A
`typeof` guard, an `instanceof`, an `in`, a `===` against a literal, a
truthiness check, an early `return` or `throw` — all of them refine the type
for the code that follows. It is not magic and it does have limits: narrowing
is lost when a value is captured in a closure that might run later, and it is
lost for a mutable property that could have changed between the check and the
use (narrow into a `const` local first if you hit that). It also does not track
across a function boundary — which is exactly the gap that user-defined type
guards, in lesson 10, exist to fill.

**Discriminated unions are the single most useful pattern in this language.**
The recipe: every member is an object type, every member has the same property
name, and each pins that property to a distinct literal type. The compiler can
then treat a comparison on that property as proof. It scales to dozens of
variants, works with `switch` and with `if`, and it is how Redux actions, React
`useReducer` state, API responses, parser results, and every `Result` type in
the wild are modelled. If you take one habit from this course, take this one.

**`never` closes the loop.** Narrowing removes members; when all of them are
removed, what is left is `never`. That is why a `default` branch of an
exhaustive switch can call `assertNever(value: never)`, and why adding a
variant later turns that call into a compile error listing exactly what you
forgot. Note the difference between this and a runtime check: `assertNever`
also throws, because a value smuggled past the compiler with a cast (or arriving
from JSON) really can reach that line. It is both a compile-time to-do list and
a runtime alarm.

**`null` and `undefined` are just union members.** With `strictNullChecks` on —
and it is on — `string | null` is an ordinary union, and `if (x)` or
`x != null` narrows it. `x != null` with the loose `!=` is the one place the
style guides forgive you, because it excludes both `null` and `undefined` in a
single check. Optional chaining `?.` and `??` are the ergonomic shorthands, and
`!` (the non-null assertion) is the escape hatch you should be able to justify
each time you write one.

## ex1 — one parameter, three types

Widening the parameter and then fixing the errors is the correct order to work
in, and it is worth noticing what the errors *were*: every method you wanted
belonged to one member, and the compiler offered you only the intersection.
That refusal is the entire value proposition. In plain JavaScript,
`value.toFixed(1)` on a string is `undefined is not a function` — at runtime, in
production, on a Friday.

The `false` case is there deliberately. A tempting implementation returns
`value ? "yes" : "no"` at the top and never checks anything, which is right for
booleans and disastrously wrong for `""` and `0`. Narrowing and truthiness are
different tools: the first asks *what type is this*, the second asks *is this
value falsy*, and confusing them is the most common bug in this lesson's
territory.

One more thing to file away: `typeof null === "object"` is a famous JavaScript
wart, and `typeof` narrowing inherits it. `typeof x === "object"` does not
exclude `null`, which is why the honest check for "a real object" is
`typeof x === "object" && x !== null`.

## ex2 — a discriminated union

The exercise is really about writing the *type*, because once the type is right
the function writes itself. That is the shape of most good TypeScript: the time
goes into modelling, and the implementation falls out.

The literal type is what makes it work. `{ kind: string }` in every member
would compile fine and narrow nothing, because comparing a `string` to
`"pass"` tells the compiler nothing about which member you have. Pinning
`kind: "pass"` makes the property a set with one element, and comparison
becomes proof. This is why lesson 05's literal types matter more than they look
like they should.

A design note interviewers like to probe: why not one interface with optional
members — `{ kind: string; attempts?: number; message?: string }`? Because it
makes illegal states representable. That shape permits a pass with a message,
a fail with neither, and a hint with an `attempts` count, and every consumer
has to defend against combinations that cannot happen. A discriminated union
makes those states unsayable, which is the whole game: *make illegal states
unrepresentable*.

## ex3 — narrowing without a discriminant

Real unions are not always yours to design. Errors arrive as `Error` instances,
API responses arrive as plain objects, a timeout arrives as whatever the
library decided. `instanceof` and `in` are the tools for unions you inherited.

`instanceof` checks the prototype chain at runtime, so it works for classes and
not for interfaces — an interface has no runtime existence to check against.
It also has a famous failure mode: across realms (iframes, worker threads, or
Node's `vm` module) there are two different `Error` constructors, and
`instanceof` returns `false` for a perfectly good error from the other side.
That is why library code often checks `error instanceof Error ||
(typeof error === "object" && error !== null && "message" in error)`.

The `in` operator narrows on property presence, and it is the pragmatic choice
for plain object unions. Its weakness is that it is only as good as your
shapes: if two members both have `code`, `in` cannot separate them. Ordering
matters too — the checks run top to bottom, so put the specific ones first.

## ex4 — make the compiler check your cases

`assertNever` is the highest-value five lines in this course. The trick is that
`never` is the empty type, so nothing can be passed to a function expecting it;
inside an exhaustive `switch`'s `default`, the value has been narrowed to
`never` and the call is legal. Miss a case and the value is
`{ kind: "triangle"; ... }`, which is not assignable to `never`, and you get an
error that names the variant.

Two details people get wrong. First, `return assertNever(shape)` rather than a
bare call, because the `return` is what convinces TypeScript that the function
always produces a number — a call alone leaves a path where control falls out
of the switch. Second, `assertNever` must throw, not return, because the type
system is erased: a triangle really can arrive from `JSON.parse`, from an `as`
cast, or from a JavaScript caller who never saw your types at all. The gate
smuggles one in with a cast precisely to make that point.

Compare with what the SQL track teaches about `CHECK` constraints: the type
system is your compile-time guard and the throw is your runtime constraint, and
serious systems want both.

## challenge — Result, by hand

The `Result` type is the "errors as values" pattern, and TypeScript models it
beautifully because a discriminated union is exactly the right shape. What it
buys you over `throw` is that the failure is in the *type* — a caller cannot
forget it exists, because they cannot read `.value` without first proving
`ok` is true. What it costs you is ceremony at every call site, and no stack
trace unless you put one in the error member.

The instructive failure is writing `{ ok: boolean; value?: string; error?:
string }`. It compiles, it looks nearly the same, and it narrows nothing:
`if (result.ok)` leaves `value` as `string | undefined`, so you are back to
defending against states that cannot happen. Literal `true` and literal `false`
in the two variants is what makes the boolean a discriminant.

Worth knowing: `partition` written with two `filter` passes loses the narrowing
— `results.filter((r) => r.ok)` gives you back `Result[]`, not the success
member, because `filter`'s signature has no way to express "the predicate
proves something". The fix is a type guard, which is lesson 10, and modern
TypeScript (5.5+) can sometimes infer one for you from a simple predicate.

## review1 — describePayment

Same pattern, third time: three variants, one literal discriminant, one
`switch`. What is worth noticing here is the `{ method: "cash" }` member, which
carries no data at all. A union member is allowed to be nothing but its tag —
and that is often exactly right, because "cash" genuinely has no extra
information. The temptation to give every variant the same members "for
symmetry" is how you end up back at optional properties and defensive code.

If you added an `assertNever` default without being asked, good. That is the
habit this lesson exists to install.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Narrowing](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html) — `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, truthiness, discriminated unions and exhaustiveness checking, in the order that builds them up.
- [Handbook: Unions and Intersection Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#union-types) — the basics, and why only shared members are available.
- [Handbook: `never` and exhaustiveness](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#exhaustiveness-checking) — the official `assertNever` recipe.
- [MDN: `instanceof`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/instanceof) — including the cross-realm caveat that bites in Node and iframes.
- [TypeScript Deep Dive: discriminated unions](https://basarat.gitbook.io/typescript/type-system/discriminated-unions) — the pattern with more worked examples, including the Redux-style reducer.

is why `toString()` works and `toUpperCase()` does not. This surprises people
who expect a union to behave like a base class. It is the opposite: a union
gets *narrower* in capability as it gets *wider* in possible values, and an
intersection (`A & B`) gets wider in capability as it gets narrower in values.
Saying that sentence out loud in an interview does you no harm at all.

**Control flow analysis is the machinery behind narrowing.** TypeScript
simulates the paths through your function and tracks what each check told it. A
`typeof` guard, an `instanceof`, an `in`, a `===` against a literal, a
truthiness check, an early `return` or `throw` — all of them refine the type
for the code that follows. It is not magic and it does have limits: narrowing
is lost when a value is captured in a closure that might run later, and it is
lost for a mutable property that could have changed between the check and the
use (narrow into a `const` local first if you hit that). It also does not track
across a function boundary — which is exactly the gap that user-defined type
guards, in lesson 10, exist to fill.

**Discriminated unions are the single most useful pattern in this language.**
The recipe: every member is an object type, every member has the same property
name, and each pins that property to a distinct literal type. The compiler can
then treat a comparison on that property as proof. It scales to dozens of
variants, works with `switch` and with `if`, and it is how Redux actions, React
`useReducer` state, API responses, parser results, and every `Result` type in
the wild are modelled. If you take one habit from this course, take this one.

**`never` closes the loop.** Narrowing removes members; when all of them are
removed, what is left is `never`. That is why a `default` branch of an
exhaustive switch can call `assertNever(value: never)`, and why adding a
variant later turns that call into a compile error listing exactly what you
forgot. Note the difference between this and a runtime check: `assertNever`
also throws, because a value smuggled past the compiler with a cast (or arriving
from JSON) really can reach that line. It is both a compile-time to-do list and
a runtime alarm.

**`null` and `undefined` are just union members.** With `strictNullChecks` on —
and it is on — `string | null` is an ordinary union, and `if (x)` or
`x != null` narrows it. `x != null` with the loose `!=` is the one place the
style guides forgive you, because it excludes both `null` and `undefined` in a
single check. Optional chaining `?.` and `??` are the ergonomic shorthands, and
`!` (the non-null assertion) is the escape hatch you should be able to justify
each time you write one.

## ex1 — one parameter, three types

Widening the parameter and then fixing the errors is the correct order to work
in, and it is worth noticing what the errors *were*: every method you wanted
belonged to one member, and the compiler offered you only the intersection.
That refusal is the entire value proposition. In plain JavaScript,
`value.toFixed(1)` on a string is `undefined is not a function` — at runtime, in
production, on a Friday.

The `false` case is there deliberately. A tempting implementation returns
`value ? "yes" : "no"` at the top and never checks anything, which is right for
booleans and disastrously wrong for `""` and `0`. Narrowing and truthiness are
different tools: the first asks *what type is this*, the second asks *is this
value falsy*, and confusing them is the most common bug in this lesson's
territory.

One more thing to file away: `typeof null === "object"` is a famous JavaScript
wart, and `typeof` narrowing inherits it. `typeof x === "object"` does not
exclude `null`, which is why the honest check for "a real object" is
`typeof x === "object" && x !== null`.

## ex2 — a discriminated union

The exercise is really about writing the *type*, because once the type is right
the function writes itself. That is the shape of most good TypeScript: the time
goes into modelling, and the implementation falls out.

The literal type is what makes it work. `{ kind: string }` in every member
would compile fine and narrow nothing, because comparing a `string` to
`"pass"` tells the compiler nothing about which member you have. Pinning
`kind: "pass"` makes the property a set with one element, and comparison
becomes proof. This is why lesson 05's literal types matter more than they look
like they should.

A design note interviewers like to probe: why not one interface with optional
members — `{ kind: string; attempts?: number; message?: string }`? Because it
makes illegal states representable. That shape permits a pass with a message,
a fail with neither, and a hint with an `attempts` count, and every consumer
has to defend against combinations that cannot happen. A discriminated union
makes those states unsayable, which is the whole game: *make illegal states
unrepresentable*.

## ex3 — narrowing without a discriminant

Real unions are not always yours to design. Errors arrive as `Error` instances,
API responses arrive as plain objects, a timeout arrives as whatever the
library decided. `instanceof` and `in` are the tools for unions you inherited.

`instanceof` checks the prototype chain at runtime, so it works for classes and
not for interfaces — an interface has no runtime existence to check against.
It also has a famous failure mode: across realms (iframes, worker threads, or
Node's `vm` module) there are two different `Error` constructors, and
`instanceof` returns `false` for a perfectly good error from the other side.
That is why library code often checks `error instanceof Error ||
(typeof error === "object" && error !== null && "message" in error)`.

The `in` operator narrows on property presence, and it is the pragmatic choice
for plain object unions. Its weakness is that it is only as good as your
shapes: if two members both have `code`, `in` cannot separate them. Ordering
matters too — the checks run top to bottom, so put the specific ones first.

## ex4 — make the compiler check your cases

`assertNever` is the highest-value five lines in this course. The trick is that
`never` is the empty type, so nothing can be passed to a function expecting it;
inside an exhaustive `switch`'s `default`, the value has been narrowed to
`never` and the call is legal. Miss a case and the value is
`{ kind: "triangle"; ... }`, which is not assignable to `never`, and you get an
error that names the variant.

Two details people get wrong. First, `return assertNever(shape)` rather than a
bare call, because the `return` is what convinces TypeScript that the function
always produces a number — a call alone leaves a path where control falls out
of the switch. Second, `assertNever` must throw, not return, because the type
system is erased: a triangle really can arrive from `JSON.parse`, from an `as`
cast, or from a JavaScript caller who never saw your types at all. The gate
smuggles one in with a cast precisely to make that point.

Compare with what the SQL track teaches about `CHECK` constraints: the type
system is your compile-time guard and the throw is your runtime constraint, and
serious systems want both.

## challenge — Result, by hand

The `Result` type is the "errors as values" pattern, and TypeScript models it
beautifully because a discriminated union is exactly the right shape. What it
buys you over `throw` is that the failure is in the *type* — a caller cannot
forget it exists, because they cannot read `.value` without first proving
`ok` is true. What it costs you is ceremony at every call site, and no stack
trace unless you put one in the error member.

The instructive failure is writing `{ ok: boolean; value?: string; error?:
string }`. It compiles, it looks nearly the same, and it narrows nothing:
`if (result.ok)` leaves `value` as `string | undefined`, so you are back to
defending against states that cannot happen. Literal `true` and literal `false`
in the two variants is what makes the boolean a discriminant.

Worth knowing: `partition` written with two `filter` passes loses the narrowing
— `results.filter((r) => r.ok)` gives you back `Result[]`, not the success
member, because `filter`'s signature has no way to express "the predicate
proves something". The fix is a type guard, which is lesson 10, and modern
TypeScript (5.5+) can sometimes infer one for you from a simple predicate.

## review1 — describePayment

Same pattern, third time: three variants, one literal discriminant, one
`switch`. What is worth noticing here is the `{ method: "cash" }` member, which
carries no data at all. A union member is allowed to be nothing but its tag —
and that is often exactly right, because "cash" genuinely has no extra
information. The temptation to give every variant the same members "for
symmetry" is how you end up back at optional properties and defensive code.

If you added an `assertNever` default without being asked, good. That is the
habit this lesson exists to install.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Narrowing](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html) — `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, truthiness, discriminated unions and exhaustiveness checking, in the order that builds them up.
- [Handbook: Unions and Intersection Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#union-types) — the basics, and why only shared members are available.
- [Handbook: `never` and exhaustiveness](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#exhaustiveness-checking) — the official `assertNever` recipe.
- [MDN: `instanceof`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/instanceof) — including the cross-realm caveat that bites in Node and iframes.
- [TypeScript Deep Dive: discriminated unions](https://basarat.gitbook.io/typescript/type-system/discriminated-unions) — the pattern with more worked examples, including the Redux-style reducer.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — Result, by hand (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Finish the `Result` union and the `Partitioned`
interface, then implement both functions:

- `unwrapOr({ ok: true, value: "green" }, "fallback")` → `"green"`
- `unwrapOr({ ok: false, error: "boom" }, "fallback")` → `"fallback"`
- `partition([{ ok: true, value: "a" }, { ok: false, error: "x" }, { ok: true, value: "b" }])`
  → `{ values: ["a", "b"], errors: ["x"] }`
- `partition([])` → `{ values: [], errors: [] }`

This is the type half of the JavaScript world's alternative to exceptions, and
you will meet it again in Rust, Go, and every `neverthrow`-shaped library.
Honest difficulty note: the code is short; the thing to get right is that the
discriminant is a *literal* `true` and a *literal* `false`, not `boolean` in
both variants. Write it the wrong way once and read the error — it is
instructive.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 04_unions_narrowing challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Result` is the shape half the TypeScript world uses instead of throwing: a
success carrying a value, or a failure carrying an error, in one type. Finish
the union, finish `Partitioned`, then write the two functions.

The discriminant here is not a string. It is a boolean, and that works just as
well - as long as each variant pins it to a *literal* `true` or `false` rather
than to `boolean`.

## Hint 2

```ts
type Result = { ok: true; value: string } | { ok: false; error: string };
```

`if (result.ok)` narrows to the first member, and the `else` narrows to the
second. Note what would break if you wrote `ok: boolean` in both variants:
`result.value` would stop being reachable, because a `boolean` cannot tell the
two apart.

`partition` walks the list once and pushes into one of two arrays.

## Hint 3

Finish the union as above, give `Partitioned` an `errors: string[]` alongside
`values`, write `unwrapOr` as a one-line conditional on `result.ok`, and write
`partition` as a loop with an `if`/`else` that pushes into the right array.

Left to you: whether `partition` uses a loop, two `filter` passes, or a
`reduce`. Try the `filter` version and see whether the narrowing survives -
what `filter` gives you back is the subject of lesson 10.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`Result` is the shape half the TypeScript world uses instead of throwing: a
success carrying a value, or a failure carrying an error, in one type. Finish
the union, finish `Partitioned`, then write the two functions.

The discriminant here is not a string. It is a boolean, and that works just as
well - as long as each variant pins it to a *literal* `true` or `false` rather
than to `boolean`.

## Hint 2

```ts
type Result = { ok: true; value: string } | { ok: false; error: string };
```

`if (result.ok)` narrows to the first member, and the `else` narrows to the
second. Note what would break if you wrote `ok: boolean` in both variants:
`result.value` would stop being reachable, because a `boolean` cannot tell the
two apart.

`partition` walks the list once and pushes into one of two arrays.

## Hint 3

Finish the union as above, give `Partitioned` an `errors: string[]` alongside
`values`, write `unwrapOr` as a one-line conditional on `result.ok`, and write
`partition` as a loop with an `if`/`else` that pushes into the right array.

Left to you: whether `partition` uses a loop, two `filter` passes, or a
`reduce`. Try the `filter` version and see whether the narrowing survives -
what `filter` gives you back is the subject of lesson 10.

## Exercise 1 — one parameter, three types

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Widen `formatCell` to accept a `string`, a `number` or
a `boolean`, and render each:

- `formatCell("ada")` → `"ada"`
- `formatCell(3)` → `"3.0"` — one decimal place
- `formatCell(9.96)` → `"10.0"`
- `formatCell(true)` → `"yes"`, `formatCell(false)` → `"no"`

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Widen the parameter first, then notice what breaks. The moment `value` can be
three things, none of the three types' methods are available on it - because
the compiler will only offer what *every* member of the union has.

That is not an obstacle to work around. It is the feature, and the way through
it is to check.

## Hint 2

A union is written with `|`:

```ts
function example(value: string | number) { ... }
```

`typeof value === "string"` inside an `if` narrows `value` to `string` for the
rest of that block - and, if you return from the block, for everything after it
as well. That second half is why a series of guard clauses reads so well.

The number branch needs one decimal place; check the README for the exact
expected strings.

## Hint 3

Widen to `string | number | boolean`, then three branches: return the string
as-is, return `value.toFixed(1)` for numbers, and return `"yes"` or `"no"` for
the boolean.

Left to you: whether the last branch tests `typeof value === "boolean"` or
simply falls through as the only remaining possibility. Both work today. Only
one of them keeps working when a fourth member joins the union - and lesson
ex4 is about making the compiler tell you which.

## Hint 1

Widen the parameter first, then notice what breaks. The moment `value` can be
three things, none of the three types' methods are available on it - because
the compiler will only offer what *every* member of the union has.

That is not an obstacle to work around. It is the feature, and the way through
it is to check.

## Hint 2

A union is written with `|`:

```ts
function example(value: string | number) { ... }
```

`typeof value === "string"` inside an `if` narrows `value` to `string` for the
rest of that block - and, if you return from the block, for everything after it
as well. That second half is why a series of guard clauses reads so well.

The number branch needs one decimal place; check the README for the exact
expected strings.

## Hint 3

Widen to `string | number | boolean`, then three branches: return the string
as-is, return `value.toFixed(1)` for numbers, and return `"yes"` or `"no"` for
the boolean.

Left to you: whether the last branch tests `typeof value === "boolean"` or
simply falls through as the only remaining possibility. Both work today. Only
one of them keeps working when a fourth member joins the union - and lesson
ex4 is about making the compiler tell you which.

## Exercise 3 — narrowing without a discriminant

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Widen `Failure` to cover the three things that go wrong
in this program, and implement `explainFailure(failure)`:

- `new Error("boom")` → `"caught: boom"`
- `{ code: 404, detail: "not found" }` → `"http 404: not found"`
- `{ timeoutMs: 250 }` → `"timed out after 250ms"`

None of these has a `kind`, so `switch` has nothing to switch on. Use
`instanceof` for the class and `in` for the plain objects — and think about the
order, because the checks are tried top to bottom.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 04_unions_narrowing ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

None of these three values carries a `kind` property, so `switch` has nothing
to switch on. TypeScript still has two narrowing tools for exactly this
situation - one for values built by a constructor, one for plain objects that
differ in which properties they have.

Order matters: check the most specific thing first.

## Hint 2

`failure instanceof Error` narrows to `Error` and gives you `.message`. It works
because `Error` is a class with a prototype at runtime, which is also why it
does *not* work for plain object types - `instanceof { code: number }` is not
even valid syntax.

For those, the `in` operator narrows on the presence of a property:

```ts
if ("code" in failure) {
  // failure is the { code, detail } member here
}
```

## Hint 3

Widen `Failure` to `Error | { code: number; detail: string } | { timeoutMs: number }`,
then: `instanceof Error` first, `"code" in failure` second, and the timeout
case last. The three output strings are in the README, including the lowercase
`http` and the trailing `ms`.

Left to you: whether the last branch checks `"timeoutMs" in failure`
explicitly. Nothing forces you to - and it is worth asking what happens to the
unchecked version the day someone adds a fourth member.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

None of these three values carries a `kind` property, so `switch` has nothing
to switch on. TypeScript still has two narrowing tools for exactly this
situation - one for values built by a constructor, one for plain objects that
differ in which properties they have.

Order matters: check the most specific thing first.

## Hint 2

`failure instanceof Error` narrows to `Error` and gives you `.message`. It works
because `Error` is a class with a prototype at runtime, which is also why it
does *not* work for plain object types - `instanceof { code: number }` is not
even valid syntax.

For those, the `in` operator narrows on the presence of a property:

```ts
if ("code" in failure) {
  // failure is the { code, detail } member here
}
```

## Hint 3

Widen `Failure` to `Error | { code: number; detail: string } | { timeoutMs: number }`,
then: `instanceof Error` first, `"code" in failure` second, and the timeout
case last. The three output strings are in the README, including the lowercase
`http` and the trailing `ms`.

Left to you: whether the last branch checks `"timeoutMs" in failure`
explicitly. Nothing forces you to - and it is worth asking what happens to the
unchecked version the day someone adds a fourth member.

## Exercise 4 — make the compiler check your cases

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. The `Shape` union is complete. Two things are not:

1. `assertNever` currently takes `unknown`, which accepts anything and proves
   nothing. Change its parameter type to `never`.
2. Implement `area(shape)` — `Math.PI * r * r`, `side * side`,
   `width * height` — with a `default` branch that calls `assertNever`.

The gate then smuggles a `{ kind: "triangle" }` past the type system with a
cast and checks that your code throws `unhandled variant: ...` rather than
returning `undefined`. Types are erased at runtime; the assertion is what
survives.

