exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two edits, and the small one is the important one. `assertNever` takes
`unknown` today, which means it accepts anything and proves nothing. Change its
parameter to the type that has no values at all, and it becomes a compile-time
assertion instead of a runtime one.

Then write `area` with a `default` branch that calls it.

## Hint 2

`never` is the empty type: no value is a `never`, so nothing can be passed to a
function expecting one. Inside an exhaustive `switch`, though, the `default`
branch is reached only when every variant has been handled - and there
TypeScript has narrowed the value to `never`, so the call compiles.

Handle one variant and leave the others out, and the same call stops compiling
with a message naming the type you forgot. That error is the feature.

## Hint 3

Change the signature to `assertNever(value: never): never`, leave the body
alone, and write `area` as a `switch (shape.kind)` with the three area formulas
plus `default: return assertNever(shape);`.

The decision left to you: whether `default` returns the call or just calls it.
Both compile. One of them makes TypeScript agree that `area` always returns a
number without any further help - try it the other way and read what it says.

## Hint 1

Two edits, and the small one is the important one. `assertNever` takes
`unknown` today, which means it accepts anything and proves nothing. Change its
parameter to the type that has no values at all, and it becomes a compile-time
assertion instead of a runtime one.

Then write `area` with a `default` branch that calls it.

## Hint 2

`never` is the empty type: no value is a `never`, so nothing can be passed to a
function expecting one. Inside an exhaustive `switch`, though, the `default`
branch is reached only when every variant has been handled - and there
TypeScript has narrowed the value to `never`, so the call compiles.

Handle one variant and leave the others out, and the same call stops compiling
with a message naming the type you forgot. That error is the feature.

## Hint 3

Change the signature to `assertNever(value: never): never`, leave the body
alone, and write `area` as a `switch (shape.kind)` with the three area formulas
plus `default: return assertNever(shape);`.

The decision left to you: whether `default` returns the call or just calls it.
Both compile. One of them makes TypeScript agree that `area` always returns a
number without any further help - try it the other way and read what it says.

lessons.briefing:
# 05 — Literal types, `as const`, and enums

In lesson 04 you wrote `{ kind: "circle" }` and the compiler treated `"circle"`
as a type. That was not a special case for discriminated unions. In TypeScript
**every literal value is also a type** — `"circle"`, `42` and `true` each name a
type with exactly one member — and that fact is what turns a union into a
closed set of options.

This is the feature that replaces most of what other languages use enums for.
`"beginner" | "intermediate" | "advanced"` is a type with three values, no
imports, no runtime object, and full narrowing support. When a codebase says
`status: string` and then compares it to string constants in nine places, this
is the fix, and it usually takes one line.

TypeScript *also* has `enum`, one of the few features that emits real
JavaScript rather than disappearing at compile time. This lesson teaches both
and is honest about when each is worth it, because "union of literals or enum?"
is a question you will be asked and will have to answer for a real codebase.

## Concept — a value that is also a type

```ts
let track = "react";          // string    - it could be reassigned
const track2 = "react";       // "react"   - it cannot, so the literal survives
```

That is **widening**: a mutable binding widens the literal to its base type, a
`const` keeps it. It explains the error everyone hits once:

```ts
type Level = "beginner" | "advanced";

let chosen = "beginner";      // widened to string
const level: Level = chosen;  // Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'Level'
```

Three ways to fix it: use `const`, annotate `let chosen: Level = "beginner"`,
or write `chosen as const`.

**`as const` on an object or array** does the same job wholesale, and adds
`readonly`:

```ts
const sizes = { small: 1, large: 2 };
//    sizes.small: number, and reassignable

const frozen = { small: 1, large: 2 } as const;
//    frozen.small: 1, and readonly - assignment is a compile error

const tracks = ["ts", "node"] as const;
//    readonly ["ts", "node"] - a readonly tuple, not string[]
```

Nothing changes at runtime; `as const` is a *type* assertion, and the emitted
JavaScript is byte-for-byte identical. What you get is a compile-time
description precise enough to derive other types from — which is the challenge
in this lesson.

**Deriving a union from data** (a preview of lesson 07, and the reason `as
const` is worth the two words):

```ts
const SIZES = { small: 1, medium: 2, large: 3 } as const;

type Size = keyof typeof SIZES;   // "small" | "medium" | "large"
```

Read it right to left. `typeof HINT_TIERS` is "the type of that value" (this is
the *type-level* `typeof`, not the runtime operator with the same spelling);
`keyof` takes the union of that type's property names. Add a fourth tier to the
object and the type updates itself — the single-source-of-truth trick that
hand-written unions cannot give you.

**Enums.** An `enum` is a named set of constants that exists at runtime:

```ts
enum Status {
  Draft = "draft",
  Published = "published",
}

Status.Draft;                 // "draft" at runtime - a real object property
const s: Status = "draft";    // ERROR: string is not assignable to Status
```

That last line is the interesting one. A string enum is **nominal**: only its
own members are assignable to it, which is unusual in this otherwise
structurally-typed language and is genuinely useful when you want a value that
cannot be faked by any old string.

What to know about the costs, because this is the interview question:

- An enum emits JavaScript — an object with the members on it — so it is not
  free, and it cannot be tree-shaken away.
- Values arriving from `JSON.parse`, a database or a form are plain strings, and
  a plain string is not assignable to a string enum, so you need a cast or a
  validation step at every boundary.
- **Numeric** enums are worse: their members are assignable from arbitrary
  numbers in more cases than you would like, and reverse mapping puts both
  `Status[0]` and `Status.Draft` on the object.
- `const enum` (fully inlined, no emit) is banned under this course's
  `isolatedModules` setting, and by most bundlers, for good reasons.

The modern default in most codebases is a union of string literals, with enums
reserved for cases where nominal typing genuinely helps. Knowing *why* is worth
more than knowing which.

## Exercise 1 — three values, not every string

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Replace `type Level = string` with a union of the three
literals, and implement `nextLevel(level)`:

- `nextLevel("beginner")` → `"intermediate"`
- `nextLevel("intermediate")` → `"advanced"`
- `nextLevel("advanced")` → `"advanced"` — the top of the ladder stays put

The type gate checks that `Level` is exactly those three strings and that
`nextLevel("expert")` does not compile.

```

```

## Exercise 2 — freeze the lookup table

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Add `as const` to `TRACK_TITLES` so its properties keep
their literal types and become read-only, then implement `titleOf(track)`:

- `titleOf("typescript")` → `"TypeScript"`
- `titleOf("node")` → `"Node.js"`
- `titleOf("react")` → `"React"`

`"TypeScript"` (not `string`) and that assigning to `TRACK_TITLES.node` is a
compile error. The body is one indexed lookup.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 05_literals_enums ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — an enum, on purpose

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Finish the `Status` enum — `Published = "published"` and
`Retired = "retired"` — and implement `statusLabel(status)`:

- `Status.Draft` → `"Draft (not visible)"`
- `Status.Published` → `"Published"`
- `Status.Retired` → `"Retired (archived)"`

type gate proves the nominal behaviour: `const sneaky: Status = "draft"` must
not compile, even though that is exactly the string the enum holds at runtime.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 05_literals_enums ex3
```

2. Replace `type Tier = string` with a type *derived* from the object's keys,

   number: `sortTiers(["almost", "nudge", "approach"])` →
   `["nudge", "approach", "almost"]`.

is here because `as const` without it is half a tool. The hints teach it. The
sort is lesson 01's copy-then-compare, one more time.

```

```

`"skip"`, and implement `verdictIcon(verdict)` returning `"ok"`, `"x"` and
`"-"` respectively.

# Reading - typescript/05_literals_enums

Literal types, const assertions, and the enum debate — with the answers an
interviewer is listening for.

## Notes

**Widening, one more time, because this is where it bites.** TypeScript infers
the narrowest useful type and then *widens* it when the binding is mutable.
`const x = "a"` is `"a"`; `let x = "a"` is `string`; `{ x: "a" }` gives `x` the
type `string`, because object properties are mutable too. That last one is the
one that surprises people, and it is exactly why `as const` exists. The three
ways to keep a literal are: make the binding `const`, annotate the target type
explicitly, or use a const assertion. Knowing which one to reach for in an
error message is a real day-to-day skill.

**`as const` is a type assertion, not a runtime freeze.** It makes every
property `readonly`, keeps every literal literal, and turns array literals into
`readonly` tuples. It emits nothing — the JavaScript is unchanged, and the
object is still mutable at runtime by anyone with a plain reference. If you
want actual immutability you want `Object.freeze`, which is a runtime call with
runtime cost; the two are complementary, and TypeScript even types
`Object.freeze` to give you the readonly type as well.

**Deriving beats repeating.** `keyof typeof CONFIG` is the smallest example of
a habit that pays off through the rest of this course: describe the data once,
derive the types from it. The alternative — a hand-written union sitting next
to the object it mirrors — is two things that must be kept in sync by
discipline, and discipline loses to deadlines. This same instinct produces
`typeof handlers`, `ReturnType<typeof makeStore>` and the mapped types of
lesson 09.

**The enum question, answered properly.** `enum` is one of a small number of
TypeScript features that emit JavaScript rather than being erased, which makes
it the odd one out in a language that otherwise disappears at build time. The
case *for* string enums: nominal typing (a plain string is not assignable, so
values cannot be faked), a single import that carries both the values and the
type, and a natural home for documentation comments. The case *against*: the
runtime object cannot be tree-shaken, values crossing a boundary
(`JSON.parse`, a database row, a form field) are plain strings that need a cast
or a validator, numeric enums have genuinely unsound assignability and reverse
mappings, and `const enum` is incompatible with `isolatedModules` and most
bundlers. The pragmatic answer most teams reach: string literal unions by
default, with `as const` objects when you also need runtime values; enums when
nominal typing earns its keep, or when a codebase already uses them
consistently.

**Template literal types exist, and this is the lesson where they start making
sense.** Since TypeScript 4.1 the type system can compute string types:

```ts
type Track = "typescript" | "node";
type GateFile = `${Track}/gate.test.ts`;   // "typescript/gate.test.ts" | "node/gate.test.ts"
```

They combine with unions by distributing over every member, and they power
things like typed route parameters and `on${Capitalize<Event>}` handler names.
Lesson 09 uses one for real.

## ex1 — three values, not every string

`type Level = string` and `type Level = "beginner" | "intermediate" |
"advanced"` produce identical JavaScript and completely different development
experiences. With the union you get autocomplete on every call site, a compile
error for a misspelled case label, and a `switch` the compiler can check for
exhaustiveness. With `string` you get none of that and a function that happily
accepts `"beginer"`.

The `advanced` → `advanced` rule is a design decision worth noticing. The
alternatives were returning `null` (making the return type `Level | null` and
pushing a check onto every caller) or throwing (making a legal input an
exception). "Saturate at the top" is the one that keeps the signature honest,
and honest signatures are how you avoid `!` and `?.` spreading through a
codebase.

The other thing to try, if you have not: write the `switch` with only two cases
and a `default` that calls the `assertNever` from lesson 04. The error names
`"advanced"` explicitly. That is what a compile-time to-do list looks like.

## ex2 — freeze the lookup table

Without `as const`, `TRACK_TITLES.typescript` is `string` and the object is
mutable, so nothing stops another module writing to it. With `as const` the
property is the literal `"TypeScript"` and the write is a compile error. Note
what did *not* change: the emitted JavaScript, byte for byte. This is the
clearest possible demonstration that types are a compile-time story about a
runtime object.

The indexed lookup `TRACK_TITLES[track]` deserves a moment. It compiles because
`track` is one of the object's literal keys — the compiler can check that every
possible value of `track` is a real property. Widen the parameter to `string`
and it stops compiling with "No index signature with a parameter of type
'string'". That error is TypeScript refusing to pretend the lookup will
succeed, and the fix is either an index signature (which lies, per lesson 03) or
a narrower key type (which does not).

## ex3 — an enum, on purpose

The runtime assertion in the gate — `expect(Status.Published).toBe("published")`
— is there to make the emit visible. Enums are not erased; `Status` is a real
object in the bundle. That has two consequences worth carrying: it costs bytes,
and it means you can iterate the members (`Object.values(Status)`), which a
literal union cannot do without an `as const` array to go with it.

The nominal behaviour is the genuinely useful part. `const s: Status = "draft"`
is an error, so a `Status` in your program provably came from your enum rather
than from a query string. The flip side is that data from outside — `JSON.parse`
of an API response, a row from a database, `req.body.status` — is a plain
string, and you will be writing `as Status` or a validator at every boundary.
Whether that boundary work is a feature (a place to validate) or a nuisance
(a place to cast blindly) depends entirely on your team's discipline, which is
the real reason the community is split.

A last practical note: prefer string enums to numeric ones. Numeric enum members
accept arbitrary numbers in more situations than they should, and a numeric
enum in a database column or a log line tells a future reader nothing.

## challenge — derive the union from the data

`keyof typeof HINT_TIERS` is two operators doing one job, and reading them
right to left is the key. The type-level `typeof` takes a *value* and gives you
its type — a different operator from the runtime `typeof` despite the shared
spelling, distinguished by appearing in a type position. `keyof` then takes a
type and gives you the union of its keys.

Without `as const` the keys are still `"nudge" | "approach" | "almost"`, so
`Tier` alone would have worked — but the *values* would widen to `number`, and
the gate checks `HINT_TIERS.almost` is the literal `3`. The habit to build is
adding `as const` to any table you intend to derive types from; it costs
nothing and it means you can go further later (mapping the values into another
type, checking exhaustiveness against the object, and so on).

The `[...tiers].sort(...)` copy is lesson 01 returning. Note that the compiler
enforces it this time: `tiers` is `readonly Tier[]` and `sort` is not on a
readonly array, so you cannot forget.

## review1 — verdictIcon

The third literal union in one lesson, on purpose. What is being trained is the
reflex to ask "is this set closed?" whenever you are about to write `string`.
Statuses, verdicts, roles, sort directions, HTTP methods, log levels, event
names — closed, all of them, and each one is a `switch` waiting to be checked.

The open question in the hint is a real one: should `verdictIcon` return
`string` or `"ok" | "x" | "-"`? Returning the narrower type gives callers
something they can `switch` on exhaustively; returning `string` gives you room
to change the icons without breaking anyone. That is the classic
narrow-vs-flexible trade, and the right answer depends on whether the icons are
data or presentation.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Everyday Types — literal types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#literal-types) — literal types, literal inference and widening, with the `as const` fix.
- [Handbook: Enums](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/enums.html) — string, numeric, `const` and reverse-mapped enums, plus the "objects vs enums" section the official docs now include.
- [TypeScript 3.4 release notes: `const` assertions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-4.html#const-assertions) — what `as const` does, from the release that introduced it.
- [Handbook: Template Literal Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/template-literal-types.html) — string types the compiler can compute, and how they distribute over unions.
- [`tsconfig` reference: `isolatedModules`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#isolatedModules) — why `const enum` is off the table in this course and in most bundled projects.

## Challenge — derive the union from the data (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Two changes and one function:

1. Add `as const` to `HINT_TIERS`.
2. Replace `type Tier = string` with a type *derived* from the object's keys,
   using `keyof typeof` as shown in the Concept section.
3. Implement `sortTiers(tiers)`, returning a new array sorted by each tier's
   number: `sortTiers(["almost", "nudge", "approach"])` →
   `["nudge", "approach", "almost"]`.

Honest difficulty note: `keyof typeof` is formally lesson 07's material, and it
is here because `as const` without it is half a tool. The hints teach it. The
sort is lesson 01's copy-then-compare, one more time.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 05_literals_enums challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Writing `type Tier = "nudge" | "approach" | "almost"` by hand works right up
until someone adds a fourth tier to the object and forgets the type. Deriving
the union from the object means that cannot happen.

Two operators do it, and they read right to left.

## Hint 2

`typeof HINT_TIERS` in a *type* position means "the type of that value", and
`keyof` takes the union of a type's keys:

```ts
const sizes = { small: 1, large: 2 } as const;
type Size = keyof typeof sizes;   // "small" | "large"
```

The `as const` matters twice here: without it the keys are still right, but the
*values* widen to `number`, and the type gate checks one of them.

The sort is by the number each tier maps to, and lesson 01 already taught you
not to sort the caller's array.

## Hint 3

Add `as const`, replace the `Tier` alias with `keyof typeof HINT_TIERS`, and
sort a copy with a comparator that subtracts the two looked-up numbers.

Left to you: whether the comparator reads `HINT_TIERS[a] - HINT_TIERS[b]` or
something with an `if`. Also worth a minute: work out why the copy has to
happen before `.sort()` even though the parameter is `readonly` - the compiler
will tell you if you forget.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Replace `type Level = string` with a union of the three
literals, and implement `nextLevel(level)`:

- `nextLevel("beginner")` → `"intermediate"`
- `nextLevel("intermediate")` → `"advanced"`
- `nextLevel("advanced")` → `"advanced"` — the top of the ladder stays put

The type gate checks that `Level` is exactly those three strings and that
`nextLevel("expert")` does not compile.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 05_literals_enums ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Level` is currently `string`, which means `"banana"` is a level and the
compiler has no way to disagree. The type you want has exactly three values in
it, and you already know how to say "one of these" from lesson 04 - the only
new part is that the members are strings rather than object types.

## Hint 2

A string literal is a type whose only value is that string:

```ts
type Answer = "yes" | "no";
```

Once `Level` says that, `switch (level)` narrows exactly as a discriminated
union did, `case "beginer"` (note the typo) becomes a compile error, and the
gate's `nextLevel("expert")` stops compiling.

The top of the ladder does not go anywhere. The README says where it stays.

## Hint 3

Declare `type Level = "beginner" | "intermediate" | "advanced"` and switch over
the three cases: beginner to intermediate, intermediate to advanced, advanced
to advanced.

Left to you: whether to write the last case at all, or to end with a `default`.
One of those two makes TypeScript prove you covered everything - and lesson 04
already showed you the trick.

## Exercise 2 — freeze the lookup table

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Add `as const` to `TRACK_TITLES` so its properties keep
their literal types and become read-only, then implement `titleOf(track)`:

- `titleOf("typescript")` → `"TypeScript"`
- `titleOf("node")` → `"Node.js"`
- `titleOf("react")` → `"React"`

The type gate asserts that `TRACK_TITLES.typescript` is the literal type
`"TypeScript"` (not `string`) and that assigning to `TRACK_TITLES.node` is a
compile error. The body is one indexed lookup.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 05_literals_enums ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Hover `TRACK_TITLES.typescript` in your editor. It says `string`, because
object properties are mutable and TypeScript widens their inferred types
accordingly. The gate wants it to say `"TypeScript"` - the literal - and it
wants an assignment to it to be rejected.

There is a two-word suffix that does both.

## Hint 2

`as const` is a *const assertion*. Applied to an object or array literal it
does two things at once: every property becomes `readonly`, and every literal
value keeps its literal type instead of widening.

```ts
const sizes = { small: 1, large: 2 } as const;
// sizes.small is 1, not number; sizes is readonly
```

The function body is then a single lookup with a computed key.

## Hint 3

Add `as const` after the closing brace of the object, and implement `titleOf`
as `return TRACK_TITLES[track];`.

That indexing works because `track` is one of the three literal keys and the
object has all three - which is the quiet payoff of literal types. Left to
you: what happens if you widen the parameter to `string`. Try it, read the
error, and you will understand index signatures better than the error message
does.

## Hint 1

Hover `TRACK_TITLES.typescript` in your editor. It says `string`, because
object properties are mutable and TypeScript widens their inferred types
accordingly. The gate wants it to say `"TypeScript"` - the literal - and it
wants an assignment to it to be rejected.

There is a two-word suffix that does both.

## Hint 2

`as const` is a *const assertion*. Applied to an object or array literal it
does two things at once: every property becomes `readonly`, and every literal
value keeps its literal type instead of widening.

```ts
const sizes = { small: 1, large: 2 } as const;
// sizes.small is 1, not number; sizes is readonly
```

The function body is then a single lookup with a computed key.

## Hint 3

Add `as const` after the closing brace of the object, and implement `titleOf`
as `return TRACK_TITLES[track];`.

That indexing works because `track` is one of the three literal keys and the
object has all three - which is the quiet payoff of literal types. Left to
you: what happens if you widen the parameter to `string`. Try it, read the
error, and you will understand index signatures better than the error message
does.

# 06 — Generics, part 1

You have now written the same function twice. Lesson 01's `zip` paired strings
with numbers; the version in this lesson pairs anything with anything, and the
body is identical. That duplication — one algorithm, many element types — is
the problem generics exist to solve.

There are two bad answers to it, and you should be able to say why both are bad
in an interview. The first is copy-paste: `zipStrings`, `zipNumbers`,
`zipUsers`. The second is `any`: one function, no checking, and every caller
back in untyped JavaScript. Generics are the third answer — one function that
*remembers* what it was given, and hands the right type back to each caller.

A generic is not a type. It is a type with a hole in it, filled in at the call
site, usually without anyone writing it down.

## Concept — a parameter for a type

```ts
function atAny(items: unknown[], index: number): unknown {
  return items[index];
}

const name = atAny(["ada", "eli"], 0);
name.toUpperCase();   // 'name' is of type 'unknown'
```

The function is honest — it really does not know what is in that array — and
useless, because the caller who *did* know has been made to forget. Now with a
type parameter:

```ts
function at<T>(items: readonly T[], index: number): T {
  return items[index];
}

const name = at(["ada", "eli"], 0);   // string
const score = at([90, 80], 1);        // number
```

`<T>` declares a type parameter, used in the rest of the signature like any
other type. Notice what you did *not* write at the call sites: no `<string>`,
no `<number>`. TypeScript **infers** the type argument from the value you
passed, which is why generics feel invisible when they are done well.

You can supply it explicitly when inference has nothing to work from:

```ts
const nothing = at<string>([], 0);   // string
```

**Naming.** `T` is conventional for one type parameter, `T`/`U` for a pair,
`K`/`V` for key/value. Longer names (`TItem`, `TResult`) are common in library
code and read better once the signature grows past two.

**Generic interfaces** put the hole in a type instead of a function:

```ts
interface Cell<T> {
  readonly value: T;
  replace<U>(next: U): Cell<U>;
}
```

Two different type parameters live there. `T` belongs to the interface — fixed
when someone writes `Cell<string>` — and `U` belongs to the method, decided
fresh at every call. Telling those apart is exercise 3, and it is the thing
people find genuinely confusing the first time.

**Why not `any`?** Because `any` is not a type, it is an off switch. It
disables checking for the value *and everything it touches*:

```ts
function firstAnyAny(items: any[]): any {
  return items[0];
}
const n = firstAnyAny([1, 2]);
n.toUpperCase();      // compiles. Explodes at runtime.
n.definitely.nope();  // also compiles.
```

`unknown` is the safe version of the same idea — you cannot touch it until you
narrow it — but it still throws away what the caller knew. A generic keeps it.
"`any` vs `unknown` vs a generic" is one of the most common TypeScript
interview questions, and the answer is: `any` opts out, `unknown` defers, a
generic *remembers*.

## Exercise 1 — the head of any list

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Make `first` generic and implement it:

- `first([10, 20])` → `10`, typed `number | undefined`
- `first(["only"])` → `"only"`, typed `string | undefined`
- `first([])` → `undefined`

The empty case is what puts `| undefined` in the return type, and the type gate
checks that a list of objects comes back as `{ id: number } | undefined` — the
element type, not `unknown`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 06_generics_1 ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — two type parameters

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Make `mapArray` generic in both directions and
implement it:

```ts
mapArray([1, 2, 3], (n) => n * 2);          // [2, 4, 6]
mapArray(["a", "bb"], (s, i) => `${i}:${s}`);  // ["0:a", "1:bb"]
mapArray([], (x) => x);                     // []
```

The callback receives the element and its index. The type gate checks that
`mapArray([1, 2], (n) => n.toFixed(1))` is `string[]` — which only works if the
callback's parameter was inferred as `number` and its return type flowed
through to the result.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 06_generics_1 ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a generic interface with a generic method

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Give `Box` a type parameter, add a `map` method, and
implement the `box` factory:

- `box(2).value` → `2`
- `box(2).map((n) => n * 3).value` → `6`
- `box("hello").map((s) => s.length).value` → `5` — a `Box<string>` became a
  `Box<number>`
- `map` returns a **new** box; the original still holds its original value

The method's type parameter is not the interface's. Write
`map<U>(transform: (value: T) => U): Box<U>` and read it out loud until it
sounds obvious.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 06_generics_1 ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — zip, one last time

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Make `zipPairs` generic in both element types:

- `zipPairs(["ada", "eli"], [90, 80])` → `[["ada", 90], ["eli", 80]]`
- `zipPairs([true, false], ["yes", "no"])` → `[[true, "yes"], [false, "no"]]`
- `zipPairs([1, 2, 3], ["only"])` → `[[1, "only"]]` — still stops at the shorter
  input

The body is the one you wrote in lesson 01. Only the signature changes, which
is exactly the point.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 06_generics_1 ex4
```

## Challenge — uniqueBy (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `uniqueBy(items, key)`, which removes
duplicates according to a key the caller computes:

```ts
uniqueBy(
  [{ id: "a", name: "Ada" }, { id: "b", name: "Eli" }, { id: "a", name: "Ada again" }],
  (learner) => learner.id,
);
// [{ id: "a", name: "Ada" }, { id: "b", name: "Eli" }]
```

- the **first** item with a given key survives; later duplicates are dropped
- input order is preserved
- `uniqueBy(["a", "A", "b"], (s) => s.toLowerCase())` → `["a", "b"]`

Honest difficulty note: one type parameter, not two — the elements go in and
the same elements come out. A `Set` makes the body five lines.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 06_generics_1 challenge
```

## Review — lastOr

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Implement `lastOr(items, fallback)`:

- `lastOr([1, 2, 3], 0)` → `3`
- `lastOr(["x"], "fallback")` → `"x"`
- `lastOr([], "fallback")` → `"fallback"`

Both parameters share one type parameter, so `lastOr([1, 2], "none")` must not
compile — and the return type has no `| undefined` in it at all.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 06_generics_1 review1
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - typescript/06_generics_1

What a type parameter actually is, how inference decides what to put in it, and
why `any` is not a shortcut to the same place.

## Notes

**A generic function is a family of functions.** `first<T>` is not one
function with a fuzzy type; it is a template the compiler instantiates at every
call site, once per type argument. At runtime there is exactly one function —
type parameters are erased like everything else — but during checking,
`first(["a"])` and `first([1])` are checked as if you had written two separate
functions with `string` and `number` substituted in. That mental model
explains almost every generic error message you will ever read: the compiler is
telling you what it substituted and where the substitution stopped working.

**Inference, in one paragraph.** TypeScript collects *candidates* for each type
parameter from the arguments you passed, then picks one. Multiple candidates in
the same position are widened to a common supertype where possible
(`first([1, "a"])` gives `T = string | number`); candidates that conflict in an
invariant position produce an error. Contextual typing runs the other way: once
`T` is fixed by the first argument, the callback's parameters are typed for you,
which is why `mapArray([1, 2], (n) => n.toFixed(1))` needs no annotation on
`n`. When inference has nothing to work from — an empty array, a callback with
no arguments — the parameter falls back to `unknown`, and that is your cue to
pass the type argument explicitly.

**`any` vs `unknown` vs a type parameter.** This trio is the most-asked
TypeScript interview question, so have a crisp answer. `any` disables checking:
every operation on an `any` compiles, and the infection spreads to anything
derived from it. `unknown` is its safe twin — you may hold one, but you must
narrow before you use it — which makes it the right type for genuinely unknown
input like `JSON.parse` output. A type parameter is different in kind from
both: it does not describe a value at all, it *carries* the caller's type
through the function so it can be handed back. Use `unknown` at the boundary,
generics in the plumbing, `any` when migrating legacy code and you have a
deadline.

**Where generics stop being worth it.** A type parameter that appears exactly
once in a signature is doing nothing. `function log<T>(value: T): void` is
`function log(value: unknown): void` with extra ceremony — the classic
"needless generic" review comment. The useful test is: does this parameter
connect two places? Input to output (`first`), one argument to another
(`lastOr`), a class field to a method (`Box`). If not, delete the angle
brackets.

**Generic defaults, constraints, and `keyof` are next.** This lesson leaves out
three things you will want almost immediately: `<T extends { id: string }>` to
require structure, `<T = string>` to supply a default, and `K extends keyof T`
to talk about property names. Lesson 07 is those three.

## ex1 — the head of any list

The exercise is a two-line function whose entire content is the signature.
`unknown[]` in and `unknown` out is a *correct* description of what the code
does and a useless one for callers: `first(["ada"]).toUpperCase()` is an error,
and the only ways out are a cast or a narrowing check, both of which throw away
information the caller already had. `T` gives it back.

`T | undefined` in the return type is the honest part. An empty array has no
first element, and pretending otherwise is how `cannot read property 'name' of
undefined` gets into production. Note the alternative designs and what each
costs: throw (callers must catch), take a fallback (review1 does this — the
return type loses the `undefined` entirely), or return `T` and lie. The third
is what `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` would prevent, and it is a flag worth
knowing about even though this course leaves it off.

## ex2 — two type parameters

`mapArray` is `Array.prototype.map` rewritten, and reading its real signature in
`lib.es5.d.ts` is worth a minute of your life:
`map<U>(callbackfn: (value: T, index: number, array: T[]) => U, thisArg?: any): U[]`.
Same shape, same reason: `T` comes from the array, `U` comes from the callback.

The subtle thing here is *contextual typing*. When you pass an inline arrow,
TypeScript types its parameters from the position it is being passed into — it
does not infer them from the body. That is why `(n) => n.toFixed(1)` works with
no annotation and why the `@ts-expect-error` probe (`n.toUpperCase()`) is a
compile error rather than a runtime one. Move the same arrow into a `const`
first and the magic disappears: standalone arrows have no context, so their
parameters become implicit `any` and `noImplicitAny` complains.

If you delegated to `items.map(...)` — good instinct, and note that
`readonly T[]` has `map` but not `push`, so the readonly parameter cost you
nothing.

## ex3 — a generic interface with a generic method

The two type parameters are the lesson. `T` is fixed when the type is written
down: a `Box<string>` holds a string forever. `U` is fixed when `map` is

# Reading - typescript/06_generics_1

What a type parameter actually is, how inference decides what to put in it, and
why `any` is not a shortcut to the same place.

## Notes

**A generic function is a family of functions.** `first<T>` is not one
function with a fuzzy type; it is a template the compiler instantiates at every
call site, once per type argument. At runtime there is exactly one function —
type parameters are erased like everything else — but during checking,
`first(["a"])` and `first([1])` are checked as if you had written two separate
functions with `string` and `number` substituted in. That mental model
explains almost every generic error message you will ever read: the compiler is
telling you what it substituted and where the substitution stopped working.

**Inference, in one paragraph.** TypeScript collects *candidates* for each type
parameter from the arguments you passed, then picks one. Multiple candidates in
the same position are widened to a common supertype where possible
(`first([1, "a"])` gives `T = string | number`); candidates that conflict in an
invariant position produce an error. Contextual typing runs the other way: once
`T` is fixed by the first argument, the callback's parameters are typed for you,
which is why `mapArray([1, 2], (n) => n.toFixed(1))` needs no annotation on
`n`. When inference has nothing to work from — an empty array, a callback with
no arguments — the parameter falls back to `unknown`, and that is your cue to
pass the type argument explicitly.

**`any` vs `unknown` vs a type parameter.** This trio is the most-asked
TypeScript interview question, so have a crisp answer. `any` disables checking:
every operation on an `any` compiles, and the infection spreads to anything
derived from it. `unknown` is its safe twin — you may hold one, but you must
narrow before you use it — which makes it the right type for genuinely unknown
input like `JSON.parse` output. A type parameter is different in kind from
both: it does not describe a value at all, it *carries* the caller's type
through the function so it can be handed back. Use `unknown` at the boundary,
generics in the plumbing, `any` when migrating legacy code and you have a
deadline.

**Where generics stop being worth it.** A type parameter that appears exactly
once in a signature is doing nothing. `function log<T>(value: T): void` is
`function log(value: unknown): void` with extra ceremony — the classic
"needless generic" review comment. The useful test is: does this parameter

## Challenge — uniqueBy (moderate)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `uniqueBy(items, key)`, which removes
duplicates according to a key the caller computes:

```ts
uniqueBy(
  [{ id: "a", name: "Ada" }, { id: "b", name: "Eli" }, { id: "a", name: "Ada again" }],
  (learner) => learner.id,
);

```

- input order is preserved

the same elements come out. A `Set` makes the body five lines.

## Exercise 1 — the head of any list

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Make `first` generic and implement it:

- `first([10, 20])` → `10`, typed `number | undefined`
- `first(["only"])` → `"only"`, typed `string | undefined`
- `first([])` → `undefined`

The empty case is what puts `| undefined` in the return type, and the type gate
checks that a list of objects comes back as `{ id: number } | undefined` — the
element type, not `unknown`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 06_generics_1 ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Nothing about taking the first element of a list depends on what the elements
are. That is the definition of a generic function: one implementation, a type
that varies with the call.

Then there is the empty list. Whatever you return for it has to be part of the
declared return type.

## Hint 2

A type parameter is declared in angle brackets before the parameter list and
used like any other type:

```ts
function last<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined { ... }
```

You do not pass `T` at the call site - TypeScript *infers* it from the
argument, so `first([1, 2])` gives `T = number`. That inference is the entire
ergonomic argument for generics over `unknown`.

## Hint 3

Write `first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined`, return `undefined` when
the list is empty, and `items[0]` otherwise.

Left to you: whether to write the body as a conditional expression or an early
return. And one thing worth trying: delete the `| undefined` and see what
TypeScript says about `items[0]` - the answer depends on a compiler flag this
course leaves off, and knowing which one is worth five minutes.

## Hint 1

Nothing about taking the first element of a list depends on what the elements
are. That is the definition of a generic function: one implementation, a type
that varies with the call.

Then there is the empty list. Whatever you return for it has to be part of the
declared return type.

## Hint 2

A type parameter is declared in angle brackets before the parameter list and
used like any other type:

```ts
function last<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined { ... }
```

You do not pass `T` at the call site - TypeScript *infers* it from the
argument, so `first([1, 2])` gives `T = number`. That inference is the entire
ergonomic argument for generics over `unknown`.

## Hint 3

Write `first<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined`, return `undefined` when
the list is empty, and `items[0]` otherwise.

Left to you: whether to write the body as a conditional expression or an early
return. And one thing worth trying: delete the `| undefined` and see what
TypeScript says about `items[0]` - the answer depends on a compiler flag this
course leaves off, and knowing which one is worth five minutes.

implement it:


callback's parameter was inferred as `number` and its return type flowed

## Exercise 3 — a generic interface with a generic method

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Give `Box` a type parameter, add a `map` method, and
implement the `box` factory:

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two separate type parameters live in this exercise, and telling them apart is
the whole lesson. One belongs to the *interface* - what this box holds. The
other belongs to the *method* - what the transform turns it into, decided fresh
at every `map` call.

## Hint 2

An interface takes type parameters the same way a function does, and a method
inside it can declare its own:

```ts
interface Cell<T> {
  readonly value: T;
  replace<U>(next: U): Cell<U>;
}
```

`box` itself is a generic function returning `Box<T>`. Its body returns an
object literal with the value and a `map` method - and the easiest `map` calls
`box` again with the transformed value.

## Hint 3

Declare `interface Box<T>` with `readonly value: T` and
`map<U>(transform: (value: T) => U): Box<U>`. Then
`export function box<T>(value: T): Box<T>` returning
`{ value, map: ... }` where `map` builds a new box from `transform(value)`.

Left to you: whether `map` is a method shorthand or an arrow property, and
whether the returned box is built by recursion into `box` or by another object
literal. One of those choices makes adding a second method much cheaper later.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two separate type parameters live in this exercise, and telling them apart is
the whole lesson. One belongs to the *interface* - what this box holds. The
other belongs to the *method* - what the transform turns it into, decided fresh
at every `map` call.

## Hint 2

An interface takes type parameters the same way a function does, and a method
inside it can declare its own:

```ts
interface Cell<T> {
  readonly value: T;
  replace<U>(next: U): Cell<U>;
}
```

`box` itself is a generic function returning `Box<T>`. Its body returns an
object literal with the value and a `map` method - and the easiest `map` calls
`box` again with the transformed value.

## Hint 3

Declare `interface Box<T>` with `readonly value: T` and
`map<U>(transform: (value: T) => U): Box<U>`. Then
`export function box<T>(value: T): Box<T>` returning
`{ value, map: ... }` where `map` builds a new box from `transform(value)`.

Left to you: whether `map` is a method shorthand or an arrow property, and
whether the returned box is built by recursion into `box` or by another object
literal. One of those choices makes adding a second method much cheaper later.

- `zipPairs(["ada", "eli"], [90, 80])` → `[["ada", 90], ["eli", 80]]`
- `zipPairs([true, false], ["yes", "no"])` → `[[true, "yes"], [false, "no"]]`
- `zipPairs([1, 2, 3], ["only"])` → `[[1, "only"]]` — still stops at the shorter
  input

is exactly the point.

```ts
function zipPairs<A, B>(a: readonly A[], b: readonly B[]): [A, B][] { ... }
```

Everything else is lesson 01: stop at the shorter length, push a two-slot tuple

Two type parameters, `readonly A[]` and `readonly B[]` in, `[A, B][]` out.

the same type - and one of the two is much easier to read when the element
type gets long.

lessons.briefing:
# 07 — Generics, part 2

Lesson 06's generics knew nothing about the types they carried, which was the
point — `first<T>` works for every `T` precisely because it never touches one.
Most real generic code is not like that. It needs the value to have a `length`,
or a key that exists, or a shape it can read a property from. That is what
**constraints** are for.

Alongside them come the two operators that make TypeScript feel like a
programming language for types rather than a labelling scheme: `keyof T`, the
union of a type's property names, and `T[K]`, the type stored at a key. With
those two you can write `pluck(learners, "name")` and have the compiler know
the answer is `string[]` — not because you told it, but because it worked it
out from the object type and the literal you passed.

By the end of this lesson you will have written a function whose third type
parameter is constrained by its second. That sounds academic; it is how every
typed configuration reader, ORM query builder and form library you have used is
built.

## Concept — constraints, `keyof`, `T[K]`, defaults

**Constraints.** `extends` in a type parameter list means "must be at least
this":

```ts
function longest<T extends { length: number }>(a: T, b: T): T {
  return b.length > a.length ? b : a;   // .length is available now
}

longest("abc", "de");     // string
longest([1, 2], [3]);     // number[]
longest(1, 2);            // Argument of type 'number' is not assignable to
                          // parameter of type '{ length: number }'
```

Two things happened at once: inside the function you may use what the
constraint promises, and outside it callers are rejected if they cannot deliver.
Note that `T` is still inferred as the *specific* type — `string`, not
`{ length: number }` — which is why the return type is useful.

**`keyof`** turns a type into a union of its property names:

```ts
interface Learner { id: string; name: string; streak: number }

type LearnerKey = keyof Learner;    // "id" | "name" | "streak"
```

**Indexed access types** read the type at a key:

```ts
type Streak = Learner["streak"];        // number
type Either = Learner["id" | "name"];   // string
```

Put them together and you get the single most reusable generic signature in the
language:

```ts
function get<T, K extends keyof T>(item: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return item[key];
}

const learner: Learner = { id: "a", name: "Ada", streak: 12 };
get(learner, "streak");   // number
get(learner, "nope");     // Argument of type '"nope"' is not assignable to
                          // parameter of type 'keyof Learner'
```

Why two type parameters instead of `key: keyof T`? Because `K` is inferred as
the *literal* `"streak"`, so `T[K]` is `number`. With `key: keyof T` the return
type would be `T[keyof T]` — `string | number` — and every caller would be back
to narrowing. Precision at the call site is the whole reason for the extra
parameter.

**Default type arguments** work like default values:

```ts
class Registry<T = string> {
  private readonly entries = new Map<string, T>();
}

new Registry();          // Registry<string>
new Registry<number>();  // Registry<number>
```

**Generic classes** parameterise their fields and methods together. The type
parameter belongs to the *instance*, so it is fixed at construction, while a
method may still declare parameters of its own. There is one rule worth
knowing: static members cannot use the class's type parameter, because there is
no instance to fix it.

## Exercise 1 — pluck

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Rewrite `pluck` so the key must be a real property and
the result carries that property's type:

- `pluck(learners, "name")` → `["Ada", "Eli"]`, typed `string[]`
- `pluck(learners, "streak")` → `[12, 3]`, typed `number[]`
- `pluck([], "name")` → `[]`
- `pluck(learners, "nickname")` must not compile

Two type parameters: the element type and the key. The body is a one-line
`map`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 07_generics_2 ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — a constraint that demands structure

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Constrain `longest` so its arguments must have a
`length`, and return the longer one:

- `longest("abc", "de")` → `"abc"`
- `longest([1, 2], [3])` → `[1, 2]`
- `longest("ab", "cd")` → `"ab"` — on a tie, the **first** argument wins
- `longest(1, 2)` must not compile

```
uv run dojo test typescript 07_generics_2 ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a generic class with a default

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Give `Registry` a type parameter defaulting to
`string`, and implement the four members over the internal `Map`:

- `set(key, value)` stores a value
- `get(key)` returns it, or `undefined` for a key that was never set
- `has(key)` returns a boolean

# Reading - typescript/07_generics_2

Constraints, `keyof`, indexed access types, defaults and generic classes — the
toolkit behind most typed library APIs.

## Notes

**A constraint is an upper bound, not a cast.** `T extends { length: number }`
means every `T` must be *at least* that shape; inside the function you may use
`.length` and nothing else, while outside, `T` is still inferred as the caller's
specific type. That combination — restricted inside, precise outside — is why
`longest("abc", "de")` returns `string` rather than `{ length: number }`. If you
find yourself writing `T extends any` or `T extends unknown`, you have written
an unconstrained parameter with extra words.

**`keyof` has sharp edges worth knowing.** `keyof` of a type with an index
signature is `string | number` (because `obj["1"]` and `obj[1]` are the same
property in JavaScript); `keyof` of `any` is `string | number | symbol`; and
`keyof` of an empty object type is `never`, which produces the wonderfully
confusing "Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type
'never'" when a generic fails to infer what you hoped. When you see `never` in a
key position, the real problem is usually one type parameter earlier.

**`T[K]` is an indexed access type and it distributes over unions.**
`Learner["id" | "name"]` is `string | string`, collapsed to `string`. That is
the same mechanism that makes `T[keyof T]` mean "the union of all value types",
which you will use in lesson 09. Note the syntax is always bracket notation —
`Learner.id` is not a type — and that it works with `number` for arrays and
tuples: `Learners[number]` is the element type of `Learners[]`, a genuinely
useful trick for deriving an item type from an `as const` array.

**Defaults, and where they belong.** `class Registry<T = string>` supplies a
type argument when the caller omits it. Defaults are useful for public APIs
where one type is overwhelmingly common (`Map<K, V = unknown>`-style
convenience) and for keeping a new type parameter backwards-compatible when you
add one to an existing generic. They interact with inference in one surprising
way: a default is only used when nothing else determines the parameter, so an
inferred type always wins over the default.

**Generic classes are less special than they look.** The type parameter is
fixed when the instance is constructed, so it behaves like an interface's — and
that is exactly why `static` members cannot refer to it: statics belong to the
class, not to an instance, so there is no `T` to point at. If you need a static
factory with its own type parameter, declare it on the method:
`static of<U>(value: U): Registry<U>`.

**Variance, if someone asks.** Is `Registry<string>` assignable to
`Registry<unknown>`? TypeScript's structural check answers by comparing members,
and because `Registry<T>` both accepts `T` (in `set`) and produces it (in
`get`), the safe answer is "no" — but TypeScript's default *method* bivariance
often lets it through anyway. That leniency is deliberate and pragmatic;
`strictFunctionTypes` tightens it for function-typed properties but not for
method syntax. This is a genuinely deep corner, and "TypeScript's methods are
bivariant for historical and ergonomic reasons" is a strong short answer.

## ex1 — pluck

The signature `<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K): T[K][]` is
the one to memorise. Every part of it is doing work: `T` comes from the array,
`K` is inferred as the *string literal* you passed, the constraint rejects keys
that do not exist, and `T[K]` reads the type at that key so the caller gets
`string[]` rather than `unknown[]`.

The instructive variation is `key: keyof T`, which the hint asks you to try.
It compiles, and the return type collapses to `T[keyof T][]` —
`(string | number)[]` for our learner — so every caller has to narrow. This is
the single clearest demonstration of why generic APIs use a separate `K`: the
literal type of the argument is information, and passing it through a type
parameter is how you avoid throwing it away.

Also worth noticing: `items.map((item) => item[key])` typechecks without a cast.
Indexing an unresolved `T` with an unresolved `K` is exactly the kind of thing
that needs `any` in weaker type systems, and TypeScript follows it precisely.

## ex2 — a constraint that demands structure

Writing the body first and watching `a.length` fail is the intended path,
because the error message *names the fix*: "Property 'length' does not exist on
type 'T'". Constraints are almost always discovered this way rather than
designed up front.

`{ length: number }` is a structural constraint, and it is worth appreciating
how much it accepts: strings, arrays, `NodeList`, `arguments`, typed arrays,
and any object you write with a `length` property. A nominal type system would
have needed an interface and every one of those types to declare it. Here the
constraint is just a shape, and everything that fits, fits.

The tie rule (`b.length > a.length ? b : a`) is a one-character decision with a
real consequence: `>=` returns `b` on a tie, `>` returns `a`. The gate checks
it because "stable" behaviour — equal inputs resolve consistently and
predictably — is what callers depend on when they chain these things together.

## ex3 — a generic class with a default

Three things were being trained here. First, that a class's type parameter
threads through fields and methods: `Map<string, T>`, `set(key, value: T)`,
`get(key): T | undefined`. Second, that `get` returning `T | undefined` is not
pessimism — `Map.get` genuinely can miss, and hiding that behind `T` is how
`undefined` gets into somewhere it will not be checked. Third, that a default
type argument keeps the common case terse.

There is a wider point about wrapping a `Map` at all. `Registry<T>` adds
nothing a `Map<string, T>` does not already do — which is the honest critique of
a lot of "service" classes. Where the wrapper earns its place is when it
constrains: a registry that validates keys, that refuses to overwrite, that
notifies on change. Keeping the field `private readonly` is what makes those
future invariants enforceable, and it is why the hint nudges at what happens
when you remove `private`.

## ex4 — indexBy

`Map<T[K], T>` is a satisfying little type: the key type is derived from the
property you chose, so `indexBy(learners, "id")` is a `Map<string, Learner>`
and `indexBy(learners, "streak")` is a `Map<number, Learner>` with no extra
work. Compare with the plain-object version, `Record<string, T>`, which cannot
express a numeric key honestly (object keys are strings at runtime) and cannot
hold object keys at all. When your keys are not strings, a `Map` is the right
data structure and TypeScript models it well.

The last-wins collision rule is the mirror of lesson 06's `uniqueBy`, which was
first-wins. Neither is more correct; what matters is that both are documented,
because a caller who assumes the wrong one gets *plausible* wrong data — the
worst kind. In an interview, saying "what should happen when two items share a
key?" before writing the function is a strong signal.

## challenge — getIn

`K2 extends keyof T[K1]` is the first time a constraint has referred to another
type parameter, and it is the shape that makes deep typed access work.
TypeScript resolves them left to right: `T` from the object, `K1` from the
first key literal, `T[K1]` from those two, then `K2` constrained by that.

Real libraries take this several steps further with template literal types and
recursion — `getIn(config, "server.port")` with a dotted path is a well-known
type-level exercise — and every one of them is built from the pieces you just
used. It is also where type-level code starts to have a cost: deeply recursive
path types are a common cause of slow editors and "Type instantiation is
excessively deep" errors. Two levels by hand is often the right engineering
answer.

The hint's closing question is the important one. The types guarantee the path
exists *in the type*, and guarantee nothing about the runtime value: if
`config` came from `JSON.parse`, `source[first]` can be `undefined` and
`source[first][second]` throws. Lesson 10 is entirely about that gap.

## review1 — firstWith

`value: T[K]` is the detail worth carrying away. The search value is typed by
the key you chose, so `firstWith(learners, "streak", "twelve")` is a compile
error rather than a search that silently finds nothing. Bugs of exactly that
shape — comparing a number to its string form and getting no match — are common
and hard to spot in review, and this signature makes them impossible.

`Array.prototype.find` returning `T | undefined` is a small gift: its type is
already exactly what you want, so nothing needs casting. When a standard
library function's type lines up with your signature that neatly, it usually
means you have modelled the problem the same way its designers did.

The `===` caveat in the hint is real. For object-valued properties, `===`
compares references, so `firstWith(items, "tags", ["a"])` will never match even
when the contents look identical. Fixing it properly means taking a comparator —
which is another callback, another type parameter, and a good example of how
"just one more feature" grows a signature.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Generics — generic constraints](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/generics.html#generic-constraints) — constraints, using type parameters in constraints, and generic classes.
- [Handbook: `keyof` type operator](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/keyof-types.html) — including the index-signature and `never` edge cases.
- [Handbook: Indexed Access Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/indexed-access-types.html) — `T[K]`, unions of keys, and `Arr[number]`.
- [Handbook: Classes — type parameters](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/classes.html#type-parameters) — generic classes and why statics cannot use them.
- [TypeScript Deep Dive: type inference and generics](https://basarat.gitbook.io/typescript/type-system/type-inference) — helpful when a constrained generic infers something you did not expect.

## Challenge — getIn (harder)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement a two-level typed getter:

```ts
const config = {
  server: { host: "localhost", port: 8080 },
  logging: { level: "debug", json: false },
};

getIn(config, "logging", "level");   // "debug", typed string
getIn(config, "server", "colour");   // must not compile
```

mentions the second (`K2 extends keyof T[K1]`). The body is one expression;
everything hard is in the signature, and getting it wrong produces error
messages that are worth reading slowly.


## Hint 1

Three type parameters, and the third one depends on the second. Say the shape
out loud: `K1` is a key of the object, and `K2` is a key of *whatever lives at
that key*.

The body is one expression. All the work is in the signature.

## Hint 2

Constraints may refer to earlier type parameters:

```ts
function twoDeep<T, A extends keyof T, B extends keyof T[A]>(...)
```

`T[A]` is the type at the first key, so `keyof T[A]` is the set of keys valid
for the second. That is what makes `getIn(config, "server", "colour")` a
compile error naming the keys it *would* have accepted.

The return type follows the same chain: `T[A][B]`.

## Hint 3

Signature: `getIn<T, K1 extends keyof T, K2 extends keyof T[K1]>(source: T, first: K1, second: K2): T[K1][K2]`,
body `return source[first][second];`.

Left to you: what this function should do if the intermediate value is
`undefined` at runtime. The types say it cannot be - but the types came from
the caller, and lesson 10 is about what to do when you do not trust them.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two promises are missing. The first: the key has to be a property that actually
exists on the elements - not any string in the world. The second: the values
that come back are whatever type that property holds, not `unknown`.

TypeScript has one operator for each half.

## Hint 2

`keyof T` is the union of `T`'s property names, and `T[K]` is the type stored
at key `K`:

```ts
interface Learner { id: string; streak: number }
type Keys = keyof Learner;        // "id" | "streak"
```

## Hint 1

Try writing the body first. `a.length` does not compile, because `T` could be
anything - a number, a boolean, `null`. The fix is not a cast; it is telling
the compiler what `T` is allowed to be.

## Hint 2

A constraint is written with `extends` in the type parameter list:

```ts
function biggest<T extends { size: number }>(a: T, b: T): T { ... }
```

Inside the function, `T` now has everything the constraint promises. At the
call site, an argument without that member is rejected - which is what the
type gate's `longest(1, 2)` probe is checking.

Strings and arrays both have `length`, so one constraint covers both.

Constrain `T extends { length: number }`, then return whichever of the two has
the greater `length`.

The decision left to you is the tie: two arguments of equal length. The README
says which one comes back, and the gate checks it - pick the comparison
operator that gets you there without an extra branch.

## Exercise 3 — a generic class with a default

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Give `Registry` a type parameter defaulting to
`string`, and implement the four members over the internal `Map`:

- `set(key, value)` stores a value
- `get(key)` returns it, or `undefined` for a key that was never set
- `has(key)` returns a boolean
- `size` (a getter) returns how many keys are stored

```ts
const scores = new Registry<number>();
scores.set("ada", 90);
scores.get("ada");      // 90, typed number | undefined
scores.get("nobody");   // undefined
new Registry().get("ts");  // typed string | undefined - the default
```

Setting the same key twice replaces the value; the size stays at 1.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Same two operators as ex1, arranged differently. The map's *keys* are the values
found at the chosen property, and the map's *values* are the whole items.

Write the return type before the body - it tells you what to construct.

## Hint 2

`Map<T[K], T>` is the type: keys of type `T[K]`, values of type `T`. Construct
it with `new Map<T[K], T>()` so the compiler checks every `set` call against
those types.

Then one pass over `items`, setting `item[key]` to `item`.

## Hint 3

Signature: `indexBy<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K): Map<T[K], T>`.
Body: build the map, loop, `index.set(item[key], item)`, return it.

Left to you: what happens when two items share a key. A `Map` overwrites, so
the last one wins - the opposite of `uniqueBy` in lesson 06. Whether that is
right depends on the caller, which is why the README says it out loud and the
gate checks it.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`keyof` and the indexed access type again, with one extra idea: the *value* you
are searching for should be typed by the key you chose. Ask for a `streak` and
the compiler should insist on a number.

## Hint 2

Three parameters, two type parameters: `items: readonly T[]`, `key: K` where
`K extends keyof T`, and `value: T[K]`.

`Array.prototype.find` returns `T | undefined`, which is exactly the return type
you want - no cast needed, and the caller is told about the miss.

## Hint 3

Write the signature as above with `T | undefined` out, and the body as
`items.find((item) => item[key] === value)`.

Left to you: `===` compares by reference for objects, so searching for an
object-valued property will not do what you hope. Whether that matters here
depends on the data - but noticing it before shipping is the skill.

## Hint 1

`keyof` and the indexed access type again, with one extra idea: the *value* you
are searching for should be typed by the key you chose. Ask for a `streak` and

## Hint 2

Three parameters, two type parameters: `items: readonly T[]`, `key: K` where
`K extends keyof T`, and `value: T[K]`.

you want - no cast needed, and the caller is told about the miss.

Write the signature as above with `T | undefined` out, and the body as
`items.find((item) => item[key] === value)`.

object-valued property will not do what you hope. Whether that matters here
depends on the data - but noticing it before shipping is the skill.

# 08 — Utility types

Every type you have written so far, you wrote out. Lesson 03's `RunOptions` and
`ResolvedOptions` were the same three members typed twice — once optional, once
required — and the moment someone adds a fourth, one of them is wrong.

TypeScript ships a small standard library of **utility types** that derive one
type from another: `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `Record`,
`Exclude`, `Extract`, `NonNullable`, `ReturnType`, `Parameters`, `Awaited`. They
are not compiler magic. Every one of them is a few lines of ordinary type code
built from `keyof`, `T[K]`, and one construct you have not formally met yet —
the **mapped type**, which this README teaches inline because you cannot
implement `Partial` without it.

The habit to leave with: describe one type, derive the rest.

## Concept — a `for` loop over keys

A mapped type walks the keys of one type and produces a member for each:

```ts
type Copy<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] };          // an exact clone of T
type Optional<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };     // every member optional
type Frozen<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
```

`[K in keyof T]` is the loop; `T[K]` is the value type at that key; `?` and
`readonly` are modifiers you can add (and, with `-?` and `-readonly`, remove).
`Partial`, `Required` and `Readonly` are exactly that pattern with one modifier
each — which is why writing them yourself is a five-token exercise rather than a
feat.

The key set does not have to be `keyof T`. Any union of keys works, and that is
what `Pick` and `Record` are built on:

```ts
type Record<K extends keyof any, V> = { [P in K]: V };

type Board = Record<"pass" | "fail", number>;   // { pass: number; fail: number }
```

`Omit` is `Pick` over the keys you did *not* name, and the subtraction is done
by `Exclude`, which filters a union:

```ts
type Rest = Exclude<"id" | "email" | "secret", "secret">;   // "id" | "email"
```

Lesson 09 explains how `Exclude` is implemented; here it is enough to know what
it does.

The three function helpers work the same way but read a *function* type apart:

```ts
type Loader = (id: string) => Promise<User>;

type A = Parameters<Loader>;              // [id: string]
type B = ReturnType<Loader>;              // Promise<User>
type C = Awaited<ReturnType<Loader>>;     // User
```

`Awaited<T>` unwraps a promise — recursively, and harmlessly on a non-promise —
which makes it the right way to say "whatever this async function eventually
produces".

Worked example, putting several together:

```ts
interface Lesson {
  slug: string;
  title: string;
  exercises: number;
}

type LessonDraft = Partial<Lesson>;                  // everything optional
type LessonCard = Pick<Lesson, "slug" | "title">;    // just two members
type LessonIndex = Record<string, Lesson>;           // a lookup table
type LessonWithoutTitle = Omit<Lesson, "title">;

function save(draft: LessonDraft): Lesson { /* ... */ }
```

None of these repeat a member name that is already written down once. Rename
`title` in `Lesson` and every derived type follows.

## Exercise 1 — Partial

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Change `applyPatch`'s second parameter so a patch may
name any subset of the object's members, and implement it:

- `applyPatch({retries: 1, label: "run", verbose: false}, {label: "nightly"})`
  → `{retries: 1, label: "nightly", verbose: false}`
- `applyPatch(base, {verbose: true, retries: 0})` → the `0` survives
- `applyPatch(base, {label: undefined})` → the base's label survives: a patch
  value of `undefined` means "no opinion"
- the base object itself is never modified

That third rule is why `{ ...base, ...patch }` is not quite the answer.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 08_utility_types ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — Pick and Omit

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Derive both aliases from `User` and implement both
functions:

- `PublicUser` is a `User` without `passwordHash`
- `UserSummary` is exactly `id` and `email`
- `toPublicUser(user)` returns an object with **no** `passwordHash` key —
  `"passwordHash" in result` must be `false`
- `toSummary(user)` returns the two-member summary
- neither modifies its input

```
uv run dojo test typescript 08_utility_types ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — write two of them yourself

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `MyPartial<T>` and `MyPick<T, K>` as mapped
types, then implement `pickKeys(source, keys)` returning `MyPick<T, K>`:

- `pickKeys(user, ["id", "email"])` → `{ id: "u1", email: "ada@example.com" }`
- `pickKeys(user, [])` → `{}`
- only the named keys appear — no `undefined` placeholders

The type gate checks your two types against the shapes the built-ins produce.
For the body you will want `{} as MyPick<T, K>` as the accumulator; the reading
explains why an honest version is so painful.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 08_utility_types ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — types derived from functions

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Two changes:

1. `Loaded` should be what the loader's promise resolves to —
   `{ id: string; title: string }`, not the `Promise` wrapping it.
2. Make `once` generic so the function it returns has the same parameters and
   return type as the one it was given.

```ts
const memo = once((a: number, b: number) => a + b);
memo(2, 3);     // 5, and the wrapped function ran
memo(10, 10);   // 5 again - the first result is cached; the function did not run
memo("2", 3);   // must not compile
```

```
uv run dojo test typescript 08_utility_types ex4
```

## Challenge — MyOmit and the runtime half (harder)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `MyOmit<T, K>` as a mapped type over the
*remaining* keys — `Exclude` is allowed, and the Concept section shows what it
does — then implement `omitKeys(source, keys)`:

- `omitKeys(user, ["passwordHash", "createdAt"])` → `{ id, email }`, and
  `"passwordHash" in result` is `false`
- `omitKeys(user, [])` → a copy of everything
- the source object is untouched

Honest difficulty note: the type is one line; the *runtime* half is where this
bites. `delete obj.prop` only compiles for optional properties, so you will need
one deliberate, documented cast — which is a real lesson about where the type
system's honesty ends.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 08_utility_types challenge
```

## Review — Record

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Replace the index signature on `ScoreBoard` with a
`Record` over the three verdicts, then implement `tallyVerdicts(verdicts)`:

- `tallyVerdicts(["pass", "fail", "pass"])` → `{ pass: 2, fail: 1, skip: 0 }`
- `tallyVerdicts([])` → `{ pass: 0, fail: 0, skip: 0 }`

Every verdict appears in the result, even at zero — and with `Record` the
compiler is what makes sure of it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 08_utility_types review1
```
