# Reading - typescript/08_utility_types

The standard library of types, what each one is made of, and the places where
the type-level story and the runtime story stop agreeing.

## Notes

**Utility types are ordinary type code.** Open `lib.es5.d.ts` in your editor
(hover `Partial` and press F12) and you will find five-line definitions built
from `keyof`, `T[K]`, mapped types and conditional types. Nothing in there is
compiler magic except `Awaited`'s recursion and a couple of intrinsics
(`Uppercase`, `Capitalize` and friends are genuinely implemented in the
compiler). Knowing this changes how you read unfamiliar library types: hover,
read, recognise the parts.

**The catalogue worth memorising.** `Partial<T>` (all optional), `Required<T>`
(all required), `Readonly<T>` (all readonly), `Pick<T, K>` (keep these keys),
`Omit<T, K>` (drop these keys), `Record<K, V>` (build from a key union),
`Exclude<U, X>` / `Extract<U, X>` (filter a union), `NonNullable<T>` (drop
`null` and `undefined`), `Parameters<F>`, `ReturnType<F>`, `Awaited<T>`,
`InstanceType<C>`. That list covers virtually every derivation you will need in
application code.

**`Omit` is the loose one.** `Pick<T, K>` constrains `K extends keyof T`, so a
typo is a compile error. `Omit<T, K>` deliberately does *not* — its `K` is
`keyof any` — so `Omit<User, "passwrodHash">` silently omits nothing. That is a
real source of bugs and a good interview detail; teams that care define a strict
version (`type StrictOmit<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>`) and use it
everywhere.

**Mapped types are where `?` and `readonly` become editable.** `+?`/`-?` and
`+readonly`/`-readonly` add and remove modifiers, which is how `Required<T>` and
`Mutable<T>` are written. Note the subtlety of `-?`: it removes the optionality
*and* strips `undefined` from the member's type, which is usually what you want
and occasionally surprising.

**`Partial<T>` and `undefined` are an awkward pair.** `Partial<Options>` allows
both "no `label` key" and "`label: undefined`", because an optional member's
type includes `undefined`. That is why `{ ...base, ...patch }` fails ex1's third
case: spreading copies the explicit `undefined` over a perfectly good value.
`exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is the compiler flag that separates the two (with
it on, `{ label: undefined }` is no longer a valid `Partial<Options>`), and it
is worth knowing about even though almost nobody turns it on.

**Runtime and type-level `Omit` are different operations.** At the type level,
removing a key is free. At runtime you have to actually not have the property —
`delete`, rest destructuring, or building a new object — and the compiler cannot
follow any of those precisely. `delete obj.prop` only compiles for optional
properties; rest destructuring (`const { secret, ...rest } = user`) is the one
form TypeScript types exactly, which is why it is the idiomatic answer.

## ex1 — Partial

The signature change is one word, and the interesting content is the third
test. `{ ...base, ...patch }` is the obvious implementation, it is what most
codebases contain, and it treats `{ label: undefined }` as an instruction to
erase `label`. Whether that is a bug depends on your API — but with a
`Partial<T>` patch it almost always is, because "the caller did not mention
this" and "the caller explicitly said undefined" arrive looking identical.

The cast on the way in (`(merged as Record<string, unknown>)[key] = value`) is
worth staring at. `Object.entries` returns `[string, any][]`, so the key you
have is a `string` and TypeScript will not accept a `string` as a key of `T` —
correctly, since a `T` could have exactly three known members. Every honest
implementation of this function contains a cast somewhere; the discipline is to
put it at the narrowest point and comment why.

## ex2 — Pick and Omit

`Omit<User, "passwordHash">` and `Pick<User, "id" | "email">` are the two
directions, and choosing between them is a design statement. Use `Omit` when the
type is "everything, minus the dangerous bit" — new members should be included
by default, and a new secret field will *not* be excluded until someone updates
the type. Use `Pick` when the type is "these specific fields" — a new member
will not leak, because it was not named. For anything security-relevant, `Pick`
is the safer default precisely because it fails closed.

The runtime half matters as much. The gate checks `"passwordHash" in publicUser`
rather than `publicUser.passwordHash === undefined`, because a serialiser will
happily ship `"passwordHash": undefined` as a key — or, worse, `JSON.stringify`
drops it while a database driver writes it. "Absent" and "present but undefined"
are different, and the type `Omit<User, "passwordHash">` promises the first.

Rest destructuring is the tool TypeScript types precisely here: `const {
passwordHash, ...rest } = user` gives `rest` the exact `Omit` type with no cast.
Some lint configs will complain about the unused `passwordHash` binding; the
conventional answer is a rule exception for rest siblings, not a `delete`.

## ex3 — write two of them yourself

Writing `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }` from memory is the point. Once you can, the
whole family becomes obvious, and the next time you need "every member optional
except `id`" you will write it in one line instead of by hand.

The accumulator cast in `pickKeys` deserves the paragraph the hint promised.
The honest version — building the object incrementally — cannot typecheck,
because after assigning one of three keys the object is not yet a
`MyPick<T, K>`, and TypeScript has no notion of "partially built". Your options
are: `{} as MyPick<T, K>` (a single, local, deliberate lie); building through
`Record<string, unknown>` and casting on return (the same lie, moved); or
`Object.fromEntries`, which returns `{ [k: string]: T }` and needs a cast
anyway. The standard library's own implementations use casts internally for
exactly this reason. Casts are not forbidden; unexplained casts are.

## ex4 — types derived from functions

`Awaited<ReturnType<Loader>>` is the idiom for "what does this async function
actually produce", and it composes: `Awaited` unwraps nested promises and leaves
non-promises alone, so it is safe to apply even when you are not sure. Before
it existed, everyone had their own `UnwrapPromise<T>` with a conditional type,
and half of them handled `PromiseLike` wrong.

The `F extends (...args: any[]) => any` constraint is the one place the
community agrees `any` is correct, and being able to explain why is a good
interview moment. The constraint's job is to say "some function"; using
`unknown[]` for the parameters breaks because function parameters are compared
*contravariantly* — a function taking `(a: number)` is not assignable to one
taking `(a: unknown)` — so real functions stop matching the constraint.
`never[]` works for the constraint but produces useless inference elsewhere.
`any` in a constraint position touches nothing outside it, because
`Parameters<F>` and `ReturnType<F>` recover the real types immediately.

The runtime behaviour — cache the first result, ignore later arguments — is
`once`, not `memoize`. A memoiser keys on the arguments and needs a `Map`, a
serialisation strategy for keys, and a story about when entries expire. Naming
the two apart in your own code saves a code review.

## challenge — MyOmit and the runtime half

`{ [P in Exclude<keyof T, K>]: T[P] }` is the definition, and `Exclude` is your
first look at a conditional type: `T extends U ? never : T`, distributed over
each member of the union. Lesson 09 explains why that distributes at all; for
now, note that "filter a union" and "subtract a union" are the same operation.

The runtime half is the real challenge, and its lesson is that `delete` is a
badly-typed operation. TypeScript only allows it on optional properties because
deleting a required one leaves the object contradicting its own type — a rule
that is *correct* and that makes the honest implementation impossible without a
cast. Two alternatives worth knowing: building the result by copying the
surviving keys (no `delete`, and no touching of inherited properties), and
`Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(source).filter(...))`, which is elegant and
loses all type information. Some performance-focused codebases ban `delete`
entirely because it can deoptimise an object's hidden class in V8 — the copy
version sidesteps that too.

## review1 — Record

`Record<Verdict, number>` versus `{ [key: string]: number }` is the same choice
as lesson 03's index signature, now with the closed-key-set option available.
The difference shows up immediately: with `Record`, `{ pass: 0, fail: 0 }` is a
compile error naming `skip`, so a new verdict added to the union produces
errors in every tally that forgot it. With the index signature, it produces
`undefined` at runtime and `NaN` after one `+= 1`.

`Record<string, T>` is still useful — it is the honest type for a genuinely open
lookup — but reach for the closed version whenever the keys are known. And
remember what `Record<string, T>` does *not* do: it does not make lookups safe.
`board["typo"]` is a `number` as far as the compiler is concerned, and
`undefined` at runtime, exactly as in lesson 03.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Utility Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html) — the full catalogue with examples, including the ones this lesson skipped.
- [Handbook: Mapped Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/mapped-types.html) — the `[K in keyof T]` loop, modifiers, and key remapping (which lesson 09 uses).
- [`tsconfig` reference: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#exactOptionalPropertyTypes) — the flag that separates "absent" from "present and undefined".
- [MDN: destructuring with rest properties](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Destructuring#rest_property) — the runtime `Omit` that TypeScript types exactly.
- [TypeScript source: `lib.es5.d.ts` utility types](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/main/src/lib/es5.d.ts) — read `Partial`, `Pick`, `Omit` and `Exclude` in their original form; they are shorter than you expect.

The runtime half is the real challenge, and its lesson is that `delete` is a
badly-typed operation. TypeScript only allows it on optional properties because
deleting a required one leaves the object contradicting its own type — a rule
that is *correct* and that makes the honest implementation impossible without a
cast. Two alternatives worth knowing: building the result by copying the
surviving keys (no `delete`, and no touching of inherited properties), and
`Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(source).filter(...))`, which is elegant and
loses all type information. Some performance-focused codebases ban `delete`
entirely because it can deoptimise an object's hidden class in V8 — the copy
version sidesteps that too.

## review1 — Record

`Record<Verdict, number>` versus `{ [key: string]: number }` is the same choice
as lesson 03's index signature, now with the closed-key-set option available.
The difference shows up immediately: with `Record`, `{ pass: 0, fail: 0 }` is a
compile error naming `skip`, so a new verdict added to the union produces
errors in every tally that forgot it. With the index signature, it produces
`undefined` at runtime and `NaN` after one `+= 1`.

`Record<string, T>` is still useful — it is the honest type for a genuinely open
lookup — but reach for the closed version whenever the keys are known. And
remember what `Record<string, T>` does *not* do: it does not make lookups safe.
`board["typo"]` is a `number` as far as the compiler is concerned, and
`undefined` at runtime, exactly as in lesson 03.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Utility Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html) — the full catalogue with examples, including the ones this lesson skipped.
- [Handbook: Mapped Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/mapped-types.html) — the `[K in keyof T]` loop, modifiers, and key remapping (which lesson 09 uses).
- [`tsconfig` reference: `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#exactOptionalPropertyTypes) — the flag that separates "absent" from "present and undefined".
- [MDN: destructuring with rest properties](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Destructuring#rest_property) — the runtime `Omit` that TypeScript types exactly.

## Challenge — MyOmit and the runtime half (harder)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `MyOmit<T, K>` as a mapped type over the
*remaining* keys — `Exclude` is allowed, and the Concept section shows what it
does — then implement `omitKeys(source, keys)`:

- `omitKeys(user, ["passwordHash", "createdAt"])` → `{ id, email }`, and
  `"passwordHash" in result` is `false`
- `omitKeys(user, [])` → a copy of everything
- the source object is untouched

Honest difficulty note: the type is one line; the *runtime* half is where this
bites. `delete obj.prop` only compiles for optional properties, so you will need
one deliberate, documented cast — which is a real lesson about where the type
system's honesty ends.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 08_utility_types challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Omit` is `Pick` over the keys you did *not* name. So the question becomes: how
do you subtract one union from another at the type level?

The standard library has a utility for exactly that, and you are allowed to use
it here - implementing it yourself is lesson 09's job.

## Hint 2

`Exclude<A, B>` removes from union `A` every member assignable to `B`:

```ts
type Rest = Exclude<"id" | "email" | "secret", "secret">;  // "id" | "email"
```

So the mapped type loops over `Exclude<keyof T, K>`.

The runtime half has a wrinkle: `delete obj.prop` is only allowed on optional
properties, so deleting from a `T` will not compile. Copy into something looser
first.

## Hint 3

`MyOmit<T, K>` is `{ [P in Exclude<keyof T, K>]: T[P] }`. For the body: spread
`source` into a `Record<string, unknown>`, `delete` each key, and cast the
result back on the way out.

Left to you: whether to build the result by *adding* the surviving keys instead
of deleting the named ones. The two versions behave differently for
inherited and non-enumerable properties - and one of them never needs `delete`,
which some codebases ban outright for performance reasons.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`Omit` is `Pick` over the keys you did *not* name. So the question becomes: how
do you subtract one union from another at the type level?

The standard library has a utility for exactly that, and you are allowed to use
it here - implementing it yourself is lesson 09's job.

## Hint 2

`Exclude<A, B>` removes from union `A` every member assignable to `B`:

```ts
type Rest = Exclude<"id" | "email" | "secret", "secret">;  // "id" | "email"
```

So the mapped type loops over `Exclude<keyof T, K>`.

The runtime half has a wrinkle: `delete obj.prop` is only allowed on optional
properties, so deleting from a `T` will not compile. Copy into something looser
first.

## Hint 3

`MyOmit<T, K>` is `{ [P in Exclude<keyof T, K>]: T[P] }`. For the body: spread
`source` into a `Record<string, unknown>`, `delete` each key, and cast the
result back on the way out.

Left to you: whether to build the result by *adding* the surviving keys instead
of deleting the named ones. The two versions behave differently for
inherited and non-enumerable properties - and one of them never needs `delete`,
which some codebases ban outright for performance reasons.

name any subset of the object's members, and implement it:

## Hint 1

One word in the signature is wrong, and one rule in the body is easy to miss.

The signature: a patch is a *subset* of the object's properties, and the
standard library has a type that turns every member of a type optional.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two aliases, two utility types, and they are opposites: one names the members to
*keep*, the other names the members to *remove*. Choose whichever makes the
intent clearer - and for a "public user", what matters is which single field
must never leave the server.

## Hint 2

```ts
type A = Pick<User, "id" | "email">;   // exactly those two members
type B = Omit<User, "passwordHash">;   // everything except that one
```

For `toPublicUser`, destructuring with a rest element removes a property
without any `delete`:

```ts
const { secret, ...rest } = source;
```

`rest` is a genuinely new object, and TypeScript types it as the original minus
the destructured member - which is `Omit` in another spelling.

## Hint 3

`PublicUser` is `Omit<User, "passwordHash">`; `UserSummary` is
`Pick<User, "id" | "email">`. Implement `toPublicUser` with rest
destructuring and `toSummary` by building the two-member object literal.

Left to you: whether `toSummary` should also be written with destructuring.
Both work. One of them stops compiling if a member is renamed, and the other
one silently keeps working - decide which failure you would rather have.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two aliases, two utility types, and they are opposites: one names the members to
*keep*, the other names the members to *remove*. Choose whichever makes the
intent clearer - and for a "public user", what matters is which single field
must never leave the server.

## Hint 2

```ts
type A = Pick<User, "id" | "email">;   // exactly those two members
type B = Omit<User, "passwordHash">;   // everything except that one
```

For `toPublicUser`, destructuring with a rest element removes a property
without any `delete`:

```ts
const { secret, ...rest } = source;
```

`rest` is a genuinely new object, and TypeScript types it as the original minus
the destructured member - which is `Omit` in another spelling.

## Hint 3

`PublicUser` is `Omit<User, "passwordHash">`; `UserSummary` is
`Pick<User, "id" | "email">`. Implement `toPublicUser` with rest
destructuring and `toSummary` by building the two-member object literal.

Left to you: whether `toSummary` should also be written with destructuring.
Both work. One of them stops compiling if a member is renamed, and the other
one silently keeps working - decide which failure you would rather have.

## Exercise 3 — write two of them yourself

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `MyPartial<T>` and `MyPick<T, K>` as mapped
types, then implement `pickKeys(source, keys)` returning `MyPick<T, K>`:

- `pickKeys(user, ["id", "email"])` → `{ id: "u1", email: "ada@example.com" }`
- `pickKeys(user, [])` → `{}`
- only the named keys appear — no `undefined` placeholders

The type gate checks your two types against the shapes the built-ins produce.
For the body you will want `{} as MyPick<T, K>` as the accumulator; the reading
explains why an honest version is so painful.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A mapped type is a `for` loop over the keys of a type. The README's Concept
section shows the syntax; the two you have to write differ only in *which* keys
they loop over and whether they add a `?`.

`MyPartial` walks every key of `T`. `MyPick` walks only the keys in `K`.

## Hint 2

```ts
type Mapped<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] };   // an exact copy of T
```

Add `?` after the bracket to make each member optional. To loop over a
different key set, put that union in place of `keyof T` - `K` is already
constrained to be a subset of `T`'s keys, so `[P in K]` is legal.

For the body of `pickKeys`, you need an accumulator the compiler will let you
write into. `{} as MyPick<T, K>` is the pragmatic idiom, and the reading
explains why an honest version is so awkward.

## Hint 3

`MyPartial<T>` is `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`. `MyPick<T, K>` is
`{ [P in K]: T[P] }`. Then loop over `keys`, assigning `source[key]` into the
accumulator.

Left to you: whether to reach for the cast at all. Try building the object with
`Object.fromEntries` instead and look at the type it hands back - it is a
perfect illustration of where TypeScript's inference gives up and why the
standard library's own implementations use casts too.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A mapped type is a `for` loop over the keys of a type. The README's Concept
section shows the syntax; the two you have to write differ only in *which* keys
they loop over and whether they add a `?`.

`MyPartial` walks every key of `T`. `MyPick` walks only the keys in `K`.

## Hint 2

```ts
type Mapped<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] };   // an exact copy of T
```

Add `?` after the bracket to make each member optional. To loop over a
different key set, put that union in place of `keyof T` - `K` is already
constrained to be a subset of `T`'s keys, so `[P in K]` is legal.

For the body of `pickKeys`, you need an accumulator the compiler will let you
write into. `{} as MyPick<T, K>` is the pragmatic idiom, and the reading
explains why an honest version is so awkward.

## Hint 3

`MyPartial<T>` is `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`. `MyPick<T, K>` is
`{ [P in K]: T[P] }`. Then loop over `keys`, assigning `source[key]` into the
accumulator.

Left to you: whether to reach for the cast at all. Try building the object with
`Object.fromEntries` instead and look at the type it hands back - it is a
perfect illustration of where TypeScript's inference gives up and why the
standard library's own implementations use casts too.

## Hint 1

Two independent problems.

`Loaded` is currently the promise. You want what the promise resolves to, and
there is a utility type whose whole job is unwrapping that - it also handles a
plainly non-promise type, and nested promises, without complaint.

`once` is a *higher-order* function: it takes a function and returns a
function. Its signature should say that the returned function has the same

`Awaited<T>` unwraps a promise; `ReturnType<F>` and `Parameters<F>` read a
function type apart.

The signature to build:

```ts
function once<F extends (...args: any[]) => any>(
  fn: F,
): (...args: Parameters<F>) => ReturnType<F> { ... }
```

Yes, `any` in that constraint - it is the one position where the community
agrees `any` is right, because the constraint is only saying "some function".
The reading explains why `unknown` does not work there.

For the body: a closure with a `called` flag and a cached `result`.

## Hint 3

`Loaded` is `Awaited<ReturnType<Loader>>`. `once` is the signature above, with
a body that returns an arrow capturing two variables - a boolean and the cached
result - and calls `fn` only when the boolean is still false.

Left to you: what happens when the wrapped function is called again with
*different* arguments. This version ignores them and returns the first result;
a memoiser would key on the arguments instead. The name you would give each of
those is the whole difference.

The index signature currently says "any string key, number value", which is the
lesson 03 answer. There are exactly three verdicts, so the key set is closed -

type Flags = Record<"a" | "b", boolean>;   // { a: boolean; b: boolean }

compile error naming the member you forgot. That is the whole difference
between this and an index signature.

counters at zero, loop the verdicts, and increment.

lessons.briefing:
# 09 — Mapped and conditional types

You have already written mapped types — `MyPartial` and `MyPick` in lesson 08
were exactly that. This lesson takes the two constructs that turn the type
system into something you can genuinely *compute* with: mapped types that
rename their keys as they go, and conditional types that branch, pattern-match
and extract with `infer`.

This is the deep end, and it is worth being honest about how much of it you
need. Most application code uses the built-in utility types and nothing more.
But every library you depend on is written in this language — every ORM's
`select`, every form library's field paths, every `zod` schema's inferred output
type — and the day you need to read one, or fix a type error coming out of one,
this is the material that lets you.

It is also, reliably, where a senior TypeScript interview goes when the
interviewer wants to find your ceiling.

## Concept — key remapping, conditionals, `infer`, distribution

**Mapped types, with modifiers.** The loop from lesson 08, plus `+`/`-` to add
or remove `readonly` and `?`:

```ts
type Loose<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };        // add ?     - every member optional
type Concrete<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };    // remove ?  - every member required
```

A `readonly` is added and removed the same way, with the modifier written in
front of the brackets rather than after them: `readonly [K in keyof T]` adds
one, and putting a minus in front of that `readonly` takes it away.

**Key remapping** with `as` lets the output key differ from the input key:

```ts
type Prefixed<T> = { [K in keyof T & string as `on${Capitalize<K>}`]: T[K] };

type Handlers = Prefixed<{ click: () => void; hover: () => void }>;
// { onClick: () => void; onHover: () => void }
```

Three pieces there: `keyof T & string` (template literal types need string
keys), `as <new key>` (the remap), and `Capitalize<K>` (one of four built-in
intrinsic string types — `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`,
`Uncapitalize`). A remapped key of `never` *drops* the member entirely, which
is how "filter the keys of an object type" is written.

**Conditional types** are a ternary for types:

```ts
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no";

type A = IsString<"hello">;   // "yes"
type B = IsString<42>;        // "no"
```

`extends` here means "is assignable to", not inheritance.

**`infer`** declares a placeholder inside the pattern and binds it if the match
succeeds:

```ts
type Unwrap<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T;
type FirstArg<F> = F extends (first: infer A, ...rest: any[]) => any ? A : never;

type A = Unwrap<Promise<string>>;              // string
type B = FirstArg<(id: number) => void>;       // number
```

This is pattern matching. `ReturnType`, `Parameters` and `Awaited` are all four
lines of `infer` in a trench coat — go and hover them.

**Distribution** is the rule that surprises everyone. When the checked type is a
*naked* type parameter and you hand it a union, the conditional is applied to
each member separately and the results are unioned:

```ts
type PairEach<T> = T extends unknown ? [T, T] : never;
type X = PairEach<string | number>;   // [string, string] | [number, number]
```

Three steps happened there: the conditional ran once for `string`, once for
`number`, and the two results were unioned.

That is also what makes `Exclude<T, U>` work. It is a one-line conditional that
returns `never` for the members you want gone — and because `never` disappears
from a union, returning it *is* subtraction:

```ts
type Y = Exclude<"a" | "b" | "c", "b">;   // "a" | never | "c"  ->  "a" | "c"
```

To *switch distribution off*, stop the checked type being naked — the
conventional way is a one-element tuple on both sides:

```ts
type PairAll<T> = [T] extends [unknown] ? [T, T] : never;
type Z = PairAll<string | number>;   // [string | number, string | number]
```

## Exercise 1 — remove a modifier

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Implement `Mutable<T>` as a mapped type that strips
`readonly` from every member, and implement `thaw(frozen)`, which returns a
writable shallow copy:

- `thaw({ retries: 1, label: "run" })` → an equal but **different** object
- the result is writable at runtime, and typed writable too

```
uv run dojo test typescript 09_mapped_conditional ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — rename the keys as you map them

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Implement `Getters<T>`, which turns every member into a
zero-argument getter with a `get`-prefixed name, and implement
`makeGetters(source)`:

```ts
const getters = makeGetters({ name: "Ada", streak: 12 });
getters.getName();     // "Ada",  typed string
getters.getStreak();   // 12,     typed number
```

Only the renamed keys exist on the result — `getters.name` must not compile.
The runtime half needs one cast on the way out; the compiler cannot follow a
property name you built from a string at runtime.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 09_mapped_conditional ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — a conditional type with `infer`

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement `ElementOf<T>` — the element type if `T` is an
array, otherwise `T` itself — and implement `flattenOnce(items)`:

- `flattenOnce([[1, 2], [3]])` → `[1, 2, 3]`
- `flattenOnce([1, 2])` → `[1, 2]`
- `flattenOnce([[[1]], [2]])` → `[[1], 2]` — one level only
- `flattenOnce([])` → `[]`

```
uv run dojo test typescript 09_mapped_conditional ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — distribution, on and off

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Three aliases and one function:

1. `MyExclude<T, U>` — remove from union `T` everything assignable to `U`
2. `BoxEach<T>` — distributes, so `BoxEach<string | number>` is
   `string[] | number[]`
3. `BoxAll<T>` — does **not** distribute, so `BoxAll<string | number>` is
   `(string | number)[]`
4. `withoutValues(values, remove)` — the runtime version of `MyExclude`:
   `withoutValues(["a", "b", "c"], ["b"])` → `["a", "c"]`, every occurrence
   removed, order preserved

The two `Box` types differ by four characters. Getting them both right is the
exercise.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 09_mapped_conditional ex4
```

## Challenge — DeepReadonly (harder)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `DeepReadonly<T>` — a mapped type that
recurses into members that are themselves objects — and `deepFreeze(value)`,
which freezes an object and everything inside it:

- `Object.isFrozen` is `true` for the object, its child, and its grandchild
- the values are unchanged
- `frozen.server.port = 8080` must not compile

Honest difficulty note: the type is three lines and recursive; the function is
five lines and recursive. The interesting part is what happens to arrays and
functions, since both are `object` — think about it before you decide your
implementation is finished.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 09_mapped_conditional challenge
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - typescript/09_mapped_conditional

Type-level programming: what the constructs are, what they cost, and how to
tell an interviewer where you would stop.

## Notes

**Mapped types are homomorphic (usually), and that word matters.** When a
mapped type has the exact form `{ [K in keyof T]: ... }`, TypeScript treats it
as *homomorphic*: it preserves `readonly` and `?` modifiers from the source,
and it distributes over arrays and tuples rather than mangling them. Add a key
remap or use a different key source and you lose that property — which is why
`Partial<string[]>` is a sensible array type while a hand-rolled
`{ [K in keyof T as K]: T[K] }` is not. If a mapped type ever destroys an array,
this is why.

**Key remapping with `as` is also a filter.** Producing `never` as the key drops
the member:

```ts
type OnlyStrings<T> = { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K] };
```

That idiom — remap to `never` to delete — shows up constantly in library types,
and it is worth recognising instantly.

**Conditional types are lazy and defer.** `T extends U ? X : Y` is only
evaluated once `T` is known; inside a generic function body, a conditional over
an unresolved type parameter stays unresolved, which is why you so often need a
cast when *returning* a conditional type. The compiler cannot prove your runtime
code produces the branch it landed on, and that limitation is by design.

**Distribution, precisely.** A conditional type distributes when its checked
type is a *naked* type parameter — `T extends U ? ... : ...`, not
`T[] extends U[] ? ...` or `[T] extends [U] ? ...`. Distribution applies the
conditional to every member of a union and unions the results. Two consequences
people trip over: `Exclude<T, U>` only works because of it, and
`T extends any ? T[] : never` with `T = never` produces `never` rather than
`never[]`, because distributing over an empty union gives an empty union. The
"naked type parameter" phrase is worth saying in an interview verbatim.

**`infer` is pattern matching, and it has options.** You can infer several
variables at once, infer from tuples (`T extends [infer A, ...infer Rest]` — the
basis of every type-level list algorithm), and since TypeScript 4.7 constrain an
inference (`T extends [infer A extends string, ...any[]] ? A : never`). Multiple
candidates for the same variable are unioned in a covariant position and
intersected in a contravariant one — which is the trick behind the famous
`UnionToIntersection` type.

**Know where to stop.** Recursive conditional types are limited to a finite
instantiation depth, and blowing past it gives "Type instantiation is
excessively deep and possibly infinite". Long before that, editor
responsiveness suffers: type-level computation runs on every keystroke.
`tsc --generateTrace` and the `--extendedDiagnostics` flag exist precisely
because clever types became a real performance problem in real codebases. A
strong senior answer to "how far would you take this?" is: derive at the
boundary, keep it shallow, name the intermediate types, and prefer a slightly
duplicated type over one nobody can debug.

## ex1 — remove a modifier

`-readonly` and `-?` are the least-known corner of mapped types and the most
immediately useful. `Mutable<T>` is the mirror of `Readonly<T>`, and the pair of
them is how DTOs get converted to editable form state and back.

The runtime half matters as much as the type. Returning `{ ...frozen }` is what
makes the promise true: the type says "writable", and a shallow copy is what
delivers it. Returning `frozen` itself with a cast would satisfy the compiler
and hand the caller a shared reference to something the rest of the program
believes is immutable — a bug that shows up far from its cause. When a type
says "copy", the code must copy.

The shallowness is the honest limitation, and the challenge in this lesson is
its counterpart: `Mutable` and `thaw` only touch the top level, so a nested
object is still shared. Whether that is fine depends on whether anything mutates
it — which is exactly why `readonly` on nested members is worth having.

## ex2 — rename the keys as you map them

`[K in keyof T & string as \`get${Capitalize<K>}\`]` is a mouthful, and it is
the single most transferable snippet in this lesson. Typed event emitters
(`on${Capitalize<Event>}`), generated action creators, `Vue`-style prop
handlers, `styled-components` variant props — all the same shape.

`keyof T & string` is there because template literal types need string keys, and
`keyof T` may include `number | symbol`. Forgetting it produces the error
"Type 'keyof T' is not assignable to type 'string | number | bigint | boolean |
null | undefined'", which is a genuinely mystifying message until you have seen
it once.

The cast in the runtime half is unavoidable and instructive. You are building
property names by string concatenation; TypeScript has no way to relate the
runtime string `"getName"` to the type-level key `` `get${Capitalize<"name">}` ``.
Every library that generates methods does the same thing: build loosely, cast
once at the boundary, and let the *declared* type be the contract. The value of
the type is undiminished — callers get full checking — but the implementation
has one honest lie in it, and it should be one line long and commented.

## ex3 — a conditional type with `infer`

`T extends readonly (infer U)[] ? U : T` reads as: "if `T` looks like an array of
something, call that something `U` and return it; otherwise return `T`". Using
`readonly (infer U)[]` rather than `(infer U)[]` is deliberate — the readonly
form matches both readonly and mutable arrays, exactly as in lesson 01, so the
type is more useful.

The two casts inside `flattenOnce` are the standard cost of a conditional return
type. `Array.isArray(item)` narrows `item` to `any[]` at runtime, but the
compiler cannot connect that to "therefore `ElementOf<T>` is the element type
here", because `T` is still unresolved. This is one of the clearest examples of
the boundary between what narrowing can prove and what a conditional type
asserts.

Worth comparing against the standard library: `Array.prototype.flat` has a
famously gnarly type using a recursive conditional `FlatArray<Arr, Depth>` with
a tuple-based depth counter. Hover it. It is the same idea as yours, iterated,
and it explains why `flat()` sometimes gives you a type you did not expect.

## ex4 — distribution, on and off

This exercise exists because distribution is the most common source of "why is

is the canonical example. The implementation you wrote is the textbook version
and it has the textbook problems: `T[K] extends object` is true for arrays

# Reading - typescript/09_mapped_conditional

Type-level programming: what the constructs are, what they cost, and how to
tell an interviewer where you would stop.

## Notes

**Mapped types are homomorphic (usually), and that word matters.** When a
mapped type has the exact form `{ [K in keyof T]: ... }`, TypeScript treats it
as *homomorphic*: it preserves `readonly` and `?` modifiers from the source,
and it distributes over arrays and tuples rather than mangling them. Add a key
remap or use a different key source and you lose that property — which is why
`Partial<string[]>` is a sensible array type while a hand-rolled
`{ [K in keyof T as K]: T[K] }` is not. If a mapped type ever destroys an array,
this is why.

**Key remapping with `as` is also a filter.** Producing `never` as the key drops
the member:

```ts
type OnlyStrings<T> = { [K in keyof T as T[K] extends string ? K : never]: T[K] };
```

That idiom — remap to `never` to delete — shows up constantly in library types,
and it is worth recognising instantly.

**Conditional types are lazy and defer.** `T extends U ? X : Y` is only
evaluated once `T` is known; inside a generic function body, a conditional over
an unresolved type parameter stays unresolved, which is why you so often need a
cast when *returning* a conditional type. The compiler cannot prove your runtime
code produces the branch it landed on, and that limitation is by design.

**Distribution, precisely.** A conditional type distributes when its checked
type is a *naked* type parameter — `T extends U ? ... : ...`, not
`T[] extends U[] ? ...` or `[T] extends [U] ? ...`. Distribution applies the
conditional to every member of a union and unions the results. Two consequences
people trip over: `Exclude<T, U>` only works because of it, and
`T extends any ? T[] : never` with `T = never` produces `never` rather than
`never[]`, because distributing over an empty union gives an empty union. The
"naked type parameter" phrase is worth saying in an interview verbatim.

**`infer` is pattern matching, and it has options.** You can infer several
variables at once, infer from tuples (`T extends [infer A, ...infer Rest]` — the
basis of every type-level list algorithm), and since TypeScript 4.7 constrain an
inference (`T extends [infer A extends string, ...any[]] ? A : never`). Multiple
candidates for the same variable are unioned in a covariant position and
intersected in a contravariant one — which is the trick behind the famous
`UnionToIntersection` type.

**Know where to stop.** Recursive conditional types are limited to a finite
instantiation depth, and blowing past it gives "Type instantiation is
excessively deep and possibly infinite". Long before that, editor
responsiveness suffers: type-level computation runs on every keystroke.
`tsc --generateTrace` and the `--extendedDiagnostics` flag exist precisely
because clever types became a real performance problem in real codebases. A
strong senior answer to "how far would you take this?" is: derive at the
boundary, keep it shallow, name the intermediate types, and prefer a slightly
duplicated type over one nobody can debug.

immediately useful. `Mutable<T>` is the mirror of `Readonly<T>`, and the pair of
them is how DTOs get converted to editable form state and back.

The runtime half matters as much as the type. Returning `{ ...frozen }` is what
makes the promise true: the type says "writable", and a shallow copy is what
delivers it. Returning `frozen` itself with a cast would satisfy the compiler
and hand the caller a shared reference to something the rest of the program
believes is immutable — a bug that shows up far from its cause. When a type
says "copy", the code must copy.

The shallowness is the honest limitation, and the challenge in this lesson is
its counterpart: `Mutable` and `thaw` only touch the top level, so a nested
object is still shared. Whether that is fine depends on whether anything mutates
it — which is exactly why `readonly` on nested members is worth having.

null | undefined'", which is a genuinely mystifying message until you have seen
it once.

The cast in the runtime half is unavoidable and instructive. You are building

Every library that generates methods does the same thing: build loosely, cast
once at the boundary, and let the *declared* type be the contract. The value of
the type is undiminished — callers get full checking — but the implementation
has one honest lie in it, and it should be one line long and commented.

asserts.

## Challenge — DeepReadonly (harder)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Implement `DeepReadonly<T>` — a mapped type that
recurses into members that are themselves objects — and `deepFreeze(value)`,
which freezes an object and everything inside it:

- `Object.isFrozen` is `true` for the object, its child, and its grandchild
- the values are unchanged
- `frozen.server.port = 8080` must not compile

Honest difficulty note: the type is three lines and recursive; the function is
five lines and recursive. The interesting part is what happens to arrays and
functions, since both are `object` — think about it before you decide your
implementation is finished.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 09_mapped_conditional challenge
```

## Hint 1

Both halves recurse. The type maps every member, and for members that are
themselves objects it applies itself again. The function walks every value, and
for values that are objects it calls itself again before freezing.

Write the type first and read its error messages; they are unusually clear
about depth.

## Hint 2

```ts
type DeepReadonly<T> = {
  readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends SomeCheck ? DeepReadonly<T[K]> : T[K];
};
```

The check is "is this member an object?", which at the type level is
`T[K] extends object`. A type alias may refer to itself inside a conditional or
mapped type - that is how recursive types are written.

At runtime, `Object.freeze` is shallow. Freeze the children before the parent,
and remember `typeof null === "object"`.

## Hint 3

The type is the mapped type above with `T[K] extends object ? DeepReadonly<T[K]>
: T[K]`. The function iterates `Object.values(value)`, recurses into anything
that is a non-null object, then returns `Object.freeze(value)` with one cast.

Left to you: arrays and functions are `object` too, so both branches of your
conditional will meet them. Decide what `DeepReadonly<string[]>` *should* be
before you decide whether this implementation gives it to you - the honest
version in a library is considerably longer, and that is the point.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Lesson 08's `Readonly<T>` added a modifier to every member. This one takes the
same modifier away, and the syntax is the same loop with one extra character in
front.

The function is a copy - a *new* object the caller may write to. Which copy
idiom you already know applies here.

## Hint 2

Inside a mapped type, `readonly` and `?` can be added with `+` (the default) or
removed with `-`:

```ts
type Required<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };
type Mutable<T>  = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
```

The minus goes immediately before the modifier, outside the brackets for
`readonly` and after them for `?`.

## Hint 3

`Mutable<T>` is `{ -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }`, and `thaw` returns
`{ ...frozen }`.

Left to you: whether the copy should be deep. This one is shallow, so a nested
object inside a frozen parent is still typed `readonly` in the original and
shared by the copy - which the challenge in this lesson takes seriously.

## Hint 1

Lesson 08's `Readonly<T>` added a modifier to every member. This one takes the
same modifier away, and the syntax is the same loop with one extra character in
front.

The function is a copy - a *new* object the caller may write to. Which copy
idiom you already know applies here.

## Hint 2

Inside a mapped type, `readonly` and `?` can be added with `+` (the default) or
removed with `-`:

```ts
type Required<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };
type Mutable<T>  = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
```

The minus goes immediately before the modifier, outside the brackets for
`readonly` and after them for `?`.

## Hint 3

`Mutable<T>` is `{ -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }`, and `thaw` returns
`{ ...frozen }`.

Left to you: whether the copy should be deep. This one is shallow, so a nested
object inside a frozen parent is still typed `readonly` in the original and
shared by the copy - which the challenge in this lesson takes seriously.

## Hint 1

A mapped type does not have to keep the key it read. There is a clause that
renames each key as it goes, and combined with a template literal type it turns
`name` into `getName`.

The values change shape too: each one becomes a function returning what the
original member held.

## Hint 2

The type has three moving parts and they compose left to right in the header:

```ts
type Example<T> = { [K in keyof T & string as `on${Capitalize<K>}`]: () => T[K] };
```

`keyof T & string` drops number and symbol keys (a template literal type needs a
string); `as` renames the key; `Capitalize<K>` is a built-in that upper-cases
the first character of a string literal type.

At runtime you are building a plain object whose values are arrows closing over
`source`. Build it as a `Record<string, () => unknown>` and cast once on the way
out - the compiler cannot follow a name you assembled from a string.

## Hint 3

`Getters<T>` maps `[K in keyof T & string as ...]` to `() => T[K]`, with the new
key built from the literal `get` and `Capitalize<K>`.

For the body: loop `Object.keys(source)`, build the name with
`key.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + key.slice(1)`, and assign an arrow that returns
`source[key as keyof T]`.

Left to you: whether the arrow reads `source` at call time or captures the value
now. Those behave differently if the source is mutated afterwards, and only one
of them deserves the name "getter".

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`ElementOf<T>` answers one question: "if `T` is an array, what is in it -
otherwise, what is `T`?". A question with two answers is a conditional type,
and the "what is in it" part needs a placeholder the compiler fills in for you.

The function then flattens one level, which is the runtime version of the same
question asked per item.

## Hint 2

```ts
type Unwrapped<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T;
```

`infer V` declares a type variable *inside* the pattern; if the match succeeds
`V` is bound to whatever fits there. For arrays the pattern is
`readonly (infer U)[]`, which also matches mutable arrays - the readonly form is
the wider one, exactly as in lesson 01.

At runtime, `Array.isArray(item)` is the check, and spreading pushes several
values at once.

## Hint 3

`ElementOf<T>` is `T extends readonly (infer U)[] ? U : T`. The body walks
`items`, spreading arrays into the accumulator and pushing everything else.
Two casts are needed because `Array.isArray` cannot narrow an unresolved `T`;
keep them local and obvious.

Left to you: whether a nested array *inside* a nested array should be flattened
too. The name says once. `Array.prototype.flat` takes a depth argument for
exactly this reason - and its type signature is worth hovering.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`ElementOf<T>` answers one question: "if `T` is an array, what is in it -
otherwise, what is `T`?". A question with two answers is a conditional type,
and the "what is in it" part needs a placeholder the compiler fills in for you.

The function then flattens one level, which is the runtime version of the same
question asked per item.

## Hint 2

```ts
type Unwrapped<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T;
```

`infer V` declares a type variable *inside* the pattern; if the match succeeds
`V` is bound to whatever fits there. For arrays the pattern is
`readonly (infer U)[]`, which also matches mutable arrays - the readonly form is
the wider one, exactly as in lesson 01.

At runtime, `Array.isArray(item)` is the check, and spreading pushes several
values at once.

## Hint 3

`ElementOf<T>` is `T extends readonly (infer U)[] ? U : T`. The body walks
`items`, spreading arrays into the accumulator and pushing everything else.
Two casts are needed because `Array.isArray` cannot narrow an unresolved `T`;
keep them local and obvious.

Left to you: whether a nested array *inside* a nested array should be flattened
too. The name says once. `Array.prototype.flat` takes a depth argument for
exactly this reason - and its type signature is worth hovering.

## Exercise 4 — distribution, on and off

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Three aliases and one function:

1. `MyExclude<T, U>` — remove from union `T` everything assignable to `U`
2. `BoxEach<T>` — distributes, so `BoxEach<string | number>` is
   `string[] | number[]`
3. `BoxAll<T>` — does **not** distribute, so `BoxAll<string | number>` is
   `(string | number)[]`
4. `withoutValues(values, remove)` — the runtime version of `MyExclude`:
   `withoutValues(["a", "b", "c"], ["b"])` → `["a", "c"]`, every occurrence
   removed, order preserved

The two `Box` types differ by four characters. Getting them both right is the
exercise.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A conditional type whose checked type is a *naked* type parameter is applied to
each member of a union separately, and the results are unioned back together.
That is called distribution, and all three aliases here are about it: two of
them differ only in whether it happens.

Write `MyExclude` first - it is the one the runtime function uses.

## Hint 2

```ts
type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;
```

Read it with `T = "a" | "b" | "c"` and `U = "b"`: the check runs three times, and
the `"b"` branch produces `never`, which vanishes from a union. That is how
subtraction falls out of a conditional.

To *stop* distribution, wrap both sides in a one-element tuple:
`[T] extends [U] ? ... : ...`. `[T]` is no longer a naked type parameter, so the
union is compared as a whole.

## Hint 3

`MyExclude<T, U>` is `T extends U ? never : T`. `BoxEach<T>` is
`T extends unknown ? T[] : never` (distributes, so a union of types becomes a
union of arrays). `BoxAll<T>` is `[T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never` (does
not, so you get one array of the union).

The function filters out anything in `remove`; a `Set` keeps it one pass, and
one cast on the way out tells the compiler what your filter proved.

Left to you: whether that cast is honest. `filter` cannot narrow `T` to
`MyExclude<T, U>` on its own - lesson 10's type guards are the tool that
sometimes can.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A conditional type whose checked type is a *naked* type parameter is applied to
each member of a union separately, and the results are unioned back together.
That is called distribution, and all three aliases here are about it: two of
them differ only in whether it happens.

Write `MyExclude` first - it is the one the runtime function uses.

## Hint 2

```ts
type MyExclude<T, U> = T extends U ? never : T;
```

Read it with `T = "a" | "b" | "c"` and `U = "b"`: the check runs three times, and
the `"b"` branch produces `never`, which vanishes from a union. That is how
subtraction falls out of a conditional.

To *stop* distribution, wrap both sides in a one-element tuple:
`[T] extends [U] ? ... : ...`. `[T]` is no longer a naked type parameter, so the
union is compared as a whole.

## Hint 3

`MyExclude<T, U>` is `T extends U ? never : T`. `BoxEach<T>` is
`T extends unknown ? T[] : never` (distributes, so a union of types becomes a
union of arrays). `BoxAll<T>` is `[T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never` (does
not, so you get one array of the union).

The function filters out anything in `remove`; a `Set` keeps it one pass, and
one cast on the way out tells the compiler what your filter proved.

Left to you: whether that cast is honest. `filter` cannot narrow `T` to
`MyExclude<T, U>` on its own - lesson 10's type guards are the tool that
sometimes can.

lessons.briefing:
# 10 — Guards, assertions, `unknown` and `satisfies`

Everything you have typed so far, you wrote. The types were true because you
made them true, and the compiler checked your work against itself.

Now the data comes from outside: `JSON.parse`, a `fetch` response, a form, a
database driver, `localStorage`, a library with optimistic typings. None of it
has been checked, and none of it will be — types are erased, so nothing at
runtime is enforcing the interface you declared. There are exactly two honest
options at that boundary. You can *check* the value, in code, and tell the
compiler what your check proved. Or you can lie with a cast and hope.

This lesson is the three tools for option one — type predicates, assertion
functions, and `unknown` — plus `satisfies`, which is how you check a value you
*did* write without losing what the compiler knew about it.

## Concept — telling the compiler what you proved

**`unknown` is the honest top type.** `any` and `unknown` both accept every
value; the difference is what you can do next:

```ts
const a: any = JSON.parse(text);
a.user.profile.name;        // compiles. Explodes at runtime, maybe.

const u: unknown = JSON.parse(text);
u.user;                     // Error: 'u' is of type 'unknown'.
```

`any` switches checking off — and it spreads, because everything derived from an
`any` is an `any`. `unknown` keeps checking on and forces a narrowing step. The
whole point of the two is that only one of them makes you look.

**Type predicates** let a *function* narrow, which `typeof` alone cannot do
across a call boundary:

```ts
function isNonEmptyString(value: unknown): value is string {
  return typeof value === "string" && value.length > 0;
}

if (isNonEmptyString(title)) {
  title.toUpperCase();   // title: string, inside this block
}
```

The `value is Lesson` return type is a promise the compiler takes at face value.
It does not check that your body actually establishes it — a predicate returning
`true` unconditionally compiles fine and is a lie. That is the trade: you get to
extend narrowing, and you own the correctness of the check.

**Assertion functions** narrow for the rest of the scope, with no `if`:

```ts
function assertIsNumber(value: unknown): asserts value is number {
  if (typeof value !== "number") throw new Error("not a number");
}

assertIsNumber(input);
input.toFixed(2);   // input: number, from here on
```

Two rules bite everyone once. The function has to be a `function` declaration or
a variable with an explicit type annotation — TypeScript will not infer an
`asserts` signature. And it must throw when the assertion fails; returning
normally makes the narrowing false for the rest of the function.

**`satisfies`** checks a value against a type *without* replacing its inferred
type:

```ts
type Endpoint = string | number;

const annotated: Record<string, Endpoint> = { host: "localhost", port: 8080 };
annotated.host.trim();   // Error: host is Endpoint, not string
annotated.hsot;          // no error - the index signature accepts anything

const checked = { host: "localhost", port: 8080 } satisfies Record<string, Endpoint>;
checked.host.trim();     // fine: host is string
checked.hsot;            // Error: no such property
```

The annotation says "treat this as `Record<string, Setting>` from now on"; the
`satisfies` says "check it against that, then carry on knowing exactly what it
is". Since TypeScript 4.9 it has been the right default for configuration
objects, palettes, route tables and anything else where you want validation
without amnesia.

The mental model to leave with: **narrow at the boundary, once, and let the rest
of your program work with real types.** Every `as` deeper than that boundary is
a place where you have decided to be right without checking.

## Exercise 1 — a type guard

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Change `isLesson` into a type predicate and implement
it:

- `isLesson({ slug: "01_types", exercises: 4 })` → `true`
- `isLesson({ slug: "01_types", exercises: 4, extra: true })` → `true` — extra
  members are fine
- `isLesson({ slug: "01_types" })` → `false`
- `isLesson({ slug: 1, exercises: 4 })` → `false`
- `isLesson(null)` → `false` — remember `typeof null === "object"`
- `isLesson("01_types")` → `false`

The type gate calls it inside an `if` and checks that `value` narrows to
`Lesson` in the true branch and stays `unknown` in the false one.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 10_guards_assertions ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — an assertion function

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Give `assertIsStringArray` an assertion signature and
implement it:

- `["a", "b"]` and `[]` pass silently
- `["a", 1]` and `"a"` throw an `Error` whose message is exactly
  `expected an array of strings`

After the call, the value must be narrowed to `string[]` for the rest of the
scope — that is what the type gate checks.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 10_guards_assertions ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — `unknown`, not `any`

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Two functions:

1. `parseJson(text)` returns the parsed value typed **`unknown`**. The type gate
   requires that reading a property off the result does not compile.
2. `readTitle(value)` digs a `title` out of an unknown value:
   - `readTitle(parseJson('{"title":"Unions"}'))` → `"Unions"`
   - `readTitle(parseJson('{"title":5}'))` → `null`
   - `readTitle(parseJson("{}"))` → `null`
   - `readTitle(null)` → `null`, `readTitle("Unions")` → `null`

```
uv run dojo test typescript 10_guards_assertions ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — `satisfies`

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Replace the `: Record<string, Setting>` annotation with
a `satisfies` clause, then implement `describeSettings()`:

- it returns `"NIGHTLY x3 (verbose)"` — the label upper-cased, the retry count
  after an `x`, and `" (verbose)"` appended only when `verbose` is true

`settings.label.toUpperCase()` is the tell: it compiles only when `label` has
kept its own type instead of widening to the union.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 10_guards_assertions ex4
```

## Challenge — a validator that collects everything (harder)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Finish the `Validated<T>` union and implement
`validateSubmission(input)`:

- valid input → `{ ok: true, value: { slug, attempts, passed } }`
- `{ slug: 1, attempts: "two", passed: true }` →
  `{ ok: false, errors: ["slug must be a string", "attempts must be a number"] }`
- `{}` → all three messages, in the order `slug`, `attempts`, `passed`
- `"nope"` and `null` → `{ ok: false, errors: ["expected an object"] }`

Honest difficulty note: the logic is straightforward; the discipline is
collecting *every* error rather than returning at the first one, and getting the
messages exactly right. This is also the shape of what `zod` does for you, which
is worth appreciating from the other side once.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 10_guards_assertions challenge
```

# Reading - typescript/10_guards_assertions

The boundary between typed code and untyped data — and the four tools that make
crossing it honest.

## Notes

**`any` vs `unknown` vs `never`, the interview answer.** `any` is the top type
with checking disabled: every operation on it compiles, and the looseness
propagates to anything derived from it. `unknown` is the top type with checking
enabled: every value is assignable *to* it, and it is assignable *from* nothing
until you narrow. `never` is the bottom type: no value has it, it is assignable
to everything, and it appears as the return type of functions that never finish
and as the result of impossible narrowing. A crisp one-liner: "`any` says stop
checking, `unknown` says check later, `never` says this cannot happen."

**A type predicate is a promise the compiler does not verify.** `value is
Lesson` tells the checker what a `true` return means, and nothing validates that
your body actually establishes it. `function isLesson(v: unknown): v is Lesson
{ return true; }` compiles. That is deliberate — the compiler cannot follow
arbitrary runtime logic — and it is why guards deserve unit tests of their own.
TypeScript 5.5 added *inferred* type predicates for simple cases (a function
whose body is just `return typeof x === "string"` may get a predicate
automatically), which is a nice improvement and does not remove the need to
write them explicitly for anything real.

**Assertion signatures have two syntactic traps.** They cannot be inferred, so
`export const assertX = (v: unknown): asserts v is T => {...}` is an error
("Assertions require every name in the call target to be declared with an
explicit type annotation") unless the *variable* carries the annotation. And
the assertion is only sound if the function throws on failure — a function
declared `asserts value is string[]` that quietly returns has told the compiler
a falsehood for the rest of the scope.

**Narrowing has limits that matter in real code.** It does not survive a
closure that might run later (`if (x) { setTimeout(() => x.foo) }` complains,
because `x` could change); it is lost for a mutable object property between the
check and the use (narrow into a `const` local instead); and `Array.prototype
.filter` does not narrow element types unless the predicate is a type guard —
`items.filter((i): i is Lesson => isLesson(i))` is the spelling that does.

**`satisfies` versus annotation versus `as`.** An annotation (`const x: T = ...`)
checks *and* widens the value to `T`. `satisfies` checks and keeps the inferred
type. `as` neither checks nor infers — it asserts, and the only safety rail is
that TypeScript refuses casts between types with no overlap (which people route
around with `as unknown as T`, the two-step cast that should always come with a
comment). Reach for `satisfies` on configuration objects, `as const satisfies T`
when you want literals *and* validation, and `as` only where you genuinely know
something the compiler cannot.

**Where schema libraries fit.** `zod`, `valibot`, `ArkType` and friends let you
declare a schema once and get both a runtime validator and a static type
(`z.infer<typeof schema>`). That is the same idea as this lesson's exercises with
the duplication removed, and it is what most production codebases use at
boundaries. Writing the hand-rolled version once — as you just did — is what
makes the library's value obvious, and what lets you debug it when the inferred
type is not what you expected.

## ex1 — a type guard

The three failing cases in the gate are the three that a careless
implementation gets wrong. `null` passes `typeof value === "object"`, which is
the oldest wart in JavaScript and the reason every object check needs
`&& value !== null`. A missing member and a member of the wrong type both need
`typeof` on the property, not just `"slug" in value` — `in` proves presence, not
type. And a bare string has no properties to check, so the object test has to
come first or the property reads throw.

The `as Record<string, unknown>` step after the object check is worth
justifying, because it looks like the cast this lesson warns about. It is
narrow, local, and true: after `typeof value === "object" && value !== null`, the
value really is an object with unknown-valued properties, and TypeScript's own
narrowing takes `unknown` to `object`, which has no index signature to read
through. The alternative is `"slug" in value &&` chains, which narrow properly
in modern TypeScript but read worse for four fields.

Extra members passing is structural typing being consistent: a guard checks
that what you need is there, not that nothing else is. If you need the stricter
version — no unknown keys — you must check `Object.keys` yourself, which is
exactly what `zod`'s `.strict()` does.

## ex2 — an assertion function

Guards and assertions are the same idea with different control flow. A guard
returns a boolean and the caller branches; an assertion throws and the caller
continues. Use a guard when both outcomes are ordinary (validation, filtering,
routing); use an assertion when the failure means the program is broken
(invariants, internal consistency, "this cannot happen" checks).

The empty-array case is a genuine JavaScript trap.
`[].every(x => typeof x === "string")` is `true` — vacuous truth — and so is
`![].some(...)`. That is correct set theory and occasionally the wrong business
rule, and the gate checks it so you have to decide rather than discover.

One more practical note: `Array.isArray` is the right check, not
`value instanceof Array`, because `instanceof` fails across realms (an array
from an iframe or a Node `vm` context has a different `Array` constructor).
`Array.isArray` was added to the language for exactly that reason.

## ex3 — `unknown`, not `any`

`JSON.parse` returning `any` is a deliberate, and much-criticised, decision in
the standard library. Its designers had no choice — the parsed shape is genuinely
unknown — but `any` means the hole propagates silently. Wrapping it in a function
that declares `unknown` is a one-line fix and a good habit; some codebases go
further and ban raw `JSON.parse` with a lint rule.

`readTitle` is what `unknown` costs, and it is the honest cost. Six lines of
checking replace an invisible assumption. Notice how the checks compose: object,
non-null, property is a string — each one narrows a little further, and only the
final `typeof` lets the value be returned as a `string`. That staircase is what
every validator, hand-written or generated, is doing underneath.

The design question in the hint — who catches `SyntaxError` — is worth having an
opinion about. `parseJson` that never throws (returning `null` or a `Result`) is
easier to compose; `parseJson` that throws matches the standard library and
keeps the error where it happened. Either is fine as long as the name says
which.

## ex4 — `satisfies`

`satisfies` closed a real gap. Before TypeScript 4.9 you had to choose between
annotating (validated, but every member widened to the annotation) and not
annotating (precise, but unchecked). The classic demonstration is a palette:

```ts
const palette = { red: [255, 0, 0], green: "#00ff00" } satisfies Record<string, string | number[]>;
palette.green.toUpperCase();   // green is string
palette.red.length;            // red is number[]
```

Both the constraint and the precision, at once.

The typo probe in the type gate makes the second half of the point. With
`: Record<string, Setting>`, `settings.retires` compiles, because an index
signature accepts every string key — the same lie lesson 03 warned about. With
`satisfies`, the object's own inferred type has exactly three keys, so the typo
is caught. That is the difference between "this value is a lookup table" and
"this value is checked against a lookup table's rules".

Pair it with `as const` when you want both immutability and validation:
`{ ... } as const satisfies Config` is the idiom for route tables, feature
flags and design tokens.

## challenge — a validator that collects everything

Returning at the first error is a guard; collecting all of them is a validator,
and a form that shows one error at a time is the user-facing symptom of getting
that wrong. The `Validated<T>` union is lesson 04's `Result` made generic, and it
composes: `Validated<Submission[]>`, `Validated<T>` returned from a parser, and
so on.

The casts when building the success value are the interesting part. You *have*
proved that `candidate.slug` is a string — but you proved it about a
`Record<string, unknown>`, and narrowing a property of a wide record does not
carry into a freshly-built object literal. Three small type guards would remove
the casts, at the cost of three more functions; a schema library removes them by
generating both halves from one declaration. All three approaches are defensible
and it is worth having written the manual one to know what you are buying.

The message ordering being part of the spec is deliberate. When errors are data
— shown in a UI, compared in tests, logged and grouped — their order and wording
are an API, and "the tests check exact strings" is a fair model of an API
consumer.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Narrowing — using type predicates](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#using-type-predicates) — the official treatment of `value is T`, plus assertion functions.
- [Handbook: `unknown`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#unknown) — why `unknown` exists and how it differs from `any`.
- [TypeScript 4.9 release notes: the `satisfies` operator](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-9.html#the-satisfies-operator) — the palette example and the motivation.
- [TypeScript 5.5 release notes: inferred type predicates](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-5-5.html#inferred-type-predicates) — when the compiler now writes the predicate for you.
- [Zod documentation](https://zod.dev/) — the schema-first version of everything in this lesson, and the standard answer in production code.

continues. Use a guard when both outcomes are ordinary (validation, filtering,
routing); use an assertion when the failure means the program is broken
(invariants, internal consistency, "this cannot happen" checks).

The empty-array case is a genuine JavaScript trap.
`[].every(x => typeof x === "string")` is `true` — vacuous truth — and so is
`![].some(...)`. That is correct set theory and occasionally the wrong business
rule, and the gate checks it so you have to decide rather than discover.

One more practical note: `Array.isArray` is the right check, not
`value instanceof Array`, because `instanceof` fails across realms (an array
from an iframe or a Node `vm` context has a different `Array` constructor).
`Array.isArray` was added to the language for exactly that reason.

## ex3 — `unknown`, not `any`

`JSON.parse` returning `any` is a deliberate, and much-criticised, decision in
the standard library. Its designers had no choice — the parsed shape is genuinely
unknown — but `any` means the hole propagates silently. Wrapping it in a function
that declares `unknown` is a one-line fix and a good habit; some codebases go
further and ban raw `JSON.parse` with a lint rule.

`readTitle` is what `unknown` costs, and it is the honest cost. Six lines of
checking replace an invisible assumption. Notice how the checks compose: object,
non-null, property is a string — each one narrows a little further, and only the
final `typeof` lets the value be returned as a `string`. That staircase is what
every validator, hand-written or generated, is doing underneath.

The design question in the hint — who catches `SyntaxError` — is worth having an
opinion about. `parseJson` that never throws (returning `null` or a `Result`) is
easier to compose; `parseJson` that throws matches the standard library and
keeps the error where it happened. Either is fine as long as the name says
which.

## ex4 — `satisfies`

`satisfies` closed a real gap. Before TypeScript 4.9 you had to choose between
annotating (validated, but every member widened to the annotation) and not
annotating (precise, but unchecked). The classic demonstration is a palette:

```ts
const palette = { red: [255, 0, 0], green: "#00ff00" } satisfies Record<string, string | number[]>;
palette.green.toUpperCase();   // green is string
palette.red.length;            // red is number[]
```

Both the constraint and the precision, at once.

The typo probe in the type gate makes the second half of the point. With
`: Record<string, Setting>`, `settings.retires` compiles, because an index
signature accepts every string key — the same lie lesson 03 warned about. With
`satisfies`, the object's own inferred type has exactly three keys, so the typo
is caught. That is the difference between "this value is a lookup table" and
"this value is checked against a lookup table's rules".

Pair it with `as const` when you want both immutability and validation:
`{ ... } as const satisfies Config` is the idiom for route tables, feature
flags and design tokens.

## challenge — a validator that collects everything

Returning at the first error is a guard; collecting all of them is a validator,
and a form that shows one error at a time is the user-facing symptom of getting
that wrong. The `Validated<T>` union is lesson 04's `Result` made generic, and it
composes: `Validated<Submission[]>`, `Validated<T>` returned from a parser, and
so on.

The casts when building the success value are the interesting part. You *have*
proved that `candidate.slug` is a string — but you proved it about a
`Record<string, unknown>`, and narrowing a property of a wide record does not
carry into a freshly-built object literal. Three small type guards would remove
the casts, at the cost of three more functions; a schema library removes them by
generating both halves from one declaration. All three approaches are defensible
and it is worth having written the manual one to know what you are buying.

The message ordering being part of the spec is deliberate. When errors are data
— shown in a UI, compared in tests, logged and grouped — their order and wording
are an API, and "the tests check exact strings" is a fair model of an API
consumer.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a validator that collects everything (harder)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Finish the `Validated<T>` union and implement
`validateSubmission(input)`:

- valid input → `{ ok: true, value: { slug, attempts, passed } }`
- `{ slug: 1, attempts: "two", passed: true }` →
  `{ ok: false, errors: ["slug must be a string", "attempts must be a number"] }`
- `{}` → all three messages, in the order `slug`, `attempts`, `passed`
- `"nope"` and `null` → `{ ok: false, errors: ["expected an object"] }`

Honest difficulty note: the logic is straightforward; the discipline is
collecting *every* error rather than returning at the first one, and getting the
messages exactly right. This is also the shape of what `zod` does for you, which
is worth appreciating from the other side once.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 10_guards_assertions challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two halves. The type `Validated<T>` needs its failure variant - lesson 04's
`Result` in generic clothing. The function then has to report *every* problem it
found, not stop at the first one, which is the difference between a validator
and a guard.

The error strings and their order are in the README, and the gate compares them
exactly.

## Hint 2

```ts
export type Validated<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; errors: string[] };
```

For the body: reject non-objects up front with the single `expected an object`
error. Otherwise collect into a `string[]`, checking each member in the order
the README lists, and return the failure variant when the array is not empty.

Building the success value needs a few casts - you have proved each member's
type with `typeof`, but you proved it about a `Record<string, unknown>`, and the
compiler does not carry that across into a new object literal.

## Hint 3

Finish the union, then: guard the non-object case, cast to
`Record<string, unknown>`, push one message per bad member, return
`{ ok: false, errors }` if any, otherwise `{ ok: true, value: { ... } }` with
the three members cast to their checked types.

Left to you: whether to write three small type guards and reuse them instead of
three inline `typeof` checks. That version is longer here and much shorter by
the time there are ten fields - which is exactly the moment most teams reach
for `zod` and let a library own this code.

## Hint 1

Two halves. The type `Validated<T>` needs its failure variant - lesson 04's
`Result` in generic clothing. The function then has to report *every* problem it
found, not stop at the first one, which is the difference between a validator
and a guard.

The error strings and their order are in the README, and the gate compares them
exactly.

## Hint 2

```ts
export type Validated<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; errors: string[] };
```

For the body: reject non-objects up front with the single `expected an object`
error. Otherwise collect into a `string[]`, checking each member in the order
the README lists, and return the failure variant when the array is not empty.

Building the success value needs a few casts - you have proved each member's
type with `typeof`, but you proved it about a `Record<string, unknown>`, and the
compiler does not carry that across into a new object literal.

## Hint 3

Finish the union, then: guard the non-object case, cast to
`Record<string, unknown>`, push one message per bad member, return
`{ ok: false, errors }` if any, otherwise `{ ok: true, value: { ... } }` with
the three members cast to their checked types.

Left to you: whether to write three small type guards and reuse them instead of
three inline `typeof` checks. That version is longer here and much shorter by
the time there are ten fields - which is exactly the moment most teams reach
for `zod` and let a library own this code.

## Exercise 1 — a type guard

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Change `isLesson` into a type predicate and implement
it:

- `isLesson({ slug: "01_types", exercises: 4 })` → `true`
- `isLesson({ slug: "01_types", exercises: 4, extra: true })` → `true` — extra
  members are fine
- `isLesson({ slug: "01_types" })` → `false`
- `isLesson({ slug: 1, exercises: 4 })` → `false`
- `isLesson(null)` → `false` — remember `typeof null === "object"`
- `isLesson("01_types")` → `false`

The type gate calls it inside an `if` and checks that `value` narrows to
`Lesson` in the true branch and stays `unknown` in the false one.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The body you are about to write is ordinary JavaScript: is this an object, is it
not null, does it have a string here and a number there. The interesting part is
the *return type*, which has to tell the compiler what a `true` answer means.

Run the type gate first and read what it says about `value` inside the `if`.

## Hint 2

A type predicate replaces `boolean` in the return position:

```ts
function isLesson(value: unknown): value is Lesson { ... }
```

Callers who write `if (isLesson(x))` now get `x` narrowed to `Lesson` inside the
block - which is narrowing that survives a function boundary, something
`typeof` alone cannot do.

Inside the body you still have an `unknown`, so check `typeof value === "object"`
and `value !== null` before you touch any property. Casting to
`Record<string, unknown>` after those two checks is the conventional way to
read properties without reaching for `any`.

## Hint 3

Signature: `isLesson(value: unknown): value is Lesson`. Body: reject non-objects
and `null`, then check `typeof candidate.slug === "string"` and
`typeof candidate.exercises === "number"`.

Left to you: whether extra properties should disqualify a value. This version
says no - it checks that the required members are present and well-typed and
ignores the rest, which is exactly what structural typing means.
