exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`parseJson` is one line. The whole exercise is which type it declares, and the
type gate is explicit: reading a property off the result must *not* compile.

`readTitle` is then the price you pay for that honesty - and the point is that
it is a price worth paying, because that is where the checking happens.

## Hint 2

`JSON.parse` returns `any`, which spreads: every property of an `any` is `any`,
and nothing downstream is checked. Declaring the return type as `unknown`
converts that hole into a question the caller has to answer.

For `readTitle`, work down the value one check at a time: is it an object, is it
non-null, is `title` a string. Anything else is `null`.

## Hint 3

`parseJson` returns `JSON.parse(text)` with `unknown` as its declared return
type. `readTitle` rejects non-objects and `null`, reads `title` through a
`Record<string, unknown>` cast, and returns it only when `typeof` says it is a
string.

Left to you: whether `parseJson` should catch a `SyntaxError` from malformed
input. The gate never passes malformed text - but every real caller will, and
"who catches this" is a design decision worth making on purpose.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`parseJson` is one line. The whole exercise is which type it declares, and the
type gate is explicit: reading a property off the result must *not* compile.

`readTitle` is then the price you pay for that honesty - and the point is that
it is a price worth paying, because that is where the checking happens.

## Hint 2

`JSON.parse` returns `any`, which spreads: every property of an `any` is `any`,
and nothing downstream is checked. Declaring the return type as `unknown`
converts that hole into a question the caller has to answer.

For `readTitle`, work down the value one check at a time: is it an object, is it
non-null, is `title` a string. Anything else is `null`.

## Hint 3

`parseJson` returns `JSON.parse(text)` with `unknown` as its declared return
type. `readTitle` rejects non-objects and `null`, reads `title` through a
`Record<string, unknown>` cast, and returns it only when `typeof` says it is a
string.

Left to you: whether `parseJson` should catch a `SyntaxError` from malformed
input. The gate never passes malformed text - but every real caller will, and
"who catches this" is a design decision worth making on purpose.

## Hint 1

Hover `settings.label` as the file stands. It is `Setting` - the whole union -
because the annotation told the compiler what the object *is allowed to be* and
it forgot what it actually saw. That is why `.toUpperCase()` does not compile.

There is an operator that checks the same constraint without the forgetting.

## Hint 2

`satisfies` goes after the expression, where you would otherwise have annotated
the variable:

```ts
const config = { host: "localhost", port: 80 } satisfies Record<string, string | number>;
config.host.trim();   // host is string, and the constraint was still checked
```

Delete the `: Record<string, Setting>` annotation and add
`satisfies Record<string, Setting>` after the closing brace. Then each member
keeps the type it was written with, and a member that violated the constraint
would still be an error.

## Hint 3

Swap the annotation for `satisfies`, then build the string: the label
upper-cased, a space, `x` and the retry count, and ` (verbose)` appended only
when the flag is on. The README has the exact expected output.

Left to you: whether to keep the `Setting` alias at all. Try
`satisfies Record<string, unknown>` and see which of the type gate's assertions
still pass - the constraint you choose decides what you are protected from.

lessons.briefing:
# 11 — Async and modules

This is the last teaching lesson of the track, and it covers the two places
where your typed code meets the outside world: **time**, in the form of
promises and async iteration, and **module boundaries**, where somebody else's
JavaScript arrives with no types at all.

Neither topic is hard in the way lesson 09 was hard. What makes them worth a
lesson is that both are where sloppiness is invisible. `Promise<User>` and
`User` look almost the same in a signature and behave completely differently at
a call site. Two `await`s in a row look almost the same as `Promise.all` and are
twice as slow. A `.d.ts` file you wrote is a *claim* about code the compiler
never sees — and nothing will tell you when it stops being true.

The challenge is the track capstone: a typed, concurrency-limited task runner
that pulls in generics, discriminated unions, `unknown` in a `catch`, and
everything you know about promises.

## Concept — promises are a type, and so is a module

**An `async` function always returns a promise**, so its return type is always
`Promise<something>`:

```ts
async function loadUser(id: string): Promise<User> {
  const response = await fetch(`/users/${id}`);
  return response.json() as User;   // ...and lesson 10 has opinions about that cast
}
```

Inside the body you `return` a plain `User` and TypeScript wraps it. A `throw`
inside an async function becomes a *rejection* rather than a synchronous
exception — the same value, delivered down a different path, and the reason
`try`/`catch` around a call without `await` catches nothing.

`Awaited<T>` (lesson 08) unwraps the promise again, and `await` does it at
runtime.

**Concurrency is a typing question too.** These two are not the same program:

```ts
const a = await loadA();       // sequential: b starts when a is done
const b = await loadB();

const [a, b] = await Promise.all([loadA(), loadB()]);   // concurrent
```

`Promise.all` over a *tuple* of promises resolves to a tuple of their values, in
order, with each element's type preserved — a small masterpiece of type
modelling that you get for free. Its siblings are worth knowing by name:
`allSettled` (never rejects; gives you a per-item status), `race` (first to
settle, win or lose), `any` (first to *fulfil*).

**Async iteration** is for sequences that arrive over time — paginated APIs,
streams, queues:

```ts
async function* ticks(): AsyncGenerator<number> {
  yield 1;
  yield 2;
}

for await (const tick of ticks()) {
  console.log(tick);
}
```

`AsyncGenerator<T>` is what an `async function*` returns; `AsyncIterable<T>` is
the wider type to *accept*, because everything iterable-over-time is one.

**Modules and declaration files.** Every file with a top-level `import` or
`export` is a module with its own scope. When you import a JavaScript file that
has no types, TypeScript looks for a **declaration file** beside it —
`legacy.js` → `legacy.d.ts` — and uses that as the truth:

```ts

export declare function slugify(title: string): string;
export declare const LEGACY_VERSION: string;
```

That is exactly what every `@types/*` package on npm is: a pile of `.d.ts` files
describing somebody else's JavaScript. Nothing verifies them against the
implementation — a `.d.ts` is a promise made by whoever wrote it.

Two smaller module details you will meet immediately. `import type { X } from
"./x"` imports a type and guarantees the import disappears at build time, which
matters under `isolatedModules` (on in this course) and avoids accidental
runtime dependencies. And module *resolution* — how `./legacy.js` becomes a file
on disk — is controlled by `moduleResolution`, set to `"bundler"` here, which is
why extensions are optional in your imports and why the `.js` extension in a
TypeScript import is not a typo but the ESM convention.

## Exercise 1 — a promise in the signature

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Make `loadLesson` asynchronous:

- `await loadLesson("04_unions_narrowing")` → `{ slug: "04_unions_narrowing",
  title: "Unions" }`
- `loadLesson("99_nope")` **rejects** with an `Error` whose message is exactly
  `unknown lesson: 99_nope`

The type gate checks the declared return type is `Promise<Lesson>` and that a
number is still not a slug.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 11_async_and_modules ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — two tasks, one wait

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Make `bothOf` generic and concurrent:

```ts
const [slow, fast] = await bothOf(
  async () => { await delay(30); return "slow-value"; },
  async () => { await delay(1);  return 42; },
);
// ["slow-value", 42] - argument order, not completion order
```

The gate records which task *finished* first, so an implementation that awaits
the first task before starting the second is detected and fails. The resolved
type must be the tuple `[A, B]`, not `unknown[]`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 11_async_and_modules ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — async iteration

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Implement both halves:

- `pages(items, size)` is an async generator yielding chunks:
  `collect(pages(["a", "b", "c"], 2))` → `[["a", "b"], ["c"]]`
- an empty input yields nothing; a size bigger than the input yields one short
  page; a size below 1 yields nothing at all rather than looping forever
- `collect(source)` drains **any** async sequence into an array, keeping its
  element type

```
uv run dojo test typescript 11_async_and_modules ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — describe an untyped module

This exercise has **two** files to edit.

`ex4/legacy.js` is plain JavaScript that already works — do not change it. Open
it and read what it exports. Then:

1. Edit `ex4/legacy.d.ts` so it describes *both* exports. One is already there;
   the other is missing.
2. Edit `ex4/solution.ts` to import the missing one and implement
   `lessonSlug(index, title)`:
   - `lessonSlug(4, "Unions and Narrowing")` → `"04_unions_and_narrowing"`
   - `lessonSlug(11, "Async & Modules!")` → `"11_async_modules"`
   - `version` re-exports `LEGACY_VERSION`, which is `"1.4.2"`

The index is padded to two digits; the title is passed through `slugify`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 11_async_and_modules ex4
```

## Challenge — the capstone: a typed task runner (hard)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Finish `TaskResult<T>` and implement
`runTasks(tasks, limit)`:

1. Every task is a `() => Promise<T>`. The result array has **one entry per
   task, in input order**, regardless of which finished first.
2. Never more than `limit` tasks in flight at once — and it must genuinely run
   them in parallel, not one at a time.
3. A task that rejects becomes `{ ok: false, error: <message> }` and does **not**
   stop the others. Use the `Error`'s `message`; a thrown non-`Error` is
   stringified.
4. A `limit` below 1 (or not a whole number) rejects with an `Error` whose
   message is exactly `runTasks: limit must be at least 1`.

Honest difficulty note: this is the hardest exercise in the track. Rules 1 and 2
interact — the trick is a small pool of workers each pulling the next index — and
rule 3 needs lesson 02's `unknown` catch handling. Take the hints in order; they
are written for exactly this.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 11_async_and_modules challenge
```

# Reading - typescript/11_async_and_modules

Promises as types, concurrency as a design decision, and what a declaration
file actually promises.

## Notes

**`Promise<T>` is an ordinary generic type, and `async` is sugar.** An `async`
function is a function that returns a promise; `await` is sugar over `.then`.
The type-level consequences are worth stating precisely: the declared return
type of an `async` function must be `Promise<something>` (TypeScript enforces
it), a `return x` inside is implicitly wrapped, and a `throw` becomes a
rejection. That last point is why `try { doAsyncThing() } catch {}` without an
`await` catches nothing at all — the rejection happens after the `try` block has
already finished — and why an unhandled rejection crashes a modern Node process.

**Forgetting `await` is the most common async type error, and annotations catch
it.** With an annotated return type, returning a `Promise<User>` where a `User`
was promised is a compile error. Without one, inference happily makes your
function return `Promise<Promise<User>>` — well, actually it flattens, which is
worse, because the mistake surfaces somewhere else entirely. The
`@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` rule exists because the type system
alone cannot see a promise nobody awaited.

**Concurrency helpers, and when each is right.** `Promise.all` fails fast — one
rejection rejects the whole thing, and the other tasks keep running unobserved.
`Promise.allSettled` never rejects and gives you `{status: "fulfilled", value}`
or `{status: "rejected", reason}` per item; it is the right default when partial
success is meaningful. `Promise.race` settles with the first result of any kind
(the timeout idiom). `Promise.any` settles with the first *success* and rejects
with an `AggregateError` if all fail. TypeScript models all four precisely,
including `all`'s tuple inference, which is the most impressive bit of typing in
the standard library.

**Unbounded concurrency is a real production failure mode.** `await
Promise.all(items.map(fetchOne))` with 10,000 items opens 10,000 sockets, and
every rate limiter, connection pool and file-descriptor table you own will
notice. That is why the capstone exists: a pool of `limit` workers is the
standard shape, and it is what `p-limit` and every job queue implement under the
hood.

**Modules: what makes a file a module.** Any file with a top-level `import` or
`export` is a module with its own scope; a file with neither is a *script*
whose declarations go into the global scope, which is a surprisingly common
cause of "duplicate identifier" errors. This course sets
`moduleDetection: "force"`, which treats every file as a module regardless.

**`import type` and `verbatimModuleSyntax`.** `import type { X } from "./x"`
states that the import is types-only and must vanish from the emitted
JavaScript. With `isolatedModules` on — as it is here, and as every bundler
requires — the compiler cannot always tell whether an imported name is a type or
a value, so being explicit avoids both accidental runtime imports and confusing
build errors.

**Declaration files are unverified promises.** A `.d.ts` describes shapes and
emits nothing. TypeScript finds a sibling `legacy.d.ts` for `./legacy.js`
automatically; for a package it looks at `types` in `package.json`, then at
`@types/<name>` from DefinitelyTyped. Nothing checks a declaration against the
implementation it describes, which is why a wrong `@types` package produces
errors that make no sense — and why `skipLibCheck: true` (on in this course) is
almost universal: it skips typechecking of `.d.ts` files, trading a class of
detection for a large amount of build time.

## ex1 — a promise in the signature

The change is small and the mental shift is not. `Lesson` and `Promise<Lesson>`
are unrelated types, and a caller who forgets `await` gets a promise where they
expected an object — usually surfacing as `undefined` when they read a property,
because a promise has no `.title`.

Rejecting rather than resolving with `null` is the design decision here, and it
has a real trade-off. Rejection keeps the happy-path type clean (`Promise<Lesson>`
rather than `Promise<Lesson | null>`) and moves the failure into `try`/`catch`,
where it is easy to forget. Resolving with `null` puts the failure in the type,
where the compiler will not let you forget, at the cost of a narrowing step at
every call site. Lesson 10's `Validated<T>` is the third option — a `Result` in a
promise — which is what most functional-leaning TypeScript codebases settle on.

The gate's `await expect(...).rejects.toThrow(...)` is worth noting as a testing
skill: without the leading `await`, the assertion returns a promise nobody
watches and the test passes whatever happens. Vitest warns about it; many test
suites contain one anyway.

## ex2 — two tasks, one wait

`Promise.all([a(), b()])` typed as `Promise<[A, B]>` is a genuinely clever piece
of the standard library's typing: the overload for a tuple preserves each
element's type positionally. Compare with `Promise.all(items.map(...))`, which
gives you `Promise<T[]>` because an array's element type is homogeneous. Both
are right; knowing which shape you passed explains the type you got back.

The concurrency test is the interesting half, and it is why the exercise takes
*thunks* (`() => Promise<A>`) rather than promises. A promise is already
running — creating it starts the work — so a function taking two promises cannot
sequence them even if it tries. Taking functions puts the decision inside your
implementation, which is exactly what real APIs do when they need to control
scheduling (retry helpers, queues, transaction wrappers).

This is a standard interview question in the form "what is wrong with this
code?", shown as two consecutive awaits of independent calls. The answer to
give: they are independent, so they should be started together with
`Promise.all`; the version as written doubles the latency for no reason.

## ex3 — async iteration

Async generators are the ergonomic way to model "a sequence that arrives over
time": paginated APIs, log tails, database cursors, message queues. The consumer
writes an ordinary `for await` loop and never sees the paging.

`collect(source: AsyncIterable<T>)` rather than `AsyncGenerator<T>` is the
"weakest thing you need" rule from lesson 01, one last time. `AsyncIterable<T>`
is satisfied by generators, by streams (Node's `Readable` is async-iterable), and
by anything with a `[Symbol.asyncIterator]` method. Asking for the generator
type would exclude all of those for no benefit.

The `size < 1` guard is the same degenerate case as lesson 01's `splitEvery`,
with a nastier failure mode: `i += 0` inside a generator is an infinite loop that
yields forever, so a consumer's `for await` never ends and the process hangs
rather than crashing. Infinite generators are a legitimate pattern — which is
exactly why nothing warns you.

## ex4 — describe an untyped module

Writing a `.d.ts` by hand is a rite of passage. The key insight is that it is
*only* a description: no bodies, no emit, no verification. Your
`export declare function slugify(title: string): string` is exactly as true as
you made it, and the compiler will happily let you describe a function that does
not exist, or give it parameters it never had.

That is what the hint's closing question is about. `slugify` in `legacy.js`
starts with `String(title)`, so it accepts numbers, booleans and `null` quite
happily. Declaring `title: string` is therefore *narrower* than the truth — and
that is usually the right call: a declaration file is where you get to impose
the contract you wish the module had, as long as you never make it *wider* than
reality. Widening (declaring a parameter `any`, or claiming a function returns
`User` when it can return `undefined`) is how a `.d.ts` becomes a lie that
crashes at runtime.

This is also the whole story of DefinitelyTyped: thousands of hand-written
descriptions of other people's JavaScript, unverified, kept honest by usage and
bug reports. When `@types/something` disagrees with reality, now you know
exactly what happened.

## challenge — the capstone

The worker-pool shape is the standard answer to bounded concurrency, and it is
worth being able to write from memory. Three properties fall out of it:
ordering, because each worker writes to `results[index]` rather than pushing;
the bound, because there are exactly `limit` workers; and full utilisation,
because a worker takes the next index the moment it is free rather than waiting
for a batch to complete. The naive "chunk the array into groups of `limit` and
`Promise.all` each chunk" alternative satisfies the bound but idles whenever one
task in a chunk is slower than the rest — a good thing to be able to compare in
an interview.

The error handling is lesson 02 and lesson 10 combined. `catch (error)` gives
you `unknown` under `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, and `error instanceof Error ?
error.message : String(error)` is the standard, honest narrowing —
because JavaScript really can `throw "just a string"`, and a library you depend
on eventually will.

Turning rejections into values rather than letting them propagate is the same
decision as lesson 04's `Result`, made at the scheduling layer. It means the
caller gets a complete picture of every task instead of the first failure, which
is what you want for a batch job and not what you want for a transaction. Say
which one you are building, and the design follows.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Everyday Types — `Promise` and async](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html) — plus [TypeScript 3.6's async iteration notes](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-6.html) for generators.
- [MDN: `Promise.all`, `allSettled`, `race`, `any`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise) — the four combinators and exactly how each settles.
- [MDN: `for await...of`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/for-await...of) — async iteration from the consumer's side.
- [Handbook: Declaration Files — Introduction](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/declaration-files/introduction.html) — how `.d.ts` files are found, written and published, including `@types` packages.
- [Handbook: Modules — module resolution](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/modules/theory.html) — what `moduleResolution: "bundler"` actually does, and why the `.js` extension appears in TypeScript imports.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the capstone: a typed task runner (hard)

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Finish `TaskResult<T>` and implement
`runTasks(tasks, limit)`:

1. Every task is a `() => Promise<T>`. The result array has **one entry per
   task, in input order**, regardless of which finished first.
2. Never more than `limit` tasks in flight at once — and it must genuinely run
   them in parallel, not one at a time.
3. A task that rejects becomes `{ ok: false, error: <message> }` and does **not**
   stop the others. Use the `Error`'s `message`; a thrown non-`Error` is
   stringified.
4. A `limit` below 1 (or not a whole number) rejects with an `Error` whose
   message is exactly `runTasks: limit must be at least 1`.

Honest difficulty note: this is the hardest exercise in the track. Rules 1 and 2
interact — the trick is a small pool of workers each pulling the next index — and
rule 3 needs lesson 02's `unknown` catch handling. Take the hints in order; they
are written for exactly this.

```
uv run dojo test typescript 11_async_and_modules challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is the capstone, so it uses most of the track: a generic type parameter, a
discriminated union for the per-task outcome, `unknown` in a `catch`, and
promises that must overlap without all starting at once.

Read the four rules in the README and write them down as four separate
problems. Solve "results in input order" and "never more than `limit` running"
last - they are the two that interact.

## Hint 2

The shape that satisfies both ordering and the limit is a small worker pool:

```ts
const results: TaskResult<T>[] = new Array(tasks.length);
let next = 0;

async function worker() {
  while (next < tasks.length) {
    const index = next++;
    // run tasks[index], store into results[index]
  }
}

await Promise.all(workers);   // `limit` workers, each pulling the next index
```

Because each worker writes to `results[index]`, order is preserved no matter
which finishes first. Because there are only `limit` workers, no more than
`limit` tasks are ever in flight.

Under `useUnknownInCatchVariables` the caught value is `unknown`, so narrow with
`instanceof Error` before reading `.message`.

## Hint 3

Finish `TaskResult<T>` with its failure variant, guard the bad `limit` with the
exact message from the README, build a `results` array the length of `tasks`,
and start `Math.min(limit, tasks.length)` workers that each loop while indexes
remain. Wrap each task call in `try`/`catch` and store the right variant.

Left to you: what a *rejected* task should do to the others. This design lets
them all finish - the opposite of `Promise.all`'s fail-fast. Deciding which
behaviour a caller wants, and being able to say why, is most of what this
capstone is testing.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This is the capstone, so it uses most of the track: a generic type parameter, a
discriminated union for the per-task outcome, `unknown` in a `catch`, and
promises that must overlap without all starting at once.

Read the four rules in the README and write them down as four separate
problems. Solve "results in input order" and "never more than `limit` running"
last - they are the two that interact.

## Hint 2

The shape that satisfies both ordering and the limit is a small worker pool:

```ts
const results: TaskResult<T>[] = new Array(tasks.length);
let next = 0;

async function worker() {
  while (next < tasks.length) {
    const index = next++;
    // run tasks[index], store into results[index]
  }
}

await Promise.all(workers);   // `limit` workers, each pulling the next index
```

Because each worker writes to `results[index]`, order is preserved no matter
which finishes first. Because there are only `limit` workers, no more than
`limit` tasks are ever in flight.

Under `useUnknownInCatchVariables` the caught value is `unknown`, so narrow with
`instanceof Error` before reading `.message`.

## Hint 3

Finish `TaskResult<T>` with its failure variant, guard the bad `limit` with the
exact message from the README, build a `results` array the length of `tasks`,
and start `Math.min(limit, tasks.length)` workers that each loop while indexes
remain. Wrap each task call in `try`/`catch` and store the right variant.

Left to you: what a *rejected* task should do to the others. This design lets
them all finish - the opposite of `Promise.all`'s fail-fast. Deciding which
behaviour a caller wants, and being able to say why, is most of what this
capstone is testing.

## Exercise 2 — two tasks, one wait

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. Make `bothOf` generic and concurrent:

```ts
const [slow, fast] = await bothOf(
  async () => { await delay(30); return "slow-value"; },
  async () => { await delay(1);  return 42; },
);
// ["slow-value", 42] - argument order, not completion order
```

The gate records which task *finished* first, so an implementation that awaits
the first task before starting the second is detected and fails. The resolved
type must be the tuple `[A, B]`, not `unknown[]`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two independent type parameters, one for each task, and a tuple out - the same
shape as lesson 06's `zipPairs`, but with promises in the middle.

The runtime half is the part people get wrong in interviews: starting the second
task only after the first has finished is *sequential*, and the gate can see the
difference.

## Hint 2

```ts
const [first, second] = await Promise.all([taskA(), taskB()]);
```

`Promise.all` on a tuple of promises resolves to a tuple of their values, in
order, and TypeScript models that precisely - which is why the return type can
be `Promise<[A, B]>` with no cast.

Both calls happen on the same line, so both are in flight before either is
awaited. `await a(); await b();` does not do that.

## Hint 3

Signature: `bothOf<A, B>(a: () => Promise<A>, b: () => Promise<B>): Promise<[A, B]>`.
Body: `return Promise.all([a(), b()]);` inside an `async` function.

Left to you: what should happen when one of the two rejects. `Promise.all`
rejects as soon as any input does, and the other task keeps running with nobody
listening. `Promise.allSettled` is the alternative - knowing which one you want
is the actual skill.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two independent type parameters, one for each task, and a tuple out - the same
shape as lesson 06's `zipPairs`, but with promises in the middle.

The runtime half is the part people get wrong in interviews: starting the second
task only after the first has finished is *sequential*, and the gate can see the
difference.

## Hint 2

```ts
const [first, second] = await Promise.all([taskA(), taskB()]);
```

`Promise.all` on a tuple of promises resolves to a tuple of their values, in
order, and TypeScript models that precisely - which is why the return type can
be `Promise<[A, B]>` with no cast.

Both calls happen on the same line, so both are in flight before either is
awaited. `await a(); await b();` does not do that.

## Hint 3

Signature: `bothOf<A, B>(a: () => Promise<A>, b: () => Promise<B>): Promise<[A, B]>`.
Body: `return Promise.all([a(), b()]);` inside an `async` function.

Left to you: what should happen when one of the two rejects. `Promise.all`
rejects as soon as any input does, and the other task keeps running with nobody
listening. `Promise.allSettled` is the alternative - knowing which one you want
is the actual skill.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`pages` is a generator: it hands back one chunk at a time instead of building
the whole list. `collect` is the opposite - it drains an async sequence into an
array, and it should work for *any* element type, not just this one.

The chunking rule is lesson 01's `splitEvery` with one difference in the
degenerate case; the README says which.

## Hint 2

An async generator is `async function*`, and it produces values with `yield`:

```ts
export async function* numbers(): AsyncGenerator<number> {
  yield 1;
  yield 2;
}
```

Consuming one uses `for await`:

```ts
for await (const value of source) { ... }
```

`collect` needs a type parameter so the array it returns holds the source's
element type, and `AsyncIterable<T>` is the widest thing you can ask for - every
async generator is one.

## Hint 3

`pages` returns early for a size below 1, then loops `i += size` yielding
`items.slice(i, i + size)`. `collect<T>(source: AsyncIterable<T>): Promise<T[]>`
pushes each value from a `for await` loop into a `T[]` and returns it.

Left to you: why `collect` takes `AsyncIterable<T>` rather than
`AsyncGenerator<T>`. Try the narrower one and think about which callers you have
just excluded - it is the same "ask for the weakest thing you need" rule from
lesson 01.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`pages` is a generator: it hands back one chunk at a time instead of building
the whole list. `collect` is the opposite - it drains an async sequence into an
array, and it should work for *any* element type, not just this one.

The chunking rule is lesson 01's `splitEvery` with one difference in the
degenerate case; the README says which.

## Hint 2

An async generator is `async function*`, and it produces values with `yield`:

```ts
export async function* numbers(): AsyncGenerator<number> {
  yield 1;
  yield 2;
}
```

Consuming one uses `for await`:

```ts
for await (const value of source) { ... }
```

`collect` needs a type parameter so the array it returns holds the source's
element type, and `AsyncIterable<T>` is the widest thing you can ask for - every
async generator is one.

## Hint 3

`pages` returns early for a size below 1, then loops `i += size` yielding
`items.slice(i, i + size)`. `collect<T>(source: AsyncIterable<T>): Promise<T[]>`
pushes each value from a `for await` loop into a `T[]` and returns it.

Left to you: why `collect` takes `AsyncIterable<T>` rather than
`AsyncGenerator<T>`. Try the narrower one and think about which callers you have
just excluded - it is the same "ask for the weakest thing you need" rule from
lesson 01.

lessons.briefing:
# d01 - Annotations and inference (drill set)

Eight problems that drill what you write down and what you let the compiler
work out for itself - lesson **01_primitives_and_inference**; redo that lesson
first if this set feels like guessing. Half of these ship with a deliberately
wrong or missing return annotation: fixing the type is part of the exercise,
and the type gate is what marks it.

## ex1 - format a reading

`formatReading(station, celsius)` returns `"<station> <celsius>C"` with the
temperature at exactly one decimal place, rounded.

- `formatReading("roof", 21.53)` -> `"roof 21.5C"`
- `formatReading("roof", 21)` -> `"roof 21.0C"`
- `formatReading("cellar", -3.24)` -> `"cellar -3.2C"`

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d01_annotations_inference ex1
```

## ex2 - a clock label

`clockLabel(seconds)` returns `mm:ss`, each half padded to two digits. Minutes
are **not** capped at 59. A fractional input never rounds up into a second that
has not happened; a negative input is clamped to zero.

- `clockLabel(65)` -> `"01:05"`, `clockLabel(3600)` -> `"60:00"`
- `clockLabel(7325)` -> `"122:05"`, `clockLabel(90.9)` -> `"01:30"`
- `clockLabel(-10)` -> `"00:00"`

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d01_annotations_inference ex2
```

## ex3 - split a station id

`splitStationId(id)` returns the tuple `[site: string, index: number]`, split at
the **last** dash. If there is no dash, or the tail after it is not made only of
digits, the whole id is the site and the index is `0`.

- `"roof-3"` -> `["roof", 3]`, `"north-wall-12"` -> `["north-wall", 12]`
- `"roof"` -> `["roof", 0]`, `"roof-x"` -> `["roof-x", 0]`, `"roof-"` -> `["roof-", 0]`

The shipped return annotation is `string[]`. That is the bug.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d01_annotations_inference ex3
```

## ex4 - the highest readings, without touching the input

`topReadings(values, count)` returns the `count` largest values, largest first,
as a **readonly** array. `count <= 0` returns nothing; a count larger than the
input returns everything. The caller's array must come back unmodified.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. The shipped return annotation hands back a mutable
array - tighten it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d01_annotations_inference ex4
```

## ex5 - one object, three numbers

`summarise(values)` returns `{ count, mean, spread }`, where `spread` is the
largest value minus the smallest. An empty list returns all three as `0`.

- `[2, 4, 9]` -> `{ count: 3, mean: 5, spread: 7 }`
- `[4]` -> `{ count: 1, mean: 4, spread: 0 }`
- `[]` -> `{ count: 0, mean: 0, spread: 0 }`

The stub has **no** return annotation at all. Write it.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d01_annotations_inference ex5
```

## ex6 - parse one CSV row

`parseCsvRow(row)` returns `[station: string, celsius: number, ok: boolean]`.
Fields are separated by commas and trimmed. A temperature that is missing,
empty or not a finite number becomes `0`; the flag is `true` only for the exact
lowercase text `true`.

- `"roof,warm,true"` -> `["roof", 0, true]`
- `"roof,21,TRUE"` -> `["roof", 21, false]`

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. The shipped annotation is `(string | number | boolean)[]`,
which is close and still wrong.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d01_annotations_inference ex6
```

## ex7 - a moving average

`movingAverage(values, window)` returns the average of every **full** window of
`window` consecutive values, left to right. A window that is not a positive
integer, or is longer than the input, produces `[]`.

- `([1, 2, 3, 4], 2)` -> `[1.5, 2.5, 3.5]`
- `([1, 2, 3], 3)` -> `[2]`, `([1, 2, 3], 4)` -> `[]`
- `([1, 2, 3], 2.5)` -> `[]`

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d01_annotations_inference ex7
```

## ex8 - run-length pairs

`runLengths(values)` collapses each run of consecutive equal values into a
`[value: number, count: number]` pair, in input order. Runs are consecutive:
this is not a tally.

- `[1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3]` -> `[[1, 2], [2, 1], [3, 3]]`
- `[1, 2, 1]` -> `[[1, 1], [2, 1], [1, 1]]`
- `[]` -> `[]`


# Reading - typescript/d01_annotations_inference

The debrief for the annotation drills: what each problem was really asking,
the mistake that costs the point, and the one sentence of reasoning behind the
model answer.

## Notes

**The skill this set drills is deciding where a type has to be written down.**
TypeScript infers a great deal - the type of a `const`, the return type of a
function whose body it can see, the parameter of a callback in a position it
already knows. It cannot infer what you never told it: the parameters of an
exported function, the shape you *intend* to return when several shapes would
compile, or the difference between an array and a tuple. Those are the three
places these eight problems keep poking at.

**Every wrong annotation in this set is a plausible one.** `string[]` really
does describe `["roof", "3"]`; `(string | number | boolean)[]` really does
describe a row of mixed cells; `number[]` really does describe the array you
just built. They are all true and all useless, because they throw away the
length, the position, or the promise not to mutate. The habit worth building
is to ask "what does this type *forbid*?" - a type that forbids nothing is
documentation, not a check.

**Tuples are the recurring shape here** - `[site, index]`, `[station, celsius,
ok]`, `[value, count]` - because a fixed-length, position-typed result is
exactly the thing an array type cannot express. The labels (`[site: string,
index: number]`) are erased at runtime and exist only so your editor and your
reader know which slot is which. Take them; they cost nothing.

**And `readonly` is an annotation about permission, not about storage.**
`readonly number[]` on a parameter is a promise you will not sort, push or
splice the caller's data; on a return type it is the same promise back to
them. Nothing is frozen at runtime - `Object.freeze` is a different tool - so
the value of `readonly` is entirely in the errors it produces at compile time.

## ex1 - format a reading

What this was testing: whether you annotate both parameters and the return
type without being reminded, and whether you know that `toFixed` produces a
*string* with a fixed number of decimals while `Math.round` produces a number
that silently drops trailing zeroes.

The classic mistake is `Math.round(celsius * 10) / 10`, which turns `21` into
`21` rather than `"21.0"` and makes the third assertion fail for a reason that
looks like a rounding bug and is really a formatting one.

The model answer is one template literal: the string work belongs to
`toFixed(1)`, and the function's only job is to glue two pieces together.

## ex2 - a clock label

What this was testing: input sanitising before arithmetic. Three inputs are
hostile - a negative, a fraction, and anything at or above an hour - and each
one breaks a different naive implementation.

The classic mistake is capping minutes with `% 60`, which is what `Date` and
most clock helpers do, and which turns 3600 seconds into `00:00`. The prompt
says minutes are not capped, and reading the prompt is part of the drill.

The model answer clamps and floors once at the top (`Math.max(0,
Math.floor(seconds))`) so that everything after it is ordinary integer
arithmetic, and pads with `String(n).padStart(2, "0")` rather than with a
hand-rolled `n < 10 ? "0" + n : n`.

## ex3 - split a station id

What this was testing: the difference between an array type and a tuple type.
`string[]` compiles happily for `["roof", 3]`? No - and that is the point: the
moment the second slot is a number, `string[]` stops being true at all, and the
compiler will not let you return it.

The classic mistake is `id.split("-")`, which is wrong twice: it splits at the
*first* dash, so `"north-wall-12"` comes back in three pieces, and it produces
strings, so the index is `"12"` rather than `12`.

The model answer finds `lastIndexOf("-")`, validates that everything after it
is digits, and falls back to `[id, 0]` in both failure cases - because a site
name is allowed to contain a dash and an index is not allowed to contain a
letter.

## ex4 - the highest readings, without touching the input

What this was testing: `readonly` in both directions, plus the oldest trap in
JavaScript arrays. `Array.prototype.sort` mutates the array it is called on and
returns that same array, so sorting a parameter is a side effect on data you
were only lent.

The classic mistake is `values.sort(...)` - which the `readonly number[]`
parameter type catches for you at compile time, which is exactly why the
annotation is worth writing. The second-classic is forgetting the numeric
comparator, because the default sort compares stringified elements and puts
`10` before `9`.

The model answer copies with a spread, sorts the copy descending, and slices -
`slice` already clamps an over-long count, so the only branch worth writing is
the zero-or-negative one.

## ex5 - one object, three numbers

What this was testing: writing an object type inline in a signature, and
noticing that a stub whose body only throws infers `never` - which satisfies
every annotation and therefore proves nothing until you supply one.

The classic mistake is seeding `min` and `max` from `0` instead of from
`values[0]`, which is invisible until a list of negatives arrives and reports a
spread that includes a value that was never in the data.

The model answer takes one pass with three accumulators and returns early for
the empty list, because `0 / 0` is `NaN`, `NaN` is not `0`, and no amount of
later arithmetic recovers from it.

## ex6 - parse one CSV row

What this was testing: a tuple whose slots have three *different* types, which
is the case an array type provably cannot describe. `(string | number |
boolean)[]` allows a row of nine booleans; the tuple allows exactly one shape.

The classic mistake is trusting `Number()`. `Number("")` is `0`, `Number("warm")`
is `NaN`, and `NaN` flows silently through every later average and comparison -
so the guard belongs at the parse boundary, not downstream.

The model answer trims every field once, then treats each slot independently:
text, a guarded number, and a strict equality against `"true"` - because
`Boolean("false")` is `true` and that is a bug generator.

## ex7 - a moving average

What this was testing: guard conditions stated as a set (not an integer, not
positive, longer than the data) and index arithmetic over a sliding window.
This is the first problem in the set where the interesting work is in the loop
rather than in the signature.

The classic mistake is emitting a partial window at the start - `[1, 1.5, 2.5,
3.5]` for `([1, 2, 3, 4], 2)` - which happens when the push is unconditional
instead of waiting for `i >= window - 1`.

The model answer keeps a running sum, adding the entering element and
subtracting the leaving one, so the whole thing is linear rather than
quadratic; the `slice`-and-`reduce` version is correct too, and saying you know
the difference is the part an interviewer marks.

## ex8 - run-length pairs

What this was testing: an array whose element type is itself a tuple, and the
distinction between a *run* and a *tally*. `[1, 2, 1]` has three runs and two
distinct values, and confusing the two is the single most common wrong answer.

The classic mistake is reading the previous input element instead of the
previous *pair*: it works until you need the count, at which point you are
carrying two pieces of state that can disagree.

The model answer keeps only the accumulator and looks at its last pair, which
makes the empty case free - there is no last pair, so the first value always
starts a run.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Everyday Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html) - annotations on parameters and returns, arrays, and where inference already has the answer.
- [Handbook: Object Types - tuple types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html#tuple-types) - fixed-length arrays, labelled elements, and `readonly` tuples.
- [Handbook: `readonly` and const assertions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html#readonly-properties) - what `readonly` forbids, and what it deliberately does not.
- [MDN: `Number.prototype.toFixed`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Number/toFixed) - rounding behaviour, and why it returns a string.
- [MDN: `Array.prototype.sort`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/sort) - in-place mutation and the default string comparison that ex4 punishes.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - a clock label

`clockLabel(seconds)` returns `mm:ss`, each half padded to two digits. Minutes
are **not** capped at 59. A fractional input never rounds up into a second that
has not happened; a negative input is clamped to zero.

- `clockLabel(65)` -> `"01:05"`, `clockLabel(3600)` -> `"60:00"`
- `clockLabel(7325)` -> `"122:05"`, `clockLabel(90.9)` -> `"01:30"`
- `clockLabel(-10)` -> `"00:00"`

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.


## Hint 1

Three jobs, in this order: make the input sane, split it into minutes and
seconds, then render each part to two characters.

`String(n).padStart(2, "0")` does the padding. `Math.floor(total / 60)` and
`total % 60` do the split. The sane-input step has to turn a negative and a
fraction into a whole, non-negative number *before* you divide, which is one
`Math.max` and one `Math.floor`.

that never reports a second that has not elapsed.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Three jobs, in this order: make the input sane, split it into minutes and
seconds, then render each part to two characters.

Minutes are not capped at 59 in this drill - 3600 seconds reads `60:00`.

## Hint 2

`String(n).padStart(2, "0")` does the padding. `Math.floor(total / 60)` and
`total % 60` do the split. The sane-input step has to turn a negative and a
fraction into a whole, non-negative number *before* you divide, which is one
`Math.max` and one `Math.floor`.

Left to you: whether a fractional input rounds or truncates. Choose the one
that never reports a second that has not elapsed.

exercises.prompt:
## ex3 - split a station id

`splitStationId(id)` returns the tuple `[site: string, index: number]`, split at
the **last** dash. If there is no dash, or the tail after it is not made only of
digits, the whole id is the site and the index is `0`.

- `"roof-3"` -> `["roof", 3]`, `"north-wall-12"` -> `["north-wall", 12]`
- `"roof"` -> `["roof", 0]`, `"roof-x"` -> `["roof-x", 0]`, `"roof-"` -> `["roof-", 0]`

The shipped return annotation is `string[]`. That is the bug.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d01_annotations_inference ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The return type is the exercise. A tuple type fixes both the length and the
type at each position: `[site: string, index: number]`. Those labels are for
readers and editor tooltips; they change nothing at runtime.

## Hint 2

`lastIndexOf("-")` finds the split point, and everything after it is the
candidate index. Two cases fall back to `[id, 0]`: no dash at all, and a tail
that is not made only of digits.

`/^\d+$/.test(tail)` is one way to ask that second question.

Left to you: a regular expression, or `Number.isInteger(Number(tail))` plus an
emptiness check. They disagree on `"roof- 3"` - decide which answer you want.

exercises.prompt:
## ex5 - one object, three numbers

`summarise(values)` returns `{ count, mean, spread }`, where `spread` is the
largest value minus the smallest. An empty list returns all three as `0`.

- `[2, 4, 9]` -> `{ count: 3, mean: 5, spread: 7 }`
- `[4]` -> `{ count: 1, mean: 4, spread: 0 }`
- `[]` -> `{ count: 0, mean: 0, spread: 0 }`

The stub has **no** return annotation at all. Write it.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d01_annotations_inference ex5
```

## ex6 - parse one CSV row

`parseCsvRow(row)` returns `[station: string, celsius: number, ok: boolean]`.
Fields are separated by commas and trimmed. A temperature that is missing,
empty or not a finite number becomes `0`; the flag is `true` only for the exact
lowercase text `true`.

- `"roof,21.5,true"` -> `["roof", 21.5, true]`
- `"roof,warm,true"` -> `["roof", 0, true]`
- `"roof,21,TRUE"` -> `["roof", 21, false]`

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`. The shipped annotation is `(string | number | boolean)[]`,
which is close and still wrong.


exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - a moving average

`movingAverage(values, window)` returns the average of every **full** window of
`window` consecutive values, left to right. A window that is not a positive
integer, or is longer than the input, produces `[]`.

- `([1, 2, 3, 4], 2)` -> `[1.5, 2.5, 3.5]`
- `([1, 2, 3], 3)` -> `[2]`, `([1, 2, 3], 4)` -> `[]`
- `([1, 2, 3], 2.5)` -> `[]`

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d01_annotations_inference ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Guard first, then slide. Three inputs produce no windows at all: a window that
is not a whole number, one that is zero or negative, and one longer than the
data. All three answer with an empty array rather than a partial window.

## Hint 2

The slow version rebuilds each window with `slice` and `reduce`. The version an
interviewer is hoping for keeps a running `sum`: add the element entering the
window, subtract the element leaving it, and push an average once the window is
full.

The index bookkeeping is the trick - the element leaving at step `i` is
`values[i - window]`, and the first full window ends at `i === window - 1`.

Left to you: running sum or slice-and-average. If you write the simple one, say
out loud that you know the other exists and what it buys.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Guard first, then slide. Three inputs produce no windows at all: a window that
is not a whole number, one that is zero or negative, and one longer than the
data. All three answer with an empty array rather than a partial window.

## Hint 2

The slow version rebuilds each window with `slice` and `reduce`. The version an
interviewer is hoping for keeps a running `sum`: add the element entering the
window, subtract the element leaving it, and push an average once the window is
full.

The index bookkeeping is the trick - the element leaving at step `i` is
`values[i - window]`, and the first full window ends at `i === window - 1`.

Left to you: running sum or slice-and-average. If you write the simple one, say
out loud that you know the other exists and what it buys.

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - run-length pairs

`runLengths(values)` collapses each run of consecutive equal values into a
`[value: number, count: number]` pair, in input order. Runs are consecutive:
this is not a tally.

- `[1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3]` -> `[[1, 2], [2, 1], [3, 3]]`
- `[1, 2, 1]` -> `[[1, 1], [2, 1], [1, 1]]`
- `[]` -> `[]`

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. The shipped annotation `number[][]` says far less than
you know.

```

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The element type is a tuple, so the return type is an array *of* that tuple:
`[value: number, count: number][]`. Write it once on the accumulator and once
as the return type, and the body will typecheck itself.

## Hint 2

Walk the input once, looking only at the last pair you pushed. If its value
equals the current one, bump the count; otherwise push a fresh `[value, 1]`.

`runs[runs.length - 1]` is `undefined` on the first iteration, so compare it
against `undefined` before reading `last[0]`.

Left to you: mutate the last tuple in place, or rebuild it. Mutating is
shorter; rebuilding is what you would do if the pairs were `readonly`.

## Hint 1

The element type is a tuple, so the return type is an array *of* that tuple:
`[value: number, count: number][]`. Write it once on the accumulator and once
as the return type, and the body will typecheck itself.

## Hint 2

Walk the input once, looking only at the last pair you pushed. If its value
equals the current one, bump the count; otherwise push a fresh `[value, 1]`.

`runs[runs.length - 1]` is `undefined` on the first iteration, so compare it
against `undefined` before reading `last[0]`.

Left to you: mutate the last tuple in place, or rebuild it. Mutating is
shorter; rebuilding is what you would do if the pairs were `readonly`.

# d02 - Function signatures (drill set)

Eight problems on the shape of a function rather than its body - optional
parameters, defaults, rest parameters, callback types, overloads and functions
that return functions. They drill lesson **02_functions**; redo it first if the
difference between an optional parameter and a defaulted one is not automatic.

Several stubs ship with a signature that is subtly too loose. The type gate is
what marks those, so read the assertions in `gate.test-d.ts` as part of the
prompt.

## ex1 - a shelf label

`shelfLabel(title, author?)` returns `"<title> - <author>"`, or just the title
when there is no author. An author that is empty or only whitespace counts as
no author.

- `shelfLabel("Dune")` -> `"Dune"`
- `shelfLabel("Dune", "Herbert")` -> `"Dune - Herbert"`
- `shelfLabel("Dune", "   ")` -> `"Dune"`

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex1
```

## ex2 - join a path

`joinPath(...segments)` joins any number of segments with `/`. Each segment is
stripped of leading and trailing slashes first, and a segment that is then
empty is dropped entirely.

- `joinPath("books", "sci-fi", "dune")` -> `"books/sci-fi/dune"`
- `joinPath("/books/", "/dune/")` -> `"books/dune"`
- `joinPath("books", "", "dune")` -> `"books/dune"`
- `joinPath()` -> `""`

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex2
```

## ex3 - count what matches

`countMatching(values, keep)` returns how many values the predicate accepted.
The predicate is called exactly once per value, in order.

- `countMatching(["a", "bb", "ccc"], (v) => v.length > 1)` -> `2`
- `countMatching([], () => true)` -> `0`

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex3
```

## ex4 - a named formatter type, with a default

Declare `Formatter`, the type of a function from a number to a string. Then
`formatAll(values, format?)` maps every value through it, defaulting to two
decimal places.

- `formatAll([1, 2.5])` -> `["1.00", "2.50"]`
- ``formatAll([1, 2], (v) => `#${v}`)`` -> `["#1", "#2"]`

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. The shipped `Formatter` returns `unknown` - tighten it.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex4
```

## ex5 - one function, two contracts

`normaliseTag` takes a tag and returns a normalised tag; take an **array** of
tags and it returns an array. Normalising means trim, lower-case, and collapse
each run of inner whitespace into a single dash.

- `normaliseTag("  Science Fiction ")` -> `"science-fiction"`
- `normaliseTag(["A B", " C "])` -> `["a-b", "c"]`

A single signature returning `string | string[]` compiles and fails the type
gate: callers would have to narrow a result they already know the shape of.
Write **overload signatures**.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex5
```

## ex6 - a counter that owns its state

`makeCounter(start?)` returns a `Counter` with three methods: `next()` hands out
the current number and advances, `peek()` shows the next number without
advancing, `reset()` returns to the start this counter was made with. The
default start is `0`.

Two counters must not share state.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex6
```

## ex7 - build a query string

`buildQuery(base, params?)` appends a query string to `base`. Keys are sorted
alphabetically, both keys and values are URL-encoded, and no params (or an empty
object) means the base is returned unchanged.

- `buildQuery("/books", { year: 1965, author: "Herbert" })` -> `"/books?author=Herbert&year=1965"`
- `buildQuery("/books", { q: "dune messiah" })` -> `"/books?q=dune%20messiah"`
- `buildQuery("/books", { draft: false })` -> `"/books?draft=false"`

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex7
```

## ex8 - a middleware chain

Declare `Middleware`: a function taking the current value **and** `next`, the
rest of the chain, and returning a value. Then `runMiddleware(input, middleware)`
runs them as an onion - the first entry is the outermost, and a middleware that
never calls `next` short-circuits everything after it.

With `upper = (v, next) => next(v.toUpperCase())` and
`exclaim = (v, next) => next(v) + "!"`:

- `runMiddleware("a", [])` -> `"a"`
- `runMiddleware("a", [upper, exclaim])` -> `"A!"`

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. The shipped `Middleware` has no `next` parameter at all.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex8
```

# Reading - typescript/d02_functions_signatures

The debrief. Per problem: what the signature was really being marked on, the
mistake that costs the point, and one sentence on why the model answer is
shaped the way it is.

## Notes

**The skill this set drills is writing the contract before the body.** Every
one of these eight problems is easy once the signature exists, and most of them
are ambiguous until it does. Optional versus defaulted, one parameter versus a
rest parameter, a callback typed by hand versus one typed by its position, one
loose signature versus a pair of overloads - those choices are the exercise,
and the runtime behaviour is the sanity check on them.

**Optional and defaulted look the same from outside and are not the same
inside.** `author?: string` gives the body `string | undefined` and forces you
to handle the missing case; `format: Formatter = fallback` gives the body a
`Formatter` with no `undefined` in sight, because the default has already run
by the time your first line executes. Both render as `?` in `Parameters<>`,
which is why the type gate cannot tell them apart and why the choice is about
the body, not the caller.

**A callback parameter is a type, and types in parameter position are
contravariant.** That is the sentence behind every "why will it not accept my
function" question: `(n: number) => boolean` is not a
`(value: string) => boolean`, because a caller of the second is entitled to
hand it any string. `strictFunctionTypes` is what turns that from a warning
into an error, and it is on here.

**Overloads exist for exactly one situation: the result type depends on the
argument type.** `string | string[]` in and `string | string[]` out is honest
and useless, because every caller must then narrow a result they already knew
the shape of. Two overload signatures over one implementation signature move
that knowledge into the type system, which is where it was all along.

**And a function that returns a function is a closure question wearing a type
question's clothes.** `makeCounter` and `runMiddleware` both live or die on
where the state is declared: inside the factory (one per counter) or inside the
returned function (recreated on every call, which is the bug).

## ex1 - a shelf label

What this was testing: that `author?: string` is what you reach for, and that
you handle three missing-ish cases rather than one. `undefined`, `""` and
`"   "` all mean "no author", and only the first is what the type system warns
you about.

The classic mistake is `author !== undefined`, which passes the type checker,
passes the first two assertions, and renders `"Dune -    "` for the third.

The model answer trims once into a local and tests that local for truthiness,
so the type question and the data question are answered in the same line.

## ex2 - join a path

What this was testing: a rest parameter, and the fact that zero arguments is a
legal call for one. `joinPath()` has to work, which rules out any implementation
that reads `segments[0]` before checking the length.

The classic mistake is `segments.join("/")` on its own: it is right for the
happy path and wrong for every segment that carries its own slashes, producing
`"/books//dune/"` from perfectly reasonable input.

The model answer normalises each segment first - strip slashes, drop what is
left if it is empty - and only then joins, which makes the empty-input case fall
out for free rather than needing a branch.

## ex3 - count what matches

What this was testing: writing a callback type by hand, and the contravariance
rule that makes a wrongly-typed predicate a compile error rather than a runtime
surprise. The gate also checks the predicate is called once per value, in order,
which rules out clever double-passes.

The classic mistake is `values.filter(keep).length`, which is correct but
allocates an array to throw it away; the interview-visible version counts as it
walks. Neither is wrong - having a reason is the point.

The model answer is one loop and one counter, and it names the callback
parameter `keep` rather than `fn`, because a predicate that reads
`if (keep(value))` documents itself.

## ex4 - a named formatter type, with a default

What this was testing: naming a function type with a `type` alias, and knowing
that a defaulted parameter is optional to the caller but not to the body. The
shipped `Formatter` returns `unknown`, which is assignable *from* everything and
therefore checks nothing.

The classic mistake is declaring `format?: Formatter` and then writing
`format ? format(value) : value.toFixed(2)` inside the loop - correct, but it
re-asks the question on every element and spreads the default across two places.

The model answer puts the default in the signature, so the body has exactly one
code path and the default is visible in the API rather than buried in an `if`.

## ex5 - one function, two contracts

What this was testing: overloads. The two overload signatures are the public
API; the implementation signature underneath is invisible to callers and can be
as loose as it needs to be, which is why `string | string[]` is fine *there* and
wrong as the only signature.

The classic mistake is making the implementation signature one of the overloads
by accident - TypeScript only exposes the declared overloads, so if you write
three signatures where the third is the implementation, callers see two.

The model answer narrows inside the implementation with a simple
`Array.isArray` check and delegates the array case to the scalar one, so the
normalising rules exist in exactly one place.

## ex6 - a counter that owns its state

What this was testing: closures, and an interface whose members are methods.
`next()`, `peek()` and `reset()` share one `let` that lives in `makeCounter`'s
scope, and `reset` needs the original `start` - which is already captured, for
free, because parameters are part of the closure.

The classic mistake is declaring the counter variable inside `next`, which
resets it on every call; the second-classic is module-level state, which makes
every counter the same counter and is caught by the last assertion in the gate.

The model answer returns an object literal of three arrow functions, so `this`
never enters the conversation - which is the honest reason most modern factory
functions avoid classes for this shape.

## ex7 - build a query string

What this was testing: an optional object parameter typed as a bag of scalars,
and the discipline of a deterministic output. Sorting the keys is not
decoration: an unsorted query string makes two identical requests cache-miss
each other.

The classic mistake is `if (!params)`, which is right, followed by forgetting
that `{}` also has to return the bare base - and then forgetting that `false`
and `0` are values, so a truthiness filter over the entries drops them.

The model answer sorts `Object.entries`, encodes both halves with
`encodeURIComponent`, and joins with `&`, treating "no pairs" and "no params" as
the same case rather than two.

## ex8 - a middleware chain

What this was testing: a recursive function type used as a parameter type, and
the onion order that Express, Koa and every HTTP framework you will meet are
built on. The gate checks `in:1, in:2, out:2, out:1`, which no `reduce`-of-
transforms implementation can produce.

The classic mistake is treating middleware as a pipeline of `(value) => value`
transforms. That gives you the right answer for `[upper]` and the wrong one the
moment a middleware wants to do something *after* the rest of the chain has run.

The model answer is a `dispatch(index)` helper that returns the `next` function
for that position; the base case - an index past the end - simply returns its
input, which is what makes an empty chain and a fully-consumed chain the same
code path.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: More on Functions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html) - optional and default parameters, rest parameters, call signatures, and the overload rules ex5 depends on.
- [Handbook: Function overloads](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#function-overloads) - why the implementation signature is not callable, and how to choose between overloads and a union.
- [TypeScript release notes: strictFunctionTypes](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#strictFunctionTypes) - the contravariance rule behind ex3.
- [MDN: Closures](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Closures) - the JavaScript half of ex6 and ex8.
- [MDN: encodeURIComponent](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/encodeURIComponent) - what it escapes and what it deliberately leaves alone.

exercises.prompt:
## ex1 - a shelf label

`shelfLabel(title, author?)` returns `"<title> - <author>"`, or just the title
when there is no author. An author that is empty or only whitespace counts as
no author.

- `shelfLabel("Dune")` -> `"Dune"`
- `shelfLabel("Dune", "Herbert")` -> `"Dune - Herbert"`
- `shelfLabel("Dune", "   ")` -> `"Dune"`

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The `?` on the parameter is only half the job. Inside the body the author is
`string | undefined`, and the prompt says three different values all mean "no
author": `undefined`, `""` and `"   "`.

## Hint 2

Collapse all three into one question by trimming first:
`const trimmed = (author ?? "").trim();`. Now a single emptiness check decides
which of the two strings you return.

Left to you: `??` before the trim, or optional chaining (`author?.trim() ?? ""`)
after it. They read differently and mean the same thing here.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - join a path

`joinPath(...segments)` joins any number of segments with `/`. Each segment is
stripped of leading and trailing slashes first, and a segment that is then
empty is dropped entirely.

- `joinPath("books", "sci-fi", "dune")` -> `"books/sci-fi/dune"`
- `joinPath("/books/", "/dune/")` -> `"books/dune"`
- `joinPath("books", "", "dune")` -> `"books/dune"`
- `joinPath()` -> `""`


## ex3 - count what matches

`countMatching(values, keep)` returns how many values the predicate accepted.
The predicate is called exactly once per value, in order.

- `countMatching([], () => true)` -> `0`

## ex4 - a named formatter type, with a default

Declare `Formatter`, the type of a function from a number to a string. Then
`formatAll(values, format?)` maps every value through it, defaulting to two
decimal places.

- `formatAll([1, 2.5])` -> `["1.00", "2.50"]`
- ``formatAll([1, 2], (v) => `#${v}`)`` -> `["#1", "#2"]`

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. The shipped `Formatter` returns `unknown` - tighten it.


Two changes. `Formatter` has to promise a `string`, not `unknown` - a type that
accepts everything checks nothing. And the default belongs in the signature,

that matters here, and whether it would in general.

exercises.prompt:
## ex5 - one function, two contracts

`normaliseTag` takes a tag and returns a normalised tag; take an **array** of
tags and it returns an array. Normalising means trim, lower-case, and collapse
each run of inner whitespace into a single dash.

- `normaliseTag("  Science Fiction ")` -> `"science-fiction"`
- `normaliseTag(["A B", " C "])` -> `["a-b", "c"]`

A single signature returning `string | string[]` compiles and fails the type
gate: callers would have to narrow a result they already know the shape of.
Write **overload signatures**.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex5
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex6 - a counter that owns its state

`makeCounter(start?)` returns a `Counter` with three methods: `next()` hands out
the current number and advances, `peek()` shows the next number without
advancing, `reset()` returns to the start this counter was made with. The
default start is `0`.

Two counters must not share state.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Where you declare the state is the whole exercise. It has to live in
`makeCounter`'s body - one `let` per call to the factory - so that the three
returned functions close over the same variable and two counters never share
one.

## Hint 2

`next()` returns the *current* value and then advances, so it needs a local
copy before the increment. `peek()` returns the same number without touching
it. `reset()` assigns the parameter back into the state - the parameter is part
of the closure too, so nothing extra needs storing.

Left to you: a defaulted parameter (`start: number = 0`) or an optional one
plus `??` in the body. One of them makes `reset()` a single line.

## Hint 1

Where you declare the state is the whole exercise. It has to live in
`makeCounter`'s body - one `let` per call to the factory - so that the three
returned functions close over the same variable and two counters never share
one.

## Hint 2

`next()` returns the *current* value and then advances, so it needs a local
copy before the increment. `peek()` returns the same number without touching
it. `reset()` assigns the parameter back into the state - the parameter is part
of the closure too, so nothing extra needs storing.

Left to you: a defaulted parameter (`start: number = 0`) or an optional one
plus `??` in the body. One of them makes `reset()` a single line.

exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - build a query string

`buildQuery(base, params?)` appends a query string to `base`. Keys are sorted
alphabetically, both keys and values are URL-encoded, and no params (or an empty
object) means the base is returned unchanged.

- `buildQuery("/books", { year: 1965, author: "Herbert" })` -> `"/books?author=Herbert&year=1965"`
- `buildQuery("/books", { q: "dune messiah" })` -> `"/books?q=dune%20messiah"`
- `buildQuery("/books", { draft: false })` -> `"/books?draft=false"`


exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - a middleware chain

Declare `Middleware`: a function taking the current value **and** `next`, the
rest of the chain, and returning a value. Then `runMiddleware(input, middleware)`
runs them as an onion - the first entry is the outermost, and a middleware that
never calls `next` short-circuits everything after it.

With `upper = (v, next) => next(v.toUpperCase())` and
`exclaim = (v, next) => next(v) + "!"`:

- `runMiddleware("a", [])` -> `"a"`
- `runMiddleware("a", [upper, exclaim])` -> `"A!"`

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`. The shipped `Middleware` has no `next` parameter at all.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d02_functions_signatures ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

First fix the type. A middleware needs two parameters: the value, and `next` -
a function from a value to a value that represents *everything after this
middleware*. That second parameter is what lets it act after the rest has run.

## Hint 2

Build the chain lazily with a helper indexed by position:

```ts
const dispatch = (index: number) => (value: string): string => { ... };
```

At `index`, look up `middleware[index]`. If there is none, the chain is over -
return the value unchanged. Otherwise call it with the value and
`dispatch(index + 1)`.

Left to you: this recursive `dispatch`, or a right-to-left `reduceRight` that
folds the array into a single function. They produce the same onion; one of
them explains itself better in an interview.

## Hint 1

First fix the type. A middleware needs two parameters: the value, and `next` -
a function from a value to a value that represents *everything after this
middleware*. That second parameter is what lets it act after the rest has run.

## Hint 2

Build the chain lazily with a helper indexed by position:

```ts
const dispatch = (index: number) => (value: string): string => { ... };
```

At `index`, look up `middleware[index]`. If there is none, the chain is over -
return the value unchanged. Otherwise call it with the value and
`dispatch(index + 1)`.

Left to you: this recursive `dispatch`, or a right-to-left `reduceRight` that
folds the array into a single function. They produce the same onion; one of
them explains itself better in an interview.

# d03 - Object shapes (drill set)

Eight problems on describing objects: required and optional members, readonly,
index signatures, nested and recursive shapes, and copying instead of mutating.
They drill lesson **03_objects_interfaces**; go back there first if "optional
member" and "member that may be undefined" feel like the same thing.

Several stubs ship with a member typed `unknown`. That is not a placeholder you
may leave - `unknown` accepts every value, so it checks nothing, and the type
gate says so.

## ex1 - one track, one line

`trackLine(track)` renders a `Track` as `"<title> - <artist> (<seconds>s)"`,
with `" [E]"` appended when the track is explicit. `explicit` is optional, and
`explicit: false` must render exactly like a missing `explicit`.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex1
```

## ex2 - defaults that respect zero

`describeAlbum(input)` returns `"<title> [<label>] <year>"`. A missing `label`
becomes `"independent"`; a missing `year` renders as the word `"unknown"`.

- `{ title: "Homework" }` -> `"Homework [independent] unknown"`
- `{ title: "Homework", year: 1997, label: "Virgin" }` -> `"Homework [Virgin] 1997"`
- `{ title: "Bootleg", year: 0 }` -> `"Bootleg [independent] 0"`
- `{ title: "Bootleg", label: "" }` -> `"Bootleg [] unknown"`

Those last two are the exercise: a default fires for `undefined` and for
nothing else.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex2
```

## ex3 - append without mutating

`addTrack(playlist, title)` returns a **new** `Playlist` with the title appended.
The playlist you were handed, and its `tracks` array, must both come back
untouched.

Mark `id` and `tracks` as `readonly` on the interface, and make `tracks` a
`readonly string[]`. The type gate proves both.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex3
```

## ex4 - two optional levels deep

`contactLine(playlist)` returns `"<owner name> <<email>>"`, falling back to
`"anonymous"` and `"no email"`. The owner is optional, the contact inside it is
optional, and the email inside that is optional - and a value that is only
whitespace counts as missing.

- `{ name: "Mix" }` -> `"anonymous <no email>"`
- `{ name: "Mix", owner: { name: "Ada", contact: { email: "ada@example.com" } } }` -> `"Ada <ada@example.com>"`

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex4
```

## ex5 - a tally of objects

`byArtist(tracks)` returns an `ArtistTotals` - an index signature from artist
name to `{ count, seconds }`. An empty input returns `{}`.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`, where the shipped index signature says the values are
`unknown`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex5
```

## ex6 - keep only the tags that exist

`presentTags(meta)` copies across only those optional members whose value is a
non-empty string once trimmed, and trims the ones it keeps. Everything else -
`undefined`, `""`, `"   "` - is dropped.

- `{ genre: "  house  ", mood: "   ", era: undefined }` -> `{ genre: "house" }`

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex6
```

## ex7 - flatten a recursive shape

`MetaTree` is an index signature whose values are either a string leaf or
another `MetaTree`. `flattenMeta(tree)` returns a flat `Record<string, string>`
whose keys are the dot-joined paths to each leaf.

- `{ a: { b: "x" }, c: "y" }` -> `{ "a.b": "x", c: "y" }`
- `{ a: {} }` -> `{}`

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex7
```

## ex8 - diff two records

`diffMeta(before, after)` returns `{ added, removed, changed }`, each an
alphabetically sorted array of keys. A key is *changed* when it exists on both
sides with values that are not strictly equal.

- `diffMeta({ a: "1", b: "2", c: "3" }, { b: "2", c: "changed", d: "4" })`
  -> `{ added: ["d"], removed: ["a"], changed: ["c"] }`
- `diffMeta({ n: 1 }, { n: "1" })` -> `{ added: [], removed: [], changed: ["n"] }`

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex8
```
