# Reading - typescript/d03_objects_shapes

The debrief. What each shape was really testing, the mistake that keeps
appearing in code review, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**The skill this set drills is saying exactly what an object has.** Not
roughly, not "some strings" - exactly. Which members are required, which may be
absent, which must not be reassigned, and whether the key set is fixed at all.
Every problem here is a different answer to that last question: a fixed set of
named members (ex1-ex4, ex6), an open set described by an index signature (ex5,
ex7, ex8), or a fixed set that nests into itself (ex7).

**Optional is a statement about the key, not about the value.** `explicit?:
boolean` says the property may be *absent*; `explicit: boolean | undefined`
says it must be present and may hold `undefined`. They behave almost
identically in your `if`, and completely differently to `in`,
`Object.keys`, spread, and anyone reading your API. Reach for `?` unless you
have a reason.

**A default fires for `undefined` and for nothing else.** This is the single
most repeated bug in this set, and ex2 makes it explicit: `year = 0` keeps the
zero, `label = ""` keeps the empty string, and `||` would silently replace
both. `??` and destructuring defaults are the nullish tools; `||` is the
falsiness tool, and the two agree only when your data has no zeroes, no empty
strings and no `false`.

**`readonly` is compile-time only, and it is shallow.** `readonly tracks:
readonly string[]` needs the modifier twice for a reason: the first stops you
reassigning the property, the second stops you pushing into the array behind
it. Nothing is frozen at runtime, and a `readonly` object can always be passed
to something that expects a mutable one via a cast - the value is entirely in
the errors you get for free while writing.

**And an index signature is a promise about every key, including the ones that
are not there.** `{ [artist: string]: Totals }` says any string key yields a
`Totals` - which is a lie the moment you read a key that was never set, and
which is why `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` exists and why the model answers here
create the entry before touching it.

## ex1 - one track, one line

What this was testing: an object type used as a parameter, and the difference
between "the property is missing" and "the property is `false`". The gate asks
for the same output in both cases, which is only easy if you check truthiness
rather than presence.

The classic mistake is `"explicit" in track ? " [E]" : ""`, which is a presence
check and renders the suffix for `explicit: false`. The mirror-image mistake is
`track.explicit!` to silence the compiler, which converts a type question into
a runtime one for no benefit.

The model answer compares against `true` (or uses plain truthiness) and builds
the suffix as a separate `const`, so the template literal at the end reads as
one line rather than as a nested ternary.

## ex2 - defaults that respect zero

What this was testing: that you know which operator fires on which values.
Destructuring defaults and `??` both trigger on `undefined` alone; `||`
triggers on every falsy value, which here means `0` and `""`.

The classic mistake is `input.label || "independent"`, which passes three of the
four assertions and quietly rewrites an intentionally empty label. The gate
includes `{ title: "Bootleg", label: "" }` for exactly that reason.

The model answer destructures with a default for `label` and handles `year`
with an explicit `undefined` check, because the year needs a *different* string
when absent rather than a different number - and a default cannot express that.

## ex3 - append without mutating

What this was testing: `readonly` in both of the places it is needed, and the
copy-then-change habit. The type gate pushes into `playlist.tracks` and assigns
to `playlist.id`, and both have to be compile errors before the exercise counts.

The classic mistake is `playlist.tracks.push(title); return playlist;` - which
returns the right data, passes a naive equality check, and fails the two
assertions that the caller's array and object are untouched. The second-classic
is `{ ...playlist, tracks: playlist.tracks }`, a new object sharing the old
array, which fails only the array identity check.

The model answer spreads both levels: a new object literal, and a new array
built with `[...playlist.tracks, title]`. Two spreads, one line.

## ex4 - two optional levels deep

What this was testing: optional chaining through more than one level, and
knowing that `?.` short-circuits the whole chain rather than one step. The extra
twist is that a present-but-blank value has to be treated as absent, which `?.`
alone will not do for you.

The classic mistake is `playlist.owner?.contact.email`, which the compiler
accepts (the `?.` covered `owner`, so `contact` looks safe) and which throws at
runtime when the owner exists without a contact. Every hop that can be missing
needs its own `?.`.

The model answer trims into two locals first, so the fallbacks are decided by a
single truthiness check each rather than by a chain of `??` that would keep the
whitespace.

## ex5 - a tally of objects

What this was testing: an index signature whose value type is itself an object,
and the "create the bucket before you use it" pattern. `unknown` as the value
type - what the stub ships - is the anti-pattern, because it makes every read
require a cast.

The classic mistake is `totals[artist].count += 1` on a key that has never been
seen, which is `undefined.count` at runtime. The type system does not stop it,
because an index signature claims every key is present.

The model answer uses `totals[artist] ??= { count: 0, seconds: 0 }` and keeps a
reference to the entry, so the bucket is created exactly once and updated in
place - one lookup instead of three.

## ex6 - keep only the tags that exist

What this was testing: iterating an object with optional members, where
`Object.entries` hands you `string | undefined` values and you have to narrow
before you can trim. It is the inverse of ex2: instead of filling holes, you are
removing them.

The classic mistake is `if (value)`, which is nearly right and drops nothing
that should survive here - but would drop a legitimate `0` in any version of
this function whose values are numbers. Being explicit (`typeof value ===
"string" && value.trim() !== ""`) documents the rule.

The model answer builds a fresh `Record<string, string>` rather than deleting
from a copy, because `delete` on a typed object fights the type system and
leaves the result's type claiming members that are gone.

## ex7 - flatten a recursive shape

What this was testing: a self-referential interface, and a walk that carries a
prefix. `interface MetaTree { [key: string]: string | MetaTree }` is legal and
lazy - the interface may mention itself because interfaces are resolved by name.

The classic mistake is emitting a key for a branch: `{ a: {} }` producing
`{ "a": {} }` or `{ "a.": "" }`. A branch contributes nothing of its own; only
leaves produce entries, which falls out naturally if the only place you write
into the accumulator is the string case.

The model answer passes the accumulated path down rather than returning partial
objects and merging them, so there is one object, one write per leaf, and no
allocation per level.

## ex8 - diff two records

What this was testing: two passes over two key sets, and a deterministic output.
Sorting is not cosmetic here - a diff that reports the same change in a
different order every run is unusable in a log or a test.

The classic mistake is a single pass over `after`, which finds everything added
and changed and silently misses everything removed. The second-classic is
comparing with `==`, which would call `1` and `"1"` equal and lose a real change.

The model answer walks `after` for added-and-changed, walks `before` for
removed, uses `in` rather than `!== undefined` (so a key explicitly set to
`undefined` still counts as present), and sorts each list before returning.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Object Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html) - optional members, `readonly`, index signatures, and excess property checks, in one page.
- [Handbook: Index signatures](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html#index-signatures) - what they promise, and why the promise is optimistic.
- [TSConfig: noUncheckedIndexedAccess](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#noUncheckedIndexedAccess) - the flag that makes the ex5 trap a compile error instead of a crash.
- [MDN: Optional chaining](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Optional_chaining) - how far `?.` short-circuits, which is the whole of ex4.
- [MDN: Nullish coalescing](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Nullish_coalescing) - `??` against `||`, with the falsy-value table ex2 is built on.

**And an index signature is a promise about every key, including the ones that
are not there.** `{ [artist: string]: Totals }` says any string key yields a
`Totals` - which is a lie the moment you read a key that was never set, and
which is why `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` exists and why the model answers here
create the entry before touching it.

## ex1 - one track, one line

What this was testing: an object type used as a parameter, and the difference
between "the property is missing" and "the property is `false`". The gate asks
for the same output in both cases, which is only easy if you check truthiness
rather than presence.

The classic mistake is `"explicit" in track ? " [E]" : ""`, which is a presence
check and renders the suffix for `explicit: false`. The mirror-image mistake is
`track.explicit!` to silence the compiler, which converts a type question into
a runtime one for no benefit.

The model answer compares against `true` (or uses plain truthiness) and builds
the suffix as a separate `const`, so the template literal at the end reads as
one line rather than as a nested ternary.

## ex2 - defaults that respect zero

What this was testing: that you know which operator fires on which values.
Destructuring defaults and `??` both trigger on `undefined` alone; `||`
triggers on every falsy value, which here means `0` and `""`.

The classic mistake is `input.label || "independent"`, which passes three of the
four assertions and quietly rewrites an intentionally empty label. The gate
includes `{ title: "Bootleg", label: "" }` for exactly that reason.

The model answer destructures with a default for `label` and handles `year`
with an explicit `undefined` check, because the year needs a *different* string
when absent rather than a different number - and a default cannot express that.

## ex3 - append without mutating

What this was testing: `readonly` in both of the places it is needed, and the
copy-then-change habit. The type gate pushes into `playlist.tracks` and assigns
to `playlist.id`, and both have to be compile errors before the exercise counts.

The classic mistake is `playlist.tracks.push(title); return playlist;` - which
returns the right data, passes a naive equality check, and fails the two
assertions that the caller's array and object are untouched. The second-classic
is `{ ...playlist, tracks: playlist.tracks }`, a new object sharing the old
array, which fails only the array identity check.

The model answer spreads both levels: a new object literal, and a new array
built with `[...playlist.tracks, title]`. Two spreads, one line.

## ex4 - two optional levels deep

What this was testing: optional chaining through more than one level, and
knowing that `?.` short-circuits the whole chain rather than one step. The extra
twist is that a present-but-blank value has to be treated as absent, which `?.`
alone will not do for you.

The classic mistake is `playlist.owner?.contact.email`, which the compiler
accepts (the `?.` covered `owner`, so `contact` looks safe) and which throws at
runtime when the owner exists without a contact. Every hop that can be missing
needs its own `?.`.

The model answer trims into two locals first, so the fallbacks are decided by a
single truthiness check each rather than by a chain of `??` that would keep the
whitespace.

## ex5 - a tally of objects

What this was testing: an index signature whose value type is itself an object,
and the "create the bucket before you use it" pattern. `unknown` as the value
type - what the stub ships - is the anti-pattern, because it makes every read
require a cast.

The classic mistake is `totals[artist].count += 1` on a key that has never been
seen, which is `undefined.count` at runtime. The type system does not stop it,
because an index signature claims every key is present.

The model answer uses `totals[artist] ??= { count: 0, seconds: 0 }` and keeps a
reference to the entry, so the bucket is created exactly once and updated in
place - one lookup instead of three.

## ex6 - keep only the tags that exist

What this was testing: iterating an object with optional members, where
`Object.entries` hands you `string | undefined` values and you have to narrow
before you can trim. It is the inverse of ex2: instead of filling holes, you are
removing them.

The classic mistake is `if (value)`, which is nearly right and drops nothing
that should survive here - but would drop a legitimate `0` in any version of
this function whose values are numbers. Being explicit (`typeof value ===
"string" && value.trim() !== ""`) documents the rule.

The model answer builds a fresh `Record<string, string>` rather than deleting
from a copy, because `delete` on a typed object fights the type system and
leaves the result's type claiming members that are gone.

## ex7 - flatten a recursive shape

What this was testing: a self-referential interface, and a walk that carries a
prefix. `interface MetaTree { [key: string]: string | MetaTree }` is legal and
lazy - the interface may mention itself because interfaces are resolved by name.

The classic mistake is emitting a key for a branch: `{ a: {} }` producing
`{ "a": {} }` or `{ "a.": "" }`. A branch contributes nothing of its own; only
leaves produce entries, which falls out naturally if the only place you write
into the accumulator is the string case.

The model answer passes the accumulated path down rather than returning partial
objects and merging them, so there is one object, one write per leaf, and no
allocation per level.

## ex8 - diff two records

What this was testing: two passes over two key sets, and a deterministic output.
Sorting is not cosmetic here - a diff that reports the same change in a
different order every run is unusable in a log or a test.

The classic mistake is a single pass over `after`, which finds everything added
and changed and silently misses everything removed. The second-classic is
comparing with `==`, which would call `1` and `"1"` equal and lose a real change.

The model answer walks `after` for added-and-changed, walks `before` for
removed, uses `in` rather than `!== undefined` (so a key explicitly set to
`undefined` still counts as present), and sorts each list before returning.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Object Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html) - optional members, `readonly`, index signatures, and excess property checks, in one page.
- [Handbook: Index signatures](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html#index-signatures) - what they promise, and why the promise is optimistic.
- [TSConfig: noUncheckedIndexedAccess](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/#noUncheckedIndexedAccess) - the flag that makes the ex5 trap a compile error instead of a crash.
- [MDN: Optional chaining](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Optional_chaining) - how far `?.` short-circuits, which is the whole of ex4.
- [MDN: Nullish coalescing](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Nullish_coalescing) - `??` against `||`, with the falsy-value table ex2 is built on.

## ex1 - one track, one line

`trackLine(track)` renders a `Track` as `"<title> - <artist> (<seconds>s)"`,
with `" [E]"` appended when the track is explicit. `explicit` is optional, and
`explicit: false` must render exactly like a missing `explicit`.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two jobs. Give `explicit` a real type - it is an optional boolean, so its type
inside the body is `boolean | undefined`. Then decide the suffix.

The prompt says `explicit: false` and a missing `explicit` render identically,
so the question you ask is about the *value*, not about the key.

## Hint 2

`"explicit" in track` asks whether the key exists, which answers the wrong
question. `track.explicit === true` (or plain truthiness) answers the right one.

Build the suffix into its own `const` and the return becomes one template
literal.

Left to you: `=== true` or plain truthiness. They agree here; say which you
would use in a codebase where the flag might be a string.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - defaults that respect zero

`describeAlbum(input)` returns `"<title> [<label>] <year>"`. A missing `label`
becomes `"independent"`; a missing `year` renders as the word `"unknown"`.

- `{ title: "Homework" }` -> `"Homework [independent] unknown"`
- `{ title: "Homework", year: 1997, label: "Virgin" }` -> `"Homework [Virgin] 1997"`
- `{ title: "Bootleg", year: 0 }` -> `"Bootleg [independent] 0"`
- `{ title: "Bootleg", label: "" }` -> `"Bootleg [] unknown"`

Those last two are the exercise: a default fires for `undefined` and for
nothing else.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

First give the two optional members real types. Then notice that they need
different treatment: a missing label becomes another *label*, but a missing year
becomes a word that is not a year at all.

## Hint 2

A destructuring default (`const { label = "independent" } = input`) fires for
`undefined` and for nothing else - which is exactly the rule the gate checks
with `label: ""`. `||` would fire for the empty string too, and would be wrong.

The year cannot use a default at all, because the replacement is a string.
Compare it against `undefined` explicitly.

Left to you: destructuring with a default, or `input.label ?? "independent"`.
They are the same rule spelled two ways.

## ex4 - two optional levels deep

`contactLine(playlist)` returns `"<owner name> <<email>>"`, falling back to
`"anonymous"` and `"no email"`. The owner is optional, the contact inside it is
optional, and the email inside that is optional - and a value that is only
whitespace counts as missing.

- `{ name: "Mix" }` -> `"anonymous <no email>"`
- `{ name: "Mix", owner: { name: "Ada", contact: { email: "ada@example.com" } } }` -> `"Ada <ada@example.com>"`

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex4
```

Every hop that might be missing needs its own `?.`. `playlist.owner?.contact.email`
compiles and still throws, because the `?.` only guarded the first hop.

`playlist.owner?.name?.trim()` gives you `string | undefined` in one expression -
`?.` on the string too, because `trim` cannot be called on `undefined`.

Then one truthiness check per half picks the fallback, and the return is a
single template literal with the angle brackets in it.

Left to you: two locals and a template literal, or one long expression. The
first is easier to read out loud, which matters more than it sounds.

## Hint 1

First say what the values are: an object with a `count` and a `seconds`, written
inline in the index signature. `unknown` would force a cast at every read, which

An index signature claims every key is present, so the compiler will not stop

`presentTags(meta)` copies across only those optional members whose value is a
non-empty string once trimmed, and trims the ones it keeps. Everything else -

```ts
if (typeof value === "string" && value.trim() !== "")
```

## Hint 1

Fix the return type first: what comes out is a bag of real strings, so
`Record<string, string>` is the promise you can keep.

Then build a *new* object rather than deleting from a copy - `delete` leaves the
type claiming members the value no longer has.

## Hint 2

`Object.entries(meta)` gives you `[key, value]` pairs whose value type is
`string | undefined`, so you have to narrow before you can trim. One condition
covers both rules:

```ts
if (typeof value === "string" && value.trim() !== "")
```

Left to you: trim once into a local and reuse it, or trim twice. The first is
cheaper and reads better; the second is one line shorter.

exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - flatten a recursive shape

`MetaTree` is an index signature whose values are either a string leaf or
another `MetaTree`. `flattenMeta(tree)` returns a flat `Record<string, string>`
whose keys are the dot-joined paths to each leaf.

- `{ a: { b: "x" }, c: "y" }` -> `{ "a.b": "x", c: "y" }`
- `{ a: {} }` -> `{}`

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An interface may mention itself by name, so
`interface MetaTree { [key: string]: string | MetaTree }` is legal and is the
type you want. Inside the loop, `typeof value === "string"` then narrows the
union to the leaf case and the branch case.

## Hint 2

Carry the path down rather than building objects on the way up. A local helper
`walk(node, prefix)` writes into one accumulator, and the path for a key is
`prefix === "" ? key : prefix + "." + key`.

Only the string case writes anything, which is what makes `{ a: {} }` produce
nothing at all without a special case.

Left to you: a nested arrow function over a shared accumulator, or a helper that
returns a fresh object per level and merges. The first is one allocation.

## Hint 1

An interface may mention itself by name, so
`interface MetaTree { [key: string]: string | MetaTree }` is legal and is the
type you want. Inside the loop, `typeof value === "string"` then narrows the
union to the leaf case and the branch case.

## Hint 2

Carry the path down rather than building objects on the way up. A local helper
`walk(node, prefix)` writes into one accumulator, and the path for a key is
`prefix === "" ? key : prefix + "." + key`.

Only the string case writes anything, which is what makes `{ a: {} }` produce
nothing at all without a special case.

Left to you: a nested arrow function over a shared accumulator, or a helper that
returns a fresh object per level and merges. The first is one allocation.

## ex8 - diff two records

`diffMeta(before, after)` returns `{ added, removed, changed }`, each an
alphabetically sorted array of keys. A key is *changed* when it exists on both
sides with values that are not strictly equal.

- `diffMeta({ a: "1", b: "2", c: "3" }, { b: "2", c: "changed", d: "4" })`
  -> `{ added: ["d"], removed: ["a"], changed: ["c"] }`
- `diffMeta({ n: 1 }, { n: "1" })` -> `{ added: [], removed: [], changed: ["n"] }`

```
uv run dojo test typescript d03_objects_shapes ex8
```

lessons.briefing:
# d04 - Interfaces and type aliases (drill set)

Eight problems on the declaration side of the language: extending an interface,
intersecting two aliases, call and construct signatures, an index signature next
to a named member, declaration merging, and `implements`. They drill lesson
**03_objects_interfaces**; go back to it first if you cannot say what an
interface can do that a `type` cannot.

The type gate is doing most of the marking in this set. Read
`gate.test-d.ts` as part of every prompt.

## ex1 - one interface built on another

`Person` has a `name`. `Player` adds a `rating` and an optional `federation`.
`describePlayer(player)` returns `"<name>, <rating>"`, or
`"<name> (<federation>), <rating>"` when there is a federation. An empty
federation counts as none.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`, where `rating` currently says `unknown`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex1
```

## ex2 - an intersection of two aliases

`Game` is `{ white, black, moves }`. `Timestamped` is `{ createdAt }`.
`GameRecord` is exactly their intersection, and `stamp(game, createdAt)`
produces one without modifying the game it was given.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex2
```

## ex3 - an interface you can call

`Scorer` is callable - `(white: number, black: number) => string`, rendering
`"3-1"` - **and** carries a `label` and a `total` that counts how many times it
has been called. `makeScorer(label)` returns one, and two scorers never share a
count.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. The shipped interface has the two members and no call
signature.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex3
```

## ex4 - an index signature beside a named member

`OpeningStats` has a `total: number` **and** an index signature mapping any
opening name to a count. `topOpening(stats)` returns the most-played opening,
skipping `total`; ties are broken alphabetically, and a table with no openings
returns `""`.

- `{ total: 6, Sicilian: 3, French: 2, London: 1 }` -> `"Sicilian"`
- `{ total: 4, Sicilian: 2, French: 2 }` -> `"French"`
- `{ total: 0 }` -> `""`

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex4
```

## ex5 - declaration merging

The first `ClubConfig` declaration is marked as shipped by a library: leave it
alone. Add a **second** `interface ClubConfig` declaration in the same file
contributing `maxPlayers: number` and `rated: boolean` - two declarations of one
interface merge into a single type, which is the one thing an interface can do
that a `type` alias cannot.

Then `describeClub(config)` returns
`"<name>: up to <maxPlayers> players, <rated|casual>"`.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex5
```

## ex6 - a class that implements an interface

`Ledger` declares `record(white, black, points)`, `pointsFor(player)` and
`standings()`. `points` is what **white** scored (1, 0.5 or 0); black scores
`1 - points`. `pointsFor` returns `0` for a player who has never appeared.
`standings()` is sorted by points descending, then by name ascending.

Declare `ArrayLedger implements Ledger` and make the type gate's
`const ledger: Ledger = new ArrayLedger()` compile.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex6
```

## ex7 - a construct signature

`Clock` is an instance type. Write `ClockConstructor` - the type of a **class**
that produces one from a start time - and `runClock(ctor, startedAt, ticks)`,
which builds an instance, ticks it that many times and returns the last value.
`ticks <= 0` returns `startedAt` unchanged.

`StepClock` is written for you; the gate also passes a class it defines itself,
which is what a construct signature is for.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`, where `ClockConstructor` is currently an ordinary method
signature.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex7
```

## ex8 - the next round of a bracket

`nextRound(round, name)` collects the winners of `round.matches`, in order, and
pairs them: first with second, third with fourth, and so on. An odd winner gets
a bye - a match against `""` with the win already recorded. A match with no
winner sends nobody through. The round you were given must come back untouched.

Both `Match` and `Round` are `readonly` throughout - two modifiers on `Round`,
three on `Match`.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - typescript/d04_interfaces_aliases

The debrief. Per problem: what the declaration was really being marked on, the
mistake that shows up in review, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**The skill this set drills is choosing a declaration form.** `interface` and
`type` overlap for about eighty percent of what you write, and the interesting
questions live in the other twenty: only an interface merges across
declarations and can be `implements`-ed idiomatically; only a `type` can name a
union, a tuple, a conditional or a mapped type. Everything else - optional
members, `readonly`, index signatures, call signatures, extension - both can do,
with different syntax.

**Extending and duplicating produce the same type.** TypeScript is structural,
so `interface Player extends Person { rating: number }` and
`interface Player { name: string; rating: number }` are indistinguishable to the
checker. `extends` is for humans and for keeping one source of truth; the
compiler will not thank you either way. The same is true of `A & B` versus
writing out the members - which is why ex1 and ex2 grade the resulting *shape*
rather than the syntax you used to reach it.

**An interface can describe things that are not plain objects.** A call
signature (`(a: number): string`) makes it callable; a construct signature
(`new (a: number): T`) makes it newable; an index signature makes its key set
open. A "hybrid" interface with a call signature *and* members is how jQuery,
Express and every `debug`-style logger are typed, and it is the shape ex3
drills.

**An index signature has to cover every named member.** `{ total: number;

`number`; add `name: string` and it stops compiling, because the index
signature promised every string key yields a number. That constraint is the
reason real code so often ends up with a nested `counts` object instead.

**And `implements` is a check, not a contract.** It tells the compiler to verify
this class against that interface and changes nothing about the class's own
type, which keeps its extra members and stays structurally usable elsewhere. A
class that satisfies an interface without saying `implements` is still
assignable to it - `implements` just moves the error from the call site to the
declaration, which is where you want it.

## ex1 - one interface built on another

What this was testing: that `extends` gives you the union of both member sets,
that an optional member is `T | undefined` inside the body, and that `unknown`
is never an acceptable placeholder for a type you know.

The classic mistake is `federation !== undefined` for the bracket decision,
which renders `"Grace (), 1500"` for a federation that is present and empty. The
gate includes that case.

The model answer builds the bracketed fragment as its own `const` from a
truthiness check, so the return stays a single template literal and the two
output shapes differ by one interpolation rather than by two branches.

## ex2 - an intersection of two aliases

What this was testing: `A & B` as a way to compose types you do not own, and the
fact that an intersection requires *both* halves - it is not a union and it is
not optional.

The classic mistake is `Object.assign(game, { createdAt })`, which returns the
right type and mutates the caller's object on the way. The gate checks the
game's own key list afterwards for exactly that reason.

The model answer is one spread into a fresh literal, which is also the answer
that keeps working when `Game` grows a member next month.

## ex3 - an interface you can call

What this was testing: a call signature inside an interface, and the fact that
functions are objects and can carry properties. This is the shape of every
"callable with configuration" API you will ever type.

The classic mistake is returning a plain arrow function and assigning the
properties afterwards without telling the type system - which either needs a
cast anyway or leaves the properties invisible. The second-classic is storing
the counter in a variable outside the returned function *and* outside

The model answer builds the function, attaches the members with

storage, not two copies.

## ex4 - an index signature beside a named member

What this was testing: that a named member and an index signature can coexist
only when the named member's type fits the index signature, and that iteration
over such an object hands you the named member too.

What this was testing: the one capability an interface has and a `type` alias
does not. Two `interface Foo` declarations in the same scope merge into one
type with the union of their members; two `type Foo` declarations are a
duplicate-identifier error.

misses the point of the exercise: merging is how you add members to a type you
do not own, which is how `declare global`, module augmentation and every

block below it, because that is exactly the shape of a real augmentation: the
library's declaration stays where it is, yours sits next to it.

What this was testing: writing a class against a declared contract, and the
ordinary bookkeeping of a scores table. `implements Ledger` is what turns a
missing method into an error on the class rather than an error at every call

through to the name when the points are equal.

What this was testing: the difference between the type of an instance and the
type of the class that makes one. `Clock` describes what you get; `new
(startedAt: number) => Clock` describes what you call `new` on, and the two are
never the same type.

class itself - `StepClock` the value is a constructor, not an instance. The

What this was testing: nested `readonly` interfaces and a pairing walk that has

## ex2 - an intersection of two aliases

`Game` is `{ white, black, moves }`. `Timestamped` is `{ createdAt }`.
`GameRecord` is exactly their intersection, and `stamp(game, createdAt)`
produces one without modifying the game it was given.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex2
```

`&` composes two object types into one that has every member of both. It is not
a union and nothing about it is optional - a `GameRecord` needs all four

caller's game on the way, which the gate checks for.

keeps working when `Game` grows a member; the explicit version does not.

## ex3 - an interface you can call

`Scorer` is callable - `(white: number, black: number) => string`, rendering
`"3-1"` - **and** carries a `label` and a `total` that counts how many times it
has been called. `makeScorer(label)` returns one, and two scorers never share a
count.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. The shipped interface has the two members and no call
signature.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A call signature inside an interface has no name and no `function` keyword:

```ts
export interface Scorer {
  (white: number, black: number): string;
  label: string;
  total: number;
}
```

That describes an object that happens to be callable - which every JavaScript
function already is.

## Hint 2

`Object.assign(fn, { label, total: 0 })` attaches the two members to the
function and hands back something that satisfies the whole interface.

The counter has to live on the returned object itself, so the arrow function
increments `scorer.total` through the closure - which is why the `const` is
declared with its type before the assignment rather than after.

Left to you: `Object.assign`, or a cast plus two assignments. Both are honest;
one of them survives someone adding a third member.

exercises.prompt:
## ex4 - an index signature beside a named member

`OpeningStats` has a `total: number` **and** an index signature mapping any
opening name to a count. `topOpening(stats)` returns the most-played opening,
skipping `total`; ties are broken alphabetically, and a table with no openings
returns `""`.

- `{ total: 6, Sicilian: 3, French: 2, London: 1 }` -> `"Sicilian"`
- `{ total: 4, Sicilian: 2, French: 2 }` -> `"French"`
- `{ total: 0 }` -> `""`

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Give the index signature a real value type. It has to be one that `total: number`
also satisfies, or the declaration will not compile at all - which is the
constraint this exercise exists to show you.

## Hint 2

Iterating the object hands you `total` along with the openings, so skip it by

## Hint 1

Write a whole second declaration, not an `extends`:

```ts
export interface ClubConfig {
  maxPlayers: number;
  rated: boolean;
}
```

Both declarations describe the same name, so TypeScript merges them into one
type with all three members. This is how module augmentation and every
`declare global` patch in the ecosystem work.

The function itself is one template literal. Pull the rated wording into a
`const` first so the interpolation stays readable.

Left to you: whether the merged declaration goes above or below the function.
Merging does not care about order - say what you would choose for a reader.

```ts
export interface ClubConfig {
  maxPlayers: number;
  rated: boolean;
}
```

Both declarations describe the same name, so TypeScript merges them into one
type with all three members. This is how module augmentation and every
`declare global` patch in the ecosystem work.

`const` first so the interpolation stays readable.

## ex7 - a construct signature

`Clock` is an instance type. Write `ClockConstructor` - the type of a **class**
that produces one from a start time - and `runClock(ctor, startedAt, ticks)`,
which builds an instance, ticks it that many times and returns the last value.
`ticks <= 0` returns `startedAt` unchanged.

`StepClock` is written for you; the gate also passes a class it defines itself,
which is what a construct signature is for.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`, where `ClockConstructor` is currently an ordinary method
signature.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A construct signature is a member with no name whose keyword is `new`:

```ts
export interface ClockConstructor {
  new (startedAt: number): Clock;
}
```

That is the type of the *class*. `Clock` is the type of what the class produces,
and a parameter typed `Clock` would refuse `StepClock` itself.

## Hint 2

Inside the function, `new ctor(startedAt)` gives you a `Clock`. Seed the result
with `startedAt` so that zero (or a negative) tick count returns it unchanged
without a special branch.

Left to you: a `for` loop or a `while`. Neither is interesting - what is
interesting is that you can explain why `typeof StepClock` would have been the
wrong parameter type.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A construct signature is a member with no name whose keyword is `new`:

```ts
export interface ClockConstructor {
  new (startedAt: number): Clock;
}
```

That is the type of the *class*. `Clock` is the type of what the class produces,
and a parameter typed `Clock` would refuse `StepClock` itself.

## Hint 2

Inside the function, `new ctor(startedAt)` gives you a `Clock`. Seed the result
with `startedAt` so that zero (or a negative) tick count returns it unchanged
without a special branch.

Left to you: a `for` loop or a `while`. Neither is interesting - what is
interesting is that you can explain why `typeof StepClock` would have been the
wrong parameter type.

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - the next round of a bracket

`nextRound(round, name)` collects the winners of `round.matches`, in order, and
pairs them: first with second, third with fourth, and so on. An odd winner gets
a bye - a match against `""` with the win already recorded. A match with no
winner sends nobody through. The round you were given must come back untouched.

Both `Match` and `Round` are `readonly` throughout - two modifiers on `Round`,
three on `Match`.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d04_interfaces_aliases ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Start with the modifiers. `readonly matches: readonly Match[]` is the pair
people miss: the first stops the property being reassigned, the second stops the
array being pushed to. The type gate has one `@ts-expect-error` for each.

## Hint 2

Two passes. First collect the winners into an array, in match order, skipping
any match whose `winner` is `undefined`. Then walk that array two at a time.

When the second index is past the end you have an odd winner: emit a match
against `""` with the `winner` already set, because there is nobody to play.

Left to you: `i += 2` over an index, or repeatedly `splice`-ing pairs off a
copy. The first does not allocate; the second reads like the bracket looks.

## Hint 1

Start with the modifiers. `readonly matches: readonly Match[]` is the pair
people miss: the first stops the property being reassigned, the second stops the
array being pushed to. The type gate has one `@ts-expect-error` for each.

## Hint 2

Two passes. First collect the winners into an array, in match order, skipping
any match whose `winner` is `undefined`. Then walk that array two at a time.

When the second index is past the end you have an odd winner: emit a match
against `""` with the `winner` already set, because there is nobody to play.

Left to you: `i += 2` over an index, or repeatedly `splice`-ing pairs off a
copy. The first does not allocate; the second reads like the bracket looks.

# d05 - Unions, the basics (drill set)

Eight problems on plain unions - the ones you get handed rather than the ones
you design. They drill lesson **04_unions_narrowing**, first half; go back there
if "the members you can touch are the intersection" does not ring a bell.

Everything here is a spreadsheet importer: cells that might be text, might be a
number, might be nothing at all.

## ex1 - how wide is this cell

`cellWidth(value)` measures a `string | number`. A string is measured after
trimming; a number is measured in **digits**, so the sign and the decimal point
do not count.

- `cellWidth("  hi  ")` -> `2`, `cellWidth("")` -> `0`
- `cellWidth(1234)` -> `4`, `cellWidth(0)` -> `1`
- `cellWidth(-12.5)` -> `3`, `cellWidth(-0.5)` -> `2`

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`, where the parameter union has one member too many.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d05_unions_basics ex1
```

## ex2 - render a cell

`toCellText(value)` takes `string | number | null` and returns text. `null` is a
dash; a number renders as itself; a string is trimmed, and a string that is
empty after trimming is also a dash.

- `toCellText(null)` -> `"-"`, `toCellText("   ")` -> `"-"`
- `toCellText(0)` -> `"0"`, `toCellText("  a ")` -> `"a"`

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d05_unions_basics ex2
```

## ex3 - add up only the numbers

`sumNumeric(values)` takes `readonly (string | number)[]` and returns the sum of
the members that really are numbers. A numeric-looking string is still a string.

- `[1, "2", 3]` -> `4`, `["a", "b"]` -> `0`, `[]` -> `0`

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d05_unions_basics ex3
```

## ex4 - one union array, two narrow arrays

`splitCells(values)` returns `{ texts: string[], numbers: number[] }`, each in
input order. Both arrays are always present, even when empty.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`, where the return type is still the union on both sides.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d05_unions_basics ex4
```

## ex5 - two kinds of id

`Id` is `string | number`. `idKey(id)` renders `"n:12"` for the number `12` and
`"s:12"` for the string `"12"`, and `sameId(a, b)` is true only when the keys
match - so `sameId(12, "12")` is `false`.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d05_unions_basics ex5
```

## ex6 - drop the nothings

`compact(values)` takes `readonly (string | null | undefined)[]` and returns
`string[]`, keeping every string - **including** the empty one - and dropping
only `null` and `undefined`.

- `["a", null, "", undefined, "b"]` -> `["a", "", "b"]`

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d05_unions_basics ex6
```

## ex7 - parse a row into cells

`Cell` is `string | number | boolean | null`. `parseCells(row)` splits on commas,
trims each field, and classifies it:

1. empty after trimming -> `null`
2. exactly `"true"` or `"false"` -> the boolean
3. a finite number -> that number
4. anything else -> the trimmed text

- `"a,1,true,,3.5"` -> `["a", 1, true, null, 3.5]`
- `" x , FALSE "` -> `["x", "FALSE"]`
- `""` -> `[null]`

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d05_unions_basics ex7
```

## ex8 - what kind is each column

`ColumnKind` is `"empty" | "string" | "number" | "boolean" | "mixed"`.
`columnKinds(rows)` reports one kind per column, where the number of columns is
the longest row. Null cells (and cells missing from a short row) are ignored; a
column with nothing but those is `"empty"`; a column whose non-null cells are
all one kind is that kind; anything else is `"mixed"`.

- `[[1, "a", null], [2, "b", true]]` -> `["number", "string", "boolean"]`
- `[[1, null], ["x", null]]` -> `["mixed", "empty"]`
- `[[1], [2, "x"]]` -> `["number", "string"]`

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d05_unions_basics ex8
```

# Reading - typescript/d05_unions_basics

The debrief. Per problem: what the union was really testing, the mistake most
people make, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**The skill this set drills is reading a union as a set of possible values.**
`string | number` is not "a thing that is sort of both" - it is "exactly one of
these, and I do not know which". That is why only the members both types share
are available before you narrow, and why every one of these eight problems
begins with a question that identifies which member you have.

**Widening the union is the expensive direction.** Six of these eight functions
would still compile if you added `boolean` or `undefined` to their parameter
type, and every one of them would be worse for it - because a union is a
promise to handle every member, and each new member is a new branch you owe the
caller. The type gate checks the exact unions for that reason: a parameter type
that accepts more than the function handles is a bug waiting for its input.

**`null` and `undefined` are ordinary members.** With `strictNullChecks` on,
`string | null` narrows with `=== null`, `!= null` or a truthiness check, and
the three are not the same: truthiness also removes `""`, which ex6 exists to
punish. `value != null` with the loose `!=` is the one place the style guides
forgive you, because it excludes both nullish values in a single check.

**Coercion is not narrowing.** `Number("2")` turns a string into a number, but
it does not tell you the value *was* a number - and ex3 and ex7 disagree
deliberately about whether the text `"2"` counts. Deciding that question at the
boundary, once, and writing the rule down is most of what a real importer does.

**And the useful shape of a union answer is often several narrow values rather
than one wide one.** ex4 turns one `(string | number)[]` into two clean arrays;
ex8 collapses a column of mixed cells into one label. Both are the same move:
do the narrowing once, at the edge, so nothing downstream has to ask again.

## ex1 - how wide is this cell

What this was testing: `typeof` narrowing on the simplest possible union, and
noticing that the two members need genuinely different arithmetic - a string is
measured in characters, a number in digits.

The classic mistake is `String(value).length` for both, which is right for
strings and wrong for `-12.5`, where the sign and the point are not digits. The
gate includes `-0.5` as well, because dropping the leading zero is the
over-correction.

The model answer narrows with `typeof value === "string"`, returns early, and
then treats the remaining branch as a number - `Math.abs` then removing the
decimal point, which is one line and says what it does.

## ex2 - render a cell

What this was testing: three members where two of them collapse to the same
output. `null` and a blank string are both "empty cell", but they are different
types and only one of them can be trimmed.

The classic mistake is `if (!value) return "-"`, which is short, handles `null`
and `""` in one go, and also swallows `0` - and `0` is a real value that must
render as `"0"`. The gate checks it.

The model answer removes `null` first with an explicit `=== null`, then handles
the number branch, and only then trims - so the truthiness question is asked of
a value that is definitely a string, where it means what you want.

## ex3 - add up only the numbers

What this was testing: that narrowing is a *question about the type*, not a
conversion. `typeof value === "number"` keeps the members that are numbers;
`Number(value)` would manufacture numbers out of strings, which the prompt
explicitly does not want.

The classic mistake is `values.reduce((a, b) => a + Number(b), 0)`, which turns
`"2"` into `2` and `"a"` into `NaN`, and `NaN` then poisons the whole sum.

The model answer is one loop with one `typeof` guard, because the alternative -
`values.filter((v) => typeof v === "number")` - only narrows the element type in
TypeScript 5.5 and later, which is worth knowing but is not something to rely on
in an interview without saying so.

## ex4 - one union array, two narrow arrays

What this was testing: doing the narrowing once and keeping the result. After
the `typeof` check, `push` into a `string[]` is allowed, which is exactly the
payoff - the two output arrays are narrow, so nothing downstream has to ask
again.

The classic mistake is two `filter` passes with casts (`as string[]`), which
works and lies: the cast is doing the job the narrowing should have done, and it
will keep compiling after someone widens the input union.

The model answer walks once and pushes into whichever array the guard selected,
so both arrays are built in input order for free and the `else` branch is
narrowed to `number` without being asked.

## ex5 - two kinds of id

What this was testing: that two members of a union can look identical once
rendered, and that "the same id" is a decision you make rather than one the
language makes for you. `12` and `"12"` compare equal with `==` and unequal with
`===`, and neither answer is automatically right.

The classic mistake is `String(a) === String(b)`, which quietly declares the
number `12` and the text `"12"` to be the same id. That is a defensible design
in some systems - but the prompt asked for the other one, and the gate says so.

The model answer tags the key with the member it came from, which is the same
trick a database uses for a polymorphic foreign key and the same one a
discriminated union will formalise in d07.

## ex6 - drop the nothings

What this was testing: the difference between "nullish" and "falsy". `null` and
`undefined` go; `""` stays; and exactly one of the obvious one-liners gets that
right.

The classic mistake is `values.filter(Boolean)`, which is idiomatic, reads well
and drops the empty string - and, in TypeScript, does not narrow the element
type either, so you end up casting on top of a bug.

The model answer tests `value !== null && value !== undefined` (or the single
`!= null`), which keeps every string and narrows the element type honestly.

## ex7 - parse a row into cells

What this was testing: writing the classification rules down in an order where
each one can assume the earlier ones failed. Order is the whole design: empty
first, then the two literal booleans, then numbers, then text as the fallback.

The classic mistake is checking numbers before booleans (harmless here) or
using `Boolean(text)` for the boolean case, which turns `"false"` into `true`
and every non-empty string into a boolean cell.

The model answer trims once, returns from each rule as it matches, and uses
`Number.isFinite(Number(text))` for the numeric test - because `Number("")` is
`0` and `Number("x")` is `NaN`, and only one of those has already been handled.

## ex8 - what kind is each column

What this was testing: folding a column of union values into a single label,
where the fold has three states - nothing seen yet, one kind seen, more than one
kind seen. That is a tiny state machine, and writing it as one is the answer.

The classic mistake is deciding the column from its first non-null cell, which
is right for the first two cases and silently wrong for the mixed one. The
second-classic is using `rows[0].length` as the width, which is wrong for ragged
input and throws for no rows at all.

The model answer computes the width as the longest row, then walks each column
with a `kind` that starts at `"empty"`, becomes the first kind it sees, and
latches to `"mixed"` the moment a second one shows up.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Union Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#union-types) - what a union means and why only shared members are available before narrowing.
- [Handbook: Narrowing with typeof](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#typeof-type-guards) - the guard behind six of these eight problems, and the `typeof null` wart.
- [Handbook: Truthiness narrowing](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#truthiness-narrowing) - exactly which values a truthiness check removes, which is the ex2 and ex6 trap.
- [MDN: Nullish coalescing operator](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Nullish_coalescing) - nullish against falsy, with the table worth memorising.
- [MDN: Number.isFinite](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Number/isFinite) - and how it differs from the global `isFinite`, which coerces first.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## ex1 - how wide is this cell

`cellWidth(value)` measures a `string | number`. A string is measured after
trimming; a number is measured in **digits**, so the sign and the decimal point
do not count.

- `cellWidth("  hi  ")` -> `2`, `cellWidth("")` -> `0`
- `cellWidth(1234)` -> `4`, `cellWidth(0)` -> `1`
- `cellWidth(-12.5)` -> `3`, `cellWidth(-0.5)` -> `2`

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`, where the parameter union has one member too many.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d05_unions_basics ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

First narrow the parameter type to the two members this function actually
handles. A union that admits a `boolean` is a promise to render one.

Then note the two measurements are genuinely different: characters for a string,
digits for a number.

## Hint 2

`typeof value === "string"` narrows, and an early `return` leaves the rest of
the body knowing it has a number.

For the number: drop the sign with `Math.abs`, render it, and remove the decimal
point before counting - `String(Math.abs(value)).replace(".", "").length`.

Left to you: `replace(".", "")` or a regular expression that keeps only digits.
They agree for ordinary numbers and disagree for `1e21` - decide whether you
care.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - render a cell

`toCellText(value)` takes `string | number | null` and returns text. `null` is a
dash; a number renders as itself; a string is trimmed, and a string that is
empty after trimming is also a dash.

- `toCellText(null)` -> `"-"`, `toCellText("   ")` -> `"-"`
- `toCellText(0)` -> `"0"`, `toCellText("  a ")` -> `"a"`

## ex5 - two kinds of id

`Id` is `string | number`. `idKey(id)` renders `"n:12"` for the number `12` and
`"s:12"` for the string `"12"`, and `sameId(a, b)` is true only when the keys
match - so `sameId(12, "12")` is `false`.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d05_unions_basics ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Trim the union to the two members the importer really has. Then notice the
problem `idKey` exists to solve: `String(12)` and `String("12")` are the same
text, so a key built from the value alone cannot tell the two ids apart.

## Hint 2

Put the member into the key. A one-character tag is enough - `n:` for the
number branch and `s:` for the string branch - and `typeof id === "number"`

## Hint 1

The return type is the promise: `string[]`. Nothing that comes out is nullish,
so nothing in the type should be either.

Then the trap: `""` is falsy and is not nullish, and the gate keeps it.

## Hint 2

`values.filter(Boolean)` reads beautifully, drops the empty string, and does not
narrow the element type - two bugs in one idiom.

`value !== null && value !== undefined` narrows honestly. So does the single
loose check `value != null`, which is the one place `!=` is idiomatic.

Left to you: `!= null` or the two strict checks. The short one needs a comment
in most teams; the long one does not.

## ex7 - parse a row into cells

`Cell` is `string | number | boolean | null`. `parseCells(row)` splits on commas,
trims each field, and classifies it:

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - what kind is each column

`ColumnKind` is `"empty" | "string" | "number" | "boolean" | "mixed"`.
`columnKinds(rows)` reports one kind per column, where the number of columns is
the longest row. Null cells (and cells missing from a short row) are ignored; a
column with nothing but those is `"empty"`; a column whose non-null cells are
all one kind is that kind; anything else is `"mixed"`.

- `[[1, "a", null], [2, "b", true]]` -> `["number", "string", "boolean"]`
- `[[1, null], ["x", null]]` -> `["mixed", "empty"]`
- `[[1], [2, "x"]]` -> `["number", "string"]`

```
uv run dojo test typescript d05_unions_basics ex8
```

`ColumnKind` is five literal strings joined by `|`. Writing it as `string` means
a typo in your own code compiles - which is exactly what the type gate objects
to.

Each column is a tiny fold with three states. Start at `"empty"`. The first
non-null cell sets the kind. Any later cell of a different kind latches it to

Treat a cell that is past the end of a short row exactly like a `null`, so
ragged input needs no separate branch.

Left to you: collect each column into an array first and classify it, or fold as
you walk. The fold allocates nothing; the collect version is easier to test in
pieces.

## Hint 1

`ColumnKind` is five literal strings joined by `|`. Writing it as `string` means
a typo in your own code compiles - which is exactly what the type gate objects
to.

Then: the number of columns is the length of the *longest* row, not of the
first one, and not of any row when there are no rows at all.

## Hint 2

Each column is a tiny fold with three states. Start at `"empty"`. The first
non-null cell sets the kind. Any later cell of a different kind latches it to
`"mixed"`, and nothing can move it back.

Treat a cell that is past the end of a short row exactly like a `null`, so
ragged input needs no separate branch.

Left to you: collect each column into an array first and classify it, or fold as
you walk. The fold allocates nothing; the collect version is easier to test in
pieces.

# d06 - Narrowing and guards (drill set)

Eight problems on proving what a value is: `typeof`, `instanceof`,
`Array.isArray`, user-defined type predicates and assertion functions. They
drill lessons **04_unions_narrowing** and **10_guards_assertions**; redo those
first if `value is T` and `asserts value is T` blur together.

Everything here is the boundary of a system - JSON that arrived from somewhere,
configuration nobody typed, values whose only honest type is `unknown`.

## ex1 - is this text

`isNonEmptyString(value)` is a type predicate over `unknown`. It is true only
for a string with something other than whitespace in it.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`, where the return type is a plain `boolean` and so tells
the caller nothing.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d06_narrowing_guards ex1
```

## ex2 - what is this, exactly

`ValueKind` is `"string" | "number" | "boolean" | "undefined" | "null" |
"array" | "object" | "function"`, and `kindOf(value)` returns the right one.
`typeof null` is `"object"` and `typeof []` is `"object"`, so both need their
own check.

- `kindOf(null)` -> `"null"`, `kindOf([1])` -> `"array"`, `kindOf(NaN)` -> `"number"`

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d06_narrowing_guards ex2
```

## ex3 - is this a point

`isPoint(value)` is a type predicate for `{ x: number; y: number }`. Extra
members are fine; a missing one, a wrong type, `null` and an array are not.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d06_narrowing_guards ex3
```

## ex4 - assert, do not ask

`assertIsRecord(value)` returns nothing and **throws** `"expected a plain
object"` for `null`, arrays and every primitive. After it returns, the caller's
value is narrowed to `Record<string, unknown>` for the rest of the scope - which
is what `asserts value is T` buys you and a `boolean` does not.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d06_narrowing_guards ex4
```

## ex5 - three ways to spell a timestamp

`toMillis(value)` takes `number | string | Date`:

- a number is already milliseconds
- a `Date` gives up its `getTime()`
- a string of digits (after trimming) is a millisecond count
- any other string is parsed as a date, and a string that is neither throws
  a message containing `cannot read a timestamp`

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`, where the parameter union has a member too many.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d06_narrowing_guards ex5
```

## ex6 - a guard that filters

`Tag` is `{ name: string; weight: number }`. Write `isTag(value)` as a type
predicate, then `collectTags(values)` over `readonly unknown[]` returns `Tag[]`
- and the guard is what makes that return type honest without a cast.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d06_narrowing_guards ex6
```

## ex7 - read a config nobody typed

`readConfig(raw)` turns `unknown` into a `Config` of `{ host, port, tls }`, or
throws on the **first** problem, in this order:

1. not a plain object -> `"config: expected an object"`
2. `host` missing, not a string, or blank -> `"config: host must be a non-empty string"`
3. `port` not a positive integer -> `"config: port must be a positive integer"`
4. `tls` not a boolean -> `"config: tls must be a boolean"`

The host is trimmed on the way out, and members the config does not declare are
dropped.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`, whose return type is currently `unknown`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d06_narrowing_guards ex7
```

## ex8 - flatten a recursive union

`TextNode` is `string | number | readonly TextNode[]`. `flattenText(node)`
renders it as one line: strings are trimmed, numbers stringified, arrays walked
depth-first, and pieces that come out empty contribute nothing - so there are
never two spaces in a row.

- `flattenText(["a", ["b", 2], "c"])` -> `"a b 2 c"`
- `flattenText(["", "a", ["", ""], "b"])` -> `"a b"`

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d06_narrowing_guards ex8
```

# Reading - typescript/d06_narrowing_guards

The debrief. Per problem: what the guard was really testing, the mistake that
gets past review, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**The skill this set drills is turning a runtime check into a compile-time
fact.** Control flow analysis already does this inside a function - a `typeof`
test refines the type for the lines that follow - but it stops dead at a
function boundary. `value is T` and `asserts value is T` are the two ways to
carry the conclusion across that boundary, and choosing between them is the
recurring question here.

**A predicate answers, an assertion insists.** `isPoint(value): value is Point`
returns a boolean and narrows inside the branch you write. `assertIsRecord(value):
asserts value is Record<string, unknown>` returns nothing, throws on failure, and
narrows the rest of the enclosing scope. Use a predicate when the caller has
something sensible to do with `false`; use an assertion when they do not.

**Both are promises the compiler does not check.** A predicate whose body
returns `true` unconditionally compiles fine and lies to every caller forever.
That is the price of the feature, and it is why a guard is one of the few places
where a unit test earns its keep even in a strongly typed codebase - which is
exactly what this drill set is.

**`typeof` has two famous holes and you will hit both.** `typeof null === "object"`
and `typeof [] === "object"`, so any "is this a plain object" check needs three
clauses: the `typeof`, an explicit `!== null`, and `!Array.isArray(value)`.
ex2, ex3, ex4 and ex7 all turn on that trio.

**And `unknown` is the honest type for data from outside.** It is `any` with the
safety on: you may hold it, pass it and store it, and you may not read a
property or call it until you have proved something. Every `JSON.parse`,
`process.env` lookup and request body in a serious codebase starts as `unknown`
and ends up narrowed by a function that looks like one of these eight.

## ex1 - is this text

What this was testing: the difference between `boolean` and `value is string` in
a return type. The runtime behaviour is identical; the type gate is the only
thing that can tell them apart, which is the point being made.

The classic mistake is `typeof value === "string" && value.length > 0`, which
accepts `"   "`. The prompt and the gate both call a whitespace-only string
empty, because that is what a form field or a CSV cell means by it.

The model answer is one expression: the `typeof` check first (so `.trim()` is
safe), then the emptiness test on the trimmed value.

## ex2 - what is this, exactly

What this was testing: knowing the shape of `typeof`'s answer set and where it
lies. Eight labels, and two of them - `"null"` and `"array"` - do not come from
`typeof` at all.

The classic mistake is checking `Array.isArray` after the `typeof === "object"`
branch has already returned `"object"`; order matters, and the two special cases
have to be tested before the general one.

The model answer returns `"null"` and `"array"` from explicit checks at the top
and then falls through to `typeof`, whose remaining answers happen to be exactly
the six labels that are left - which is also why the return type is a literal
union rather than `string`.

## ex3 - is this a point

What this was testing: a structural guard over `unknown`, and the property
access problem that comes with it - you cannot read `value.x` until you have
proved `value` is an object, and even then TypeScript does not know `x` exists.

The classic mistake is `typeof value === "object" && typeof value.x === "number"`,
which does not compile, followed by `value as Point` to make it compile - which
throws the check away entirely, since the cast is what you were trying to
justify.

The model answer casts once to a `{ x?: unknown; y?: unknown }` shape (or
indexes through `Record<string, unknown>`) after establishing the value is a
non-null object, then checks both members with `typeof`. One documented cast,
inside the guard, is the accepted answer.

## ex4 - assert, do not ask

What this was testing: the `asserts` return type, and the fact that its
narrowing applies to everything after the call rather than to a branch. The type
gate calls it and then checks the type on the very next line.

The classic mistake is writing the body as `if (ok) return true` - an assertion
function returns `void` and communicates by throwing. The second-classic is
forgetting `Array.isArray`, because an array is genuinely a `Record<string,
unknown>` structurally and almost never what "a plain object" means.

The model answer is one negated condition and one `throw`, which is also why
assertion functions read so well at the top of a request handler: three lines of
preamble and the rest of the function is typed.

## ex5 - three ways to spell a timestamp

What this was testing: `instanceof` alongside `typeof`, and the ordering that
makes them cooperate. `typeof new Date()` is `"object"`, so the `Date` branch has
to be an `instanceof`, and it is cheapest to take it first.

The classic mistake is `Number(value)` for the whole string branch: `Number("2026-03-01")`
is `NaN`, so every ISO date falls into the error path. Splitting the string case
into "digits" and "everything else" is the fix.

The model answer checks `Date` first, then `number`, then treats the remaining
string in two steps - and it is worth knowing that `instanceof` fails across
realms (an iframe, a worker, Node's `vm`), which is why library code often adds a
duck-typed fallback.

## ex6 - a guard that filters

What this was testing: that `Array.prototype.filter` has an overload taking a
type predicate, so `values.filter(isTag)` returns `Tag[]` with no cast. That
overload is the single most useful consequence of writing guards.

The classic mistake is `values.filter((v) => isTag(v))`, which wraps the
predicate in an arrow whose return type is plain `boolean` - and the narrowing
is lost. Pass the guard itself.

The model answer is one line in `collectTags`, which is the whole argument for
putting the work in the guard: the interesting code is written once and reused
by `filter`, `find`, `some` and every `if` in the codebase.

## ex7 - read a config nobody typed

What this was testing: an ordered validation walk over `unknown`, where each
check both rejects bad input and narrows the value for the next one. This is
what every `zod`-style library is doing under the hood.

The classic mistake is checking the fields in a different order than the prompt
states, which passes four assertions and fails one - the gate deliberately hands
`{}` to prove `host` is checked first. The second-classic is spreading `raw`
into the result, which copies members the config never declared.

The model answer narrows to a `Record<string, unknown>` once, then validates
each field with a `typeof` plus a domain rule (non-blank, positive integer), and
builds a fresh object from the three values it proved - so the returned `Config`
contains only what it promises.

## ex8 - flatten a recursive union

What this was testing: a type alias that refers to itself through an array, and
a walk with three cases where two are leaves. `type TextNode = string | number |
readonly TextNode[]` is legal because the recursion goes through an array type.

The classic mistake is joining with `" "` unconditionally, which produces double
spaces for empty children - `["", "a"]` becoming `" a"`. Filter the empty pieces
out before joining, not after.

The model answer returns early for the two leaf cases and, for the array case,
collects the non-empty renderings of the children and joins them once - so
`[[[["deep"]]]]` costs four frames and no string concatenation until the end.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Narrowing](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html) - `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, truthiness and control flow analysis in one page.
- [Handbook: Using type predicates](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#using-type-predicates) - the `value is T` return type and the `filter` overload that makes ex6 one line.
- [Handbook: Assertion functions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-7.html#assertion-functions) - `asserts value is T`, and the annotation rule that makes it work only for declared names.
- [MDN: typeof](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/typeof) - the complete answer table, including the two holes ex2 exists for.
- [MDN: Date.parse](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date/parse) - what is specified (ISO 8601) and what is implementation-defined.

That is the price of the feature, and it is why a guard is one of the few places
where a unit test earns its keep even in a strongly typed codebase - which is
exactly what this drill set is.

**`typeof` has two famous holes and you will hit both.** `typeof null === "object"`
and `typeof [] === "object"`, so any "is this a plain object" check needs three
clauses: the `typeof`, an explicit `!== null`, and `!Array.isArray(value)`.
ex2, ex3, ex4 and ex7 all turn on that trio.

**And `unknown` is the honest type for data from outside.** It is `any` with the
safety on: you may hold it, pass it and store it, and you may not read a
property or call it until you have proved something. Every `JSON.parse`,
`process.env` lookup and request body in a serious codebase starts as `unknown`
and ends up narrowed by a function that looks like one of these eight.

## ex1 - is this text

What this was testing: the difference between `boolean` and `value is string` in
a return type. The runtime behaviour is identical; the type gate is the only
thing that can tell them apart, which is the point being made.

The classic mistake is `typeof value === "string" && value.length > 0`, which
accepts `"   "`. The prompt and the gate both call a whitespace-only string
empty, because that is what a form field or a CSV cell means by it.

The model answer is one expression: the `typeof` check first (so `.trim()` is
safe), then the emptiness test on the trimmed value.

## ex2 - what is this, exactly

What this was testing: knowing the shape of `typeof`'s answer set and where it
lies. Eight labels, and two of them - `"null"` and `"array"` - do not come from
`typeof` at all.

The classic mistake is checking `Array.isArray` after the `typeof === "object"`
branch has already returned `"object"`; order matters, and the two special cases
have to be tested before the general one.

The model answer returns `"null"` and `"array"` from explicit checks at the top
and then falls through to `typeof`, whose remaining answers happen to be exactly
the six labels that are left - which is also why the return type is a literal
union rather than `string`.

## ex3 - is this a point

What this was testing: a structural guard over `unknown`, and the property
access problem that comes with it - you cannot read `value.x` until you have
proved `value` is an object, and even then TypeScript does not know `x` exists.

The classic mistake is `typeof value === "object" && typeof value.x === "number"`,
which does not compile, followed by `value as Point` to make it compile - which
throws the check away entirely, since the cast is what you were trying to
justify.

The model answer casts once to a `{ x?: unknown; y?: unknown }` shape (or
indexes through `Record<string, unknown>`) after establishing the value is a
non-null object, then checks both members with `typeof`. One documented cast,
inside the guard, is the accepted answer.

## ex4 - assert, do not ask

What this was testing: the `asserts` return type, and the fact that its
narrowing applies to everything after the call rather than to a branch. The type
gate calls it and then checks the type on the very next line.

The classic mistake is writing the body as `if (ok) return true` - an assertion
function returns `void` and communicates by throwing. The second-classic is
forgetting `Array.isArray`, because an array is genuinely a `Record<string,
unknown>` structurally and almost never what "a plain object" means.

The model answer is one negated condition and one `throw`, which is also why
assertion functions read so well at the top of a request handler: three lines of
preamble and the rest of the function is typed.

## ex5 - three ways to spell a timestamp

What this was testing: `instanceof` alongside `typeof`, and the ordering that
makes them cooperate. `typeof new Date()` is `"object"`, so the `Date` branch has
to be an `instanceof`, and it is cheapest to take it first.

The classic mistake is `Number(value)` for the whole string branch: `Number("2026-03-01")`
is `NaN`, so every ISO date falls into the error path. Splitting the string case
into "digits" and "everything else" is the fix.

The model answer checks `Date` first, then `number`, then treats the remaining
string in two steps - and it is worth knowing that `instanceof` fails across
realms (an iframe, a worker, Node's `vm`), which is why library code often adds a
duck-typed fallback.

## ex6 - a guard that filters

What this was testing: that `Array.prototype.filter` has an overload taking a
type predicate, so `values.filter(isTag)` returns `Tag[]` with no cast. That
overload is the single most useful consequence of writing guards.

The classic mistake is `values.filter((v) => isTag(v))`, which wraps the
predicate in an arrow whose return type is plain `boolean` - and the narrowing
is lost. Pass the guard itself.

The model answer is one line in `collectTags`, which is the whole argument for
putting the work in the guard: the interesting code is written once and reused
by `filter`, `find`, `some` and every `if` in the codebase.

## ex7 - read a config nobody typed

What this was testing: an ordered validation walk over `unknown`, where each
check both rejects bad input and narrows the value for the next one. This is
what every `zod`-style library is doing under the hood.

The classic mistake is checking the fields in a different order than the prompt
states, which passes four assertions and fails one - the gate deliberately hands
`{}` to prove `host` is checked first. The second-classic is spreading `raw`
into the result, which copies members the config never declared.

The model answer narrows to a `Record<string, unknown>` once, then validates
each field with a `typeof` plus a domain rule (non-blank, positive integer), and
builds a fresh object from the three values it proved - so the returned `Config`
contains only what it promises.

## ex8 - flatten a recursive union

What this was testing: a type alias that refers to itself through an array, and
a walk with three cases where two are leaves. `type TextNode = string | number |
readonly TextNode[]` is legal because the recursion goes through an array type.

The classic mistake is joining with `" "` unconditionally, which produces double
spaces for empty children - `["", "a"]` becoming `" a"`. Filter the empty pieces
out before joining, not after.

The model answer returns early for the two leaf cases and, for the array case,
collects the non-empty renderings of the children and joins them once - so
`[[[["deep"]]]]` costs four frames and no string concatenation until the end.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Narrowing](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html) - `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, truthiness and control flow analysis in one page.
- [Handbook: Using type predicates](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#using-type-predicates) - the `value is T` return type and the `filter` overload that makes ex6 one line.
- [Handbook: Assertion functions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-7.html#assertion-functions) - `asserts value is T`, and the annotation rule that makes it work only for declared names.
- [MDN: typeof](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/typeof) - the complete answer table, including the two holes ex2 exists for.
- [MDN: Date.parse](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Date/parse) - what is specified (ISO 8601) and what is implementation-defined.

here; one of them reads like the sentence in the prompt.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The return type is the exercise: `value is string` instead of `boolean`. Both
return `true` or `false` at runtime; only one of them narrows for the caller,
and the type gate checks exactly that.

## Hint 2

The body is a single `&&`. The `typeof` check has to come first, because
`.trim()` cannot be called on an `unknown` - and because `&&` short-circuits,
the second half only runs once the first has proved the type.

Left to you: `value.trim() !== ""` or `value.trim().length > 0`. Identical
here; one of them reads like the sentence in the prompt.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - what is this, exactly

`ValueKind` is `"string" | "number" | "boolean" | "undefined" | "null" |
"array" | "object" | "function"`, and `kindOf(value)` returns the right one.
`typeof null` is `"object"` and `typeof []` is `"object"`, so both need their
own check.

- `kindOf(null)` -> `"null"`, `kindOf([1])` -> `"array"`, `kindOf(NaN)` -> `"number"`

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d06_narrowing_guards ex2
```
