exercises.prompt:
## ex3 - a tally with declared buckets

`tally(keys, values)` returns a `Record<K, number>` with **every** declared key
present, counting how many times each appears in `values`. A value that is not a
declared key is ignored.

- `tally(["a", "b"], ["a", "a", "c"])` -> `{ a: 2, b: 0 }`

The buckets come from `keys`, so `K` must stay a union of literals rather than
widening to `string`.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d10_generic_constraints ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Return `Record<K, number>`, not `Record<string, number>`. `K extends string` is
what makes inference keep `"a" | "b"` instead of widening to `string`, and the
whole point of the exercise is that the result type names its own buckets.

## Hint 2

`const counts: Record<K, number> = {}` will not compile - an empty object is not
a complete record. `{} as Record<K, number>` is the accepted cast, and it is
honest because the next loop fills every key.

Seed all the declared buckets at zero *before* counting; that is what makes
`b: 0` appear and an unlisted value get ignored.

Left to you: how to test membership - `value in counts`, or a `Set` built from
the keys. One of them needs a cast at the increment; the other does not.

## Hint 1

Return `Record<K, number>`, not `Record<string, number>`. `K extends string` is
what makes inference keep `"a" | "b"` instead of widening to `string`, and the
whole point of the exercise is that the result type names its own buckets.

## Hint 2

`const counts: Record<K, number> = {}` will not compile - an empty object is not
a complete record. `{} as Record<K, number>` is the accepted cast, and it is
honest because the next loop fills every key.

Seed all the declared buckets at zero *before* counting; that is what makes
`b: 0` appear and an unlisted value get ignored.

Left to you: how to test membership - `value in counts`, or a `Set` built from
the keys. One of them needs a cast at the increment; the other does not.

## ex4 - defaults under a value

`withDefaults(value, defaults)` returns `T & D`: every member of `defaults`,
overridden by every member of `value`. Neither argument is modified, and a
supplied `0` beats a default.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.


One spread expression does the work, and the order is the behaviour: defaults

## Hint 1

A default goes after the constraint: `K extends string | number = string`. That
is what makes `makeCache<number>()` legal with one type argument while
`makeCache<string, number>()` still lets a caller choose numeric keys.

Note the parameter order: the one you want to default comes last.

## Hint 2

The storage is a `Map<K, V>` declared inside `makeCache`, so every call gets its
own - the gate builds two caches and checks they do not share.

The four methods are one-line delegates to that map.

Left to you: an object literal of arrow functions, or a class. The literal keeps
`this` out of the conversation entirely.

exercises.prompt:
## ex6 - group into a Map

`groupToMap(items, groupOf)` returns `Map<G, T[]>`, where `G` is constrained to
`string | number` - the things that make sensible keys. Groups appear in
first-seen order and each list keeps input order.

- `groupToMap(["a", "bb", "cc"], (w) => w.length)` -> `Map { 1 => ["a"], 2 => ["bb", "cc"] }`

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d10_generic_constraints ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two type parameters that are unrelated: `T` is what is in the list, `G` is what
the callback returns. Only `G` is constrained, and only because it has to be
usable as a key.

Return `Map<G, T[]>`.

## Hint 2

Ask the map for the bucket once. If it is missing, `set` a new one-element
array; otherwise push. That single lookup is also what gives you first-seen
group order for free.

Do not stringify the key - `Map` takes any key type, which is exactly why the
constraint can stay as wide as `string | number`.

Left to you: `groups.get(key) ?? []` followed by an unconditional `set`, or the
branch above. One of them writes to the map on every item.

exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - merge two objects, deeply

`deepMerge(a, b)` returns `A & B`. When **both** sides hold a plain object at a
key, merge them recursively; otherwise `b` wins outright. Arrays and `null`
replace rather than merge, and neither input is modified at any depth.

- `deepMerge({ a: { x: 1, y: 2 }, k: 1 }, { a: { y: 3, z: 4 }, m: 2 })`
  -> `{ a: { x: 1, y: 3, z: 4 }, k: 1, m: 2 }`

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.


exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - a store that refuses stale writes

`VersionedStore<T extends { id: string; version: number }>` has:

- `put(item)` - stores it and returns `true`, unless an item with that id is
  already stored at the **same or a newer** version, in which case it changes
  nothing and returns `false`
- `get(id)` - the item or `undefined`
- `all()` - every item, sorted by id
- `size` - a getter

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`, whose constraint has forgotten about versions.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d10_generic_constraints ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The constraint has to name every member the class reads, so add the version:
`T extends { id: string; version: number }`.

Then `put` needs one comparison and two outcomes, and neither of them may modify
what is stored when the write is refused.

## Hint 2

A `Map<string, T>` keyed by id is the store. Refuse when there is already an
entry whose version is **greater than or equal to** the incoming one - the gate
writes the same version twice, so `>` alone is not enough.

Sort in `all()` rather than keeping the map ordered: reads are where the order
is wanted.

Left to you: whether `all()` should hand back the stored objects or copies. The
gate does not care - a caller who mutates one of them will.

## Hint 1

The constraint has to name every member the class reads, so add the version:
`T extends { id: string; version: number }`.

Then `put` needs one comparison and two outcomes, and neither of them may modify
what is stored when the write is refused.

## Hint 2

A `Map<string, T>` keyed by id is the store. Refuse when there is already an
entry whose version is **greater than or equal to** the incoming one - the gate
writes the same version twice, so `>` alone is not enough.

Sort in `all()` rather than keeping the map ordered: reads are where the order
is wanted.

Left to you: whether `all()` should hand back the stored objects or copies. The
gate does not care - a caller who mutates one of them will.

# d11 - keyof and indexed access (drill set)

Eight problems on the two operators that let a generic function talk about the
*members* of a type: `keyof T` for its keys and `T[K]` for what lives at one.
They drill lesson **07_generics_2**; go back there if `K extends keyof T` still
looks like noise.

**Most stubs here return `unknown`** where they should return `T[K]`,
`T[keyof T]` or a `Pick`. Reconnecting the result to the input is the exercise.

## ex1 - read one member

`getValue(source, key)` returns whatever lives at that key, typed. Passing a key
the object does not have is a compile error.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d11_keyof_indexed_access ex1
```

## ex2 - write one member, immutably

`setValue(source, key, value)` returns a **new** object with that one member
replaced. `value` has to be of the type that key holds, and the source is never
modified.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d11_keyof_indexed_access ex2
```

## ex3 - collect the values

`valuesOf(source)` returns `T[keyof T][]` - every value, in key order.
`{ a: 1, b: "x" }` gives `(number | string)[]`.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d11_keyof_indexed_access ex3
```

## ex4 - index an array type

`sample(values, index)` returns `T[number] | undefined`. A negative index counts
back from the end; anything out of range, and any fractional index, is
`undefined`.

- `sample([1, 2, 3], -1)` -> `3`, `sample([1, 2, 3], 3)` -> `undefined`
- with a `readonly ["a", "b"]` tuple the result type is `"a" | "b" | undefined`

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d11_keyof_indexed_access ex4
```

## ex5 - two levels of indexed access

`pluckNested(items, outer, inner)` returns `T[K][I][]` - one value per row,
read from `row[outer][inner]`.

- `pluckNested(rows, "user", "name")` -> the names, typed `string[]`

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d11_keyof_indexed_access ex5
```

## ex6 - a table read both ways

`ROLES` is `{ admin: 3, editor: 2, viewer: 1 } as const`. Derive both:

- `Role` = `keyof typeof ROLES`
- `RoleLevel` = `(typeof ROLES)[Role]` - the union of the **values**

Then `roleFor(level)` finds the role with that level, and `atLeastRole(role,
min)` compares two roles through the table.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d11_keyof_indexed_access ex6
```

## ex7 - select columns

`project(rows, keys)` returns `Pick<T, K>[]` - one object per row containing
only the named members, in the order the keys were given. No keys means one
empty object per row.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d11_keyof_indexed_access ex7
```

## ex8 - sort by several keys

`SortKey<T>` is `{ key: keyof T; direction: "asc" | "desc" }`, and
`sortRows(rows, by)` sorts a copy by each key in turn. Numbers compare
numerically, everything else compares as text, and the sort is **stable**, so
rows that tie on every key keep their input order.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`, where `SortKey` will accept any string as a key.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d11_keyof_indexed_access ex8
```

# Reading - typescript/d11_keyof_indexed_access

The debrief. Per problem: what the key relationship was really buying, the
mistake that breaks it, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**The skill this set drills is describing a member without naming it.**
`keyof T` is the union of `T`'s keys; `T[K]` is the type stored at `K`; and the
pair `<T, K extends keyof T>` is the single most reused signature in typed
JavaScript. It appears in `lodash`, in every ORM, in every form library, and in
about half the utility functions you will write.

**`K extends keyof T` is what keeps the key literal.** Without the constraint,
`key: string` widens and `source[key]` stops typechecking; with it, calling
`getValue(item, "qty")` infers `K = "qty"` and the return type is exactly the
type of `qty`. The constraint is doing inference work, not just validation.

**Indexed access composes.** `T[K][I]` reads two levels; `T[keyof T]` unions
every value type; `T[number]` reads the element type of an array or tuple - and
on a `readonly ["a", "b"]` that is `"a" | "b"`, which is the same trick that
turned an `as const` list into a literal union back in d08.

**`Object.keys` is typed `string[]`, on purpose.** Structural typing means a
value may always carry more properties than its type declares, so the compiler
cannot promise the key list matches. Every implementation in this set therefore
contains one cast - `Object.keys(source) as (keyof T)[]`, or `{} as Pick<T, K>` -
and being able to explain *why* rather than apologising for it is the point.

**And "an object under construction" is the other recurring cast.** You cannot
declare `const picked: Pick<T, K> = {}` because an empty object is not one yet;
you assert the type up front and fill it immediately. The alternative -
`Object.fromEntries` - trades the cast for a different one and loses the key
literals on the way.

## ex1 - read one member

What this was testing: the canonical `<T, K extends keyof T>(source: T, key: K):
T[K]`. Three type positions, all connected, and a body that is one line.

The classic mistake is `key: string`, which fails to compile at `source[key]` -
and the fix people reach for is `(source as any)[key]`, which returns `any` and
poisons every call site downstream.

The model answer writes the constraint and returns `source[key]`; the interesting
work is entirely in the signature, which is exactly what the drill wants you to
notice.

## ex2 - write one member, immutably

What this was testing: the same pair used in an argument position rather than a
return position. `value: T[K]` is what rejects `setValue(item, "a", "2")`.

The classic mistake is `source[key] = value; return source;`, which mutates the
caller's object - the gate keeps the original and checks it.

The model answer spreads into a new object with a computed key,
`{ ...source, [key]: value }`, and casts the result to `T`. TypeScript widens a
computed-key spread to an index signature and cannot see that it produced a `T`,
so the cast is expected - and it is safe because `value` was already constrained
to `T[K]`.

## ex3 - collect the values

What this was testing: `T[keyof T]`, which indexes by *every* key at once and so
unions the value types. For `{ a: number; b: string }` that is `number | string`.

The classic mistake is `Object.values(source)`, which is typed `any[]` for a
generic `T` and quietly loses everything - it looks like the right answer and
returns the wrong type.

The model answer maps `Object.keys` with one cast to `keyof T`, which is the
honest version of what `Object.values` pretends to do.

## ex4 - index an array type

What this was testing: `T[number]`, the array-and-tuple form of indexed access.
On a `number[]` it is `number`; on a `readonly ["a", "b"]` it is `"a" | "b"`, and
the gate checks both so the tuple case cannot be an accident.

The classic mistake is handling the negative index with `values[index]`, which
JavaScript happily reads as the property `"-1"` and returns `undefined` - correct
by luck for out-of-range and wrong for `-1`, which should be the last element.

The model answer converts a negative index once (`values.length + index`), then
runs a single range check that also rejects fractions, so there is exactly one
place that decides whether an index is usable.

## ex5 - two levels of indexed access

What this was testing: chaining constraints. `I extends keyof T[K]` reads as "a
key of whatever lives at `K`", and it is the moment `keyof` stops feeling like
syntax and starts feeling like a small language.

The classic mistake is `I extends keyof T`, which compiles for the outer key and
rejects every inner one - the error message points at the argument rather than
at the signature, which is why it takes a minute to spot.

The model answer maps `item[outer][inner]`; the body is trivial once the three
type parameters are written down, which is the recurring shape of this whole
lesson.

## ex6 - a table read both ways

What this was testing: deriving *two* types from one value. `keyof typeof ROLES`
gives the names; `(typeof ROLES)[Role]` gives the levels; and `as const` is what
stops the second one collapsing to `number`.

The classic mistake is writing `type RoleLevel = number`, which compiles, passes
the runtime tests, and lets `roleFor(4)` through - the gate rejects exactly that
call.

The model answer looks the level up by scanning the table's keys, with one cast
on `Object.keys`, and compares roles by reading the same table - so the numbers
live in exactly one place and both functions agree by construction.

## ex7 - select columns

What this was testing: `Pick<T, K>` as a return type built from an inferred key
union. `project(rows, ["id", "name"])` infers `K = "id" | "name"` and the result
is `Pick<Row, "id" | "name">[]`, with no mention of `Row` in the call.

The classic mistake is building the object with `Object.fromEntries`, which
returns `{ [k: string]: T[K] }` and needs a broader cast that also loses the key
literals - it works, and it says less.

The model answer starts each row from `{} as Pick<T, K>` and assigns the named
keys in the order they were given, which is what makes `Object.keys` on the
result come out in that order too.

## ex8 - sort by several keys

What this was testing: `keyof T` inside a generic *interface*, plus a comparator
that has to work for values whose type it does not know. `SortKey<T>["key"]`
being `keyof T` is what rejects a typo in the sort specification.

The classic mistake is comparing with `<` directly on `a[key]`, which does not
compile for a generic value type - and the second-classic is `String(a) <
String(b)` for everything, which sorts `120` before `90`. The gate sorts a
numeric column descending to catch it.

The model answer walks the sort keys in order, returning as soon as one
distinguishes the rows, and delegates the comparison to a small helper that
handles numbers numerically and everything else as text - relying on
`Array.prototype.sort` being stable, which it has been since ES2019.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: keyof Type Operator](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/keyof-types.html) - `keyof` on objects, on index signatures, and on arrays.
- [Handbook: Indexed Access Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/indexed-access-types.html) - `T[K]`, `T[keyof T]`, `T[number]` and how they chain.
- [Handbook: typeof Type Operator](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/typeof-types.html) - the `keyof typeof` pairing ex6 is built on.
- [Handbook: Pick](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html#picktype-keys) - the utility ex7 returns, and its definition as a mapped type.
- [MDN: Array.prototype.sort](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/sort) - the stability guarantee ex8 depends on, and the comparator contract.

gives the names; `(typeof ROLES)[Role]` gives the levels; and `as const` is what
stops the second one collapsing to `number`.

The classic mistake is writing `type RoleLevel = number`, which compiles, passes
the runtime tests, and lets `roleFor(4)` through - the gate rejects exactly that
call.

The model answer looks the level up by scanning the table's keys, with one cast
on `Object.keys`, and compares roles by reading the same table - so the numbers
live in exactly one place and both functions agree by construction.

## ex7 - select columns

What this was testing: `Pick<T, K>` as a return type built from an inferred key
union. `project(rows, ["id", "name"])` infers `K = "id" | "name"` and the result
is `Pick<Row, "id" | "name">[]`, with no mention of `Row` in the call.

The classic mistake is building the object with `Object.fromEntries`, which
returns `{ [k: string]: T[K] }` and needs a broader cast that also loses the key
literals - it works, and it says less.

The model answer starts each row from `{} as Pick<T, K>` and assigns the named
keys in the order they were given, which is what makes `Object.keys` on the
result come out in that order too.

## ex8 - sort by several keys

What this was testing: `keyof T` inside a generic *interface*, plus a comparator
that has to work for values whose type it does not know. `SortKey<T>["key"]`
being `keyof T` is what rejects a typo in the sort specification.

The classic mistake is comparing with `<` directly on `a[key]`, which does not
compile for a generic value type - and the second-classic is `String(a) <
String(b)` for everything, which sorts `120` before `90`. The gate sorts a
numeric column descending to catch it.

The model answer walks the sort keys in order, returning as soon as one
distinguishes the rows, and delegates the comparison to a small helper that
handles numbers numerically and everything else as text - relying on
`Array.prototype.sort` being stable, which it has been since ES2019.

## ex1 - read one member

`getValue(source, key)` returns whatever lives at that key, typed. Passing a key
the object does not have is a compile error.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d11_keyof_indexed_access ex1
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`T[K]` is the type stored at key `K`. That is the return type, and once it is
written the body is a single `return source[key]`.

## Hint 2

Notice what `K extends keyof T` is doing besides validation: it keeps the key
*literal*, so `getValue(item, "qty")` infers `K = "qty"` rather than widening to
`string`. Widen it and `source[key]` stops compiling.

Left to you: nothing much here - which is the point. Be able to write this
signature from memory, because half the utilities you will ever type start with
it.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`T[K]` is the type stored at key `K`. That is the return type, and once it is
written the body is a single `return source[key]`.

## Hint 2

Notice what `K extends keyof T` is doing besides validation: it keeps the key
*literal*, so `getValue(item, "qty")` infers `K = "qty"` rather than widening to
`string`. Widen it and `source[key]` stops compiling.

Left to you: nothing much here - which is the point. Be able to write this
signature from memory, because half the utilities you will ever type start with
it.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`value: T[K]` is the whole type-level fix: the value has to be of the type that
key holds, which is what makes `setValue(item, "a", "2")` a compile error.

## Hint 2

The body spreads into a fresh object with a computed key:
`{ ...source, [key]: value }`.

TypeScript widens a computed-key spread to an index signature and cannot see
that the result is still a `T`, so one `as T` is expected. It is safe precisely
because `value` was already constrained.

Left to you: the cast, or a mapped-type return that describes the change. The
second is a real exercise in its own right - know that it exists.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`T[keyof T]` indexes the type by *all* of its keys at once, which unions the
value types: `{ a: number; b: string }` gives `number | string`.

That is the element type of the array you return.

## Hint 2

`Object.values(source)` is typed `any[]` for a generic `T` - it looks right and
loses everything.

`Object.keys` is typed `string[]` on purpose (a value may always carry more
properties than its type declares), so one cast to `(keyof T)[]` is the accepted
answer, and the `map` after it is fully typed.

Left to you: cast the keys and map, or cast the result of `Object.values`. One
of those two casts is a claim you can justify.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## ex4 - index an array type

`sample(values, index)` returns `T[number] | undefined`. A negative index counts
back from the end; anything out of range, and any fractional index, is
`undefined`.

- `sample([1, 2, 3], -1)` -> `3`, `sample([1, 2, 3], 3)` -> `undefined`
- with a `readonly ["a", "b"]` tuple the result type is `"a" | "b" | undefined`

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d11_keyof_indexed_access ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`T[number]` is the element type of an array or tuple - `number` for a
`number[]`, and `"a" | "b"` for a `readonly ["a", "b"]`. Add `| undefined`,
because the index may miss.

## Hint 2

Convert a negative index once, then range-check once. `values[-1]` in JavaScript
reads a property named `"-1"` and returns `undefined`, so a negative index has to
be turned into `values.length + index` before it is used.

The fractional case is easiest to reject up front with `Number.isInteger`.

Left to you: your own bounds check, or `Array.prototype.at`, which already
handles negatives. If you use `at`, you still owe the fractional case an answer.

## Hint 1

`T[number]` is the element type of an array or tuple - `number` for a
`number[]`, and `"a" | "b"` for a `readonly ["a", "b"]`. Add `| undefined`,
because the index may miss.

## Hint 2

Convert a negative index once, then range-check once. `values[-1]` in JavaScript
reads a property named `"-1"` and returns `undefined`, so a negative index has to
be turned into `values.length + index` before it is used.

The fractional case is easiest to reject up front with `Number.isInteger`.

Left to you: your own bounds check, or `Array.prototype.at`, which already
handles negatives. If you use `at`, you still owe the fractional case an answer.

## Hint 1

Constrain the inner key to the keys of whatever lives at the outer one:

```ts
I extends keyof T[K]
```

Then the element type of the result is `T[K][I]`, and the array type is that

## ex6 - a table read both ways

`ROLES` is `{ admin: 3, editor: 2, viewer: 1 } as const`. Derive both:

- `Role` = `keyof typeof ROLES`

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Pick<T, K>` is the type of a row containing only the named members, so the
return type is `Pick<T, K>[]`. `K` is inferred from the array of keys, which is
why the call site never has to mention the row type.

## Hint 2

An object under construction cannot be declared as the finished type - `const
projected: Pick<T, K> = {}` is an error, because an empty object is not one yet.
`{} as Pick<T, K>` followed immediately by the loop that fills it is the
accepted answer.

Assigning in the order the keys were given is what makes `Object.keys` on the
result come out in that order.

Left to you: this loop, or `Object.fromEntries(keys.map(...))`. The second needs
a broader cast and loses the key literals - say which trade you prefer.

## Hint 1

`Pick<T, K>` is the type of a row containing only the named members, so the
return type is `Pick<T, K>[]`. `K` is inferred from the array of keys, which is
why the call site never has to mention the row type.

## Hint 2

An object under construction cannot be declared as the finished type - `const
projected: Pick<T, K> = {}` is an error, because an empty object is not one yet.
`{} as Pick<T, K>` followed immediately by the loop that fills it is the
accepted answer.

Assigning in the order the keys were given is what makes `Object.keys` on the
result come out in that order.

Left to you: this loop, or `Object.fromEntries(keys.map(...))`. The second needs
a broader cast and loses the key literals - say which trade you prefer.

## ex8 - sort by several keys

`SortKey<T>` is `{ key: keyof T; direction: "asc" | "desc" }`, and
`sortRows(rows, by)` sorts a copy by each key in turn. Numbers compare
numerically, everything else compares as text, and the sort is **stable**, so
rows that tie on every key keep their input order.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`, where `SortKey` will accept any string as a key.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d11_keyof_indexed_access ex8
```

## Hint 1

`key: keyof T` is the fix that turns a typo in a sort specification into a
compile error - and the return type is `T[]`, not `unknown[]`.

`a[key] < b[key]` will not compile for a generic value type, and casting both
sides to make it compile is how `120` ends up sorting before `90`.

wherever `String()` does - decide whether that is good enough to ship.

lessons.briefing:
# d12 - Built-in utility types (drill set)

Eight problems on the utility types that ship with TypeScript: `Required`,
`Exclude`, `Extract`, `NonNullable`, `Parameters`, `ReturnType`, `Partial`,
`Awaited`, `ConstructorParameters`, `InstanceType`, `Omit` and `Readonly`. They
drill lesson **08_utility_types**; go back there if you cannot say what
`Pick` and `Omit` have to do with each other.

**Every stub here has given up on a derived type** - returning the input type
instead of the transformed one, or `unknown[]` instead of a real argument list.
The type gate marks each one.

## ex1 - fill a draft

`JobDraft` has three optional members. `complete(draft)` returns
`Required<JobDraft>` with the holes filled: `"untitled"`, `0`, `false`.

An explicitly supplied `0`, `false` or `""` is a value, not a hole.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d12_builtin_utilities ex1
```

## ex2 - cut a union in two

`Status` is `"draft" | "open" | "paused" | "closed" | "archived"`. Derive both
halves:

- `Live` = `Exclude<Status, "closed" | "archived">`
- `Dead` = `Extract<Status, "closed" | "archived">`

Then `isLive(status)` is a type predicate for `Live` - so the `else` branch
narrows to `Dead` - and `liveOnly(statuses)` returns `Live[]`.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d12_builtin_utilities ex2
```

## ex3 - the first value that is really there

`firstDefined(values)` returns `NonNullable<T> | undefined` - the first element
that is neither `null` nor `undefined`. `0` and `""` are values.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d12_builtin_utilities ex3
```

## ex4 - take a function type apart

`loadPosting` is written for you. Derive `LoadArgs` with `Parameters<typeof
loadPosting>` and `Loaded` with `ReturnType<typeof loadPosting>`, then write

# Reading - typescript/d12_builtin_utilities

The debrief. Per problem: which utility was really being tested, the mistake
that makes it decorative, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**The skill this set drills is deriving a type instead of writing a second
one.** Every utility here takes a type you already have and produces the one you
need: without the `Partial`, the `Omit` or the `Awaited`, you would hand-write a
near-copy that silently stops matching the day the original changes. That
divergence is the bug these types exist to prevent, and it is why every stub in
this set fails by returning the *input* type.

**They are all ordinary type-level code.** `Partial<T>` is a mapped type with a
`?` added, `Omit<T, K>` is `Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>`, `NonNullable<T>` is
`T & {}` these days, and `Parameters<F>` is a conditional type with `infer`.
Nothing in `lib.es5.d.ts` is magic - d13 asks you to write several of them from
scratch, and knowing they are only a few lines each is the point.

**Distributive utilities work on unions, member by member.** `Exclude` and
`Extract` look like set difference and intersection because that is exactly
what they are: `Exclude<Status, "closed" | "archived">` visits each member of
`Status` and keeps the ones that do not match. That is also why they do nothing
useful on object types - `Exclude<Posting, ...>` is not how you drop a member;
`Omit` is.

**`typeof` is the bridge from a value to a type.** `Parameters<typeof
loadPosting>`, `ReturnType<typeof loadPosting>`, `ConstructorParameters<typeof
Search>` and `InstanceType<typeof Search>` all begin by turning a value you have
into a type you can transform. Note that `typeof Search` is the type of the
*class* and `InstanceType<typeof Search>` (which is just `Search`) is the type
of what it makes - the same distinction as the construct signature in d04.

**And the utilities compose.** `Readonly<Omit<Posting, "internalNotes" |
"recruiterEmail">>` reads outside-in and does exactly what it says. Reaching for
two of them at once is normal; reaching for five is a sign the underlying type
wanted splitting up.

## ex1 - fill a draft

What this was testing: `Required<T>`, which removes `?` from every member - the
exact inverse of `Partial<T>`. The return type is the promise that no hole is
left, and the body has to keep it.

The classic mistake is `draft.salary || 0`, which is right for `undefined` and
wrong for a supplied `0`; the gate hands you `{ salary: 0, remote: false }` and
`{ title: "" }` precisely to catch the falsy-versus-nullish confusion.

The model answer builds a fresh object with `??` on each member, so the returned
value has all three keys present whatever the input looked like.

## ex2 - cut a union in two

What this was testing: `Exclude` and `Extract` as set difference and
intersection over a union of literals, plus a type predicate that hands the
result to control flow analysis. The `else` branch narrowing to `Dead` is the
payoff.

The classic mistake is writing `Live` out by hand. It compiles, it passes today,
and it silently stops matching the day a `"expired"` status is added to
`Status` - which is the entire argument for deriving it.

The model answer excludes the two dead statuses in the type and checks for those
same two in the predicate; keeping the list in two places is the one real
weakness of the approach, and worth saying out loud.

## ex3 - the first value that is really there

What this was testing: `NonNullable<T>` in a return type, and the difference
between "nullish" and "falsy" one more time. The gate returns `0` and `""` from
this function on purpose.

The classic mistake is `values.find(Boolean)`, which is short, idiomatic and
skips `0`, `""`, `false` and `NaN` - and does not narrow the element type
either.

The model answer loops with an explicit `!== null && !== undefined` and asserts
`NonNullable<T>` on the way out, because TypeScript cannot see that the two
checks removed exactly the two members the return type removes.

## ex4 - take a function type apart

What this was testing: `Parameters<F>` and `ReturnType<F>`, and the `typeof`
that turns the function *value* into a function *type*. `LoadArgs` is a labelled
tuple, which is why spreading it into the call typechecks.

The classic mistake is `Parameters<loadPosting>`, without `typeof` - a value
where a type was expected, and the error message is one of the more confusing
ones TypeScript produces.

The model answer is `return loadPosting(...args)`; the tuple type carries both
the arity and the order, so passing one argument too few is a compile error
rather than an `undefined` at runtime.

## ex5 - a patch of what changed

What this was testing: `Partial<T>` as a return type, and the distinction
between an absent key and a key holding `undefined`. `"title" in patch` has to
be `false`, which rules out building the object with every key and blanking the
unchanged ones.

The classic mistake is `{ ...after }` filtered afterwards, or assigning
`undefined` for unchanged members - both produce a patch that a naive `Object.assign`
would then use to erase good data.

The model answer starts from `{}` and writes only the changed members, with one
cast at the assignment - because TypeScript cannot verify that `patch[key] =
after[key]` lines up when `key` is a union of several keys at once.

## ex6 - unwrap a promise type

What this was testing: `Awaited<T>`, which unwraps a promise (and a promise of a
promise, recursively). `ReturnType<typeof fetchPosting>` is
`Promise<{ id, title }>`; `Awaited<...>` of that is the shape you actually hold
after the `await`.

The classic mistake is stopping at `ReturnType`, which leaves a `Promise` inside
the type - so `Fetched[]` becomes an array of promises and the whole signature
is quietly wrong.

The model answer resolves the ids with `Promise.all`, which is the one line that
turns an array of promises into a promise of an array - and note that it fails
fast on the first rejection, which is worth knowing before you rely on it.

## ex7 - take a class apart

What this was testing: the class-shaped versions of ex4.
`ConstructorParameters<typeof Search>` is the argument tuple for `new`, and
`InstanceType<typeof Search>` is what `new` produces - which is `Search`, and
saying so is the point of the exercise.

The classic mistake is `Parameters<typeof Search>`, which does not apply to a
class at all, or `ConstructorParameters<Search>`, which passes the instance type
where the constructor type was wanted.

The model answer is `new Search(...args)`, and the `run` method lower-cases both
sides once before comparing and slices to the limit - so a shorter result is
never padded.

## ex8 - a public view of a posting

What this was testing: composing two utilities, and the fact that `Omit` removes
a member from the *type* while a spread with destructuring removes it from the
*value*. Both halves are needed, and the gate checks each with `in`.

The classic mistake is assigning `undefined` to the private members instead of
removing them - the key is still there for `JSON.stringify`, which is exactly
the leak this function exists to prevent. The second-classic is mutating the
input with `delete`.

The model answer destructures the two private members out and pushes the rest,
skipping the dead statuses on the way - so a published posting is a new object
with three keys, readonly by type and complete by construction.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Utility Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html) - the full list, each with its definition; worth reading end to end once.
- [Handbook: Exclude and Extract](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html#excludeuniontype-excludedmembers) - and why they distribute over unions.
- [Handbook: Awaited](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html#awaitedtype) - recursive unwrapping, and the thenable rules behind it.
- [TypeScript source: lib.es5.d.ts](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/main/src/lib/es5.d.ts) - the actual definitions; `Partial`, `Pick` and `Omit` are three lines each.
- [MDN: Promise.all](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/all) - the ex6 one-liner, including its fail-fast behaviour.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - cut a union in two

`Status` is `"draft" | "open" | "paused" | "closed" | "archived"`. Derive both
halves:

- `Live` = `Exclude<Status, "closed" | "archived">`
- `Dead` = `Extract<Status, "closed" | "archived">`

Then `isLive(status)` is a type predicate for `Live` - so the `else` branch
narrows to `Dead` - and `liveOnly(statuses)` returns `Live[]`.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d12_builtin_utilities ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Exclude<Union, Members>` keeps everything that is not in `Members`;
`Extract<Union, Members>` keeps everything that is. They distribute over the
union member by member, which is why they read like set difference and
intersection.

Derive both - writing `"draft" | "open" | "paused"` out by hand compiles and
stops matching the day a sixth status appears.

## Hint 2

`isLive` has to be a type **predicate** (`status is Live`), not a boolean.
That is what makes the `else` branch a `Dead` and what lets
`statuses.filter(isLive)` return `Live[]` with no cast at all.

Left to you: whether the dead statuses should live in a shared `as const` list
that both the type and the predicate read. It removes the duplication and costs
you a `readonly` cast - say which you would ship.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`Exclude<Union, Members>` keeps everything that is not in `Members`;
`Extract<Union, Members>` keeps everything that is. They distribute over the
union member by member, which is why they read like set difference and
intersection.

Derive both - writing `"draft" | "open" | "paused"` out by hand compiles and
stops matching the day a sixth status appears.

## Hint 2

`isLive` has to be a type **predicate** (`status is Live`), not a boolean.
That is what makes the `else` branch a `Dead` and what lets
`statuses.filter(isLive)` return `Live[]` with no cast at all.

Left to you: whether the dead statuses should live in a shared `as const` list
that both the type and the predicate read. It removes the duplication and costs
you a `readonly` cast - say which you would ship.

## ex3 - the first value that is really there

```
uv run dojo test typescript d12_builtin_utilities ex3
```

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`NonNullable<T>` removes `null` and `undefined` from a type. The return type is
`NonNullable<T> | undefined` - the `undefined` at the end is the "found nothing"
answer, not a value that survived the filter.

## Hint 2

`values.find(Boolean)` is the tempting one-liner and it skips `0`, `""` and
`false` - all of which are defined. The gate returns `0` from this function.

Check `value !== null && value !== undefined` (or the single `value != null`).
TypeScript will not see that those two checks remove exactly the two members
`NonNullable` removes, so one assertion on the way out is expected.

Left to you: the loop, or `find` with a type predicate helper. The second is
reusable and takes three more lines.

`Partial<T>` makes every member optional, which is exactly what a patch is: some
members, maybe none.

The gate checks with `in`, so an unchanged member has to be **absent** rather

several at once - so one narrow cast at the assignment is the accepted answer.

## Hint 1

`Partial<T>` makes every member optional, which is exactly what a patch is: some
members, maybe none.

The gate checks with `in`, so an unchanged member has to be **absent** rather
than present holding `undefined`.

Start from `{}` and write only the members that differ. Comparing with `!==`
means `false` counts as a change when the old value was `true`.

Assigning through a `keyof Posting` variable does not typecheck on its own -
TypeScript cannot line up the key and the value when the key is a union of
several at once - so one narrow cast at the assignment is the accepted answer.

Left to you: the loop with a cast, or four explicit `if`s with no cast at all.
The second is longer, needs editing when the interface grows, and is completely
honest.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`ReturnType<typeof fetchPosting>` is `Promise<{ id, title }>` - the type of what
the call gives you, not the type of what you hold after awaiting it.

`Awaited<T>` unwraps that, recursively, so `Fetched` is the plain object.

## Hint 2

`ids.map((id) => fetchPosting(id))` gives you an array of promises.
`Promise.all` turns that into a promise of an array, which is what the return
type asks for.

Left to you: `Promise.all` or a sequential `for await`. The first is one line
and fails fast on the first rejection; the second is slower and gives you a
place to keep going. Say which the caller would want.

## ex8 - a public view of a posting

`PublicPosting` is `Readonly<Omit<Posting, "internalNotes" | "recruiterEmail">>`.
`publish(postings)` drops every posting whose status is `"closed"` or
`"archived"`, and strips the two private members from the rest - **removed**,
not blanked. Input order is kept and the source postings are never modified.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d12_builtin_utilities ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two utilities, read outside-in: `Readonly<Omit<Posting, "internalNotes" |
"recruiterEmail">>`. `Omit` removes the members from the type; `Readonly` stops
the caller writing to what is left.

## Hint 2

`Omit` changes the type; it does not change the value. Removing the members from
the object is a separate job, and destructuring does it in one line:

```ts
const { internalNotes, recruiterEmail, ...rest } = posting;
```

Setting them to `undefined` instead would leave the keys in place for
`JSON.stringify`, which is exactly the leak this function exists to prevent -
and the gate checks with `in`.

Left to you: filter first and strip second, or the other way round. Same output;
one of them does less work on the postings nobody will ever see.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two utilities, read outside-in: `Readonly<Omit<Posting, "internalNotes" |
"recruiterEmail">>`. `Omit` removes the members from the type; `Readonly` stops
the caller writing to what is left.

## Hint 2

`Omit` changes the type; it does not change the value. Removing the members from
the object is a separate job, and destructuring does it in one line:

```ts
const { internalNotes, recruiterEmail, ...rest } = posting;
```

Setting them to `undefined` instead would leave the keys in place for
`JSON.stringify`, which is exactly the leak this function exists to prevent -
and the gate checks with `in`.

Left to you: filter first and strip second, or the other way round. Same output;
one of them does less work on the postings nobody will ever see.

# d13 - Implement the utility types (drill set)

Eight built-in-style utility types, written from scratch. Lesson **08** taught
you to use `Partial`, `Pick` and friends and had you build two of them; this set
makes the rest automatic, with `infer` from lesson **09** carrying the second
half. Redo those two lessons first if mapped types still feel like syntax.

Every exercise here is **type-level only**: each stub is a deliberately weak or
wrong alias that compiles fine and proves nothing. There is no runtime gate in
this set - the whole gate is `gate.test-d.ts`, and `// @ts-expect-error` lines
in it are assertions in reverse: they pass only when your type makes the next
line illegal.

## ex1 - MyReadonly

`MyReadonly<T>` locks every member: same keys, same value types, all `readonly`.
`MyReadonly<{ name: string }>` is `{ readonly name: string }`.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d13_implement_utilities ex1
```

## ex2 - MyRequired

`MyRequired<T>` removes every `?`: `MyRequired<{ title?: string }>` is
`{ title: string }`. A type with nothing optional passes through unchanged.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d13_implement_utilities ex2
```

## ex3 - MyRecord

`MyRecord<K, V>` builds an object type with exactly the keys in `K`, each
holding a `V`. `MyRecord<"pass" | "fail", number>` is
`{ pass: number; fail: number }` - and a value missing one of those keys must
not compile. The stub's index signature is precisely what a `Record` is not.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d13_implement_utilities ex3
```

## ex4 - MyParameters

`MyParameters<F>` is the parameter list of the function type `F`, as a tuple -
labels, optionality and all. `MyParameters<() => void>` is `[]`.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d13_implement_utilities ex4
```

## ex5 - MyInstanceType

`MyInstanceType<C>` is what the construct signature `C` builds:
`MyInstanceType<typeof Beacon>` is `Beacon`, and
`MyInstanceType<new () => Map<string, number>>` is `Map<string, number>`.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d13_implement_utilities ex5
```

## ex6 - MyAwaited

`MyAwaited<T>` unwraps promises **recursively** - `Promise<Promise<string>>`
becomes `string` - and passes non-promises through untouched. Handed a union,
it unwraps each member separately.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d13_implement_utilities ex6
```

## ex7 - PartialBy

`PartialBy<T, K>` makes **only** the keys in `K` optional and leaves the rest
exactly as they were. `PartialBy<Session, "expiresAt">` still requires `user`
and `token`, no longer requires `expiresAt`, and invents no new keys. Two
built-ins you have already written by hand compose into this one.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d13_implement_utilities ex7
```

## ex8 - Merge

`Merge<A, B>` is one object type with every key from either shape; where both
declare a key, **B wins**. The stub is the classic wrong answer - an
intersection, which turns every disagreement into `never` instead of an
override.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d13_implement_utilities ex8
```

# Reading - typescript/d13_implement_utilities

The debrief. Per problem: what the utility was really made of, the mistake that
looks right, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**Every built-in utility type is a few lines of ordinary type code**, and this
set exists to make you the person who can write those lines cold. There are only
three ingredients. A *mapped type* (`[K in keyof T]`) walks keys and rebuilds an
object, and its modifiers (`readonly`, `?`, and the `-` that removes them) are
the whole story of `Readonly`, `Partial`, `Required` and `Mutable`. A
*conditional type with `infer`* pattern-matches a type and pulls a piece out,
which is the whole story of `Parameters`, `ReturnType`, `InstanceType` and
`Awaited`. And *composition* - one utility written in terms of two others - is
how everything else gets made, `Omit` and this set's `PartialBy` included.

Two habits separate a memorised answer from a working one. First, know which
ingredient you are reaching for before you type: "same keys, different
decoration" is a mapped type; "a piece of a bigger type" is `infer`; "both" is
composition. Second, test your type on the degenerate inputs the gate uses -
the type with nothing optional, the zero-argument function, the non-promise -
because that is where a wrong branch or a missing `-` hides.

The `any[]` in the two function-reading exercises deserves a note: the real
`Parameters` and `InstanceType` constrain with `(...args: any) => any` too,
because a constraint of `unknown[]` would reject perfectly good functions whose
parameters are narrower. It is one of the few places `any` is the honest tool -
it appears in a constraint, where nothing unsound can flow out of it.

## ex1 - MyReadonly

What this was testing: the mapped-type loop plus one modifier. `{ readonly [K in
keyof T]: T[K] }` is five tokens longer than a clone and completely different in
meaning.

The classic mistake is thinking `readonly` has to be *removed* from somewhere or
listed per key - or reaching for `Object.freeze`, which is a runtime tool and no
help to a type alias.

The model answer writes the modifier in front of the bracket, and the gate's
assignment probe (`locked.tier = 3`) is what proves it took: a clone compiles
that line, and the unused `@ts-expect-error` fails the test.

## ex2 - MyRequired

What this was testing: modifiers can be removed, not just added. `-?` strips the
optional marker, and with it the `undefined` that `?` had mixed into every read.

The classic mistake is mapping without the minus - `{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] }` -
which looks like it should "normalise" the type but is homomorphic: it
faithfully *preserves* the `?` you were trying to delete.

The model answer is `{ [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }`, and the second assertion (a
type with nothing optional passes through unchanged) is free: removing a marker
that is not there does nothing.

## ex3 - MyRecord

What this was testing: the key set of a mapped type does not have to be
`keyof` anything - any union of keys works, and that is the difference between
a `Record` and an index signature.

The classic mistake is the stub itself: `{ [key: string]: V }` accepts every
string key and demands none, so `{ up: 1 }` satisfies it even when `down` was
promised. An index signature is a claim about *whatever keys exist*; a `Record`
is a claim that *specific keys exist*.

The model answer maps over the parameter directly - `{ [P in K]: V }` - and
constrains `K extends PropertyKey`, exactly as the built-in does.

## ex4 - MyParameters

What this was testing: `infer` in the argument position of a function pattern.
`F extends (...args: infer P) => unknown ? P : never` binds the entire
parameter list, as a tuple, labels and all.

The classic mistake is inferring one parameter (`(first: infer A, ...rest:
any[])`) or declaring the result `unknown[]` like the stub - both throw away
arity, so `[]` and `[slug: string, attempts: number]` come out looking the same.

The model answer lets rest-parameter syntax do the collecting: `...args: infer
P` makes `P` the tuple, and the conditional's false branch is `never` because a
non-function has no parameters to speak of.

## ex5 - MyInstanceType

What this was testing: construct signatures are function types with `new` in
front, and `infer` works on them the same way - in the *return* position this
time.

The classic mistake is pattern-matching without the `new` (which fails to match
`typeof Beacon` at all) or confusing the class `Beacon`-the-type (an instance)
with `typeof Beacon` (the constructor). The gate's `() => Beacon` probe exists
for exactly that confusion: right return type, wrong kind of signature.

The model answer is `C extends new (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never`,
and hovering the built-in `InstanceType` shows the same shape.

## ex6 - MyAwaited

What this was testing: a recursive conditional type. One `extends
Promise<infer V>` unwraps one layer; writing `MyAwaited<V>` in the true branch
unwraps them all, and the false branch is what lets non-promises through
untouched.

The classic mistake is stopping at one layer - `T extends Promise<infer V> ? V
: T` - which leaves `Promise<Promise<string>>` half-opened as
`Promise<string>`. The gate's nested case exists to catch it.

The model answer recurses, and the union assertion comes along for free:
`MyAwaited<Promise<number> | string>` distributes because the checked type is a
naked parameter, unwrapping each member separately.

## ex7 - PartialBy

What this was testing: composition. Split `T` into the keys you were told to
loosen and the keys you were not, apply `Partial` to one half, and glue the
halves back together with an intersection.

The classic mistake is `Partial<T>` (which loosens everything, so the gate's
"user is still required" probe fails) or trying to write one mapped type with
two different modifiers, which the syntax simply does not allow - the two-halves
intersection is not a workaround, it is the idiom.

The model answer is `Omit<T, K> & Partial<Pick<T, K>>`, and the gate grades it
by behaviour - what may be omitted, what must stay, what may not be added -
precisely so that any equivalent composition passes too.

## ex8 - Merge

What this was testing: a mapped type over a key set built from *two* types, with
a conditional choosing each value. `keyof A | keyof B` is the union of keys;
`K extends keyof B ? B[K] : ...` is the override rule, written so B is checked
first.

The classic mistake is the stub: `A & B` looks like a merge and is a
*constraint* - both sides must hold at once, so `retries: number` meets
`retries: string` and produces `never`, a member no value can satisfy. The
spread operator at runtime overrides; the intersection type does not.

The model answer checks `keyof B` before `keyof A` so the second shape wins,
and the final `never` arm is unreachable but required to finish the
conditional.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Utility Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html) - every built-in this set rebuilds, with its real definition one hover away.
- [Handbook: Mapped Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/mapped-types.html) - the loop, the modifiers, and the `-` that removes them (ex1-ex3).
- [Handbook: Conditional Types - inferring](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html#inferring-within-conditional-types) - `infer` in parameter, return and construct positions (ex4-ex6).
- [Handbook: Intersection Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html#intersection-types) - what `&` really means, and why it is the ex7 idiom and the ex8 trap at once.

This is a mapped type with one modifier added: walk every key of `T` with
`[K in keyof T]` and decorate each member. Lesson 08's Concept section shows

The modifier goes in front of the bracket: `{ readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }`.

a plain clone of `T` compiles the assignment and fails the test.

## Hint 1

A construct signature is written `new (...args) => Something`, and `infer`
works in its return position exactly as it does for a plain function. Match
that shape, not a plain call signature.

## Hint 2

`C extends new (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never`. The `new` keyword in
the pattern is what makes `typeof Beacon` match and `() => Beacon` fail - the
gate probes both.

## ex6 - MyAwaited

`MyAwaited<T>` unwraps promises **recursively** - `Promise<Promise<string>>`
becomes `string` - and passes non-promises through untouched. Handed a union,
it unwraps each member separately.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```

```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

One conditional with `infer` unwraps one promise layer. The gate feeds you a
promise *inside* a promise - what do you do with the value you just inferred?

## Hint 2

Name the alias in its own true branch: `T extends Promise<infer V> ?
MyAwaited<V> : T`. Recursion keeps unwrapping until the `extends` stops
matching, and the false branch is what passes plain values through.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`A & B` is the trap, not the answer: an intersection demands both sides at
once, so two different declarations of `retries` collapse into `never`. A merge
has to *choose*, and choosing is what conditional types do.

## Hint 2

Build the result as one mapped type whose key set covers both shapes:
`[K in keyof A | keyof B]`. For each key, decide where the value comes from.

## Hint 3

In the value position, check `K extends keyof B` first - that order is what
"B wins" means - and fall back to `A[K]` when only A has the key. Left to you:
the final arm of the conditional. It can never be reached (every `K` came from
one of the two), but the syntax demands you write something there - pick the
type that says "impossible".

lessons.briefing:
# d14 - Mapped types (drill set)

Eight problems on the mapped-type loop: modifiers on and off, values rewritten,
keys renamed, members filtered, and two ex7/ex8 tricks interviews love. They
drill lesson **09_mapped_conditional** (with lesson 08's plain loop underneath);
redo those if `[K in keyof T]` still reads like noise.

Every exercise is **type-level only** - each stub compiles and is wrong, and
there is no runtime gate: the whole gate is `gate.test-d.ts`. The
`// @ts-expect-error` lines are assertions in reverse; they pass only when your
type makes the next line illegal.

## ex1 - Nullable

`Nullable<T>` keeps every key and lets every value also be `null`:
`Nullable<{ count: number }>` is `{ count: number | null }`.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d14_mapped_types ex1
```

## ex2 - Locked

`Locked<T>` applies two modifiers in one pass: every member becomes `readonly`
**and** required. The stub already locks; it forgets to remove the question
marks.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d14_mapped_types ex2
```

## ex3 - Boxed

`Boxed<T>` wraps every value: `Boxed<{ count: number }>` is
`{ count: { value: number } }`. Same keys, new value shape.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d14_mapped_types ex3
```

## ex4 - Watchers

`Watchers<T>` renames as it maps: every member `title` becomes a callback
member `titleChanged: (value: <old type>) => void`, and the original names are
gone from the result.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d14_mapped_types ex4
```

## ex5 - PickByType

`PickByType<T, V>` keeps only the members whose value type is assignable to
`V`, and deletes the rest - `PickByType<Metric, string>` has the two string
members and nothing else. Deleting means remapping the key to `never`.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d14_mapped_types ex5
```

## ex6 - Toggles

`Toggles<K>` maps over a **union of names**, not over `keyof` anything:
`Toggles<"audio" | "video">` is `{ hasAudio: boolean; hasVideo: boolean }`.
One of the four intrinsic string types does the capitalising.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d14_mapped_types ex6
```

## ex7 - Invert

`Invert<T>` swaps each key with its value: `Invert<{ ok: "OK"; bad: "ERR" }>`
is `{ OK: "ok"; ERR: "bad" }`, and it works for number values too. The values
are constrained to `PropertyKey`, because they are about to become keys.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d14_mapped_types ex7
```

## ex8 - OptionalKeys

`OptionalKeys<T>` is the union of the keys a value of `T` may omit:
`OptionalKeys<{ a: number; b?: string }>` is `"b"`, and a type with nothing
optional yields `never`. The trick is asking, per key, whether `{}` satisfies
`Pick<T, K>`.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d14_mapped_types ex8
```

# Reading - typescript/d14_mapped_types The debrief. Per problem: what the map was really doing, the mistake that looks right, and one sentence on the model answer. ## Notes **A mapped type is one loop with four levers**, and this set pulls each of them in isolation before combining them. The levers: what the *key set* is (usually `keyof T`, but any union of keys works - ex6); what happens to the *value* (`T[K]` untouched, widened with `| null`, wrapped in an object - ex1, ex3); what happens to the *modifiers* (`readonly` and `?`, added or removed with `+` and `-` - ex2); and what happens to the *key itself* (`as` remapping, which can rename with a template literal or delete by producing `never` - ex4, ex5, ex7). Keep the homomorphic rule from lesson 09 in view while you work: the plain form `{ [K in keyof T]: ... }` silently preserves each member's `readonly` and `?`. That is a feature right up until you wanted them gone - ex2's stub is exactly that failure - and it is lost the moment you remap keys, which is why ex7's inverted table comes out clean of modifiers. The two hard problems are hard for type-level reasons worth naming. Inversion (ex7) uses `as T[K]`: the *value* type becomes the key, which is legal only because the constraint promises every value is a `PropertyKey`. And ex8 turns a mapped type inside out - map each key to itself-or-`never`, then index with `[keyof T]` to collapse the object into a union. That map-then-index idiom is how most "which keys...?" utilities in real codebases are written. ## ex1 - Nullable What this was testing: the simplest possible value rewrite - `T[K] | null` - and that you resist doing anything else to the type while you are in there. The classic mistake is reaching for `?` instead of `| null`: an optional member may be *absent*, which is a different contract from "present but null", and the gate's equality assertion tells them apart. The model answer is `{ [K in keyof T]: T[K] | null }`, homomorphic on purpose so keys and modifiers ride through untouched. ## ex2 - Locked What this was testing: two modifiers on one mapped type - `readonly` written before the bracket, `-?` written after it - and the knowledge that they are independent levers. The classic mistake is the stub: locking without `-?`. Because the plain map is homomorphic, every `?` survives, and `Locked` still allows an absent `theme` on an object that claims to be fully resolved. The model answer is `{ readonly [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] }` - one line, both levers, no second pass. ## ex3 - Boxed What this was testing: the value position of a mapped type can be any type expression that mentions `T[K]`, including a brand-new object type built around it. The classic mistake is defining a separate `Box` and mapping to `Box` or `Box` - the wrapper survives but the connection to the member's own type is cut, and `boxed.count.value` comes out `unknown`. The model answer writes `{ value: T[K] }` inline (a named `Box` used as `Box` is just as good), keeping each box tied to its own member. ## ex4 - Watchers What this was testing: key remapping with `as` plus a template literal - the `` `${K}Changed` `` suffix pattern - and the `keyof T & string` intersection that template literals force on you. The classic mistake is forgetting that intersection: `keyof T` may include `number | symbol`, which cannot be spliced into a template literal, and the error message it produces is famously unhelpful. The second mistake is mapping values to callbacks but leaving the names alone, which is the stub. The model answer is `[K in keyof T & string as `${K}Changed`]: (value: T[K]) => void` - and the probe on `watchers.title` proves the old names really are gone, not merely joined by new ones. ## ex5 - PickByType What this was testing: the remap-to-`never`-deletes idiom, driven by a conditional on the *value* type: `as T[K] extends V ? K : never`. The classic mistake is putting the conditional in the value position instead of the key position - `T[K] extends V ? T[K] : never` keeps every key and fills the losers with `never`, which is a very different (and mostly useless) type. Where the conditional sits decides whether you filter members or mangle values. The model answer filters in the key position and leaves the value as plain `T[K]`, so the members that survive are exactly what they were before. ## ex6 - Toggles What this was testing: a mapped type over a plain union - no `keyof` in sight - plus one intrinsic. `[P in K]` iterates `"audio" | "video"` directly, and `Capitalize

` shapes the new name inside the template literal. The classic mistake is trying to route through an object first (`keyof Record`) or reaching for `Uppercase` and producing `hasAUDIO`. The four intrinsics do four different jobs; this one needs only the first letter raised. The model answer is `{ [P in K as `has${Capitalize

}`]: boolean }`, and the probe on `toggles.audio` checks the raw names never leaked into the result. ## ex7 - Invert What this was testing: `as T[K]` - remapping each key to its own *value*. The key and value positions swap roles, which is legal because the constraint `Record` promises every value can serve as a key. The classic mistake is writing the swap in the value position only (the stub: `{ [K in keyof T]: K }`), which relabels values but moves nothing - or dropping the constraint and watching `as T[K]` fail, because an arbitrary value type has no business being a key. The model answer is `{ [K in keyof T as T[K]]: K }`: three tokens moved, whole meaning reversed - and it handles the numeric table for free, since numbers are already `PropertyKey`s. ## ex8 - OptionalKeys What this was testing: the map-then-index idiom, plus the `{} extends Pick` probe. `Pick` isolates one member; if the empty object satisfies it, that member was optional; collapse the survivors with `[keyof T]`. The classic mistake is testing `undefined extends T[K]`, which confuses "may be absent" with "may hold undefined" - a required `title: string | undefined` would be misreported as optional. Absence is a property of the *key*, not the value, which is why the probe is phrased with `Pick` and `{}`. The model answer maps with `-?` (so the collected union is clean of `undefined`), keeps `K` for optional members and `never` for required ones, and indexes with `[keyof T]` - `never` vanishes from the union, which is what makes the all-required case come out as `never`. ## Further reading - [Handbook: Mapped Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/mapped-types.html) - modifiers, key remapping via `as`, and mapping over arbitrary unions. - [Handbook: Template Literal Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/template-literal-types.html) - the `${K}Changed` pattern and the four intrinsic string types. - [Handbook: Conditional Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html) - the `? K : never` filter that drives ex5 and ex8. - [Handbook: keyof and Indexed Access Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/indexed-access-types.html) - the `[keyof T]` collapse that turns ex8's map into a union.

## ex7 - Invert

`Invert<T>` swaps each key with its value: `Invert<{ ok: "OK"; bad: "ERR" }>`
is `{ OK: "ok"; ERR: "bad" }`, and it works for number values too. The values
are constrained to `PropertyKey`, because they are about to become keys.

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - OptionalKeys

`OptionalKeys<T>` is the union of the keys a value of `T` may omit:
`OptionalKeys<{ a: number; b?: string }>` is `"b"`, and a type with nothing
optional yields `never`. The trick is asking, per key, whether `{}` satisfies
`Pick<T, K>`.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d14_mapped_types ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two steps: build a mapped type where each key becomes either itself or `never`,
then collapse the whole object into a union by indexing it with `[keyof T]` -
`never` disappears from unions, taking the required keys with it.

## Hint 2

The per-key question is "may a value omit this member?", and the honest probe
is `{} extends Pick<T, K>`: pick the single member out, and ask whether the
empty object satisfies the result. Do not test `undefined extends T[K]` - a
required member typed `string | undefined` would lie to you.

## Hint 3

The shape is `{ [K in keyof T]-?: {} extends Pick<T, K> ? K : never }[keyof
T]`. Left to you: why the `-?` is there. Remove it and inspect what
`OptionalKeys<Prefs>` becomes - the answer teaches you what optional members do
to the values you collect.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Two steps: build a mapped type where each key becomes either itself or `never`,
then collapse the whole object into a union by indexing it with `[keyof T]` -
`never` disappears from unions, taking the required keys with it.

## Hint 2

The per-key question is "may a value omit this member?", and the honest probe
is `{} extends Pick<T, K>`: pick the single member out, and ask whether the
empty object satisfies the result. Do not test `undefined extends T[K]` - a
required member typed `string | undefined` would lie to you.

## Hint 3

The shape is `{ [K in keyof T]-?: {} extends Pick<T, K> ? K : never }[keyof
T]`. Left to you: why the `-?` is there. Remove it and inspect what
`OptionalKeys<Prefs>` becomes - the answer teaches you what optional members do
to the values you collect.

# d15 - Conditional types (drill set)

Eight problems on `T extends U ? X : Y`: the question it really asks, what
distribution does to it, and the three "is it *that* type?" probes that every
type-level library ships. They drill lesson **09_mapped_conditional**; reread
its conditional section if the arrow still reads like an `if`.

Every exercise here is **type-level only** - each stub compiles and is wrong,
and the whole gate is `gate.test-d.ts`. `// @ts-expect-error` is an assertion
in reverse: it passes only when the very next line fails to compile, so the
expressions it guards are deliberately kept to one line.

## ex1 - is it an array

`IsArray<T>` is `true` when `T` is any array or tuple type - mutable,
`readonly`, or a fixed-length tuple - and `false` otherwise. The answers are
the *literal* types `true` and `false`, not `boolean`.

- `IsArray<string[]>` -> `true`, `IsArray<readonly number[]>` -> `true`
- `IsArray<[1, 2]>` -> `true`, `IsArray<{ length: number }>` -> `false`

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex1
```

## ex2 - distribute over the union

`ToArray<T>` turns a type into an array of it, **member by member**:

- `ToArray<string>` -> `string[]`
- `ToArray<string | number>` -> `string[] | number[]` (not `(string | number)[]`)
- `ToArray<never>` -> `never`

That last case is the tell: a distributive conditional over the empty union
produces the empty union.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex2
```

## ex3 - and now do not distribute

`ToArrayAll<T>` is the same question with the opposite answer: one array that
holds the whole union.

- `ToArrayAll<string | number>` -> `(string | number)[]`
- `ToArrayAll<never>` -> `never[]`, not `never`

Write it as a conditional type, with distribution deliberately switched off -
returning `T[]` directly is not the exercise.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex3
```

## ex4 - name the family

`Kind<T>` reports which family a type belongs to, as a string literal:
`"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"bigint"`, `"null"`, `"undefined"`,
`"array"`, or `"object"` - and `"other"` for anything left over.

- `Kind<"ready">` -> `"string"` (a literal still belongs to its family)
- `Kind<readonly [1, 2]>` -> `"array"`, and `Kind<{ id: string }>` -> `"object"`
- `Kind<string | number>` -> `"string" | "number"` - it distributes

Order matters: an array *is* an object, so one of those checks has to come
first.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex4
```

## ex5 - widen a literal

`Widen<T>` is what `let` does to a literal, expressed as a type: a string
literal becomes `string`, a numeric literal becomes `number`, `true` becomes
`boolean`, a bigint literal becomes `bigint`. Everything else is returned
untouched, including object types.

- `Widen<"ready">` -> `string`, `Widen<7>` -> `number`, `Widen<10n>` -> `bigint`
- `Widen<"a" | 3>` -> `string | number` (it distributes)
- `Widen<{ id: 1 }>` -> `{ id: 1 }` - only the top level is widened

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex5
```

## ex6 - is it never

`IsNever<T>` is `true` only when `T` is `never`.

- `IsNever<never>` -> `true`
- `IsNever<string>` -> `false`, `IsNever<never | string>` -> `false`
- `IsNever<Extract<"a" | "b", "c">>` -> `true` - the realistic way to get one

The naive version - `T extends never ? true : false` - returns `never` for
`never`, which is neither `true` nor `false`. Work out why before you fix it.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex6
```

## ex7 - is it any

`IsAny<T>` is `true` only for `any`.

- `IsAny<any>` -> `true`
- `IsAny<unknown>` -> `false`, `IsAny<never>` -> `false`, `IsAny<string>` -> `false`

The obvious tests all fail: `any` is assignable to everything *and* everything
is assignable to `any`, so any conditional whose condition mentions `T`
directly takes both branches and returns `boolean`. You need a condition that
is false for every real type and that `any` alone can make true.

The lever: intersecting anything with `any` gives `any`, while intersecting
two unrelated types gives `never`.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex7
```

## ex8 - are these two types identical

`Equals<X, Y>` is `true` when the two types are *identical*, not merely
mutually assignable.

- `Equals<string, string>` -> `true`, `Equals<"a" | "b", "b" | "a">` -> `true`
- `Equals<{ id: string }, { id: string }>` -> `true`, `Equals<never, never>` -> `true`
- `Equals<any, string>` -> `false`, `Equals<unknown, any>` -> `false`
- `Equals<1, number>` -> `false`, `Equals<{ id: string }, { id?: string }>` -> `false`

Mutual assignability is not enough: `any` is assignable both ways to
everything, so the two-sided `extends` test says `true` for `Equals<any,
string>`. The escape hatch is that the compiler compares two *deferred*
conditional types structurally - two generic function types whose bodies are
conditionals are related only when the conditionals are written against
identical types.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex8
```
