# Reading - typescript/d15_conditional_types

The debrief. Per problem: what the conditional was really asking, the version
that looks right and is not, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**A conditional type is one question - "is `X` assignable to `Y`?" - and two
answers.** Everything else in this set is a consequence of that. The question
is assignability, not equality and not "what is it really", which is why a
literal answers yes to its base type (ex5), an array answers yes to `object`
(ex4), and `any` answers yes to everything at once (ex7).

**Distribution is the rule that makes conditionals feel haunted.** When the
checked type is a bare type parameter, the conditional is applied to each
member of a union separately and the results are unioned back. That gives you
`ToArray<string | number>` as `string[] | number[]` for free (ex2), and it
gives you `IsNever<never>` as `never` for free too (ex6) - because the union
with no members distributes into no results, and the union of no results is
`never`.

**So the first thing to decide about any conditional you write is whether you
want distribution.** If you do, keep the parameter naked. If you do not, wrap
both sides in a tuple: `[T] extends [U]`. That is the whole of ex3, and it is
the reason the tuple wrapper appears in every type-level library you will read.

**The last three problems are the standard probes**, and they are a family:
`IsNever` needs distribution switched off, `IsAny` needs the parameter out of
the checked position entirely, and `Equals` needs two conditionals the compiler
refuses to evaluate. Each one is a workaround for a place where the ordinary
rules cannot express the question - which is the useful thing to remember about
them, more than the syntax.

## ex1 - is it an array

What this was testing: that a conditional type is a *question about
assignability*, and that its branches may be literal types rather than
`boolean`. `boolean` is the union `true | false` - answering with it is
answering "yes and no".

The classic mistake is writing `T extends unknown[]`, which says `false` for
`readonly number[]` because a readonly array is not assignable to a mutable
one. Constraints run in the direction of assignability, and `readonly` is the
weaker requirement, so it is the one to test against.

The model answer is `T extends readonly unknown[] ? true : false` - one line,
and the tuple case falls out for free because every tuple is assignable to a
readonly array of its element union.

## ex2 - distribute over the union

What this was testing: the rule that a conditional type whose checked type is
a bare type parameter is applied to each member of a union separately and the
results are unioned back together. `ToArray<string | number>` is really two
evaluations, `string[]` and `number[]`, joined with `|`.

The classic mistake is thinking `T[]` and `ToArray<T>` are the same thing.
They agree on every non-union input and diverge on the first union anyone
passes, which is exactly the kind of bug that surfaces months later in
someone else's call site.

The model answer uses `T extends unknown ? T[] : never`: the false branch is
unreachable, and its only job is to make the type conditional so that
distribution applies - including the `never` case, where the empty union has
no members to distribute over and the result stays `never`.

## ex3 - and now do not distribute

What this was testing: the counterpart to ex2. Once you know distribution is
triggered by the bare parameter, turning it off is a syntax trick rather than
a new concept - and it is the trick that makes `IsNever` and every "compare
two types" helper possible.

The classic mistake is reaching for the tuple wrapper without understanding
it, and then writing `[T] extends [U] ? ... : ...` everywhere out of
superstition. Distribution is usually what you want; you switch it off when
the question is about the union *as a whole*.

The model answer is `[T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never` - the condition is
still always true, but `T` is now inside a tuple, so the compiler evaluates it
once with the full union in hand.

## ex4 - name the family

What this was testing: chained conditionals, and the fact that assignability -
not some notion of "the real type" - decides which branch is taken. Every
question in the chain is `extends`, so the specific cases have to come before
the general ones.

The classic mistake is putting `T extends object` early and wondering why
arrays come back as `"object"`; the second-classic is forgetting that a
literal like `"ready"` is assignable to `string`, and adding a special case
for it that never fires.

The model answer is one nested chain from most specific to least, with `null`
and `undefined` first (they are assignable to nothing else here) and `"other"`
as the fallthrough - so adding `symbol` later means inserting one line.

## ex5 - widen a literal

What this was testing: that literal types are subtypes of their base types,
and that a conditional chain plus a fallthrough of `T` gives you a total
function over types. It is also a compact model of what the compiler does on
its own every time you write `let` instead of `const`.

The classic mistake is ending the chain with `never` or `unknown` instead of
`T`, which quietly destroys every object type passed in - the gate's
`{ id: 1 }` case exists to catch precisely that.

The model answer is a four-step chain ending in `T`, and it distributes for
free, so `Widen<"a" | 3>` comes out as `string | number` without a word about
unions anywhere in the definition.

## ex6 - is it never

What this was testing: the single most surprising consequence of distribution.
`T extends never ? true : false` applied to `never` runs the body zero times
and unions zero results, and the union of nothing is `never` - so the type
answers `never` to a yes/no question.

The classic mistake is not noticing, because `IsNever<never>` still *looks*
falsy at a glance and most call sites only ever ask about real types. It shows
up as an unreachable branch or a mysteriously empty result, usually far from
here.

The model answer is `[T] extends [never] ? true : false`: the tuple wrapper
makes the compiler compare the whole type at once, so `never` is checked
against `never` and answers `true`.

## ex7 - is it any

What this was testing: that `any` is not a type in the lattice so much as a
hole in it, and that detecting it needs a condition whose *checked* side does
not mention `T` at all. Every straightforward probe returns `boolean`, because
`any` satisfies both branches simultaneously.

The classic mistake is `T extends any ? true : false` - true for everything -
or its mirror `unknown extends T ? true : false`, which is also true for
`unknown`, and so cannot tell the two apart. The gate checks `unknown`
explicitly for that reason.

The model answer is `0 extends 1 & T ? true : false`: the intersection is
`never` for unrelated types, `1` when `T` is `1` or a supertype of it, and
`any` only when `T` is `any` - and `0` extends only that last one.

## ex8 - are these two types identical

What this was testing: the difference between mutual assignability and
identity, and the one probe that can tell them apart. `any` is the reason the
distinction matters - it is assignable in both directions to everything, so
`X extends Y ? Y extends X ? ...` reports every type as equal to `any`.

The classic mistake is shipping the two-sided `extends` version and trusting
it, usually inside a test helper. It also gets optional members wrong in the
other direction, which is why the gate compares `{ id: string }` with
`{ id?: string }`.

The model answer defers both conditionals behind a generic function type; the
compiler cannot evaluate either one, so it compares them structurally, and two
unevaluated conditionals are identical only when the types they branch on are.
That is an implementation detail rather than a documented rule, and it is worth
knowing which of the two you are relying on.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Conditional Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html) - the base rule, and the section on distributive conditional types that ex2, ex3 and ex6 all turn on.
- [Handbook: Everyday Types - literal types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#literal-types) - why `"ready" extends string` is true, which is the engine behind ex4 and ex5.
- [Handbook: `any`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#any) - assignable in both directions to everything, which is exactly what ex7 and ex8 are working around.
- [TypeScript 2.8 release notes: conditional types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-2-8.html) - the original write-up, including the deferred-conditional behaviour ex8 relies on.

results are unioned back together. `ToArray<string | number>` is really two
evaluations, `string[]` and `number[]`, joined with `|`.

The classic mistake is thinking `T[]` and `ToArray<T>` are the same thing.
They agree on every non-union input and diverge on the first union anyone
passes, which is exactly the kind of bug that surfaces months later in
someone else's call site.

The model answer uses `T extends unknown ? T[] : never`: the false branch is
unreachable, and its only job is to make the type conditional so that
distribution applies - including the `never` case, where the empty union has
no members to distribute over and the result stays `never`.

## ex3 - and now do not distribute

What this was testing: the counterpart to ex2. Once you know distribution is
triggered by the bare parameter, turning it off is a syntax trick rather than
a new concept - and it is the trick that makes `IsNever` and every "compare
two types" helper possible.

The classic mistake is reaching for the tuple wrapper without understanding
it, and then writing `[T] extends [U] ? ... : ...` everywhere out of
superstition. Distribution is usually what you want; you switch it off when
the question is about the union *as a whole*.

The model answer is `[T] extends [unknown] ? T[] : never` - the condition is
still always true, but `T` is now inside a tuple, so the compiler evaluates it
once with the full union in hand.

## ex4 - name the family

What this was testing: chained conditionals, and the fact that assignability -
not some notion of "the real type" - decides which branch is taken. Every
question in the chain is `extends`, so the specific cases have to come before
the general ones.

The classic mistake is putting `T extends object` early and wondering why
arrays come back as `"object"`; the second-classic is forgetting that a
literal like `"ready"` is assignable to `string`, and adding a special case
for it that never fires.

The model answer is one nested chain from most specific to least, with `null`
and `undefined` first (they are assignable to nothing else here) and `"other"`
as the fallthrough - so adding `symbol` later means inserting one line.

## ex5 - widen a literal

What this was testing: that literal types are subtypes of their base types,
and that a conditional chain plus a fallthrough of `T` gives you a total
function over types. It is also a compact model of what the compiler does on
its own every time you write `let` instead of `const`.

The classic mistake is ending the chain with `never` or `unknown` instead of
`T`, which quietly destroys every object type passed in - the gate's
`{ id: 1 }` case exists to catch precisely that.

The model answer is a four-step chain ending in `T`, and it distributes for
free, so `Widen<"a" | 3>` comes out as `string | number` without a word about
unions anywhere in the definition.

## ex6 - is it never

What this was testing: the single most surprising consequence of distribution.
`T extends never ? true : false` applied to `never` runs the body zero times
and unions zero results, and the union of nothing is `never` - so the type
answers `never` to a yes/no question.

The classic mistake is not noticing, because `IsNever<never>` still *looks*
falsy at a glance and most call sites only ever ask about real types. It shows
up as an unreachable branch or a mysteriously empty result, usually far from
here.

The model answer is `[T] extends [never] ? true : false`: the tuple wrapper
makes the compiler compare the whole type at once, so `never` is checked
against `never` and answers `true`.

## ex7 - is it any

What this was testing: that `any` is not a type in the lattice so much as a
hole in it, and that detecting it needs a condition whose *checked* side does
not mention `T` at all. Every straightforward probe returns `boolean`, because
`any` satisfies both branches simultaneously.

The classic mistake is `T extends any ? true : false` - true for everything -
or its mirror `unknown extends T ? true : false`, which is also true for
`unknown`, and so cannot tell the two apart. The gate checks `unknown`
explicitly for that reason.

The model answer is `0 extends 1 & T ? true : false`: the intersection is
`never` for unrelated types, `1` when `T` is `1` or a supertype of it, and
`any` only when `T` is `any` - and `0` extends only that last one.

## ex8 - are these two types identical

What this was testing: the difference between mutual assignability and
identity, and the one probe that can tell them apart. `any` is the reason the
distinction matters - it is assignable in both directions to everything, so
`X extends Y ? Y extends X ? ...` reports every type as equal to `any`.

The classic mistake is shipping the two-sided `extends` version and trusting
it, usually inside a test helper. It also gets optional members wrong in the
other direction, which is why the gate compares `{ id: string }` with
`{ id?: string }`.

The model answer defers both conditionals behind a generic function type; the
compiler cannot evaluate either one, so it compares them structurally, and two
unevaluated conditionals are identical only when the types they branch on are.
That is an implementation detail rather than a documented rule, and it is worth
knowing which of the two you are relying on.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Conditional Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html) - the base rule, and the section on distributive conditional types that ex2, ex3 and ex6 all turn on.
- [Handbook: Everyday Types - literal types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#literal-types) - why `"ready" extends string` is true, which is the engine behind ex4 and ex5.
- [Handbook: `any`](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#any) - assignable in both directions to everything, which is exactly what ex7 and ex8 are working around.
- [TypeScript 2.8 release notes: conditional types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-2-8.html) - the original write-up, including the deferred-conditional behaviour ex8 relies on.

exercises.prompt:
## ex1 - is it an array

`IsArray<T>` is `true` when `T` is any array or tuple type - mutable,
`readonly`, or a fixed-length tuple - and `false` otherwise. The answers are
the *literal* types `true` and `false`, not `boolean`.

- `IsArray<string[]>` -> `true`, `IsArray<readonly number[]>` -> `true`
- `IsArray<[1, 2]>` -> `true`, `IsArray<{ length: number }>` -> `false`

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The two branches of a conditional type can be literal types. `true` and
`false` are types as well as values - that is the whole of lesson 05.

## Hint 2

The check has to admit `readonly` arrays and tuples too. A mutable `string[]`
is assignable to `readonly unknown[]`, and so is `[1, 2]`, so one constraint
covers all three - the other direction does not.

Left to you: `unknown` or `any` as the element type in that constraint. Both
work here; only one of them keeps `noImplicitAny` honest elsewhere.

## Hint 1

The two branches of a conditional type can be literal types. `true` and
`false` are types as well as values - that is the whole of lesson 05.

## Hint 2

The check has to admit `readonly` arrays and tuples too. A mutable `string[]`
is assignable to `readonly unknown[]`, and so is `[1, 2]`, so one constraint
covers all three - the other direction does not.

Left to you: `unknown` or `any` as the element type in that constraint. Both
work here; only one of them keeps `noImplicitAny` honest elsewhere.

// d15_conditional_types / ex1 - reference solution (author only).

export type IsArray<T> = T extends readonly unknown[] ? true : false;

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - distribute over the union

`ToArray<T>` turns a type into an array of it, **member by member**:

- `ToArray<string>` -> `string[]`
- `ToArray<string | number>` -> `string[] | number[]` (not `(string | number)[]`)
- `ToArray<never>` -> `never`

That last case is the tell: a distributive conditional over the empty union
produces the empty union.

Distribution is triggered by a *naked* type parameter on the left of
`extends`. So stop it from being naked.

## Hint 2

Wrapping both sides in a one-element tuple - `[T] extends [U]` - asks the same
assignability question about a type the compiler will not split apart. The
`never` case proves it worked: `never[]` rather than `never`.

Left to you: tuples are the usual wrapper, but any position that is not the
bare parameter works. Try one and see whether it still reads.

exercises.prompt:
## ex4 - name the family

`Kind<T>` reports which family a type belongs to, as a string literal:
`"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"`, `"bigint"`, `"null"`, `"undefined"`,
`"array"`, or `"object"` - and `"other"` for anything left over.

- `Kind<"ready">` -> `"string"` (a literal still belongs to its family)
- `Kind<readonly [1, 2]>` -> `"array"`, and `Kind<{ id: string }>` -> `"object"`
- `Kind<string | number>` -> `"string" | "number"` - it distributes

Order matters: an array *is* an object, so one of those checks has to come
first.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Conditional types nest in the false branch, exactly like a chain of ternaries
in JavaScript - and they read the same way once you stop trying to align them.

## Hint 2

Two orderings will bite you. An array is assignable to `object`, so the array
check must come before the object check. And `boolean` is `true | false`, so
distribution splits it before the check even runs - which is harmless here,
because both halves land on the same answer.

Left to you: how to lay the chain out. Nested ternaries or one long line - the
compiler does not care, and your reviewer will.

## Hint 1

Conditional types nest in the false branch, exactly like a chain of ternaries
in JavaScript - and they read the same way once you stop trying to align them.

## Hint 2

Two orderings will bite you. An array is assignable to `object`, so the array
check must come before the object check. And `boolean` is `true | false`, so
distribution splits it before the check even runs - which is harmless here,
because both halves land on the same answer.

Left to you: how to lay the chain out. Nested ternaries or one long line - the
compiler does not care, and your reviewer will.

export type Kind<T> = T extends null
  ? "null"
  : T extends undefined
    ? "undefined"
    : T extends readonly unknown[]
      ? "array"
      : T extends string
        ? "string"
        : T extends number
          ? "number"
          : T extends boolean
            ? "boolean"
            : T extends bigint
              ? "bigint"
              : T extends object
                ? "object"
                : "other";

exercises.prompt:
## ex5 - widen a literal

`Widen<T>` is what `let` does to a literal, expressed as a type: a string
literal becomes `string`, a numeric literal becomes `number`, `true` becomes
`boolean`, a bigint literal becomes `bigint`. Everything else is returned
untouched, including object types.

- `Widen<"ready">` -> `string`, `Widen<7>` -> `number`, `Widen<10n>` -> `bigint`
- `Widen<"a" | 3>` -> `string | number` (it distributes)
- `Widen<{ id: 1 }>` -> `{ id: 1 }` - only the top level is widened


`IsNever<T>` is `true` only when `T` is `never`.

exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - is it any

`IsAny<T>` is `true` only for `any`.

- `IsAny<any>` -> `true`
- `IsAny<unknown>` -> `false`, `IsAny<never>` -> `false`, `IsAny<string>` -> `false`

The obvious tests all fail: `any` is assignable to everything *and* everything
is assignable to `any`, so any conditional whose condition mentions `T`
directly takes both branches and returns `boolean`. You need a condition that
is false for every real type and that `any` alone can make true.

The lever: intersecting anything with `any` gives `any`, while intersecting
two unrelated types gives `never`.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Pick two literal types that are definitely not assignable to one another - say
`0` and `1`. `0 extends 1` is false, and it stays false no matter what.

## Hint 2

Now intersect one of them with `T`. For every ordinary `T`, `1 & T` is either
`1` or `never`, and `0` extends neither. For `any`, `1 & any` collapses to
`any`, and `0` extends `any`.

Note that the checked type is `0`, not `T`, so nothing distributes - which is
also why `IsAny<string | number>` comes out as a single `false`.

Left to you: which two literals to use. Any non-assignable pair works; pick
the one that will still read as deliberate in six months.

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - are these two types identical

`Equals<X, Y>` is `true` when the two types are *identical*, not merely
mutually assignable.

- `Equals<string, string>` -> `true`, `Equals<"a" | "b", "b" | "a">` -> `true`
- `Equals<{ id: string }, { id: string }>` -> `true`, `Equals<never, never>` -> `true`
- `Equals<any, string>` -> `false`, `Equals<unknown, any>` -> `false`
- `Equals<1, number>` -> `false`, `Equals<{ id: string }, { id?: string }>` -> `false`

Mutual assignability is not enough: `any` is assignable both ways to
everything, so the two-sided `extends` test says `true` for `Equals<any,
string>`. The escape hatch is that the compiler compares two *deferred*
conditional types structurally - two generic function types whose bodies are
conditionals are related only when the conditionals are written against
identical types.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d15_conditional_types ex8
```

## Hint 1

Do not try to compare `X` and `Y` directly - every test you can write is one
`any` away from lying. Compare two *things built from* `X` and `Y` instead.

## Hint 2

Build a generic function type on each side whose return type is a conditional
mentioning the type under test: `<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2`. Neither
conditional can be resolved (nothing is known about `T`), so the compiler falls
back to comparing them as written - and they match only when `X` and `Y` are
the same type.

## Hint 3

Then the whole thing is one `extends` between those two function types, with
`true` and `false` as the branches. Watch the parentheses: the conditional in
the return position and the outer conditional are easy to tangle.

Left to you: this is a compiler-internals trick with no specification behind
it. Decide for yourself whether it belongs in a codebase you maintain, or only
in the tests that guard your utility types.

lessons.briefing:
# d16 - infer patterns (drill set)

Eight problems on `infer`: the keyword that lets a conditional type ask "what
was in there?" and keep the answer. Arrays, parameter lists, tuple heads and
tails, nested callbacks, and the two recursive patterns interviewers reach for.
They drill lesson **09_mapped_conditional**; go back to its `infer` section if
the keyword still looks like a declaration.

Every exercise is **type-level only** - each stub compiles and is wrong, and
the whole gate is `gate.test-d.ts`. The one rule to keep in front of you:
`infer X` may appear only inside the `extends` clause of a conditional type,
and `X` is usable only in the true branch.

## ex1 - the element of an array

`ElementOf<T>` is the element type of an array or tuple, and `never` for
anything that is not one.

- `ElementOf<string[]>` -> `string`, `ElementOf<readonly number[]>` -> `number`
- `ElementOf<[1, "a"]>` -> `1 | "a"` - a tuple's elements collapse to their union
- `ElementOf<string>` -> `never`

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex1
```

## ex2 - the first parameter

`FirstArg<F>` is the type of a function's **first** parameter - not the whole
parameter tuple.

- `FirstArg<(id: string, retries: number) => void>` -> `string`
- `FirstArg<(rows: number[]) => string>` -> `number[]`
- `FirstArg<() => void>` -> `unknown` - there was nothing to infer, and an
  uninferred `infer` falls back to `unknown`
- `FirstArg<string>` -> `never` - not a function at all

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex2
```

## ex3 - everything after the head

`TailOf<T>` drops the first element of a tuple and returns the rest as a tuple.

- `TailOf<[1, 2, 3]>` -> `[2, 3]`, `TailOf<[string]>` -> `[]`
- `TailOf<readonly ["a", "b"]>` -> `["b"]` - the result is a mutable tuple
- `TailOf<[]>` -> `never` - an empty tuple has no head to drop

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex3
```

## ex4 - the far end of a tuple

`LastOf<T>` is the type of a tuple's **last** element.

- `LastOf<[1, 2, 3]>` -> `3`, `LastOf<[string]>` -> `string`
- `LastOf<readonly ["a", "b"]>` -> `"b"`, `LastOf<[]>` -> `never`

The interesting part is that the variadic part of the pattern does not have to
come last.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex4
```

## ex5 - unwrap all the way down

`Flatten<T>` strips every layer of array nesting, however deep.

- `Flatten<number[][][]>` -> `number`, `Flatten<string[]>` -> `string`
- `Flatten<string>` -> `string` - not an array, so it is already flat
- `Flatten<readonly (readonly boolean[])[]>` -> `boolean`

This one recurses. A conditional type may refer to itself in its own branches,
and here the base case is "`T` is not an array".

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex5
```

## ex6 - the state a store publishes

`StateOf<T>` recovers the state type from a store-like object: something with a
`subscribe` method that takes a listener, where the listener takes the state.

Given `interface Store { subscribe(listener: (state: { count: number }) => void): () => void }`,
`StateOf<Store>` is `{ count: number }`.

- `StateOf<{ subscribe: string }>` -> `never`, `StateOf<{ count: number }>` -> `never`

The `infer` sits two levels deep: inside the parameter of the parameter.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex6
```

## ex7 - turn a union into an intersection

`UnionToIntersection<U>` converts `A | B` into `A & B`.

- `UnionToIntersection<{ a: string } | { b: number }>` -> `{ a: string } & { b: number }`
- `UnionToIntersection<{ a: string }>` -> `{ a: string }`
- three members intersect just as happily as two

There is no direct operator for this. The route is two steps: distribute the
union into a union of *function types* that take it as a parameter, then infer
one parameter type back out. Because parameters are compared
contravariantly, inferring from several call signatures at once produces the
**intersection** of the candidates rather than their union.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex7
```

## ex8 - curry a signature

`Curried<F>` rewrites a function type as a chain of one-argument functions.

- `Curried<(a: string, b: number) => boolean>` -> `(a: string) => (b: number) => boolean`
- `Curried<(a: 1, b: 2, c: 3) => 4>` -> `(a: 1) => (b: 2) => (c: 3) => 4`
- `Curried<(a: string) => number>` -> `(a: string) => number` - already one argument
- `Curried<() => number>` -> `() => number` - nothing to split
- `Curried<string>` -> `never`

Two `infer`s in the outer pattern (the parameter tuple and the return type),
then recursion over the tuple.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - typescript/d16_infer_patterns

The debrief. Per problem: what the pattern was really matching, the capture
that looks close enough, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**`infer` is pattern matching for types.** You write the shape you expect on
the right of `extends`, put `infer X` where the interesting part lives, and if
the shape matches, `X` is bound in the true branch. The two hard rules: it is
legal only inside a conditional type's `extends` clause, and the name is
visible only in the true branch - which is also a decent way to remember why
the false branch has to invent its own answer.

**Be specific where you are capturing and vague everywhere else.** Half the
failures in this set are patterns that were too narrow in a position nobody
cared about: `(infer E)[]` instead of `readonly (infer E)[]` (ex1), a `void`
return where a real function returned an unsubscriber (ex6), an `unknown[]`
rest that would not absorb a narrower parameter (ex2). A pattern is a
*constraint*, so every detail you write is a way for a real type to miss.

**Tuple patterns are positional and the rest element can sit anywhere.**
`[unknown, ...infer Rest]` peels the head (ex3), `[...unknown[], infer Last]`
reads the tail (ex4), and requiring a fixed element is what makes the empty
tuple fall through to the false branch. Together with recursion that gives you
a loop over a parameter list, which is all ex8 is.

**Recursion needs a base case and a shrinking argument.** `Flatten` recurses on
the captured element and stops when the pattern fails to match (ex5); `Curried`
recurses on a rebuilt signature and stops when the tuple runs out (ex8). If you
cannot say in one sentence what gets smaller each step, the compiler will say
it for you, at depth 50, in a much longer sentence.

**And two of these are not really about `infer` at all.** ex7 works because
parameters are contravariant, so inferring one type from several call
signatures yields their intersection; `infer` is only the tool that reads the
result out. That is the pattern behind most union-manipulation utilities you
will meet in the wild.

## ex1 - the element of an array

What this was testing: the smallest complete use of `infer` - one pattern, one
capture, one branch that uses it. Everything later in this set is this shape
with a more interesting pattern.

The classic mistake is `T extends unknown[] ? T[number] : never`, which works
but throws away the point of the exercise, or `T extends (infer E)[]`, which
answers `never` for `readonly number[]` because a readonly array is not
assignable to a mutable one.

The model answer is `T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? E : never`; the tuple
case falls out for free, because `[1, "a"]` is assignable to
`readonly (1 | "a")[]` and that is the widest capture the compiler can make.

## ex2 - the first parameter

What this was testing: an `infer` in one *position* of a larger pattern rather
than the whole of it, plus a rest parameter used as a wildcard. This is how
`Parameters`, `ReturnType` and every hand-rolled variation of them are built.

The classic mistake is capturing `...args: infer A` and then indexing with
`A[0]`, which is a longer way to the same place and gives `undefined` in the
union once optional parameters are involved. The second is using `unknown[]`
for the rest wildcard, which fails to match a function whose later parameters
are narrower.

The model answer matches `(first: infer A, ...rest: never[]) => unknown`, so
the first parameter is captured by name and everything after it is ignored -
and the empty-parameter case leaves `A` uninferred, which the compiler resolves
to `unknown`.

## ex3 - everything after the head

What this was testing: variadic tuple patterns, and the fact that requiring a
leading element is what distinguishes "has a head" from "is empty". The
compiler matches these positionally, so the pattern reads exactly like the
value-level destructuring it mirrors.

The classic mistake is `[infer First, ...infer Rest]` with `First` unused,
which is harmless but noisy, or forgetting `readonly` in the pattern and then
being unable to explain why a `readonly ["a", "b"]` came back `never`.

The model answer is `T extends readonly [unknown, ...infer Rest] ? Rest : never`
- and the captured `Rest` comes out as a mutable tuple, because that is the
form the compiler infers for a rest element.

## ex4 - the far end of a tuple

What this was testing: that the variadic element of a tuple pattern is not
pinned to the end, which is the whole reason `LastOf` is expressible at all.
Once you have seen it, `[...unknown[], infer Last]` reads as naturally as
`[unknown, ...infer Rest]`.

The classic mistake is the stub's version - capture the element type of the
array and call it the last one. It is right for a one-element tuple and gives
`1 | 2 | 3` for the gate's first case, which is a union masquerading as an
answer.

The model answer is `T extends readonly [...unknown[], infer Last] ? Last : never`,
one pattern with no recursion - unlike the union-based `LastOf` you may have
seen, which is solving the much harder problem of ordering a union.

## ex5 - unwrap all the way down

What this was testing: recursion in a conditional type, with `infer` supplying
the smaller input for the next step. The pattern - match, capture, recurse on
the capture, fall through to `T` - is the skeleton of `DeepReadonly`,
`DeepPartial` and every "walk the whole type" utility.

The classic mistake is the stub: one unwrap, which passes the shallow test and
returns `number[][]` for a triple-nested array. The second is writing `never`
as the base case, which erases every non-array type instead of returning it.

The model answer is `T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? Flatten<E> : T` - four
tokens more than the stub, and the difference between a utility and a demo.

## ex6 - the state a store publishes

What this was testing: that `infer` is positional inside an arbitrarily nested
structural pattern. Nothing new happens at depth - the compiler matches the
shape and binds whatever sits where the `infer` is - but it is the first time
in this set that the pattern is a whole interface.

The classic mistake is being too specific about the parts you are not
capturing: writing `): void` for `subscribe`'s return type makes `Store` fail
to match, because it returns an unsubscribe function. Wildcards in a pattern
should be as wide as you can make them.

The model answer matches `{ subscribe(listener: (state: infer S) => void): unknown }`
and returns `S` - `unknown` in the return position accepts anything, and the
listener's `void` return accepts any listener because `void` in a return
position is deliberately permissive.

## ex7 - turn a union into an intersection

What this was testing: contravariance, expressed as a type-level trick. When
the compiler infers from several call signatures at once it must satisfy all of
them, and for a parameter position "satisfies all" means an intersection - the
exact opposite of what happens in a return position.

The classic mistake is expecting a union-to-intersection operator to exist and
searching for it. The second is forgetting the parentheses around the
distributive step, which produces a type error far from its cause.

The model answer distributes `U` into `(arg: U) => void` and then infers a
single parameter type back out; the number of union members never appears in
the definition, because distribution does the counting.

## ex8 - curry a signature

What this was testing: two `infer`s in one pattern, recursion driven by a tuple,
and the discipline of enumerating base cases before writing the recursive one.
It is the type-level half of the `curry` every functional-programming interview
asks for, and it is the half that people skip.

The classic mistake is forgetting the one-parameter base case and producing
`(a: string) => () => number`: an extra empty call that nothing at the call site
expects. The second is recursing on `Rest` directly, which type-errors because
`Curried` is written to take a function type.

The model answer peels one parameter per step and rebuilds the remainder as a
new signature, so the recursion always has the same shape of input - and the
zero-parameter case is handled first, where it cannot be forgotten.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Conditional Types - inferring within conditional types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html#inferring-within-conditional-types) - the rules for where `infer` may appear and where its name is visible.
- [Handbook: Variadic tuple types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-0.html#variadic-tuple-types) - the `[...unknown[], infer Last]` and `[unknown, ...infer Rest]` patterns from ex3 and ex4.
- [Handbook: Recursive conditional types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-1.html#recursive-conditional-types) - what makes ex5 and ex8 legal, and where the depth limit lives.
- [Handbook: Type inference in conditional types and variance](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#assignability-of-functions) - parameter contravariance, which is the whole mechanism behind ex7.
lessons.fullReadme:
# d16 - infer patterns (drill set)

Eight problems on `infer`: the keyword that lets a conditional type ask "what
was in there?" and keep the answer. Arrays, parameter lists, tuple heads and
tails, nested callbacks, and the two recursive patterns interviewers reach for.
They drill lesson **09_mapped_conditional**; go back to its `infer` section if
the keyword still looks like a declaration.

Every exercise is **type-level only** - each stub compiles and is wrong, and
the whole gate is `gate.test-d.ts`. The one rule to keep in front of you:
`infer X` may appear only inside the `extends` clause of a conditional type,
and `X` is usable only in the true branch.

## ex1 - the element of an array

`ElementOf<T>` is the element type of an array or tuple, and `never` for
anything that is not one.

- `ElementOf<string[]>` -> `string`, `ElementOf<readonly number[]>` -> `number`
- `ElementOf<[1, "a"]>` -> `1 | "a"` - a tuple's elements collapse to their union
- `ElementOf<string>` -> `never`

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex1
```

## ex2 - the first parameter

`FirstArg<F>` is the type of a function's **first** parameter - not the whole
parameter tuple.

- `FirstArg<(id: string, retries: number) => void>` -> `string`
- `FirstArg<(rows: number[]) => string>` -> `number[]`
- `FirstArg<() => void>` -> `unknown` - there was nothing to infer, and an
  uninferred `infer` falls back to `unknown`
- `FirstArg<string>` -> `never` - not a function at all

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex2
```

## ex3 - everything after the head

`TailOf<T>` drops the first element of a tuple and returns the rest as a tuple.

- `TailOf<[1, 2, 3]>` -> `[2, 3]`, `TailOf<[string]>` -> `[]`
- `TailOf<readonly ["a", "b"]>` -> `["b"]` - the result is a mutable tuple
- `TailOf<[]>` -> `never` - an empty tuple has no head to drop

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex3
```

## ex4 - the far end of a tuple

`LastOf<T>` is the type of a tuple's **last** element.

- `LastOf<[1, 2, 3]>` -> `3`, `LastOf<[string]>` -> `string`
- `LastOf<readonly ["a", "b"]>` -> `"b"`, `LastOf<[]>` -> `never`

The interesting part is that the variadic part of the pattern does not have to
come last.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex4
```

## ex5 - unwrap all the way down

`Flatten<T>` strips every layer of array nesting, however deep.

- `Flatten<number[][][]>` -> `number`, `Flatten<string[]>` -> `string`
- `Flatten<string>` -> `string` - not an array, so it is already flat
- `Flatten<readonly (readonly boolean[])[]>` -> `boolean`

This one recurses. A conditional type may refer to itself in its own branches,
and here the base case is "`T` is not an array".

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex5
```

## ex6 - the state a store publishes

`StateOf<T>` recovers the state type from a store-like object: something with a
`subscribe` method that takes a listener, where the listener takes the state.

Given `interface Store { subscribe(listener: (state: { count: number }) => void): () => void }`,
`StateOf<Store>` is `{ count: number }`.

- `StateOf<{ subscribe: string }>` -> `never`, `StateOf<{ count: number }>` -> `never`

The `infer` sits two levels deep: inside the parameter of the parameter.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex6
```

## ex7 - turn a union into an intersection

`UnionToIntersection<U>` converts `A | B` into `A & B`.

- `UnionToIntersection<{ a: string } | { b: number }>` -> `{ a: string } & { b: number }`
- `UnionToIntersection<{ a: string }>` -> `{ a: string }`
- three members intersect just as happily as two

There is no direct operator for this. The route is two steps: distribute the
union into a union of *function types* that take it as a parameter, then infer
one parameter type back out. Because parameters are compared
contravariantly, inferring from several call signatures at once produces the
**intersection** of the candidates rather than their union.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex7
```

## ex8 - curry a signature

`Curried<F>` rewrites a function type as a chain of one-argument functions.

- `Curried<(a: string, b: number) => boolean>` -> `(a: string) => (b: number) => boolean`
- `Curried<(a: 1, b: 2, c: 3) => 4>` -> `(a: 1) => (b: 2) => (c: 3) => 4`
- `Curried<(a: string) => number>` -> `(a: string) => number` - already one argument
- `Curried<() => number>` -> `() => number` - nothing to split
- `Curried<string>` -> `never`

Two `infer`s in the outer pattern (the parameter tuple and the return type),
then recursion over the tuple.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex8
```

## The gate

This is the entire gate, `gate.test-d.ts`:

```ts
// Type gate for typescript/d16_infer_patterns. Quoted verbatim in README.md.
import { describe, expectTypeOf, test } from "vitest";

import type { ElementOf } from "./ex1/solution";
import type { FirstArg } from "./ex2/solution";
import type { TailOf } from "./ex3/solution";
import type { LastOf } from "./ex4/solution";
import type { Flatten } from "./ex5/solution";
import type { StateOf } from "./ex6/solution";
import type { UnionToIntersection } from "./ex7/solution";
import type { Curried } from "./ex8/solution";

interface Store {
  subscribe(listener: (state: { count: number }) => void): () => void;
}

interface Poller {
  subscribe(listener: (state: string[]) => void): () => void;
}

describe("d16_infer_patterns", () => {
  test("ex1 - ElementOf<T> pulls the element type out of an array", () => {
    expectTypeOf<ElementOf<string[]>>().toEqualTypeOf<string>();
    expectTypeOf<ElementOf<readonly number[]>>().toEqualTypeOf<number>();
    expectTypeOf<ElementOf<[1, "a"]>>().toEqualTypeOf<1 | "a">();
    expectTypeOf<ElementOf<string>>().toEqualTypeOf<never>();
    const first: ElementOf<{ id: string }[]> = { id: "a" };
    expectTypeOf(first).toEqualTypeOf<{ id: string }>();
  });

  test("ex2 - FirstArg<F> reads only the first parameter", () => {
    expectTypeOf<FirstArg<(id: string, retries: number) => void>>().toEqualTypeOf<string>();
    expectTypeOf<FirstArg<(rows: number[]) => string>>().toEqualTypeOf<number[]>();
    expectTypeOf<FirstArg<() => void>>().toEqualTypeOf<unknown>();
    expectTypeOf<FirstArg<string>>().toEqualTypeOf<never>();
  });

  test("ex3 - TailOf<T> drops the head of a tuple", () => {
    expectTypeOf<TailOf<[1, 2, 3]>>().toEqualTypeOf<[2, 3]>();
    expectTypeOf<TailOf<[string]>>().toEqualTypeOf<[]>();
    expectTypeOf<TailOf<readonly ["a", "b"]>>().toEqualTypeOf<["b"]>();
    expectTypeOf<TailOf<[]>>().toEqualTypeOf<never>();
  });

  test("ex4 - LastOf<T> reads the far end of a tuple", () => {
    expectTypeOf<LastOf<[1, 2, 3]>>().toEqualTypeOf<3>();
    expectTypeOf<LastOf<[string]>>().toEqualTypeOf<string>();
    expectTypeOf<LastOf<readonly ["a", "b"]>>().toEqualTypeOf<"b">();
    expectTypeOf<LastOf<[]>>().toEqualTypeOf<never>();
  });

  test("ex5 - Flatten<T> keeps unwrapping until there is nothing left", () => {
    expectTypeOf<Flatten<number[][][]>>().toEqualTypeOf<number>();
    expectTypeOf<Flatten<string[]>>().toEqualTypeOf<string>();
    expectTypeOf<Flatten<string>>().toEqualTypeOf<string>();
    expectTypeOf<Flatten<readonly (readonly boolean[])[]>>().toEqualTypeOf<boolean>();
    expectTypeOf<Flatten<{ id: string }[][]>>().toEqualTypeOf<{ id: string }>();
  });

  test("ex6 - StateOf<T> digs two levels into a method signature", () => {
    expectTypeOf<StateOf<Store>>().toEqualTypeOf<{ count: number }>();
    expectTypeOf<StateOf<Poller>>().toEqualTypeOf<string[]>();
    expectTypeOf<StateOf<{ subscribe: string }>>().toEqualTypeOf<never>();
    expectTypeOf<StateOf<{ count: number }>>().toEqualTypeOf<never>();
  });

  test("ex7 - UnionToIntersection<U> turns or into and", () => {
    expectTypeOf<UnionToIntersection<{ a: string } | { b: number }>>().toMatchTypeOf<{
      a: string;
      b: number;
    }>();
    expectTypeOf<UnionToIntersection<{ a: string }>>().toEqualTypeOf<{ a: string }>();
    expectTypeOf<
      UnionToIntersection<{ a: string } | { b: number } | { c: boolean }>
    >().toMatchTypeOf<{ a: string; b: number; c: boolean }>();
    const both = { a: "x", b: 1 } as UnionToIntersection<{ a: string } | { b: number }>;
    expectTypeOf(both.b).toEqualTypeOf<number>();
  });

  test("ex8 - Curried<F> splits a signature one argument at a time", () => {
    expectTypeOf<Curried<(a: string, b: number) => boolean>>().toEqualTypeOf<
      (a: string) => (b: number) => boolean
    >();
    expectTypeOf<Curried<(a: string) => number>>().toEqualTypeOf<(a: string) => number>();
    expectTypeOf<Curried<() => number>>().toEqualTypeOf<() => number>();
    expectTypeOf<Curried<(a: 1, b: 2, c: 3) => 4>>().toEqualTypeOf<
      (a: 1) => (b: 2) => (c: 3) => 4
    >();
    expectTypeOf<Curried<string>>().toEqualTypeOf<never>();
  });
});
```

## Ten-pass spaced repetition

Use this ladder after completing **d16 - infer patterns (drill set)**. Each pass changes the retrieval
task so repetition strengthens recall instead of becoming answer recognition.
Do the named exercise from a blank starting point whenever practical, and only
open its hints after recording your first attempt.

| Pass | When | Practice target | Retrieval task |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | now | `ex1` | Close the notes and state the central rule in one precise sentence. |
| 2 | 3 days | `ex2` | Rebuild the smallest valid example from memory, then explain each part. |
| 3 | 7 days | `ex3` | Predict the result or behavior before running anything; reconcile surprises. |
| 4 | 21 days | `ex4` | Solve from a blank file and name the first tempting mistake you avoided. |
| 5 | 60 days | `ex5` | Contrast this technique with its nearest alternative and choose between them. |
| 6 | 120 days | `ex6` | Add one realistic constraint and adapt the solution without consulting notes. |
| 7 | 240 days | `ex7` | Debug a deliberately broken version; explain the evidence before the repair. |
| 8 | 1 year | `ex8` | Teach the idea aloud in two minutes, including one boundary case. |
| 9 | 18 months | `ex1` | Transfer the pattern to a new domain and verify the result with the gate. |
| 10 | 3 years | `ex2` | Complete a cold, timed solution and write the rule you want to retain long-term. |

A failed pass is useful evidence: return to pass 1 after three days. A clean
pass advances to the next interval. After pass 10, revisit the skill every
three years or whenever real work exposes a weak edge case.

# Reading - typescript/d16_infer_patterns

The debrief. Per problem: what the pattern was really matching, the capture
that looks close enough, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**`infer` is pattern matching for types.** You write the shape you expect on
the right of `extends`, put `infer X` where the interesting part lives, and if
the shape matches, `X` is bound in the true branch. The two hard rules: it is
legal only inside a conditional type's `extends` clause, and the name is
visible only in the true branch - which is also a decent way to remember why
the false branch has to invent its own answer.

**Be specific where you are capturing and vague everywhere else.** Half the
failures in this set are patterns that were too narrow in a position nobody
cared about: `(infer E)[]` instead of `readonly (infer E)[]` (ex1), a `void`
return where a real function returned an unsubscriber (ex6), an `unknown[]`
rest that would not absorb a narrower parameter (ex2). A pattern is a
*constraint*, so every detail you write is a way for a real type to miss.

**Tuple patterns are positional and the rest element can sit anywhere.**
`[unknown, ...infer Rest]` peels the head (ex3), `[...unknown[], infer Last]`
reads the tail (ex4), and requiring a fixed element is what makes the empty
tuple fall through to the false branch. Together with recursion that gives you
a loop over a parameter list, which is all ex8 is.

**Recursion needs a base case and a shrinking argument.** `Flatten` recurses on
the captured element and stops when the pattern fails to match (ex5); `Curried`
recurses on a rebuilt signature and stops when the tuple runs out (ex8). If you
cannot say in one sentence what gets smaller each step, the compiler will say
it for you, at depth 50, in a much longer sentence.

**And two of these are not really about `infer` at all.** ex7 works because
parameters are contravariant, so inferring one type from several call
signatures yields their intersection; `infer` is only the tool that reads the
result out. That is the pattern behind most union-manipulation utilities you
will meet in the wild.

## ex1 - the element of an array

What this was testing: the smallest complete use of `infer` - one pattern, one
capture, one branch that uses it. Everything later in this set is this shape
with a more interesting pattern.

The classic mistake is `T extends unknown[] ? T[number] : never`, which works
but throws away the point of the exercise, or `T extends (infer E)[]`, which
answers `never` for `readonly number[]` because a readonly array is not
assignable to a mutable one.

The model answer is `T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? E : never`; the tuple
case falls out for free, because `[1, "a"]` is assignable to
`readonly (1 | "a")[]` and that is the widest capture the compiler can make.

## ex2 - the first parameter

What this was testing: an `infer` in one *position* of a larger pattern rather
than the whole of it, plus a rest parameter used as a wildcard. This is how
`Parameters`, `ReturnType` and every hand-rolled variation of them are built.

The classic mistake is capturing `...args: infer A` and then indexing with
`A[0]`, which is a longer way to the same place and gives `undefined` in the
union once optional parameters are involved. The second is using `unknown[]`
for the rest wildcard, which fails to match a function whose later parameters
are narrower.

The model answer matches `(first: infer A, ...rest: never[]) => unknown`, so
the first parameter is captured by name and everything after it is ignored -
and the empty-parameter case leaves `A` uninferred, which the compiler resolves
to `unknown`.

## ex3 - everything after the head

What this was testing: variadic tuple patterns, and the fact that requiring a
leading element is what distinguishes "has a head" from "is empty". The
compiler matches these positionally, so the pattern reads exactly like the
value-level destructuring it mirrors.

The classic mistake is `[infer First, ...infer Rest]` with `First` unused,
which is harmless but noisy, or forgetting `readonly` in the pattern and then
being unable to explain why a `readonly ["a", "b"]` came back `never`.

The model answer is `T extends readonly [unknown, ...infer Rest] ? Rest : never`
- and the captured `Rest` comes out as a mutable tuple, because that is the
form the compiler infers for a rest element.

## ex4 - the far end of a tuple

What this was testing: that the variadic element of a tuple pattern is not
pinned to the end, which is the whole reason `LastOf` is expressible at all.
Once you have seen it, `[...unknown[], infer Last]` reads as naturally as
`[unknown, ...infer Rest]`.

The classic mistake is the stub's version - capture the element type of the
array and call it the last one. It is right for a one-element tuple and gives
`1 | 2 | 3` for the gate's first case, which is a union masquerading as an
answer.

The model answer is `T extends readonly [...unknown[], infer Last] ? Last : never`,
one pattern with no recursion - unlike the union-based `LastOf` you may have
seen, which is solving the much harder problem of ordering a union.

## ex5 - unwrap all the way down

What this was testing: recursion in a conditional type, with `infer` supplying
the smaller input for the next step. The pattern - match, capture, recurse on
the capture, fall through to `T` - is the skeleton of `DeepReadonly`,
`DeepPartial` and every "walk the whole type" utility.

The classic mistake is the stub: one unwrap, which passes the shallow test and
returns `number[][]` for a triple-nested array. The second is writing `never`
as the base case, which erases every non-array type instead of returning it.

The model answer is `T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? Flatten<E> : T` - four
tokens more than the stub, and the difference between a utility and a demo.

## ex6 - the state a store publishes

What this was testing: that `infer` is positional inside an arbitrarily nested
structural pattern. Nothing new happens at depth - the compiler matches the
shape and binds whatever sits where the `infer` is - but it is the first time
in this set that the pattern is a whole interface.

The classic mistake is being too specific about the parts you are not
capturing: writing `): void` for `subscribe`'s return type makes `Store` fail
to match, because it returns an unsubscribe function. Wildcards in a pattern
should be as wide as you can make them.

The model answer matches `{ subscribe(listener: (state: infer S) => void): unknown }`
and returns `S` - `unknown` in the return position accepts anything, and the
listener's `void` return accepts any listener because `void` in a return
position is deliberately permissive.

## ex7 - turn a union into an intersection

What this was testing: contravariance, expressed as a type-level trick. When
the compiler infers from several call signatures at once it must satisfy all of
them, and for a parameter position "satisfies all" means an intersection - the
exact opposite of what happens in a return position.

The classic mistake is expecting a union-to-intersection operator to exist and
searching for it. The second is forgetting the parentheses around the
distributive step, which produces a type error far from its cause.

The model answer distributes `U` into `(arg: U) => void` and then infers a
single parameter type back out; the number of union members never appears in
the definition, because distribution does the counting.

## ex8 - curry a signature

What this was testing: two `infer`s in one pattern, recursion driven by a tuple,
and the discipline of enumerating base cases before writing the recursive one.
It is the type-level half of the `curry` every functional-programming interview
asks for, and it is the half that people skip.

The classic mistake is forgetting the one-parameter base case and producing
`(a: string) => () => number`: an extra empty call that nothing at the call site
expects. The second is recursing on `Rest` directly, which type-errors because
`Curried` is written to take a function type.

The model answer peels one parameter per step and rebuilds the remainder as a
new signature, so the recursion always has the same shape of input - and the
zero-parameter case is handled first, where it cannot be forgotten.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Conditional Types - inferring within conditional types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html#inferring-within-conditional-types) - the rules for where `infer` may appear and where its name is visible.
- [Handbook: Variadic tuple types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-0.html#variadic-tuple-types) - the `[...unknown[], infer Last]` and `[unknown, ...infer Rest]` patterns from ex3 and ex4.
- [Handbook: Recursive conditional types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-1.html#recursive-conditional-types) - what makes ex5 and ex8 legal, and where the depth limit lives.
- [Handbook: Type inference in conditional types and variance](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#assignability-of-functions) - parameter contravariance, which is the whole mechanism behind ex7.

## ex1 - the element of an array

`ElementOf<T>` is the element type of an array or tuple, and `never` for
anything that is not one.

- `ElementOf<string[]>` -> `string`, `ElementOf<readonly number[]>` -> `number`
- `ElementOf<[1, "a"]>` -> `1 | "a"` - a tuple's elements collapse to their union
- `ElementOf<string>` -> `never`

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex1
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - the first parameter

`FirstArg<F>` is the type of a function's **first** parameter - not the whole
parameter tuple.

- `FirstArg<(id: string, retries: number) => void>` -> `string`
- `FirstArg<(rows: number[]) => string>` -> `number[]`
- `FirstArg<() => void>` -> `unknown` - there was nothing to infer, and an
  uninferred `infer` falls back to `unknown`
- `FirstArg<string>` -> `never` - not a function at all

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex2
```

## ex3 - everything after the head

`TailOf<T>` drops the first element of a tuple and returns the rest as a tuple.

A tuple type may have its rest element anywhere, not only at the end:

one of them accepts every tuple you might be handed.

## Hint 1

A tuple type may have its rest element anywhere, not only at the end:
`[...unknown[], infer Last]` is a legal pattern and means what it looks like.

## Hint 2

The leading rest absorbs any number of elements, including none, so a
one-element tuple still matches - and an empty tuple does not, because there is
no final element to bind.

Left to you: whether `unknown[]` or `never[]` belongs in the leading rest. Only
one of them accepts every tuple you might be handed.

references.solution.ts:
// d16_infer_patterns / ex4 - reference solution (author only).

export type LastOf<T> = T extends readonly [...unknown[], infer Last] ? Last : never;

exercises.prompt:
## ex5 - unwrap all the way down

`Flatten<T>` strips every layer of array nesting, however deep.

- `Flatten<number[][][]>` -> `number`, `Flatten<string[]>` -> `string`
- `Flatten<string>` -> `string` - not an array, so it is already flat
- `Flatten<readonly (readonly boolean[])[]>` -> `boolean`

This one recurses. A conditional type may refer to itself in its own branches,
and here the base case is "`T` is not an array".

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex5
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - turn a union into an intersection

`UnionToIntersection<U>` converts `A | B` into `A & B`.

- `UnionToIntersection<{ a: string } | { b: number }>` -> `{ a: string } & { b: number }`
- `UnionToIntersection<{ a: string }>` -> `{ a: string }`
- three members intersect just as happily as two

There is no direct operator for this. The route is two steps: distribute the
union into a union of *function types* that take it as a parameter, then infer
one parameter type back out. Because parameters are compared
contravariantly, inferring from several call signatures at once produces the
**intersection** of the candidates rather than their union.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex7
```

Step two matches that union against a single `(arg: infer I) => void`. The
compiler has to find one parameter type that works for *every* member of the
union, and for parameters that means the intersection.

Wrap step one in parentheses before the outer `extends`, or the two
conditionals will bind in the wrong order and the error will be about

## ex8 - curry a signature

`Curried<F>` rewrites a function type as a chain of one-argument functions.

- `Curried<(a: string, b: number) => boolean>` -> `(a: string) => (b: number) => boolean`
- `Curried<(a: 1, b: 2, c: 3) => 4>` -> `(a: 1) => (b: 2) => (c: 3) => 4`
- `Curried<(a: string) => number>` -> `(a: string) => number` - already one argument
- `Curried<() => number>` -> `() => number` - nothing to split
- `Curried<string>` -> `never`

Two `infer`s in the outer pattern (the parameter tuple and the return type),
then recursion over the tuple.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d16_infer_patterns ex8
```

// d16_infer_patterns / ex8 - reference solution (author only).

export type Curried<F> = F extends (...args: infer Args) => infer R
  ? Args extends [infer First, ...infer Rest]
    ? Rest extends []
      ? (arg: First) => R
      : (arg: First) => Curried<(...args: Rest) => R>
    : () => R
  : never;

lessons.briefing:
# d17 - Template literal types (drill set)

Eight problems on the string type that is also a template: building names,
matching prefixes, cutting strings into tuples and putting them back, and
finally reading a route's parameters out of its path. They drill lesson
**09_mapped_conditional**, whose key-remapping section introduced the syntax -
but this set treats it as a subject in its own right, so `reading.md` starts
from the construct rather than assuming it.

Every exercise is **type-level only** - each stub compiles and is wrong, and
the whole gate is `gate.test-d.ts`. `// @ts-expect-error` only suppresses the
line immediately after it, so the expressions it guards are kept to one line.

## ex1 - one name from two

`Prefixed<P, K>` joins a namespace and an event name with a colon.

- `Prefixed<"user", "created">` -> `"user:created"`
- `Prefixed<"user", "created" | "deleted">` -> `"user:created" | "user:deleted"`
- `Prefixed<"user" | "team", "created">` -> `"user:created" | "team:created"`

Both parameters are constrained to `string`. A union in either position
produces every combination - that happens on its own, with nothing in your
definition mentioning unions.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d17_template_literal_types ex1
```

## ex2 - capitalise as you prefix

`GetterName<K>` turns a property name into the name of its getter.

- `GetterName<"title">` -> `"getTitle"`, `GetterName<"URL">` -> `"getURL"`
- `GetterName<"id" | "name">` -> `"getId" | "getName"`
- `GetterName<"">` -> `"get"`

TypeScript ships four intrinsic string types - `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`,
`Capitalize`, `Uncapitalize` - and one of them does exactly this.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d17_template_literal_types ex2
```

# Reading - typescript/d17_template_literal_types

The debrief, and the tutorial the numbered lessons only had room to sketch.
Per problem: what the pattern was really doing, the version that looks right,
and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**A template literal type is a string type with holes in it.** Written with
backticks in type position - `` `${P}:${K}` `` - it means the same thing to the
type system that a template string means at runtime, except that the holes hold
types. Every placeholder must be something the compiler can stringify, which in
practice means `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, or
a literal of one of those - hence the `extends string` constraints all over
this set.

**Placeholders holding unions expand to every combination.** `` `${"a" | "b"}:${"x" | "y"}` ``
is four string literals, not one. This is a cross product, so it is also how
you accidentally create a type with forty thousand members; the compiler has a
hard cap of 100,000 and will tell you when you find it.

**The same syntax works as a pattern.** On the right-hand side of `extends`, a
template is matched rather than built: `` S extends `${P}${string}` `` asks
whether `S` starts with `P` (ex3), and `` S extends `${P}${infer Rest}` ``
captures what came after (ex4). Inside a pattern, `string` is a wildcard that
matches anything including nothing, and `infer` is the same wildcard with a
name attached. When a placeholder is followed by a literal, the match is
non-greedy - it stops at the *first* occurrence - which is what makes `Split`
walk left to right.

**Four intrinsic types come with the compiler**: `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`,
`Capitalize` and `Uncapitalize`. They are implemented in the compiler itself,
not in `lib.d.ts`, so there is no source to read - and they compose inside
templates like anything else, which is the whole of ex2 and half of ex7.

**Recursion is how the interesting ones are built.** Match, capture, do
something to the capture, recurse on the remainder, and stop when the pattern
stops matching. Each step must consume at least one character, or the compiler
will stop you at depth 50 with a message about excessive recursion. `Split`
(ex5), `Join` (ex6, over a tuple instead of a string), `SnakeToCamel` (ex7) and
`RouteParams` (ex8) are four variations on that one shape.

**And the last rule is a design rule.** When a recursion needs to produce an
object, collect a union of keys on the way down and map over it once at the
end. Building the object as you go means intersecting types at every step,
which typechecks and produces tooltips nobody can read.

## ex1 - one name from two

What this was testing: the basic construct - backticks in type position, with
type parameters in the holes - and the cross-product rule that comes with it.
When a placeholder holds a union, the template is expanded once per member, and
two unions expand into every pairing.

The classic mistake is a missing or duplicated separator, which is invisible
until a call site compares the produced string with a hand-written one. The
second is leaving off `extends string`, which fails to compile with an error
about the placeholder rather than about the constraint.

The model answer is a single line, and the union behaviour is free: nothing in
`` `${P}:${K}` `` says anything about unions, yet six inputs produce six names.

## ex2 - capitalise as you prefix

What this was testing: the intrinsic string manipulation types, and the fact
that they compose inside a template like any other type. `Capitalize` is
implemented in the compiler rather than in `lib.d.ts`, which is why you cannot
find its definition by clicking through.

The classic mistake is hand-rolling it - matching `` `${infer First}${infer Rest}` ``
and uppercasing `First` - which works and is three lines longer than the
built-in. The second is reaching for `Uppercase`, which gives `"getID"`.

The model answer is `` `get${Capitalize<K>}` ``, and the empty-string case falls
out for free because `Capitalize<"">` is `""`.

## ex3 - does it start with that

What this was testing: template literal types as patterns rather than as
builders, with `string` acting as a wildcard. This is the same machinery as
ex1, read in the other direction - and it is the reason a literal like
`"/api/users"` is assignable to `` `/api${string}` ``.

The classic mistake is the stub's equality check, which is right only for exact
matches. A close second is `` `${P}${infer _}` `` with an unused capture, which
works but says you have not noticed that `string` alone is enough.

The model answer is `` S extends `${P}${string}` ? true : false ``, and the
`boolean` result for a union input is distribution doing its job - two members,
two answers, unioned back together.

## ex4 - cut the prefix off

What this was testing: `infer` inside a template literal pattern, which is
where the string-manipulation types stop being a curiosity and start being
useful. Everything from ex5 onwards is this, in a loop.

The classic mistake is returning `never` when the prefix is absent, which turns
a no-op into a type error somewhere downstream. The second is capturing the
prefix as well - `` `${infer _}${infer Rest}` `` - which matches ambiguously
and gives an answer nobody predicted.

The model answer is `` S extends `${P}${infer Rest}` ? Rest : S ``: one capture,
and the empty result for a full-length prefix falls out because a placeholder
may match the empty string.

## ex5 - cut a string into a tuple

What this was testing: recursion over a string, driven by a template pattern
with two captures. The compiler matches the *first* occurrence of the
delimiter, so `Head` is the shortest possible match and the recursion walks
left to right - which is also what makes the result order match
`String.prototype.split`.

The classic mistake is a base case of `[]` instead of `[S]`, which silently
drops the last segment: `Split<"a,b", ",">` comes out `["a"]`. The second is
expecting empty segments to disappear, which is a habit from other languages'
split functions.

The model answer is three lines, and it terminates because every recursive step
is applied to a strictly shorter string - the delimiter itself is consumed.

## ex6 - put a tuple back together

What this was testing: recursion over a tuple that *builds* a string, plus the
separator-placement problem every join has. The type-level version makes the
off-by-one visible, because a stray trailing comma shows up in the type rather
than in a log line.

The classic mistake is `` `${Head}${D}${Join<Rest, D>}` `` with no base case for
the last element, which appends a delimiter to the end of every joined string.
The second is forgetting `readonly` in the pattern, so a `readonly ["a", "b"]`
falls through to `""`.

The model answer peels the head with `infer Head extends string`, returns it
alone when the remainder is empty, and otherwise glues head, delimiter and the
recursive join together - one branch per case, no arithmetic.

## ex7 - snake_case to camelCase

What this was testing: composing recursion with an intrinsic, and the order in
which the two are applied. Both orderings agree on a single underscore and
disagree on two, which is why the gate uses `"user_first_name"`.

The classic mistake is capitalising the tail before recursing, which produces
`"userFirst_name"` - the recursive call then sees a string whose first
character is already uppercase and has nothing left to fix at the second
underscore. The second is replacing the underscore rather than consuming it.

The model answer recurses first and capitalises the result, so each segment
after the first is capitalised exactly once, and the union case distributes for
free.

## ex8 - read the params out of a path

What this was testing: everything in the set at once - patterns, wildcards,
captures, recursion - plus the decision to collect a union and map it at the
end rather than build the object as you go. It is also the actual mechanism
behind typed routers, so the shape is worth keeping.

The classic mistake is a single pattern. A path's last parameter has no
trailing slash, so a pattern that requires one silently drops it, and
`"/users/:id"` comes back with no keys at all. The second is building
`{ [K in Param]: string } & RouteParams<Rest>`, which is correct but produces a
chain of intersections that no editor tooltip will ever render legibly.

The model answer collects names into a union with a two-branch recursion and
then maps once - so `never` for a path with no parameters becomes an empty
object without a special case, and the whole public type is one line.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Template Literal Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/template-literal-types.html) - the construct, the cross-product rule, and the four intrinsic string types.
- [Handbook: Conditional Types - inferring within conditional types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html#inferring-within-conditional-types) - `infer` inside a template pattern, which is what ex4 through ex8 all lean on.
- [TypeScript 4.1 release notes](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-1.html) - where template literal types and key remapping were introduced, with the original motivating examples.
- [MDN: String.prototype.split](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/split) - the runtime behaviour ex5 is expected to mirror, empty segments included.

# d17 - Template literal types (drill set)

Eight problems on the string type that is also a template: building names,
matching prefixes, cutting strings into tuples and putting them back, and
finally reading a route's parameters out of its path. They drill lesson
**09_mapped_conditional**, whose key-remapping section introduced the syntax -
but this set treats it as a subject in its own right, so `reading.md` starts
from the construct rather than assuming it.

the whole gate is `gate.test-d.ts`. `// @ts-expect-error` only suppresses the
line immediately after it, so the expressions it guards are kept to one line.

- `Prefixed<"user" | "team", "created">` -> `"user:created" | "team:created"`

```ts
// Type gate for typescript/d17_template_literal_types. Quoted verbatim in README.md.
import { describe, expectTypeOf, test } from "vitest";

import type { Prefixed } from "./ex1/solution";
import type { GetterName } from "./ex2/solution";
import type { StartsWith } from "./ex3/solution";
import type { StripPrefix } from "./ex4/solution";
import type { Split } from "./ex5/solution";
import type { Join } from "./ex6/solution";
import type { SnakeToCamel } from "./ex7/solution";
import type { RouteParams } from "./ex8/solution";

describe("d17_template_literal_types", () => {
  test("ex1 - Prefixed<P, K> builds one name from two", () => {
    expectTypeOf<Prefixed<"user", "created">>().toEqualTypeOf<"user:created">();
    expectTypeOf<Prefixed<"user", "created" | "deleted">>().toEqualTypeOf<
      "user:created" | "user:deleted"
    >();
    expectTypeOf<Prefixed<"user" | "team", "created">>().toEqualTypeOf<
      "user:created" | "team:created"
    >();
    const topic: Prefixed<"user", "created"> = "user:created";
    expectTypeOf(topic).toEqualTypeOf<"user:created">();
    // @ts-expect-error - the separator is part of the type, so this literal does not fit.
    const wrong: Prefixed<"user", "created"> = "usercreated";
  });

  test("ex2 - GetterName<K> capitalises as it prefixes", () => {
    expectTypeOf<GetterName<"title">>().toEqualTypeOf<"getTitle">();
    expectTypeOf<GetterName<"id" | "name">>().toEqualTypeOf<"getId" | "getName">();
    expectTypeOf<GetterName<"URL">>().toEqualTypeOf<"getURL">();
    expectTypeOf<GetterName<"">>().toEqualTypeOf<"get">();
  });

  test("ex3 - StartsWith<S, P> matches a prefix", () => {
    expectTypeOf<StartsWith<"/api/users", "/api">>().toEqualTypeOf<true>();
    expectTypeOf<StartsWith<"/api", "/api">>().toEqualTypeOf<true>();
    expectTypeOf<StartsWith<"users", "/api">>().toEqualTypeOf<false>();
    expectTypeOf<StartsWith<"abc", "">>().toEqualTypeOf<true>();
    expectTypeOf<StartsWith<"/api" | "users", "/">>().toEqualTypeOf<boolean>();
  });

  test("ex4 - StripPrefix<S, P> keeps whatever came after", () => {
    expectTypeOf<StripPrefix<"/api/users", "/api">>().toEqualTypeOf<"/users">();
    expectTypeOf<StripPrefix<"onClick", "on">>().toEqualTypeOf<"Click">();
    expectTypeOf<StripPrefix<"users", "/api">>().toEqualTypeOf<"users">();
    expectTypeOf<StripPrefix<"/api", "/api">>().toEqualTypeOf<"">();
  });

  test("ex5 - Split<S, D> cuts a string into a tuple", () => {
    expectTypeOf<Split<"a,b,c", ",">>().toEqualTypeOf<["a", "b", "c"]>();
    expectTypeOf<Split<"a", ",">>().toEqualTypeOf<["a"]>();
    expectTypeOf<Split<"", ",">>().toEqualTypeOf<[""]>();
    expectTypeOf<Split<"a,,b", ",">>().toEqualTypeOf<["a", "", "b"]>();
    expectTypeOf<Split<"users/42/posts", "/">>().toEqualTypeOf<["users", "42", "posts"]>();
  });

  test("ex6 - Join<T, D> puts a tuple back together", () => {
    expectTypeOf<Join<["a", "b", "c"], ",">>().toEqualTypeOf<"a,b,c">();
    expectTypeOf<Join<["a"], ",">>().toEqualTypeOf<"a">();
    expectTypeOf<Join<[], ",">>().toEqualTypeOf<"">();
    expectTypeOf<Join<["users", "42"], "/">>().toEqualTypeOf<"users/42">();
    expectTypeOf<Join<readonly ["a", "b"], "-">>().toEqualTypeOf<"a-b">();
  });

  test("ex7 - SnakeToCamel<S> renames a column", () => {
    expectTypeOf<SnakeToCamel<"created_at">>().toEqualTypeOf<"createdAt">();
    expectTypeOf<SnakeToCamel<"user_first_name">>().toEqualTypeOf<"userFirstName">();
    expectTypeOf<SnakeToCamel<"id">>().toEqualTypeOf<"id">();
    expectTypeOf<SnakeToCamel<"created_at" | "updated_at">>().toEqualTypeOf<
      "createdAt" | "updatedAt"
    >();
  });

  test("ex8 - RouteParams<S> reads the params out of a path", () => {
    expectTypeOf<RouteParams<"/users/:id">>().toEqualTypeOf<{ id: string }>();
    expectTypeOf<RouteParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">>().toEqualTypeOf<{
      userId: string;
      postId: string;
    }>();
    expectTypeOf<keyof RouteParams<"/health">>().toEqualTypeOf<never>();
    const params: RouteParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId"> = { userId: "1", postId: "2" };
    expectTypeOf(params.postId).toEqualTypeOf<string>();
    // @ts-expect-error - slug is not a parameter of this path.
    params.slug;
  });
});
```
