# Reading - typescript/d17_template_literal_types

The debrief, and the tutorial the numbered lessons only had room to sketch.
Per problem: what the pattern was really doing, the version that looks right,
and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**A template literal type is a string type with holes in it.** Written with
backticks in type position - `` `${P}:${K}` `` - it means the same thing to the
type system that a template string means at runtime, except that the holes hold
types. Every placeholder must be something the compiler can stringify, which in
practice means `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, or
a literal of one of those - hence the `extends string` constraints all over
this set.

**Placeholders holding unions expand to every combination.** `` `${"a" | "b"}:${"x" | "y"}` ``
is four string literals, not one. This is a cross product, so it is also how
you accidentally create a type with forty thousand members; the compiler has a
hard cap of 100,000 and will tell you when you find it.

**The same syntax works as a pattern.** On the right-hand side of `extends`, a
template is matched rather than built: `` S extends `${P}${string}` `` asks
whether `S` starts with `P` (ex3), and `` S extends `${P}${infer Rest}` ``
captures what came after (ex4). Inside a pattern, `string` is a wildcard that
matches anything including nothing, and `infer` is the same wildcard with a
name attached. When a placeholder is followed by a literal, the match is
non-greedy - it stops at the *first* occurrence - which is what makes `Split`
walk left to right.

**Four intrinsic types come with the compiler**: `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`,
`Capitalize` and `Uncapitalize`. They are implemented in the compiler itself,
not in `lib.d.ts`, so there is no source to read - and they compose inside
templates like anything else, which is the whole of ex2 and half of ex7.

**Recursion is how the interesting ones are built.** Match, capture, do
something to the capture, recurse on the remainder, and stop when the pattern
stops matching. Each step must consume at least one character, or the compiler
will stop you at depth 50 with a message about excessive recursion. `Split`
(ex5), `Join` (ex6, over a tuple instead of a string), `SnakeToCamel` (ex7) and
`RouteParams` (ex8) are four variations on that one shape.

**And the last rule is a design rule.** When a recursion needs to produce an
object, collect a union of keys on the way down and map over it once at the
end. Building the object as you go means intersecting types at every step,
which typechecks and produces tooltips nobody can read.

## ex1 - one name from two

What this was testing: the basic construct - backticks in type position, with
type parameters in the holes - and the cross-product rule that comes with it.
When a placeholder holds a union, the template is expanded once per member, and
two unions expand into every pairing.

The classic mistake is a missing or duplicated separator, which is invisible
until a call site compares the produced string with a hand-written one. The
second is leaving off `extends string`, which fails to compile with an error
about the placeholder rather than about the constraint.

The model answer is a single line, and the union behaviour is free: nothing in
`` `${P}:${K}` `` says anything about unions, yet six inputs produce six names.

## ex2 - capitalise as you prefix

What this was testing: the intrinsic string manipulation types, and the fact
that they compose inside a template like any other type. `Capitalize` is
implemented in the compiler rather than in `lib.d.ts`, which is why you cannot
find its definition by clicking through.

The classic mistake is hand-rolling it - matching `` `${infer First}${infer Rest}` ``
and uppercasing `First` - which works and is three lines longer than the
built-in. The second is reaching for `Uppercase`, which gives `"getID"`.

The model answer is `` `get${Capitalize<K>}` ``, and the empty-string case falls
out for free because `Capitalize<"">` is `""`.

## ex3 - does it start with that

What this was testing: template literal types as patterns rather than as
builders, with `string` acting as a wildcard. This is the same machinery as
ex1, read in the other direction - and it is the reason a literal like
`"/api/users"` is assignable to `` `/api${string}` ``.

The classic mistake is the stub's equality check, which is right only for exact
matches. A close second is `` `${P}${infer _}` `` with an unused capture, which
works but says you have not noticed that `string` alone is enough.

The model answer is `` S extends `${P}${string}` ? true : false ``, and the
`boolean` result for a union input is distribution doing its job - two members,
two answers, unioned back together.

## ex4 - cut the prefix off

What this was testing: `infer` inside a template literal pattern, which is
where the string-manipulation types stop being a curiosity and start being
useful. Everything from ex5 onwards is this, in a loop.

The classic mistake is returning `never` when the prefix is absent, which turns
a no-op into a type error somewhere downstream. The second is capturing the
prefix as well - `` `${infer _}${infer Rest}` `` - which matches ambiguously
and gives an answer nobody predicted.

The model answer is `` S extends `${P}${infer Rest}` ? Rest : S ``: one capture,
and the empty result for a full-length prefix falls out because a placeholder
may match the empty string.

## ex5 - cut a string into a tuple

What this was testing: recursion over a string, driven by a template pattern
with two captures. The compiler matches the *first* occurrence of the
delimiter, so `Head` is the shortest possible match and the recursion walks
left to right - which is also what makes the result order match
`String.prototype.split`.

The classic mistake is a base case of `[]` instead of `[S]`, which silently
drops the last segment: `Split<"a,b", ",">` comes out `["a"]`. The second is
expecting empty segments to disappear, which is a habit from other languages'
split functions.

The model answer is three lines, and it terminates because every recursive step
is applied to a strictly shorter string - the delimiter itself is consumed.

## ex6 - put a tuple back together

What this was testing: recursion over a tuple that *builds* a string, plus the
separator-placement problem every join has. The type-level version makes the
off-by-one visible, because a stray trailing comma shows up in the type rather
than in a log line.

The classic mistake is `` `${Head}${D}${Join<Rest, D>}` `` with no base case for
the last element, which appends a delimiter to the end of every joined string.
The second is forgetting `readonly` in the pattern, so a `readonly ["a", "b"]`
falls through to `""`.

The model answer peels the head with `infer Head extends string`, returns it
alone when the remainder is empty, and otherwise glues head, delimiter and the
recursive join together - one branch per case, no arithmetic.

## ex7 - snake_case to camelCase

What this was testing: composing recursion with an intrinsic, and the order in
which the two are applied. Both orderings agree on a single underscore and
disagree on two, which is why the gate uses `"user_first_name"`.

The classic mistake is capitalising the tail before recursing, which produces
`"userFirst_name"` - the recursive call then sees a string whose first
character is already uppercase and has nothing left to fix at the second
underscore. The second is replacing the underscore rather than consuming it.

The model answer recurses first and capitalises the result, so each segment
after the first is capitalised exactly once, and the union case distributes for
free.

## ex8 - read the params out of a path

What this was testing: everything in the set at once - patterns, wildcards,
captures, recursion - plus the decision to collect a union and map it at the
end rather than build the object as you go. It is also the actual mechanism
behind typed routers, so the shape is worth keeping.

The classic mistake is a single pattern. A path's last parameter has no
trailing slash, so a pattern that requires one silently drops it, and
`"/users/:id"` comes back with no keys at all. The second is building
`{ [K in Param]: string } & RouteParams<Rest>`, which is correct but produces a
chain of intersections that no editor tooltip will ever render legibly.

The model answer collects names into a union with a two-branch recursion and
then maps once - so `never` for a path with no parameters becomes an empty
object without a special case, and the whole public type is one line.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Template Literal Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/template-literal-types.html) - the construct, the cross-product rule, and the four intrinsic string types.
- [Handbook: Conditional Types - inferring within conditional types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html#inferring-within-conditional-types) - `infer` inside a template pattern, which is what ex4 through ex8 all lean on.
- [TypeScript 4.1 release notes](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-1.html) - where template literal types and key remapping were introduced, with the original motivating examples.
- [MDN: String.prototype.split](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/split) - the runtime behaviour ex5 is expected to mirror, empty segments included.

## ex1 - one name from two

`Prefixed<P, K>` joins a namespace and an event name with a colon.

- `Prefixed<"user", "created">` -> `"user:created"`
- `Prefixed<"user", "created" | "deleted">` -> `"user:created" | "user:deleted"`
- `Prefixed<"user" | "team", "created">` -> `"user:created" | "team:created"`

Both parameters are constrained to `string`. A union in either position
produces every combination - that happens on its own, with nothing in your
definition mentioning unions.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d17_template_literal_types ex1
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - capitalise as you prefix

`GetterName<K>` turns a property name into the name of its getter.

- `GetterName<"title">` -> `"getTitle"`, `GetterName<"URL">` -> `"getURL"`
- `GetterName<"id" | "name">` -> `"getId" | "getName"`
- `GetterName<"">` -> `"get"`

TypeScript ships four intrinsic string types - `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`,
`Capitalize`, `Uncapitalize` - and one of them does exactly this.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d17_template_literal_types ex2
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex3 - does it start with that

`StartsWith<S, P>` is `true` when the string type `S` begins with the string
type `P`.

- `StartsWith<"/api/users", "/api">` -> `true`, `StartsWith<"/api", "/api">` -> `true`
- `StartsWith<"users", "/api">` -> `false`, `StartsWith<"abc", "">` -> `true`
- `StartsWith<"/api" | "users", "/">` -> `boolean` - it distributes, and the
  two members disagree

The trick is that `string` is usable *inside* a template as a wildcard.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```

```

exercises.prompt:
## ex5 - cut a string into a tuple

`Split<S, D>` splits the string type `S` on the delimiter `D` and returns the
parts as a tuple, exactly like `String.prototype.split` does at runtime.

- `Split<"a,b,c", ",">` -> `["a", "b", "c"]`
- `Split<"a", ",">` -> `["a"]`, `Split<"", ",">` -> `[""]`
- `Split<"a,,b", ",">` -> `["a", "", "b"]` - an empty part is still a part
- `Split<"users/42/posts", "/">` -> `["users", "42", "posts"]`

This one recurses, and the base case is "no delimiter left".

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d17_template_literal_types ex5
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex6 - put a tuple back together

`Join<T, D>` is ex5 backwards: a tuple of string literals and a delimiter
become one string literal.

- `Join<["a", "b", "c"], ",">` -> `"a,b,c"`
- `Join<["a"], ",">` -> `"a"` - no trailing delimiter
- `Join<[], ",">` -> `""`
- `Join<readonly ["a", "b"], "-">` -> `"a-b"` - readonly tuples too

`T` is constrained to `readonly string[]`.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You already know how to peel the head off a tuple (d16 ex3). Do that, then
build a template out of the head, the delimiter, and the joined rest.

## Hint 2

The delimiter goes *between* parts, so the one-element case needs its own
branch - otherwise `Join<["a"], ",">` comes out `"a,"`. Ask whether the
remainder is the empty tuple.

## Hint 3

A capture used inside a template has to be known to be a string, or the
compiler refuses the placeholder. `infer Head extends string` states that
constraint in the pattern itself, which is cleaner than a nested conditional.

Left to you: whether to special-case one element or to special-case the empty
remainder. They are the same check written from opposite sides; pick the one
you can explain.

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - read the params out of a path

`RouteParams<S>` takes an Express-style path and produces an object type whose
keys are its parameters, all typed `string`.

- `RouteParams<"/users/:id">` -> `{ id: string }`
- `RouteParams<"/users/:userId/posts/:postId">` -> `{ userId: string; postId: string }`
- `RouteParams<"/health">` -> an object with no keys

Two shapes to match: a parameter with a path segment after it (`:userId/...`)
and a parameter at the very end (`:postId`). Collect the names first, then map
over the union you collected - a mapped type over a union of string literals is
the last step, not the first.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d17_template_literal_types ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Split the job in two: a helper that produces the *union of parameter names*,
and a one-line mapped type that turns that union into an object. Trying to
build the object during the recursion means intersecting object types, which
works and reads much worse.

## Hint 2

The helper needs two patterns, in this order: `` `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}` ``
for a parameter with more path after it, then `` `${string}:${infer Param}` ``
for the last one. The leading `${string}` skips whatever came before the colon.

## Hint 3

The base case is `never`, and it is doing real work: mapping over `never`
produces an object with no keys, which is exactly what a path with no
parameters should give you.

Left to you: whether the helper is exported. The gate only asks about
`RouteParams`, so this is a question about what you want the public surface to
be.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Split the job in two: a helper that produces the *union of parameter names*,
and a one-line mapped type that turns that union into an object. Trying to
build the object during the recursion means intersecting object types, which
works and reads much worse.

## Hint 2

The helper needs two patterns, in this order: `` `${string}:${infer Param}/${infer Rest}` ``
for a parameter with more path after it, then `` `${string}:${infer Param}` ``
for the last one. The leading `${string}` skips whatever came before the colon.

## Hint 3

The base case is `never`, and it is doing real work: mapping over `never`
produces an object with no keys, which is exactly what a path with no
parameters should give you.

Left to you: whether the helper is exported. The gate only asks about
`RouteParams`, so this is a question about what you want the public surface to
be.

lessons.briefing:
# d18 - Guards, harder (drill set)

Eight problems on predicates that carry real information: guards that prove a
list has a head, guards that add a key, assertion functions, and two
combinators that build guards out of other guards. They drill lesson
**10_guards_assertions**; go back if `value is T` still looks like a return
type.

Both gates run here. `gate.test.ts` checks what the guard *does* at runtime and
`gate.test-d.ts` checks what it *proves* to the compiler - and an exercise is
green only when both agree. That pairing is the point of the set: a guard that
lies is worse than no guard, and only one of the two gates can catch a liar.

## ex1 - prove the list has a head

`isNonEmpty(values)` returns `true` when the array has at least one element,
and narrows it to the tuple type `[T, ...T[]]` so that `values[0]` is a `T`
rather than a `T | undefined`.

- `isNonEmpty([1])` -> `true`, `isNonEmpty([])` -> `false`
- `isNonEmpty([undefined])` -> `true` - one element is one element

The signature is the exercise as much as the body is.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex1
```

## ex2 - prove a key exists

`hasKey(value, key)` reports whether `value` has `key` as its **own** property,
and narrows `value` so that `value[key]` is readable as `unknown`.

- `hasKey({ total: 3 }, "total")` -> `true`, `hasKey({ total: 3 }, "missing")` -> `false`
- `hasKey({ total: undefined }, "total")` -> `true` - the key exists
- an inherited property is **not** an own property, so `in` is the wrong operator

`key` is generic and constrained to `PropertyKey`; the narrowed type is
`Record<K, unknown>`.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex2
```

## ex3 - narrow a string to a list

`isOneOf(allowed, value)` reports whether the string `value` appears in
`allowed`, and narrows it from `string` to the union of the list's literal
types.

- with `const permissions = ["read", "write"] as const`, a `string` that passes
  `isOneOf(permissions, raw)` is `"read" | "write"` inside the branch
- `isOneOf([], "read")` -> `false`

`allowed` is `readonly T[]` where `T extends string`; `value` is a plain
`string`.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex3
```

## ex4 - assert a row or throw

`Row` is `{ id: string; amount: number }`. `assertRow(value)` takes an
`unknown` and either returns normally - after which `value` is a `Row` for the
rest of the scope - or throws a `TypeError` whose message **names the field
that failed**.

- a valid row passes silently
- `{ id: 1, amount: 12 }` throws, and the message contains `id`
- `{ id: "r1" }` throws, and the message contains `amount`
- `null` and `[]` both throw

The signature is `asserts value is Row`, which is a different animal from
`value is Row`: the caller gets narrowing without a branch.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex4
```

## ex5 - filter a discriminated union

`Task` is the union
`{ kind: "email"; to: string } | { kind: "sms"; number: string } | { kind: "push"; token: string }`.

`onlyKind(tasks, kind)` returns the tasks with that discriminant, in input
order - and the return type is the *matching member only*, not `Task[]`.

- `onlyKind(tasks, "email")` -> `{ kind: "email"; to: string }[]`
- `onlyKind([], "email")` -> `[]`
- `onlyKind(tasks, "fax")` is a compile error

The input is never modified.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex5
```

## ex6 - two guards, one built on the other

Two guards in one file.

`isRecord(value)` is `true` for any non-null, non-array object, and narrows to
`Record<string, unknown>`.

- `isRecord({})` -> `true`, `isRecord(null)` -> `false`, `isRecord([1, 2])` -> `false`

`isStringRecord(value)` is `true` when `value` is a record **and every one of
its values is a string**, and narrows to `Record<string, string>`.

- `isStringRecord({ a: "x" })` -> `true`, `isStringRecord({ a: 1 })` -> `false`
- `isStringRecord({})` -> `true` - vacuously

Build the second on the first.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex6
```

## ex7 - lift a guard over a list

`everyIs(guard)` takes a guard for one value and returns a guard for a whole
list: the returned function is `true` when **every** element passes, and it
narrows `readonly T[]` to `readonly S[]`.

- `everyIs(isString)(["a", "b"])` -> `true`, `everyIs(isString)(["a", 1])` -> `false`
- `everyIs(isString)([])` -> `true` - vacuously, like `Array.prototype.every`

The signature has two type parameters, `T` and `S extends T`, and the returned
function's own return type is a type predicate.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex7
```

## ex8 - a guard built from a shape

`objectOf(shape)` takes an object whose values are guards and returns a guard
for an object of the corresponding types.

```ts
const isUser = objectOf({ id: isString, age: isNumber });
```

- `isUser({ id: "u1", age: 30 })` -> `true`, and inside the branch the value is
  `{ id: string; age: number }`
- `isUser({ id: "u1", age: "30" })` -> `false`, `isUser({ id: "u1" })` -> `false`
- `isUser({ id: "u1", age: 30, extra: true })` -> `true` - extra keys are fine
- `isUser(null)` and `isUser([])` -> `false`
- `objectOf({})` accepts any object

`Guard<T>` is given in the stub. You will need a second type that reads the
narrowed type back out of a guard, and a mapped type that applies it to every
member of the shape.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex8
```

# Reading - typescript/d18_guards_advanced

The debrief. Per problem: what the predicate was really claiming, the version
that runs correctly and proves nothing, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**A guard makes two promises and the compiler only checks one.** `value is T`
says "if I return true, treat this as a `T`" - and TypeScript takes your word
for it. Nothing verifies that the body actually establishes the claim. That
asymmetry is why this lesson runs a runtime gate and a type gate side by side:
the runtime gate catches a guard that returns the wrong answer, the type gate
catches a guard that returns the right answer and tells the compiler nothing,
and only both together catch a guard that lies.

**Narrowing is always to a subtype.** `[T, ...T[]]` narrows `T[]` (ex1),
`Record<K, unknown>` narrows `object` (ex2), a literal union narrows `string`
(ex3). If the compiler rejects your predicate, the usual cause is that you
promised something the declared parameter type does not allow - and the fix is
almost never a cast.

**Claim the least you can.** `hasKey` proves a key exists, so it narrows to
`Record<K, unknown>` and not to anything about the value behind it. Every extra
word in a narrowed type is a claim the body has to justify, and the compiler
will not ask you for the justification.

**Assertion functions are guards without the branch.** `asserts value is Row`
narrows for the remainder of the scope and throws otherwise, which is the right
shape at a parsing boundary where "carry on with an unvalidated value" is not
an option. They have one sharp edge: the thing you call has to have an explicit
declared type, which is why they are always written as declarations or as
annotated consts.

**And predicates compose.** A predicate is part of a function *type*, so a
function can take guards and return guards (ex7, ex8) - which is how every
runtime schema library you have used is built. What none of them can do is get
the predicate by inference: TypeScript will infer `boolean` every time, so the
`value is T` has to be written by hand at every level.

## ex1 - prove the list has a head

What this was testing: that a type predicate may narrow to a *tuple*, not only
to a union member. The payoff is `values[0]`, which under
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` or a hand-written union would otherwise be
`T | undefined` forever.

The classic mistake is returning `boolean`: the runtime behaves perfectly and
the compiler learns nothing, so every caller still writes a non-null assertion
after the check. That is why this lesson runs two gates.

The model answer is `values.length > 0` with `values is [T, ...T[]]` in the
return position - the whole exercise is in the signature, and the body is the
part you could have guessed.

## ex2 - prove a key exists

What this was testing: a type predicate whose narrowed type is built from a
generic parameter, plus the own-versus-inherited distinction that `in` gets
wrong. `Record<K, unknown>` is the smallest honest claim: the key is there, and
you know nothing about what is behind it.

The classic mistake is narrowing to `Record<K, string>` or some other concrete
value type, which is a lie the compiler will happily believe - the guard
checked for existence and said something about the contents. The second is
using `key in value`, which the gate catches with an inherited property.

The model answer is `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(value, key)` with
`value is Record<K, unknown>` in the return position: one own-property check,
one honest claim.

## ex3 - narrow a string to a list

What this was testing: a predicate on a parameter other than the first, and the
inference chain from `as const` at the call site to a literal union in the
narrowed branch. This is how a validated string from a request body becomes a
usable union without a cast.

The classic mistake is `allowed.includes(value as T)`, which asserts the answer
before asking the question - and would return `true`-shaped types for values
that are not in the list at all if the body were ever refactored. Widen the
array, never the value.

The model answer widens `allowed` to `readonly string[]` for the `includes`
call and declares `value is T`, so the only unchecked claim in the function is
the one the guard exists to make.

## ex4 - assert a row or throw

What this was testing: assertion signatures, and the discipline of validating
the container before its contents. `asserts value is Row` narrows the caller's
variable with no `if` at the call site, which is what makes it the right tool
for parsing at a boundary.

The classic mistake is reading `value.id` before proving `value` is an object,
which is a `TypeError` at runtime on `null` and a compile error on `unknown`.
The second is throwing a bare `Error("invalid")`, which turns a five-second
debugging session into a twenty-minute one - the gate matches on the field name
for that reason.

The model answer checks the container, casts once to `Record<string, unknown>`,
and then checks each field with its own message, so the thrown error always
says which field and what was expected.

## ex5 - filter a discriminated union

What this was testing: two ideas at once - `Extract` over a discriminated
union, and `filter`'s type-predicate overload. Either alone gives you half the
answer: `Extract` with a plain filter callback returns `Task[]` and needs a
cast; a predicate callback without `Extract` has nothing to narrow *to*.

The classic mistake is `tasks.filter((task) => task.kind === kind) as Extract<Task, { kind: K }>[]`,
which produces the right type by assertion rather than by proof - and keeps
producing it after someone changes the comparison.

The model answer names the predicate in the callback so the compiler derives
the return type, and the generic `K` means `onlyKind(tasks, "fax")` is caught
at the call site rather than returning an empty array.

## ex6 - two guards, one built on the other

What this was testing: guard composition, and the two values that `typeof
"object"` lets through by accident. `isStringRecord` is only interesting
because it reuses `isRecord` - the narrowing from the first call is what makes
the `Object.values` line legal without a cast.

The classic mistake is `typeof value === "object"` alone, which is `true` for
`null` and for every array, and then crashes one line later. The second is
re-implementing the object check inside the second guard, which passes the gate
and drifts the moment one of the two definitions changes.

The model answer narrows once in `isRecord` and leans on it in
`isStringRecord`, where short-circuit evaluation carries the narrowing across
the `&&` - the same flow analysis that makes `if (x && x.y)` work.

## ex7 - lift a guard over a list

What this was testing: that a type predicate is part of a *function type*, and
so can be produced by a higher-order function rather than written at a fixed
call site. This is the combinator pattern that runtime validators are built
from.

The classic mistake is expecting inference to produce the predicate. TypeScript
never infers `value is S` - if you do not write it in the return type, you get
`boolean`, the guard silently stops narrowing, and only a type gate notices.
The second is forgetting `S extends T`, which makes the predicate illegal.

The model answer spells the predicate out in both places - once on `everyIs`'s
return type, once on the arrow it returns - and the body is a single `every`
call whose vacuous-truth behaviour is exactly what the prompt asks for.

## ex8 - a guard built from a shape

What this was testing: the whole set at once. A guard combinator whose *type*
is computed from its argument - `infer` to read a guard's narrowed type
(d16), a mapped type to apply it across the shape (d14), and a type predicate
to hand the result to the caller (lesson 10).

The classic mistake is constraining `S` to `Record<string, Guard<unknown>>` and
then finding that every field narrows to `unknown`: the constraint is not what
the mapped type reads, but it is what a careless implementation ends up
propagating. The second is `guard(record[key])` without the presence check,
which lets `{ id: "u1" }` through whenever a guard happens to accept
`undefined`.

The model answer keeps the constraint loose so inference preserves the real
signatures, derives the object type with one mapped type over `GuardType`, and
validates container, presence and value in that order - which is also the order
the error messages would want.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Narrowing - using type predicates](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#using-type-predicates) - the `value is T` form and the subtype rule every exercise here obeys.
- [Handbook: Assertion functions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-7.html#assertion-functions) - `asserts value is T`, including why the call target needs an explicit type.
- [Handbook: Discriminated unions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#discriminated-unions) - the shape ex5 filters, and why `Extract` is the right utility for it.
- [MDN: Object.hasOwn](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/hasOwn) - own versus inherited properties, which is the trap in ex2.
- [MDN: Array.prototype.every](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/every) - including the vacuous-truth behaviour ex7 and ex8 both depend on.

## ex1 - prove the list has a head

What this was testing: that a type predicate may narrow to a *tuple*, not only
to a union member. The payoff is `values[0]`, which under
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` or a hand-written union would otherwise be
`T | undefined` forever.

The classic mistake is returning `boolean`: the runtime behaves perfectly and
the compiler learns nothing, so every caller still writes a non-null assertion
after the check. That is why this lesson runs two gates.

The model answer is `values.length > 0` with `values is [T, ...T[]]` in the
return position - the whole exercise is in the signature, and the body is the
part you could have guessed.

## ex2 - prove a key exists

What this was testing: a type predicate whose narrowed type is built from a
generic parameter, plus the own-versus-inherited distinction that `in` gets
wrong. `Record<K, unknown>` is the smallest honest claim: the key is there, and
you know nothing about what is behind it.

The classic mistake is narrowing to `Record<K, string>` or some other concrete
value type, which is a lie the compiler will happily believe - the guard
checked for existence and said something about the contents. The second is
using `key in value`, which the gate catches with an inherited property.

The model answer is `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(value, key)` with
`value is Record<K, unknown>` in the return position: one own-property check,
one honest claim.

## ex3 - narrow a string to a list

What this was testing: a predicate on a parameter other than the first, and the
inference chain from `as const` at the call site to a literal union in the
narrowed branch. This is how a validated string from a request body becomes a
usable union without a cast.

The classic mistake is `allowed.includes(value as T)`, which asserts the answer
before asking the question - and would return `true`-shaped types for values
that are not in the list at all if the body were ever refactored. Widen the
array, never the value.

The model answer widens `allowed` to `readonly string[]` for the `includes`
call and declares `value is T`, so the only unchecked claim in the function is
the one the guard exists to make.

## ex4 - assert a row or throw

What this was testing: assertion signatures, and the discipline of validating
the container before its contents. `asserts value is Row` narrows the caller's
variable with no `if` at the call site, which is what makes it the right tool
for parsing at a boundary.

The classic mistake is reading `value.id` before proving `value` is an object,
which is a `TypeError` at runtime on `null` and a compile error on `unknown`.
The second is throwing a bare `Error("invalid")`, which turns a five-second
debugging session into a twenty-minute one - the gate matches on the field name
for that reason.

The model answer checks the container, casts once to `Record<string, unknown>`,
and then checks each field with its own message, so the thrown error always
says which field and what was expected.

## ex5 - filter a discriminated union

What this was testing: two ideas at once - `Extract` over a discriminated
union, and `filter`'s type-predicate overload. Either alone gives you half the
answer: `Extract` with a plain filter callback returns `Task[]` and needs a
cast; a predicate callback without `Extract` has nothing to narrow *to*.

The classic mistake is `tasks.filter((task) => task.kind === kind) as Extract<Task, { kind: K }>[]`,
which produces the right type by assertion rather than by proof - and keeps
producing it after someone changes the comparison.

The model answer names the predicate in the callback so the compiler derives
the return type, and the generic `K` means `onlyKind(tasks, "fax")` is caught
at the call site rather than returning an empty array.

## ex6 - two guards, one built on the other

What this was testing: guard composition, and the two values that `typeof
"object"` lets through by accident. `isStringRecord` is only interesting
because it reuses `isRecord` - the narrowing from the first call is what makes
the `Object.values` line legal without a cast.

The classic mistake is `typeof value === "object"` alone, which is `true` for
`null` and for every array, and then crashes one line later. The second is
re-implementing the object check inside the second guard, which passes the gate
and drifts the moment one of the two definitions changes.

The model answer narrows once in `isRecord` and leans on it in
`isStringRecord`, where short-circuit evaluation carries the narrowing across
the `&&` - the same flow analysis that makes `if (x && x.y)` work.

## ex7 - lift a guard over a list

What this was testing: that a type predicate is part of a *function type*, and
so can be produced by a higher-order function rather than written at a fixed
call site. This is the combinator pattern that runtime validators are built
from.

The classic mistake is expecting inference to produce the predicate. TypeScript
never infers `value is S` - if you do not write it in the return type, you get
`boolean`, the guard silently stops narrowing, and only a type gate notices.
The second is forgetting `S extends T`, which makes the predicate illegal.

The model answer spells the predicate out in both places - once on `everyIs`'s
return type, once on the arrow it returns - and the body is a single `every`
call whose vacuous-truth behaviour is exactly what the prompt asks for.

## ex8 - a guard built from a shape

What this was testing: the whole set at once. A guard combinator whose *type*
is computed from its argument - `infer` to read a guard's narrowed type
(d16), a mapped type to apply it across the shape (d14), and a type predicate
to hand the result to the caller (lesson 10).

The classic mistake is constraining `S` to `Record<string, Guard<unknown>>` and
then finding that every field narrows to `unknown`: the constraint is not what
the mapped type reads, but it is what a careless implementation ends up
propagating. The second is `guard(record[key])` without the presence check,
which lets `{ id: "u1" }` through whenever a guard happens to accept
`undefined`.

The model answer keeps the constraint loose so inference preserves the real
signatures, derives the object type with one mapped type over `GuardType`, and
validates container, presence and value in that order - which is also the order
the error messages would want.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Narrowing - using type predicates](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#using-type-predicates) - the `value is T` form and the subtype rule every exercise here obeys.
- [Handbook: Assertion functions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-7.html#assertion-functions) - `asserts value is T`, including why the call target needs an explicit type.
- [Handbook: Discriminated unions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#discriminated-unions) - the shape ex5 filters, and why `Extract` is the right utility for it.
- [MDN: Object.hasOwn](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/hasOwn) - own versus inherited properties, which is the trap in ex2.
- [MDN: Array.prototype.every](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/every) - including the vacuous-truth behaviour ex7 and ex8 both depend on.

exercises.prompt:
## ex1 - prove the list has a head

`isNonEmpty(values)` returns `true` when the array has at least one element,
and narrows it to the tuple type `[T, ...T[]]` so that `values[0]` is a `T`
rather than a `T | undefined`.

- `isNonEmpty([1])` -> `true`, `isNonEmpty([])` -> `false`
- `isNonEmpty([undefined])` -> `true` - one element is one element

The signature is the exercise as much as the body is.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A type predicate is written in the return position: `values is <the narrower
type>`. The narrower type here is a tuple with one required element and a rest.

## Hint 2

`[T, ...T[]]` is assignable to `T[]`, which is the rule a predicate has to obey:
you may only narrow to a subtype of the declared parameter type.

The body is one comparison. Resist writing `!!values.length` - it is the same
check with the reasoning removed.

Left to you: `values.length > 0` or `values.length !== 0`. Identical here; one
of them still reads correctly if `length` is ever a floating-point number.

`[T, ...T[]]` is assignable to `T[]`, which is the rule a predicate has to obey:
you may only narrow to a subtype of the declared parameter type.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - prove a key exists

`hasKey(value, key)` reports whether `value` has `key` as its **own** property,
and narrows `value` so that `value[key]` is readable as `unknown`.

- `hasKey({ total: 3 }, "total")` -> `true`, `hasKey({ total: 3 }, "missing")` -> `false`
- `hasKey({ total: undefined }, "total")` -> `true` - the key exists
- an inherited property is **not** an own property, so `in` is the wrong operator

`key` is generic and constrained to `PropertyKey`; the narrowed type is
`Record<K, unknown>`.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The narrowed type has to mention the *generic* key: `value is Record<K, unknown>`.
That is what makes `value.total` readable after the check and `value.missing`
still an error.

## Hint 2

`in` walks the prototype chain and the gate builds an object with
`Object.create` to prove it. `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(value, key)`
does not - and calling it that way survives objects with a null prototype or a
property literally named `hasOwnProperty`.

Left to you: `Object.hasOwn` is the modern spelling of the same check. Look up
which runtimes have it before you decide.

## ex3 - narrow a string to a list

`isOneOf(allowed, value)` reports whether the string `value` appears in
`allowed`, and narrows it from `string` to the union of the list's literal
types.

`allowed` is `readonly T[]` where `T extends string`; `value` is a plain
`string`.

exercises.prompt:
## ex4 - assert a row or throw

`Row` is `{ id: string; amount: number }`. `assertRow(value)` takes an
`unknown` and either returns normally - after which `value` is a `Row` for the
rest of the scope - or throws a `TypeError` whose message **names the field
that failed**.

- a valid row passes silently
- `{ id: 1, amount: 12 }` throws, and the message contains `id`
- `{ id: "r1" }` throws, and the message contains `amount`
- `null` and `[]` both throw

The signature is `asserts value is Row`, which is a different animal from
`value is Row`: the caller gets narrowing without a branch.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`asserts value is Row` in the return position means "if this returns at all,
`value` is a `Row`". There is no boolean to return - the only two outcomes are
returning and throwing.

## Hint 2

Check the container first: `typeof value === "object"`, not `null`, not an
array. Only then can you read fields off it, and you will need one cast to a
`Record<string, unknown>` to do so - that cast is safe precisely because of the
check above it.

Left to you: one message per field, or one message listing everything wrong.
The gate only requires the failing field's name to appear; ex4 of lesson 10's
challenge argued for collecting them all.

## ex5 - filter a discriminated union

`Task` is the union
`{ kind: "email"; to: string } | { kind: "sms"; number: string } | { kind: "push"; token: string }`.

`onlyKind(tasks, kind)` returns the tasks with that discriminant, in input
order - and the return type is the *matching member only*, not `Task[]`.

- `onlyKind(tasks, "email")` -> `{ kind: "email"; to: string }[]`
- `onlyKind([], "email")` -> `[]`
- `onlyKind(tasks, "fax")` is a compile error

The input is never modified.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Extract<Task, { kind: K }>` is the union member whose discriminant is `K`.
That is the return element type; the parameter `K` is constrained to
`Task["kind"]` so a typo is a compile error.

`Array.prototype.filter` has an overload that takes a type predicate and
returns the narrowed element type. Writing the callback as
`(task): task is Extract<Task, { kind: K }> => task.kind === kind` is what
selects it.

exercises.prompt:
## ex6 - two guards, one built on the other

Two guards in one file.

`isRecord(value)` is `true` for any non-null, non-array object, and narrows to
`Record<string, unknown>`.

- `isRecord({})` -> `true`, `isRecord(null)` -> `false`, `isRecord([1, 2])` -> `false`

`isStringRecord(value)` is `true` when `value` is a record **and every one of
its values is a string**, and narrows to `Record<string, string>`.

- `isStringRecord({ a: "x" })` -> `true`, `isStringRecord({ a: 1 })` -> `false`
- `isStringRecord({})` -> `true` - vacuously

Build the second on the first.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex6
```

`typeof null` is `"object"`. Every object guard in JavaScript starts by ruling
that out, and the gate checks it first for exactly that reason.

The second guard should call the first. Once `isRecord(value)` has returned
`true`, `value` is a `Record<string, unknown>` inside the `&&`, so

exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - lift a guard over a list

`everyIs(guard)` takes a guard for one value and returns a guard for a whole
list: the returned function is `true` when **every** element passes, and it
narrows `readonly T[]` to `readonly S[]`.

- `everyIs(isString)(["a", "b"])` -> `true`, `everyIs(isString)(["a", 1])` -> `false`
- `everyIs(isString)([])` -> `true` - vacuously, like `Array.prototype.every`

The signature has two type parameters, `T` and `S extends T`, and the returned
function's own return type is a type predicate.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d18_guards_advanced ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The predicate you have to write is on the *returned* function, not on
`everyIs` itself. A function type may carry a predicate:
`(values: readonly T[]) => values is readonly S[]`.

## Hint 2

Write the returned arrow with that return type spelled out. TypeScript will not
infer a type predicate for you - inference gives `boolean`, which is the stub.

## Hint 3

`S extends T` is what makes the narrowing legal: you may only narrow to a
subtype of what was declared. Drop the constraint and the compiler will
complain about the predicate rather than about the constraint, which is a
confusing place to start debugging.

Left to you: `values.every((value) => guard(value))` or `values.every(guard)`.
Both work; one of them changes meaning if `guard` ever grows a second
parameter.

## Hint 1

The predicate you have to write is on the *returned* function, not on
`everyIs` itself. A function type may carry a predicate:
`(values: readonly T[]) => values is readonly S[]`.

## Hint 2

Write the returned arrow with that return type spelled out. TypeScript will not
infer a type predicate for you - inference gives `boolean`, which is the stub.

## Hint 3

`S extends T` is what makes the narrowing legal: you may only narrow to a
subtype of what was declared. Drop the constraint and the compiler will
complain about the predicate rather than about the constraint, which is a
confusing place to start debugging.

Left to you: `values.every((value) => guard(value))` or `values.every(guard)`.
Both work; one of them changes meaning if `guard` ever grows a second
parameter.

## ex8 - a guard built from a shape

`objectOf(shape)` takes an object whose values are guards and returns a guard
for an object of the corresponding types.

```ts
const isUser = objectOf({ id: isString, age: isNumber });
```

- `isUser({ id: "u1", age: 30 })` -> `true`, and inside the branch the value is
  `{ id: string; age: number }`
- `isUser({ id: "u1", age: "30" })` -> `false`, `isUser({ id: "u1" })` -> `false`
- `isUser({ id: "u1", age: 30, extra: true })` -> `true` - extra keys are fine
- `isUser(null)` and `isUser([])` -> `false`
- `objectOf({})` accepts any object

`Guard<T>` is given in the stub. You will need a second type that reads the
narrowed type back out of a guard, and a mapped type that applies it to every
member of the shape.


lessons.briefing:
# d19 - unknown, any and never (drill set)

Eight problems on the three types that are not really types: `unknown` (the
value you have not earned the right to use), `any` (the value that stops the
compiler asking), and `never` (the value that does not exist). They drill
lesson **10_guards_assertions**, whose third exercise made the case for
`unknown`; this set makes it eight times.

Both gates run. `gate.test.ts` checks behaviour and `gate.test-d.ts` checks
what the signature promises - because most of the mistakes in this area are
correct programs with dishonest types. ex5 is type-level only and appears in
the type gate alone.

## ex1 - parse into unknown

`parseJson(text)` parses JSON and returns **`unknown`**, and throws when the
text is not valid JSON.

- `parseJson('{"a":1}')` -> `{ a: 1 }`, `parseJson("null")` -> `null`
- `parseJson("{")` throws

`JSON.parse` is typed as returning `any`, which is the single most common way
`any` gets into a codebase. The exercise is to stop it at the door.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex1
```

## ex2 - unknown in, number or null out

`toNumber(value)` takes an `unknown` and returns `number | null`.

- a **finite** number is itself; `NaN` and `Infinity` are `null`
- a string is trimmed first: `"42"` -> `42`, `"  7  "` -> `7`
- `""` and `"   "` are `null` - **not** `0`
- `"abc"` -> `null`
- booleans, `null`, `undefined` and objects are all `null`

The return type is part of the exercise: the stub declares `unknown`.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex2
```

## ex3 - never as the exhaustiveness check

`Shipment` is the union
`{ status: "pending" } | { status: "shipped"; trackingId: string } | { status: "delivered"; signedBy: string } | { status: "cancelled"; reason: string }`.

`describeShipment(shipment)` returns:

- `"waiting to ship"`, `"in transit as TR9"`, `"delivered to Ada"`,
  `"cancelled: out of stock"`

and its `default` branch calls `assertUnreachable(shipment)`.

`assertUnreachable(value: never): never` throws, and its message contains the
value it was handed. Its parameter type is `never`, so passing anything the
switch did not already narrow away is a **compile error** - which is how a
newly added union member becomes a build failure instead of a runtime
surprise.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex3
```

## ex4 - an untyped store with a typed door

`createCache()` returns an object with three members:

- `set(key: string, value: unknown): void`
- `get<T>(key: string, guard: (value: unknown) => value is T): T | null`
- `has(key: string): boolean`

The store holds `unknown` internally. `get` returns the value only if the
guard accepts it, and `null` otherwise - including when the key is absent.

- `cache.set("count", 3)`, then `cache.get("count", isNumber)` -> `3`
- `cache.get("count", isString)` -> `null` - the guard is the only proof
- `cache.get("missing", isNumber)` -> `null`

The `Cache` interface is exported; the stub's `get` returns `unknown`, which
is what you have to fix.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex4
```

## ex5 - never as a filter

Type-level only, and the one exercise here with no runtime half.

`OmitNever<T>` removes every member whose type is `never`.

- `OmitNever<{ a: string; b: never; c: number }>` -> `{ a: string; c: number }`
- `OmitNever<{ a: string }>` -> `{ a: string }`
- `OmitNever<{ a: never }>` -> an object with no keys
- `OmitNever<{ a: never; b: undefined }>` -> `{ b: undefined }` - `undefined`
  is a value and stays

Members typed `never` show up whenever a conditional type filters something
out, which is why a utility that sweeps them away is worth having.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex5
```

## ex6 - walk a path through unknown

`deepGet(value, path)` follows a list of string keys into an unknown value and
returns whatever it finds - as `unknown`. It returns `undefined` the moment the
path stops working.

- `deepGet({ server: { name: "edge" } }, ["server", "name"])` -> `"edge"`
- `deepGet({ server: { ports: [8080, 9090] } }, ["server", "ports", "1"])` -> `9090`
- `deepGet(config, [])` -> the value itself
- a missing key, a walk into a string, `null` and `undefined` all give `undefined`

Only own properties count.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex6
```

## ex7 - narrow unknown to JSON

`JsonValue` is given:

```ts
export type JsonValue =
  | string
  | number
  | boolean
  | null
  | JsonValue[]
  | { [key: string]: JsonValue };
```

`isJsonValue(value)` narrows an `unknown` to it. Accept exactly what JSON can
hold:

- `{ a: [1, "x", null, { b: true }] }` -> `true`, `[]` and `{}` -> `true`
- `null` -> `true`, `undefined` -> `false`
- `NaN` -> `false` - JSON has no spelling for it
- a function -> `false`, and one bad value anywhere fails the whole document

The guard has to recurse.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex7
```

## ex8 - a function that never returns

Two exports.

`fail(message: string): never` throws an `Error` with that message. Because it
returns `never`, the compiler treats any code after a call to it as
unreachable - which means it can be used as the last expression of a function
that is declared to return something else, and as the `else` of a ternary.

`requirePort(raw: unknown): number` returns a valid port, or calls `fail`. A
valid port is an integer from 1 to 65535; a numeric string is accepted after
trimming. The thrown message contains the word `port`.

- `requirePort(8080)` -> `8080`, `requirePort("443")` -> `443`, `requirePort("  22  ")` -> `22`
- `requirePort(0)`, `requirePort(70000)`, `requirePort(80.5)`, `requirePort("abc")`
  and `requirePort(null)` all throw

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex8
```
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - typescript/d19_unknown_any_never

The debrief. Per problem: which of the three types was really at issue, the
version that runs correctly and lies, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**The three types sit at the two ends of the scale and outside it.** `unknown`
is the top: everything is assignable *to* it, and it is assignable to nothing,
so holding one obliges you to prove something before you use it. `never` is the
bottom: nothing is assignable to it, and it is assignable to everything, which
is why a `never`-returning function can appear wherever a value is expected.
`any` is not on the scale at all - it is assignable in both directions to
everything, which is another way of saying the compiler has agreed to stop
looking.

**`unknown` is the correct type at every boundary.** JSON you just parsed (ex1),
a value pulled from a heterogeneous store (ex4), a step in a path walk (ex6), a
document you are about to validate (ex7). The pattern is always the same: take
`unknown` in, narrow with `typeof` or a guard, hand back a type that says what
you proved. The alternative - accepting `any` and hoping - produces code that
compiles identically and fails differently.

**`any` spreads.** It is not confined to the variable that holds it: every
property read, call and arithmetic operation on an `any` produces another
`any`, so one untyped import can quietly disable checking across a module. Two
stubs in this set return `any` for exactly that reason, and the type gate is
the only thing that notices.

**`never` has three jobs, and they look unrelated until they do not.** As a
*parameter* type it means "this can only be called with something that cannot
exist", which is the exhaustiveness check (ex3). As a *return* type it means

## ex1 - parse into unknown

`parseJson(text)` parses JSON and returns **`unknown`**, and throws when the
text is not valid JSON.

- `parseJson('{"a":1}')` -> `{ a: 1 }`, `parseJson("null")` -> `null`
- `parseJson("{")` throws

`JSON.parse` is typed as returning `any`, which is the single most common way
`any` gets into a codebase. The exercise is to stop it at the door.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex1
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - unknown in, number or null out

`toNumber(value)` takes an `unknown` and returns `number | null`.

- a **finite** number is itself; `NaN` and `Infinity` are `null`
- a string is trimmed first: `"42"` -> `42`, `"  7  "` -> `7`
- `""` and `"   "` are `null` - **not** `0`
- `"abc"` -> `null`
- booleans, `null`, `undefined` and objects are all `null`

The return type is part of the exercise: the stub declares `unknown`.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex2
```

`Number("")` is `0` and `Number("  ")` is `0` as well - JavaScript treats an
empty string as zero, and the gate checks both. Trim first, reject the empty
result, and only then convert.

## Hint 1

Two `typeof` branches and a fallthrough. Everything the prompt does not name is
`null`, so write the two cases you do handle and return `null` at the end.

## Hint 2

`Number("")` is `0` and `Number("  ")` is `0` as well - JavaScript treats an
empty string as zero, and the gate checks both. Trim first, reject the empty
result, and only then convert.

`Number.isFinite` covers `NaN` and both infinities in one call, which is why
the number branch and the string branch can end the same way.

Left to you: whether `"1e3"` should be `1000`. The prompt does not say; decide
and be able to justify it, because a real parser has to.

exercises.prompt:
## ex3 - never as the exhaustiveness check

`Shipment` is the union
`{ status: "pending" } | { status: "shipped"; trackingId: string } | { status: "delivered"; signedBy: string } | { status: "cancelled"; reason: string }`.

`describeShipment(shipment)` returns:

- `"waiting to ship"`, `"in transit as TR9"`, `"delivered to Ada"`,
  `"cancelled: out of stock"`

and its `default` branch calls `assertUnreachable(shipment)`.

`assertUnreachable(value: never): never` throws, and its message contains the
value it was handed. Its parameter type is `never`, so passing anything the
switch did not already narrow away is a **compile error** - which is how a
newly added union member becomes a build failure instead of a runtime
surprise.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`never` has no values, so a parameter typed `never` can only be passed
something the compiler has already narrowed to nothing. In the `default` branch
of an exhaustive switch, that is exactly what the discriminant has become.

## Hint 2

The return type is `never` too, which is what lets the `default` branch say
`return assertUnreachable(shipment)` without upsetting the string return type
of the function around it.

The thrown message has to include the value - `String(value)` is enough, and
the gate checks for it. A value that "cannot happen" is exactly the value you
will want to see printed when it does.

Left to you: `return assertUnreachable(...)` or a bare call followed by
nothing. Both compile; one of them keeps working if the function is later
converted to an expression.

exercises.prompt:
## ex4 - an untyped store with a typed door

`createCache()` returns an object with three members:

- `set(key: string, value: unknown): void`
- `get<T>(key: string, guard: (value: unknown) => value is T): T | null`
- `has(key: string): boolean`

The store holds `unknown` internally. `get` returns the value only if the
guard accepts it, and `null` otherwise - including when the key is absent.

- `cache.set("count", 3)`, then `cache.get("count", isNumber)` -> `3`
- `cache.get("count", isString)` -> `null` - the guard is the only proof
- `cache.get("missing", isNumber)` -> `null`

The `Cache` interface is exported; the stub's `get` returns `unknown`, which
is what you have to fix.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex4
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex5 - never as a filter

Type-level only, and the one exercise here with no runtime half.

`OmitNever<T>` removes every member whose type is `never`.

- `OmitNever<{ a: string; b: never; c: number }>` -> `{ a: string; c: number }`
- `OmitNever<{ a: string }>` -> `{ a: string }`
- `OmitNever<{ a: never }>` -> an object with no keys
- `OmitNever<{ a: never; b: undefined }>` -> `{ b: undefined }` - `undefined`
  is a value and stays

Members typed `never` show up whenever a conditional type filters something
out, which is why a utility that sweeps them away is worth having.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex5
```
exercises.hints:

Key remapping (d14 ex4, ex5) is the tool: `[K in keyof T as <new key>]`. A

So the new key is a conditional: `never` when the member's type is `never`, and

Left to you: whether the check should be `T[K] extends never` or

## Hint 1

Key remapping (d14 ex4, ex5) is the tool: `[K in keyof T as <new key>]`. A
remap that produces `never` deletes the member.

## Hint 2

So the new key is a conditional: `never` when the member's type is `never`, and
`K` otherwise. Note which way round that is - it is easy to write the branches
backwards and delete everything else instead.

Left to you: whether the check should be `T[K] extends never` or
`[T[K]] extends [never]`. Both pass this gate; d15 ex6 explains when they part
company, and it is worth deciding on purpose.

## ex6 - walk a path through unknown

`deepGet(value, path)` follows a list of string keys into an unknown value and
returns whatever it finds - as `unknown`. It returns `undefined` the moment the
path stops working.

- `deepGet({ server: { name: "edge" } }, ["server", "name"])` -> `"edge"`
- `deepGet({ server: { ports: [8080, 9090] } }, ["server", "ports", "1"])` -> `9090`
- `deepGet(config, [])` -> the value itself
- a missing key, a walk into a string, `null` and `undefined` all give `undefined`

Only own properties count.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex6
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - narrow unknown to JSON

`JsonValue` is given:

```ts
export type JsonValue =
  | string
  | number
  | boolean
  | null
  | JsonValue[]
  | { [key: string]: JsonValue };
```

`isJsonValue(value)` narrows an `unknown` to it. Accept exactly what JSON can
hold:

- `{ a: [1, "x", null, { b: true }] }` -> `true`, `[]` and `{}` -> `true`
- `null` -> `true`, `undefined` -> `false`
- `NaN` -> `false` - JSON has no spelling for it
- a function -> `false`, and one bad value anywhere fails the whole document

The guard has to recurse.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex7
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - a function that never returns

Two exports.

`fail(message: string): never` throws an `Error` with that message. Because it
returns `never`, the compiler treats any code after a call to it as
unreachable - which means it can be used as the last expression of a function
that is declared to return something else, and as the `else` of a ternary.

`requirePort(raw: unknown): number` returns a valid port, or calls `fail`. A
valid port is an integer from 1 to 65535; a numeric string is accepted after
trimming. The thrown message contains the word `port`.

- `requirePort(8080)` -> `8080`, `requirePort("443")` -> `443`, `requirePort("  22  ")` -> `22`
- `requirePort(0)`, `requirePort(70000)`, `requirePort(80.5)`, `requirePort("abc")`
  and `requirePort(null)` all throw

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d19_unknown_any_never ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`never` as a return type is a promise that the function does not finish
normally. Write it on `fail` and the compiler will let you call it where a
value of any type is expected, and will treat the code after it as dead.

## Hint 2

In `requirePort`, convert the string case first and then validate once. After
an `if` block that ends in a call to `fail`, the compiler narrows the value to
`number` for the `return` below - no cast, no non-null assertion.

## Hint 3

Order the conditions so each one is legal: `typeof value !== "number"` has to
come before any comparison, because `<` on an `unknown` is an error. The `||`
chain narrows as it goes, which is what makes the later operands compile.

Left to you: whether `requirePort` should accept `"8080\n"`. Trimming says yes;
a stricter reading of the prompt says nothing at all about newlines.

## Hint 1

`never` as a return type is a promise that the function does not finish
normally. Write it on `fail` and the compiler will let you call it where a
value of any type is expected, and will treat the code after it as dead.

## Hint 2

In `requirePort`, convert the string case first and then validate once. After
an `if` block that ends in a call to `fail`, the compiler narrows the value to
`number` for the `return` below - no cast, no non-null assertion.

## Hint 3

Order the conditions so each one is legal: `typeof value !== "number"` has to
come before any comparison, because `<` on an `unknown` is an error. The `||`
chain narrows as it goes, which is what makes the later operands compile.

Left to you: whether `requirePort` should accept `"8080\n"`. Trimming says yes;
a stricter reading of the prompt says nothing at all about newlines.

# d20 - satisfies and as const (drill set)

Eight problems on the two operators that decide how much the compiler is
allowed to forget: `as const`, which stops widening, and `satisfies`, which
checks a value against a type *without* replacing what was inferred. They drill
lessons **10_guards_assertions** (its `satisfies` exercise) and
**05_literals_enums**; go back if "widening" is still a word rather than a
behaviour.

Most of these exercises are declarations, so the type gate is where they are
graded: `gate.test-d.ts` covers all eight, and `gate.test.ts` covers the three
that have a function to run. Nearly every stub is the *annotated* version -
`const X: Shape = {...}` - which is the habit this whole set exists to break.

## ex1 - freeze a config object

`RETRY` holds `{ attempts: 3, backoffMs: 250, jitter: false }` and its type is
exactly

```ts
{ readonly attempts: 3; readonly backoffMs: 250; readonly jitter: false }
```

- `RETRY.attempts` is the literal `3`, not `number`
- `RETRY.attempts = 4` is a compile error

The values in the stub are already right. The type is not.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex1
```

## ex2 - return a pair, not an array

`minMax(values)` returns the smallest and largest values as a **readonly pair**:
its return type is `readonly [number, number]`, not `number[]`.

- `minMax([3, 1, 2])` -> `[1, 3]`, `minMax([5])` -> `[5, 5]`
- `minMax([])` -> `[Infinity, -Infinity]` - `Math.min()` with no arguments is
  `Infinity`, and `Math.max()` is `-Infinity`. That is the documented empty
  case, not a special branch.

Do not write the return type out by hand; get it from the returned expression.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex2
```

## ex3 - check without erasing

`PALETTE` holds three colours - `primary`, `danger`, `muted` - and each value
is a hex string. Two things have to be true at once:

- `keyof typeof PALETTE` is `"primary" | "danger" | "muted"`, so `PALETTE.accent`
  is a compile error
- every value is checked against `` `#${string}` ``, so a colour written as
  `"0055ff"` would be rejected at the declaration

An annotation of `Record<string, string>` gives you the second half and throws
away the first. There is an operator that gives you both.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex3
```

## ex4 - a route table that publishes its paths

`ROUTES` is a list of three entries:

```
{ path: "/",      method: "GET" }
{ path: "/users", method: "GET" }
{ path: "/users", method: "POST" }
```

checked against `readonly { path: string; method: "GET" | "POST" }[]`, and
frozen so that the literals survive. Two types are derived from it:

- `RoutePath` -> `"/" | "/users"`
- `RouteMethod` -> `"GET" | "POST"`

`(typeof ROUTES)["length"]` is `3`, and `ROUTES[0].path = "/other"` is a
compile error.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex4
```

## ex5 - satisfies against as

`Settings` is `{ mode: "strict" | "lenient"; retries: number; tags: readonly string[] }`.

`CONFIG` holds `{ mode: "strict", retries: 3, tags: ["core"] }` and must be
checked against `Settings` **without** taking `Settings` as its type:

- `CONFIG.mode` is the literal `"strict"`, so `CONFIG.mode = "lenient"` is a
  compile error
- `CONFIG.retries` is `number` - the target type asked for `number`, so nothing
  is preserved there

The stub uses `as Settings`. That is a type assertion: it changes the type and
performs almost no checking - and it is the habit this exercise is aimed at.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex5
```

## ex6 - as const on the callee side

`tupleOf(values)` returns its argument unchanged, but its type parameter is
declared `const`, so a literal passed to it is inferred as a readonly tuple of
literals - without the caller writing `as const`.

- `tupleOf([1, "a"])` -> type `readonly [1, "a"]`
- `tupleOf(["ready"])` -> type `readonly ["ready"]`
- `tupleOf([])` -> type `readonly []`

At runtime it just hands the values back.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex6
```

## ex7 - derive two unions from one table

`PLANS` describes three plans:

```
free:  { seats: 1,   features: ["basic"] }
pro:   { seats: 10,  features: ["basic", "api"] }
scale: { seats: 100, features: ["basic", "api", "sso"] }
```

frozen, and checked against
`Record<string, { seats: number; features: readonly string[] }>`. Two types
come out of it:

- `PlanName` -> `"free" | "pro" | "scale"`
- `Feature` -> `"basic" | "api" | "sso"` - every feature named anywhere in the
  table, deduplicated

`PLANS.pro.seats` is the literal `10`, and `PLANS.enterprise` is a compile
error. The two derived types are already written in the stub; making them true
is the exercise.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex7
```

## ex8 - a flag spec that types its own defaults

`FLAGS` describes a command-line interface:

```
verbose: { kind: "boolean", default: false }
retries: { kind: "number",  default: 3 }
out:     { kind: "string",  default: "dist" }
```

frozen, and checked against
`Record<string, { kind: "boolean" | "number" | "string"; default: boolean | number | string }>`.

From it:

- `FlagName` -> `"verbose" | "retries" | "out"`
- `Flags` -> `{ verbose: boolean; retries: number; out: string }` - one member
  per flag, with the type chosen by that flag's `kind`
- `defaults()` returns `{ verbose: false, retries: 3, out: "dist" }` typed as
  `Flags`

`Flags` is a mapped type over `FlagName` whose value is a conditional on each
flag's `kind`. `FlagName` and `Flags` are declared in the stub; the declaration
of `FLAGS` and the body of `defaults()` are yours.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex8
```
