# Reading - typescript/d20_satisfies_asconst

The debrief. Per problem: which operator was really at stake, the annotation
that quietly destroys the answer, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**Four ways to attach a type to a value, and they are not interchangeable.** An
*annotation* (`const x: T = ...`) checks the value and then uses `T` as the
type, discarding whatever was inferred. An *assertion* (`x as T`) replaces the
type and checks almost nothing - `as` only requires the two types to overlap. A
*const assertion* (`x as const`) checks nothing and preserves everything: no
widening, and `readonly` on every member. And `satisfies T` checks fully and
preserves the inferred type. Most of the stubs in this set are annotations, and
most of the fixes are one of the other three.

**Widening is the default and it is usually right.** `let mode = "strict"` gives
`string`, because you are going to reassign it. It is wrong exactly when the
value *is* the specification - a config object, a route table, a plan matrix -
and `as const` is how you say so.

**`satisfies` exists because annotations are a trade.** Before it, checking an
object against a shape meant accepting that shape as the object's type, which
is why so many codebases have a `Record<string, string>` sitting on top of a
constant whose three keys everyone wanted to know about. `satisfies` removes the
trade: full checking, no loss.

**They compose, in one order.** `expr as const satisfies T` freezes first and
checks second, which is what ex4, ex7 and ex8 all need. The other order is
legal and useless, and the frozen value forces the target type to be readonly -
a readonly tuple is not assignable to a mutable array, which is the error most
people meet first here.

**And `const` type parameters move the decision to the callee.** `<const T>`
infers as though the caller had written `as const`, so a helper can insist on
literal inference instead of documenting a convention. It is the newest piece
in this set and the one most likely to be missing from code you inherit.

**The payoff, in every case, is derivation.** `keyof typeof`, `[number]` and
indexed access turn a frozen table into the unions and mapped types around it -
so the data and the types cannot drift, because there is only one of them.

## ex1 - freeze a config object

What this was testing: that an annotation and a const assertion pull in
opposite directions. `const RETRY: { attempts: number } = { attempts: 3 }`
throws away the one fact worth keeping - that the value is 3 - and hands back
something writable.

The classic mistake is thinking `const` already prevents this. `const` protects
the binding, not the object: without an assertion, `RETRY.attempts` is a
mutable `number`, because that is what the compiler infers for a property of an
object literal.

The model answer is the same literal with `as const` after it, which freezes
the values as literal types and marks every member `readonly` - one operator,
both effects.

## ex2 - return a pair, not an array

What this was testing: that `as const` applies to any literal expression, not
only to a top-level declaration - and that on an array literal it produces a
tuple, which is what makes `const [low, high] = minMax(rows)` typecheck without
either element being `number | undefined`.

The classic mistake is annotating the return type as `number[]` and then
wondering why destructuring gives possibly-undefined elements. The second is
writing the tuple type out by hand, which works until the body changes and the
two drift.

The model answer omits the return type and puts `as const` on the returned
array literal, so the signature is derived from the implementation and says
exactly what the caller gets.

## ex3 - check without erasing

What this was testing: the core of `satisfies` - a check that does not become
the type. The annotation `Record<string, string>` is a strictly worse
description of this object than the one the compiler would have worked out on
its own, and swapping it for a `satisfies` clause is the whole fix.

The classic mistake is believing that an annotation is the only way to get a
value validated, and accepting the loss of key information as the price. The
second is dropping the constraint entirely, which keeps the keys and stops
checking the values.

The model answer keeps the object literal exactly as written and appends a
`satisfies` clause naming the hex-string record, so a mistyped colour is caught
at the declaration and the three key names stay in the type.

## ex4 - a route table that publishes its paths

What this was testing: the `as const satisfies` pair, and indexed access with
`[number]` to turn a tuple of objects into a union of one of their fields. This
is how a route table, a menu definition or a migration list can be the single
source of truth for the types around it.

The classic mistake is picking one operator. `as const` alone leaves the entries
unchecked, so a typo in `method` is only caught wherever the value is used;
`satisfies` alone (without `as const`) leaves `path` widened to `string`, and
`RoutePath` becomes useless.

The model answer freezes first and checks second, so the literals survive into
`typeof ROUTES` and the derived unions come out of the data rather than being
maintained beside it.

## ex5 - satisfies against as

What this was testing: the three-way difference between an annotation, an
assertion and `satisfies`. An annotation checks and replaces. An assertion
replaces and barely checks - `as` only requires the two types to overlap, so it
will happily accept a value with a missing field if the shapes are close
enough. `satisfies` checks fully and replaces nothing.

The classic mistake is reaching for `as` to silence an error, which is the one
option that can make a genuine mistake invisible. The second is expecting
`satisfies` to preserve every literal; it preserves what the target type leaves
room for, which is why `retries` comes out as `number`.

The model answer swaps `as Settings` for `satisfies Settings` and changes
nothing else - the value is validated more strictly than before, and the
inferred type is more precise than before.

## ex6 - as const on the callee side

What this was testing: `const` type parameters, which move the decision about
widening from the caller to the function. Before them, a helper that wanted
literal inference had to document "call me with `as const`" and hope; now the
signature can ask for it.

The classic mistake is putting `as const` inside the body - `return values as
const` - which does nothing, because the widening already happened during
inference at the call site. By the time the body runs, `T` has been decided.

The model answer adds one keyword to the type parameter and returns the
argument, and the gate's three assertions all change from widened arrays to
readonly tuples of literals.

## ex7 - derive two unions from one table

What this was testing: `as const satisfies` on a nested structure, and a
three-step indexed access that turns a table into a union of leaf values. The
result is that adding a fourth plan with a new feature updates `Feature`
automatically, which is the entire argument for keeping data and types in one
place.

The classic mistake is the stub's annotation, which is easy to defend
("`Record` documents the shape") and destroys both derived types at once -
`keyof` an index signature is `string`, so `PlanName` says nothing and `Feature`
follows it down.

The model answer freezes the table, checks it, and lets the two derived types do
their work: `keyof typeof` for the names, and
`[PlanName]["features"][number]` for the features - a union of unions of
unions, deduplicated by the type system for free.

## ex8 - a flag spec that types its own defaults

What this was testing: the whole set, plus d14 and d15. A frozen, checked spec;
`keyof typeof` for the names; a mapped type over those names; a conditional type
that reads each entry's `kind` to pick a member type; and a function whose
return type is the result. Nothing here is new - the point is that they compose
into a small typed CLI with one source of truth.

The classic mistake is the annotation on `FLAGS`, and it is worth being precise
about the damage: `FlagName` becomes `string`, so the mapped type becomes an
index signature, so `Flags` accepts any key with the wrong type, so
`defaults()` typechecks while returning nonsense. One annotation, four
consequences.

The model answer freezes and checks the spec, leaves the two derived types
untouched, and reads the defaults straight back out of `FLAGS` - so adding a
fourth flag means editing one object and nothing else.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: const assertions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-4.html#const-assertions) - what `as const` does to literals, arrays and objects.
- [TypeScript 4.9 release notes: the satisfies operator](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-9.html#the-satisfies-operator) - the motivating examples, including the palette in ex3.
- [TypeScript 5.0 release notes: const type parameters](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-5-0.html#const-type-parameters) - the `<const T>` modifier from ex6.
- [Handbook: Literal types and widening](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html#literal-inference) - why `const` on the binding does not stop the properties widening.
- [Handbook: keyof and Indexed Access Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/indexed-access-types.html) - the `[number]` and `[PlanName]` steps that derive the unions in ex4, ex7 and ex8.

maintained beside it.

## ex5 - satisfies against as

What this was testing: the three-way difference between an annotation, an
assertion and `satisfies`. An annotation checks and replaces. An assertion
replaces and barely checks - `as` only requires the two types to overlap, so it
will happily accept a value with a missing field if the shapes are close
enough. `satisfies` checks fully and replaces nothing.

The classic mistake is reaching for `as` to silence an error, which is the one
option that can make a genuine mistake invisible. The second is expecting
`satisfies` to preserve every literal; it preserves what the target type leaves
room for, which is why `retries` comes out as `number`.

The model answer swaps `as Settings` for `satisfies Settings` and changes
nothing else - the value is validated more strictly than before, and the
inferred type is more precise than before.

## ex6 - as const on the callee side

What this was testing: `const` type parameters, which move the decision about
widening from the caller to the function. Before them, a helper that wanted
literal inference had to document "call me with `as const`" and hope; now the
signature can ask for it.

The classic mistake is putting `as const` inside the body - `return values as
const` - which does nothing, because the widening already happened during
inference at the call site. By the time the body runs, `T` has been decided.

The model answer adds one keyword to the type parameter and returns the
argument, and the gate's three assertions all change from widened arrays to
readonly tuples of literals.

## ex7 - derive two unions from one table

What this was testing: `as const satisfies` on a nested structure, and a
three-step indexed access that turns a table into a union of leaf values. The
result is that adding a fourth plan with a new feature updates `Feature`
automatically, which is the entire argument for keeping data and types in one
place.

The classic mistake is the stub's annotation, which is easy to defend
("`Record` documents the shape") and destroys both derived types at once -
`keyof` an index signature is `string`, so `PlanName` says nothing and `Feature`
follows it down.

The model answer freezes the table, checks it, and lets the two derived types do
their work: `keyof typeof` for the names, and
`[PlanName]["features"][number]` for the features - a union of unions of
unions, deduplicated by the type system for free.

## ex8 - a flag spec that types its own defaults

What this was testing: the whole set, plus d14 and d15. A frozen, checked spec;
`keyof typeof` for the names; a mapped type over those names; a conditional type
that reads each entry's `kind` to pick a member type; and a function whose
return type is the result. Nothing here is new - the point is that they compose
into a small typed CLI with one source of truth.

The classic mistake is the annotation on `FLAGS`, and it is worth being precise
about the damage: `FlagName` becomes `string`, so the mapped type becomes an
index signature, so `Flags` accepts any key with the wrong type, so
`defaults()` typechecks while returning nonsense. One annotation, four
consequences.

The model answer freezes and checks the spec, leaves the two derived types
untouched, and reads the defaults straight back out of `FLAGS` - so adding a
fourth flag means editing one object and nothing else.

## ex1 - freeze a config object

`RETRY` holds `{ attempts: 3, backoffMs: 250, jitter: false }` and its type is
exactly

```ts
{ readonly attempts: 3; readonly backoffMs: 250; readonly jitter: false }
```

- `RETRY.attempts` is the literal `3`, not `number`
- `RETRY.attempts = 4` is a compile error

The values in the stub are already right. The type is not.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An annotation tells the compiler what to *use*; a const assertion tells it what
to *keep*. You want the second, so the annotation has to go.

## Hint 2

`as const` on an object literal does two things at once: no literal is widened,
and every member becomes `readonly`. Both are checked by the gate, and both are
lost the moment an annotation is put back.

Left to you: `Object.freeze` also produces readonly members and does so at
runtime. Work out what it does *not* do that `as const` does, before deciding
they are interchangeable.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

An annotation tells the compiler what to *use*; a const assertion tells it what
to *keep*. You want the second, so the annotation has to go.

## Hint 2

`as const` on an object literal does two things at once: no literal is widened,
and every member becomes `readonly`. Both are checked by the gate, and both are
lost the moment an annotation is put back.

Left to you: `Object.freeze` also produces readonly members and does so at
runtime. Work out what it does *not* do that `as const` does, before deciding
they are interchangeable.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - return a pair, not an array

`minMax(values)` returns the smallest and largest values as a **readonly pair**:
its return type is `readonly [number, number]`, not `number[]`.

- `minMax([3, 1, 2])` -> `[1, 3]`, `minMax([5])` -> `[5, 5]`
- `minMax([])` -> `[Infinity, -Infinity]` - `Math.min()` with no arguments is
  `Infinity`, and `Math.max()` is `-Infinity`. That is the documented empty
  case, not a special branch.

Do not write the return type out by hand; get it from the returned expression.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex2
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex4 - a route table that publishes its paths

`ROUTES` is a list of three entries:

```
{ path: "/",      method: "GET" }
{ path: "/users", method: "GET" }
{ path: "/users", method: "POST" }
```

checked against `readonly { path: string; method: "GET" | "POST" }[]`, and
frozen so that the literals survive. Two types are derived from it:

- `RoutePath` -> `"/" | "/users"`
- `RouteMethod` -> `"GET" | "POST"`

`(typeof ROUTES)["length"]` is `3`, and `ROUTES[0].path = "/other"` is a
compile error.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You want both operators, in this order: `as const` to keep the literals and
make the tuple readonly, then `satisfies` to check the frozen value against the
shape. `expr as const satisfies T` is legal and reads left to right.

## Hint 2

Because `as const` makes the array readonly, the `satisfies` target has to be
`readonly ...[]` as well - a readonly array is not assignable to a mutable one.

The derived types are already written for you; they only start saying something
once `typeof ROUTES` is a tuple of literal objects.

Left to you: whether `RoutePath` should be `"/" | "/users"` or should include
duplicates. Unions deduplicate on their own, which is worth noticing rather than
assuming.

## ex5 - satisfies against as

`Settings` is `{ mode: "strict" | "lenient"; retries: number; tags: readonly string[] }`.

`CONFIG` holds `{ mode: "strict", retries: 3, tags: ["core"] }` and must be
checked against `Settings` **without** taking `Settings` as its type:

- `CONFIG.mode` is the literal `"strict"`, so `CONFIG.mode = "lenient"` is a
  compile error
- `CONFIG.retries` is `number` - the target type asked for `number`, so nothing
  is preserved there

The stub uses `as Settings`. That is a type assertion: it changes the type and
performs almost no checking - and it is the habit this exercise is aimed at.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex5
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex6 - as const on the callee side

`tupleOf(values)` returns its argument unchanged, but its type parameter is
declared `const`, so a literal passed to it is inferred as a readonly tuple of
literals - without the caller writing `as const`.

- `tupleOf([1, "a"])` -> type `readonly [1, "a"]`
- `tupleOf(["ready"])` -> type `readonly ["ready"]`
- `tupleOf([])` -> type `readonly []`

At runtime it just hands the values back.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex6
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - derive two unions from one table

`PLANS` describes three plans:

```
free:  { seats: 1,   features: ["basic"] }
pro:   { seats: 10,  features: ["basic", "api"] }
scale: { seats: 100, features: ["basic", "api", "sso"] }
```

frozen, and checked against
`Record<string, { seats: number; features: readonly string[] }>`. Two types
come out of it:

- `PlanName` -> `"free" | "pro" | "scale"`
- `Feature` -> `"basic" | "api" | "sso"` - every feature named anywhere in the
  table, deduplicated

`PLANS.pro.seats` is the literal `10`, and `PLANS.enterprise` is a compile
error. The two derived types are already written in the stub; making them true
is the exercise.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex7
```

first so the keys and the nested literals survive, then `satisfies` so a plan

## Hint 2

Check the `satisfies` target against what `as const` produced: the nested
`features` arrays are now readonly tuples, so the target has to say
`readonly string[]` rather than `string[]`.

## Hint 3

Read `Feature` slowly: index the table by *every* plan name at once, take the
`features` member of the result, then index that with `[number]`. Each step
produces a union, and the last one flattens three tuples into one union of
strings.

Left to you: whether `Feature` should be defined that way or as
`(typeof PLANS)[PlanName]["features"][number]` written in stages with a helper
type. The one-liner is shorter; the staged version is the one you can debug.

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - a flag spec that types its own defaults

`FLAGS` describes a command-line interface:

```
verbose: { kind: "boolean", default: false }
retries: { kind: "number",  default: 3 }
out:     { kind: "string",  default: "dist" }
```

frozen, and checked against
`Record<string, { kind: "boolean" | "number" | "string"; default: boolean | number | string }>`.

From it:

- `FlagName` -> `"verbose" | "retries" | "out"`
- `Flags` -> `{ verbose: boolean; retries: number; out: string }` - one member
  per flag, with the type chosen by that flag's `kind`
- `defaults()` returns `{ verbose: false, retries: 3, out: "dist" }` typed as
  `Flags`

`Flags` is a mapped type over `FlagName` whose value is a conditional on each
flag's `kind`. `FlagName` and `Flags` are declared in the stub; the declaration
of `FLAGS` and the body of `defaults()` are yours.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d20_satisfies_asconst ex8
```

lessons.briefing:
# d21 - Typing async code (drill set)

Eight problems on promises with types on them: sequential and concurrent
loading, settled results, async iteration, retries, races, a concurrency limit,
and a tuple-shaped `Promise.all`. They drill lesson **11_async_and_modules**;
go back if `Promise<T>` and `T` still look interchangeable in a signature.

Both gates run. Everything here is **deterministic** - no real timers and no
wall-clock waiting. Where an exercise needs something to be pending, the gate
hands it a deferred promise and resolves it by hand, which is also how you
should test this kind of code at work.

## ex1 - one at a time, in order

`mapSeries(values, fn)` applies an async `fn` to each value **sequentially** -
the next call does not start until the previous one has settled - and resolves
with the results in input order.

- `mapSeries([1, 2, 3], double)` -> `[2, 4, 6]`
- the callback receives `(value, index)`
- an empty list resolves to `[]`

Two type parameters: the element type going in and the result type coming out.
The return type is `Promise<R[]>`, not `Promise<R>[]`.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d21_async_typing ex1
```

## ex2 - three loaders, one wait

`Profile` is `{ user: { id: string; name: string }; orders: readonly { id: string }[]; unread: number }`.

`loadProfile(loadUser, loadOrders, loadUnread)` calls all three loaders,
**starts them all before awaiting any of them**, and resolves with the
assembled `Profile`.

The gate proves the concurrency: it hands you three loaders that record when
they are called and return promises that nobody has resolved yet, then checks
that all three were called.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d21_async_typing ex2
```

## ex3 - split the settled results

`partitionSettled(tasks)` waits for every promise - it never rejects - and
resolves with `{ fulfilled: T[]; rejected: unknown[] }`.

- rejection reasons are `unknown`, because a promise may be rejected with
  anything at all

- one rejection must not lose the values that did arrive

```

```

## ex4 - walk the pages

Two exports.

`pages(fetchPage)` is an **async generator** that yields items across a cursor
API. It calls `fetchPage(null)` first; each page is
`{ items: readonly T[]; next: string | null }`; it yields every item, then
follows `next` until `next` is `null`.

`collect(source)` takes any `AsyncIterable<T>` and resolves with all of its
items as an array.

- three pages of `["a", "b"]`, `["c"]`, `["d"]` collect to `["a", "b", "c", "d"]`

- an empty first page with `next: null` collects to `[]`

`Promise<T[]>`.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d21_async_typing ex4
```

## ex5 - try again, up to a point

`withRetry(task, attempts)` calls `task()` and returns its value. If it
rejects, it calls it again, up to `attempts` times in total. If the last
attempt rejects, that rejection is what comes out.

- a task that fails twice then succeeds resolves on the third attempt, with
  `attempts` set to 3
- with `attempts` set to 2, the same task rejects, and the reason is the one
  from the second attempt
- a task that succeeds first time is called exactly once

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d21_async_typing ex5
```

`withTimeout(task, expire, message)` resolves with `task`'s value if `task`
settles first, and rejects with `new Error(message)` if `expire` resolves
first.

- if `task` rejects first, **its own reason** comes out - the timeout message
  does not replace it
- the return type is `Promise<T>`: the expiry contributes nothing to it

them by hand, so there is no timer anywhere - which is exactly how you make
timeout code testable.

```

```

`createQueue(limit)` returns `{ add<T>(task: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> }`.

- at most `limit` tasks run at once
- waiting tasks start in the order they were added
- each `add` call resolves (or rejects) with its own task's result

have started, resolves the first, and checks that the third then starts.

# Reading - typescript/d21_async_typing

The debrief. Per problem: what the signature was really promising, the version
that runs and lies about its shape, and one sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**An `async` function's annotation describes what the promise resolves to.**
`Promise<R[]>` is one promise of many results; `Promise<R>[]` is many promises;
`R[]` on an `async` function is a compile error. Most of the type slips in this
area are a misplaced pair of brackets, and they are caught the moment somebody
tries to `await` the thing.

**Where the `await` sits decides the concurrency, and the types cannot see it.**
Three awaits in a row and one `Promise.all` have identical signatures and
different latency (ex1, ex2). That is why this lesson's runtime gate records
*when* things start rather than only what they return - it is the only
observable difference.

**The four combinators answer four different questions.** `Promise.all` is
all-or-nothing and gives you a tuple. `Promise.allSettled` never rejects and
gives you a discriminated union per input. `Promise.race` takes the first to
settle, rejection included. `Promise.any` takes the first to *fulfil*. Picking
the wrong one is a behaviour bug the type system will happily wave through.

**`never` and `Awaited` do quiet work in these signatures.** A promise that only
rejects is `Promise<never>`, so racing it against `Promise<T>` leaves
`Promise<T>` untouched (ex6). `Awaited<T>` unwraps any depth of promise and
leaves plain values alone, which is what lets one mapped type handle a tuple of
mixed inputs (ex8).

**And async code is testable without waiting.** Every exercise here that needs
something to be pending gets a deferred promise - a promise plus its `resolve`
and `reject`, kept by the test - so the test controls the interleaving exactly.
No `setTimeout`, no flaky ordering, no sleeping in a test suite. Where a real
timeout is needed, inject it as a promise (ex6) rather than reaching for a timer
inside the function.

## ex1 - one at a time, in order

What this was testing: the shape of an async return type, and the difference
between mapping and sequencing. `async` functions always return a promise, so
the annotation describes what the promise resolves to - writing `Promise<R>[]`
there is a common slip that typechecks at the declaration and fails at every
call site.

The classic mistake is `values.map(fn)` followed by `Promise.all`, which
produces the right array in the right order and starts everything at once.
Sometimes that is what you want; when it is not - a rate-limited API, a
database that will deadlock - it is a bug the type system cannot see, which is
why the gate records the interleaving.

The model answer awaits inside the loop and pushes, so at most one call is in
flight and the results array is built in order by construction.

## ex2 - three loaders, one wait

What this was testing: concurrency as a property of *where the awaits are*, and
`Promise.all`'s tuple typing. Three sequential awaits and one `Promise.all` are
indistinguishable in the type signature and differ by a factor of three in
latency, which is why the gate measures behaviour rather than shape.

The classic mistake is `const user = await loadUser();` on three consecutive
lines. It reads beautifully and serialises three independent requests. The fix
is to separate starting from waiting.

The model answer starts all three in the argument list of `Promise.all` and
destructures the resulting tuple, so each name has its own type without a single
annotation in the body.

## ex3 - split the settled results

What this was testing: `Promise.allSettled` and the discriminated union it
resolves to. The point of the exercise is that partial failure is a normal
outcome - three of four dashboards loading is worth showing - and that
`Promise.all` cannot express it, because the first rejection discards the rest.

The classic mistake is reading `result.value` without checking `result.status`,
which does not compile - the standard library types this as a proper union
precisely so it cannot be got wrong. The second is typing the reasons as
`Error[]`: a promise can be rejected with a string, a number or `undefined`, so
`unknown` is the only claim you can defend.

The model answer awaits `allSettled`, walks the results once, and pushes into
the list the discriminant selects - so the fulfilled values stay in input order
and no rejection can take them down with it.

## ex4 - walk the pages

What this was testing: async generators as the natural type for a paginated
API, and the fact that `for await...of` consumes anything that implements
`AsyncIterable`. The generator hides the cursor entirely - the consumer sees a
stream of items and never learns that there were pages.

The classic mistake is fetching every page into an array before yielding
anything, which works and defeats the purpose: the point of a generator is that
the consumer can stop after ten items without the twentieth page ever being
requested. The second is checking `next` before yielding the current page's
items, which silently drops the last page.

The model answer loops forever, yields each item as it arrives, and returns when
`next` is `null` - and `collect` takes the widest type it can, `AsyncIterable<T>`,
so it is not tied to this generator.

## ex5 - try again, up to a point

What this was testing: the generic wrapper shape - `T` in, `Promise<T>` out -
and the one situation where `return await` earns its keep. A wrapper that
loosens the type is a wrapper every call site has to undo.

The classic mistake is `return task()` inside the `try`. The promise is handed
back before it settles, the `try` block exits successfully, and a rejection
lands on the caller with no retry ever happening. The second is throwing a new
`Error("all attempts failed")`, which is exactly the moment the original reason
was needed.

The model answer loops, returns on the first success, remembers the last error
as `unknown`, and rethrows it - so the failure the caller sees is the failure
that happened.

## ex6 - whichever settles first

What this was testing: `Promise.race`, and `never` as the return type of
something that only ever rejects. The union arithmetic is the pleasing part -
`Promise<T | never>` collapses to `Promise<T>`, so the timeout branch adds a
failure mode without widening the success type.

The classic mistake is racing `expire` as it is and then rejecting afterwards,
which resolves the race with `undefined` and hands the caller a value it never
asked for. The second is catching the task's rejection and rethrowing the
timeout message, which erases the real error.

The model answer maps the expiry to a `Promise<never>` that throws, races the
two, and stops there - and the fact that the losing task keeps running is a
property of promises, not an oversight.

## ex7 - at most n at a time

What this was testing: a small piece of concurrency machinery with an honest
signature. Every property that matters here - the limit, the ordering, the
per-call result type - is invisible to the type system except the last one, so
the runtime gate does most of the work and the type gate makes sure `add` did
not quietly become `Promise<unknown>`.

The classic mistake is decrementing the counter only on success, so one rejected
task permanently costs a slot; `finally` is the fix and is the reason it exists.
The second is putting the generic on `createQueue`, which forces every task in
one queue to return the same type.

The model answer counts running tasks, queues closures for the rest, and settles
each caller's promise from inside its own closure - so a task that fails rejects
its own `add` and nobody else is affected.

## ex8 - a tuple-shaped Promise.all

What this was testing: the whole toolkit pointed at one signature - a `const`
type parameter to preserve the tuple (d20), a mapped type over that tuple with
the `readonly` modifier removed (d14), and `Awaited` to unwrap each member
(d12). The runtime is one line; the exercise is the type.

The classic mistake is dropping `const`, after which `T` is
`(Promise<number> | Promise<string>)[]`, the mapped type produces an array
rather than a tuple, and both positions come out as the same union. The second
is hand-rolling the unwrap with a conditional, which is right until someone
passes a `Promise<Promise<T>>`.

The model answer is one mapped type and one cast, and it is the shape the
standard library itself uses for `Promise.all` - reading `lib.es2015.promise.d.ts`
after finishing this is worth the five minutes.

## Further reading

- [MDN: Promise.all](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/all) - and the sibling pages for `allSettled`, `race` and `any`, which are ex2, ex3 and ex6.
- [MDN: for await...of](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/for-await...of) - the consumer side of the async generator in ex4.
- [Handbook: Awaited and Promise improvements](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-5.html#the-awaited-type-and-promise-improvements) - what `Awaited<T>` does that a hand-written conditional does not (ex8).
- [Handbook: Utility types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html) - `Awaited`, `ReturnType` and the rest, as the standard library defines them.
- [MDN: AsyncGenerator](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/AsyncGenerator) - the three type parameters ex4 asks you to fill in.

exercises.prompt:
## ex1 - one at a time, in order

`mapSeries(values, fn)` applies an async `fn` to each value **sequentially** -
the next call does not start until the previous one has settled - and resolves
with the results in input order.

- `mapSeries([1, 2, 3], double)` -> `[2, 4, 6]`
- the callback receives `(value, index)`
- an empty list resolves to `[]`

Two type parameters: the element type going in and the result type coming out.
The return type is `Promise<R[]>`, not `Promise<R>[]`.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d21_async_typing ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Promise<R[]>` is one promise of many results. `Promise<R>[]` is many promises
and is what `values.map(fn)` gives you - the difference is the whole exercise.

## Hint 2

Sequential means the `await` has to be inside the loop. `values.map(fn)` starts
every call immediately, and `await Promise.all(...)` on the result keeps the
order but not the sequencing - the gate logs the starts and ends to tell the two
apart.

Left to you: a `for` loop with an index, or `for...of` with `entries()`. Both
give you the index; only one of them needs a cast under stricter index settings.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - three loaders, one wait

`Profile` is `{ user: { id: string; name: string }; orders: readonly { id: string }[]; unread: number }`.

`loadProfile(loadUser, loadOrders, loadUnread)` calls all three loaders,
**starts them all before awaiting any of them**, and resolves with the
assembled `Profile`.

The gate proves the concurrency: it hands you three loaders that record when
they are called and return promises that nobody has resolved yet, then checks
that all three were called.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d21_async_typing ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Call all three loaders first, then wait. `await loadUser()` on its own line
means the second loader has not even been called yet.

## Hint 2

`Promise.all` over an array literal of three differently typed promises gives a
promise of a **tuple**, so destructuring the result keeps each type. That
inference is the reason the assembled object needs no annotations inside.

exercises.prompt:
## ex3 - split the settled results

`partitionSettled(tasks)` waits for every promise - it never rejects - and
resolves with `{ fulfilled: T[]; rejected: unknown[] }`.

- fulfilled values keep input order
- rejection reasons are `unknown`, because a promise may be rejected with
  anything at all
- `partitionSettled([])` -> `{ fulfilled: [], rejected: [] }`
- one rejection must not lose the values that did arrive

exercises.prompt:
## ex4 - walk the pages

Two exports.

`pages(fetchPage)` is an **async generator** that yields items across a cursor
API. It calls `fetchPage(null)` first; each page is
`{ items: readonly T[]; next: string | null }`; it yields every item, then
follows `next` until `next` is `null`.

`collect(source)` takes any `AsyncIterable<T>` and resolves with all of its
items as an array.

- three pages of `["a", "b"]`, `["c"]`, `["d"]` collect to `["a", "b", "c", "d"]`
- the cursors requested are `null`, then whatever each page returned
- an empty first page with `next: null` collects to `[]`

`pages` returns `AsyncGenerator<T, void, undefined>`; `collect` returns
`Promise<T[]>`.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d21_async_typing ex4
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex5 - try again, up to a point

`withRetry(task, attempts)` calls `task()` and returns its value. If it
rejects, it calls it again, up to `attempts` times in total. If the last
attempt rejects, that rejection is what comes out.

- a task that fails twice then succeeds resolves on the third attempt, with
  `attempts` set to 3
- with `attempts` set to 2, the same task rejects, and the reason is the one
  from the second attempt
- a task that succeeds first time is called exactly once

There are no delays between attempts - this is a retry, not a backoff.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d21_async_typing ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`return await task()` inside a `try` is the shape. Without the `await`, the
promise is returned before it can reject and the `catch` never runs - which is
the one place where `return await` is not redundant.

## Hint 2

Keep the last error in a variable typed `unknown` (`useUnknownInCatchVariables`
gives you that anyway) and rethrow it after the loop, so the caller sees the
real failure rather than a message you invented.

Left to you: what `attempts` of 0 should do. The gate does not ask; decide
whether it means "never call" or "call once", and make the loop say so.

## Hint 1

`return await task()` inside a `try` is the shape. Without the `await`, the
promise is returned before it can reject and the `catch` never runs - which is
the one place where `return await` is not redundant.

## Hint 2

Keep the last error in a variable typed `unknown` (`useUnknownInCatchVariables`
gives you that anyway) and rethrow it after the loop, so the caller sees the
real failure rather than a message you invented.

Left to you: what `attempts` of 0 should do. The gate does not ask; decide
whether it means "never call" or "call once", and make the loop say so.

exercises.prompt:
## ex6 - whichever settles first

`withTimeout(task, expire, message)` resolves with `task`'s value if `task`
settles first, and rejects with `new Error(message)` if `expire` resolves
first.

- if `task` rejects first, **its own reason** comes out - the timeout message
  does not replace it
- the return type is `Promise<T>`: the expiry contributes nothing to it

`expire` is a `Promise<void>`. The gate supplies deferred promises and settles
them by hand, so there is no timer anywhere - which is exactly how you make
timeout code testable.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d21_async_typing ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Promise.race` settles with whichever input settles first, rejection included.
That is what gives you "the task rejected first, so its reason wins" without
any extra code.

## Hint 2

Turn the expiry into a promise that *rejects*: `expire.then(() => { throw ... })`.
Its type is `Promise<never>`, which is why racing it against `Promise<T>` still
gives `Promise<T>` - `T | never` is `T`.

Left to you: whether this function should also stop the task when the timeout
wins. It cannot, and that is worth sitting with: a promise has no cancel, and
the abort signal is a separate mechanism.

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - a tuple-shaped Promise.all

`allOf(values)` is `Promise.all` with the types written out: it takes a tuple of
promises and plain values, and resolves with a tuple of the awaited results, in
the same positions.

- `allOf([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.resolve("a")])` -> `Promise<[number, string]>`
- `allOf([Promise.resolve(true), 2])` -> resolves to `[boolean, 2]` - a plain
  value passes through, and its literal type survives
- `allOf([])` -> resolves to `[]`
- one rejection rejects the whole call

Three pieces: a `const` type parameter so the argument is inferred as a tuple, a
mapped type over that tuple, and `Awaited` on each member.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d21_async_typing ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Without a `const` type parameter (d20 ex6), an array literal argument widens to
an array of a union and the positions are gone before the mapped type ever
runs.

## Hint 2

A mapped type over a tuple stays a tuple: `{ [K in keyof T]: ... }` applied to
`readonly [A, B]` gives `readonly [f<A>, f<B>]`. Add `-readonly` to hand the
caller a mutable tuple, which is what `Promise.all` actually resolves with.

## Hint 3

`Awaited<T[K]>` unwraps a promise and leaves a plain value alone, which is
exactly the rule the prompt describes for mixed inputs - and it handles nesting,
which `T[K] extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T[K]` does not.

Left to you: the body needs one assertion, because `Promise.all`'s own
signature cannot see through your mapped type. Decide where to put it and write
the comment that justifies it.

## Hint 1

Without a `const` type parameter (d20 ex6), an array literal argument widens to
an array of a union and the positions are gone before the mapped type ever
runs.

## Hint 2

A mapped type over a tuple stays a tuple: `{ [K in keyof T]: ... }` applied to
`readonly [A, B]` gives `readonly [f<A>, f<B>]`. Add `-readonly` to hand the
caller a mutable tuple, which is what `Promise.all` actually resolves with.

## Hint 3

`Awaited<T[K]>` unwraps a promise and leaves a plain value alone, which is
exactly the rule the prompt describes for mixed inputs - and it handles nesting,
which `T[K] extends Promise<infer U> ? U : T[K]` does not.

Left to you: the body needs one assertion, because `Promise.all`'s own
signature cannot see through your mapped type. Decide where to put it and write
the comment that justifies it.

# d22 - Declaration merging and ambient types (drill set)

Eight problems on the part of TypeScript that describes code rather than
containing it: declaration merging, namespaces, overload signatures and global
augmentation - the vocabulary every `.d.ts` file is written in. They drill
lesson **11_async_and_modules**, whose fourth exercise described an untyped
module, and lesson i1's declaration-merging question.

Both gates run: `gate.test.ts` checks that the values exist at runtime and
`gate.test-d.ts` checks that the declarations say so. Everything lives in
ordinary `.ts` files here, because that is where these constructs are graded -
but every one of them is exactly what you would write in a hand-authored
declaration file.

## ex1 - a function with members

`parseTag(raw)` splits `"dojo:ts"` into `{ scope: "dojo", name: "ts" }`. With no
colon, the whole string is the name and the scope is `""`.

The same name also carries two members:

- `parseTag.VERSION` - a `string` whose value is `"1.0"`
- `parseTag.isValid(raw)` - `true` when the string contains a colon

`Tag` is exported as an interface. Getting members onto a function without
writing `Object.assign` is the exercise.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex1
```

## ex2 - two signatures, one function

`box(value)` has two **overload signatures**:

- `box(value: string)` returns `{ kind: "text"; value: string }`
- `box(value: number)` returns `{ kind: "count"; value: number }`

and `box(true)` is a compile error.

- `box("hello")` -> `{ kind: "text", value: "hello" }`
- `box(0)` -> `{ kind: "count", value: 0 }` - the branch is on the *type*, not
  on truthiness

The implementation signature is not callable from outside; it exists only to
be wide enough for both overloads.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex2
```

## ex3 - add something to globalThis

Two exports plus one global.

`registerBuild(name, version)` records a build number on a global registry;
`readBuild(name)` reads it back and returns `number | undefined`.

The registry lives at `globalThis.__d22BuildRegistry`, typed
`Record<string, number> | undefined`, and it has to be **declared** so that
every module in the program can see the type - which is what a `.d.ts` file in
a real project would do for a polyfill, a test helper or a bundler-injected
constant.

- `readBuild("nothing")` -> `undefined` before anything is registered
- registering the same name twice overwrites

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex3
```

## ex4 - a namespace of types and values

`Api` is a namespace holding all three kinds of declaration at once:

- `Api.Row` - an interface, `{ id: string; amount: number }`
- `Api.Id` - a type alias equal to `Row["id"]`, so `string`
- `Api.VERSION` - a value, the `number` `2`

`makeRow(id, amount)` takes an `Api.Id` and a `number` and returns an `Api.Row`.

Namespaced types are written `Api.Row`, with a dot, in type position.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex4
```

## ex5 - one interface, two declarations

`RequestContext` is declared **twice** in the file, once with `requestId: string`
and once with `locale: string`. The two declarations merge, so the type has both
members.

`describeContext(context)` returns `` `${requestId}@${locale}` ``.

- `describeContext({ requestId: "req-1", locale: "en-GB" })` -> `"req-1@en-GB"`

Interfaces merge; type aliases do not. That asymmetry is the reason libraries
publish their extension points as interfaces.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex5
```

## ex6 - an enum with helpers

`Level` is a numeric enum - `Debug = 10`, `Info = 20`, `Error = 40` - merged
with a namespace of the same name that adds two functions:

- `Level.isAtLeast(value, minimum)` - inclusive, so `isAtLeast(Info, Info)` is
  `true`
- `Level.parse(name)` - `Level | undefined`; `parse("Error")` is `40`,
  `parse("Fatal")` is `undefined`, and `parse("20")` is `undefined` too

That last case is the trap: a numeric enum object has entries in both
directions, so `Level["20"]` is the string `"Error"`, and a string is not a
level.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex6
```

## ex7 - a registry other files can extend

`CommandRegistry` is an interface declared **empty** and then extended by two
further declarations - one adding `build: { target: string }`, one adding
`test: { pattern: string }`. That is the plugin-registry pattern: the base
declares the extension point, and each feature adds its own entry.

From it:

- `CommandName` is `keyof CommandRegistry`, so `"build" | "test"`
- `dispatch(name, payload)` is generic over `K extends CommandName` and takes
  `CommandRegistry[K]` as its payload, so `dispatch("build", { pattern: "x" })`
  is a compile error

`dispatch("build", { target: "web" })` -> `"build:web"`, and
`dispatch("test", { pattern: "*.ts" })` -> `"test:*.ts"`.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex7
```

## ex8 - a class, a type and a namespace

`Money` is one name in three declaration spaces at once - the capstone of this
set.

The class: `new Money(amount, currency)` with `readonly amount: number` and
`readonly currency: Money.Currency`.

- `plus` is overloaded: `plus(other: Money): Money` and `plus(amount: number): Money`.
  Adding two different currencies throws, and the message contains `currency`.
- `toString()` is the symbol followed by the amount to two decimal places, so
  `new Money(3, "USD").toString()` is `"$3.00"`

The namespace, merged onto the class:

- `Money.Currency` - the type `"USD" | "EUR"`
- `Money.SYMBOLS` - `Record<Currency, string>`, mapping `USD` to `$` and `EUR`
  to `E`
- `Money.zero(currency)` - a `Money` with an amount of `0`

`Money.zero("GBP")` is a compile error.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex8
```

# Reading - typescript/d22_declaration_files

The debrief. Per problem: which declaration space was really in play, the
version that has the value but not the type (or the reverse), and one sentence
on the model answer.

## Notes

**Every name in TypeScript lives in up to three spaces: value, type and
namespace.** `const x` occupies the value space. `interface X` occupies the type
space. `class X` occupies both. `namespace X` occupies the namespace space and,
if it has runtime members, the value space too. Declaration merging is simply
the rule that two declarations of the same name in *different* spaces coexist -
and that some declarations in the *same* space combine rather than collide.

**Interfaces merge; type aliases do not.** Two `interface X` declarations become
one interface with the members of both (ex5, ex7); two `type X` declarations are
a duplicate-identifier error. That single asymmetry is why every extensible API
- a router's route table, a store's action map, a plugin registry - is published
as an interface.

**Namespaces merge onto almost anything.** Onto a function, so a callable can
have members (ex1). Onto an enum, so a level can carry its own helpers (ex6).
Onto a class, so one name can hold nested types and factories (ex8). The rule is
always the same: the function, enum or class comes first, the namespace second,
and the namespace's exports become properties of the value.

**Overload signatures are declarations without an implementation** (ex2, and the
`plus` method in ex8). Only the overloads are visible to callers; the
implementation signature is invisible and is allowed to be wider. They are the
tool for "the return type depends on the argument" in any situation where you
are describing code rather than writing it.

**`declare` says "this exists, I am not creating it".** `declare global` reopens
the global scope from inside a module (ex3) - the standard way to type a
polyfill, a bundler-injected constant or a test helper. Use `var` there, because
only `var` declarations become properties of `globalThis`.

**And the ordinary rules still apply to the values.** Nothing here removes the
need for the runtime object to exist: a merged namespace produces real
properties, an overload set produces one real function, and a `declare global`
block produces nothing at all - which is exactly why ex3 also has to write to
`globalThis` itself.

## ex1 - a function with members

What this was testing: function-and-namespace merging, which is how libraries
like `moment` or Node's own `require` are described - a thing you can call that
also has properties. Written by hand at runtime it needs `Object.assign` and a
cast; declared as a merge it needs neither.

The classic mistake is declaring the namespace *before* the function, which is
an error, or reaching for an interface with a call signature - which describes
the shape but does not create the value.

The model answer declares the function, then a namespace of the same name whose
exports become its members - one construct, and the runtime object and its type
are produced together.

## ex2 - two signatures, one function

What this was testing: overload signatures, which are the declaration-file way
of saying "the result depends on the argument" without a conditional type. They
are also the only shape available when the implementation is in JavaScript and
you are describing it from outside.

The classic mistake is thinking the implementation signature is callable. It is
not - `box(true)` is an error even though the implementation would happily
handle it - and that gap is deliberate: the implementation is allowed to be
wider than the contract.

The model answer lists the two signatures above one implementation whose
parameter is the union and whose return type is the union of the two shapes, and
narrows once with `typeof` inside.

## ex3 - add something to globalThis

What this was testing: global augmentation, the construct behind every
`declare global` block in a project's `types/` folder. The declaration creates
no value; it tells the compiler that something else will, which is exactly the
contract a `.d.ts` file offers.

The classic mistake is `const` instead of `var` inside `declare global`, which
declares a global binding that is *not* a property of `globalThis` - so
`globalThis.__d22BuildRegistry` still does not typecheck. The second is putting
the block in a file with no imports or exports, where it silently becomes a
script and takes its other declarations global with it.

The model answer declares the `var`, creates the object on first write, and
reads with optional chaining - so the `undefined` in the declared type is
handled rather than asserted away.

## ex4 - a namespace of types and values

What this was testing: that a namespace is a container for declarations in all
three declaration spaces - type, value and namespace - and that the dotted form
`Api.Row` works in type position. This is the shape almost every hand-written
`.d.ts` for a UMD library takes.

The classic mistake is exporting a type from a namespace and then trying to
`import { Row }` - the name is `Api.Row`, and `import type { Api }` followed by
`Api.Row` is how you reach it. The second is repeating the id type instead of
deriving it, which is the same duplication `keyof` and indexed access exist to
remove.

The model answer keeps `Row` as the source of truth, derives `Id` from it with
an indexed access, and puts the one runtime value alongside them - so the
namespace describes an API surface rather than merely grouping names.

## ex5 - one interface, two declarations

What this was testing: interface declaration merging, in its simplest form. Two
declarations, one type - and unlike an intersection, the result is a single
interface, so error messages and tooltips still name it.

The classic mistake is assuming a type alias behaves the same way; `type X` twice
is a duplicate-identifier error, which is exactly why `interface` is the right
choice for anything a consumer might want to extend. The second is expecting a
conflicting member to merge: two declarations of the same property with
different types is an error, not a union.

The model answer is two interface declarations and a template string, and the
interesting line is the one that is not there - nothing joins the declarations
together, because the compiler does it by name.

## ex6 - an enum with helpers

What this was testing: enum-and-namespace merging, and the double-entry nature
of a numeric enum's runtime object. Attaching helpers to an enum is one of the
few places a namespace is still clearly the best tool - the alternative is a
separate `LevelHelpers` object that call sites have to import alongside it.

The classic mistake is `parse` returning whatever the lookup produced. A
numeric enum has a reverse mapping, so `Level["20"]` is `"Error"`, and a parse
that accepts it will hand a string to code expecting a level. The gate checks
that case directly.

The model answer merges the namespace onto the enum, indexes the enum object
once, and accepts the result only when it is a number - which is also the check
that rejects unknown names, for free.

## ex7 - a registry other files can extend

What this was testing: the registry pattern - an interface that other
declarations extend, with `keyof` and indexed access turning the extensions into
a checked API. This is how a router types its routes, how a store types its
actions, and how libraries let consumers register their own names without the
library knowing them.

The classic mistake is the stub's index signature, which looks like a
generalisation and is actually an abdication: `keyof` becomes `string`, the
payload becomes `unknown`, and `dispatch` accepts anything.

The model answer declares the interface three times, derives the names with
`keyof`, and pairs each name with a handler - and the single cast in the body is
the well-known limit of correlated unions rather than a shortcut.

## ex8 - a class, a type and a namespace

What this was testing: everything in the set, on one identifier. A class is
already a value and a type; the namespace adds nested types and statics-by-merge;
the overloads give one method two contracts. This is the exact shape of the
hand-written declaration for a library whose main export is a class with a few
constants hanging off it.

The classic mistake is trying to put `Currency` inside the class body - a class
cannot contain a type alias, which is precisely the gap the merged namespace
fills. The second is declaring the namespace before the class, which compiles as
a namespace and then fails to merge.

The model answer keeps the class first, adds the namespace after it, and lets the
class body reference `Money.Currency` freely - and the runtime object ends up
with `SYMBOLS` and `zero` attached to the constructor, which is what a static
would have given you without the nested type.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Declaration Merging](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/declaration-merging.html) - the declaration spaces table, and every merge in this set.
- [Handbook: Namespaces](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/namespaces.html) - what they still do well, and when a module is the better container.
- [Handbook: Functions - overload signatures](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#function-overloads) - including why the implementation signature is not callable.
- [Handbook: Declaration files - deep dive](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/declaration-files/deep-dive.html) - `declare`, ambient contexts and global augmentation, written from the `.d.ts` side.
- [MDN: globalThis](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/globalThis) - and why `var` is the declaration form that lands on it (ex3).

reads with optional chaining - so the `undefined` in the declared type is
handled rather than asserted away.

## ex4 - a namespace of types and values

What this was testing: that a namespace is a container for declarations in all
three declaration spaces - type, value and namespace - and that the dotted form
`Api.Row` works in type position. This is the shape almost every hand-written
`.d.ts` for a UMD library takes.

The classic mistake is exporting a type from a namespace and then trying to
`import { Row }` - the name is `Api.Row`, and `import type { Api }` followed by
`Api.Row` is how you reach it. The second is repeating the id type instead of
deriving it, which is the same duplication `keyof` and indexed access exist to
remove.

The model answer keeps `Row` as the source of truth, derives `Id` from it with
an indexed access, and puts the one runtime value alongside them - so the
namespace describes an API surface rather than merely grouping names.

## ex5 - one interface, two declarations

What this was testing: interface declaration merging, in its simplest form. Two
declarations, one type - and unlike an intersection, the result is a single
interface, so error messages and tooltips still name it.

The classic mistake is assuming a type alias behaves the same way; `type X` twice
is a duplicate-identifier error, which is exactly why `interface` is the right
choice for anything a consumer might want to extend. The second is expecting a
conflicting member to merge: two declarations of the same property with
different types is an error, not a union.

The model answer is two interface declarations and a template string, and the
interesting line is the one that is not there - nothing joins the declarations
together, because the compiler does it by name.

## ex6 - an enum with helpers

What this was testing: enum-and-namespace merging, and the double-entry nature
of a numeric enum's runtime object. Attaching helpers to an enum is one of the
few places a namespace is still clearly the best tool - the alternative is a
separate `LevelHelpers` object that call sites have to import alongside it.

The classic mistake is `parse` returning whatever the lookup produced. A
numeric enum has a reverse mapping, so `Level["20"]` is `"Error"`, and a parse
that accepts it will hand a string to code expecting a level. The gate checks
that case directly.

The model answer merges the namespace onto the enum, indexes the enum object
once, and accepts the result only when it is a number - which is also the check
that rejects unknown names, for free.

## ex7 - a registry other files can extend

What this was testing: the registry pattern - an interface that other
declarations extend, with `keyof` and indexed access turning the extensions into
a checked API. This is how a router types its routes, how a store types its
actions, and how libraries let consumers register their own names without the
library knowing them.

The classic mistake is the stub's index signature, which looks like a
generalisation and is actually an abdication: `keyof` becomes `string`, the
payload becomes `unknown`, and `dispatch` accepts anything.

The model answer declares the interface three times, derives the names with
`keyof`, and pairs each name with a handler - and the single cast in the body is
the well-known limit of correlated unions rather than a shortcut.

## ex8 - a class, a type and a namespace

What this was testing: everything in the set, on one identifier. A class is
already a value and a type; the namespace adds nested types and statics-by-merge;
the overloads give one method two contracts. This is the exact shape of the
hand-written declaration for a library whose main export is a class with a few
constants hanging off it.

The classic mistake is trying to put `Currency` inside the class body - a class
cannot contain a type alias, which is precisely the gap the merged namespace
fills. The second is declaring the namespace before the class, which compiles as
a namespace and then fails to merge.

The model answer keeps the class first, adds the namespace after it, and lets the
class body reference `Money.Currency` freely - and the runtime object ends up
with `SYMBOLS` and `zero` attached to the constructor, which is what a static
would have given you without the nested type.

- [Handbook: Declaration Merging](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/declaration-merging.html) - the declaration spaces table, and every merge in this set.
- [Handbook: Namespaces](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/namespaces.html) - what they still do well, and when a module is the better container.
- [Handbook: Functions - overload signatures](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#function-overloads) - including why the implementation signature is not callable.

- [MDN: globalThis](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/globalThis) - and why `var` is the declaration form that lands on it (ex3).

exercises.prompt:
## ex1 - a function with members

`parseTag(raw)` splits `"dojo:ts"` into `{ scope: "dojo", name: "ts" }`. With no
colon, the whole string is the name and the scope is `""`.

The same name also carries two members:

- `parseTag.VERSION` - a `string` whose value is `"1.0"`
- `parseTag.isValid(raw)` - `true` when the string contains a colon

`Tag` is exported as an interface. Getting members onto a function without
writing `Object.assign` is the exercise.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `namespace` declared with the same name as a function *merges* with it: the
namespace's exports become properties of the function object, at runtime and in
the type.

## Hint 2

Order matters. The function declaration has to come first, or the compiler
cannot tell which of the two is the value being extended.

`export namespace parseTag { ... }` next to `export function parseTag(...)` is
the whole mechanism - no `Object.assign`, no interface describing the callable.

Left to you: whether `VERSION` should be annotated `string` or left to infer
`"1.0"`. The gate wants `string`; note which of the two an ordinary `const`
gives you.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A `namespace` declared with the same name as a function *merges* with it: the
namespace's exports become properties of the function object, at runtime and in
the type.

## Hint 2

Order matters. The function declaration has to come first, or the compiler
cannot tell which of the two is the value being extended.

`export namespace parseTag { ... }` next to `export function parseTag(...)` is
the whole mechanism - no `Object.assign`, no interface describing the callable.

Left to you: whether `VERSION` should be annotated `string` or left to infer
`"1.0"`. The gate wants `string`; note which of the two an ordinary `const`
gives you.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - two signatures, one function

`box(value)` has two **overload signatures**:

- `box(value: string)` returns `{ kind: "text"; value: string }`
- `box(value: number)` returns `{ kind: "count"; value: number }`

and `box(true)` is a compile error.

- `box("hello")` -> `{ kind: "text", value: "hello" }`
- `box(0)` -> `{ kind: "count", value: 0 }` - the branch is on the *type*, not
  on truthiness

The implementation signature is not callable from outside; it exists only to
be wide enough for both overloads.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex2
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex3 - add something to globalThis

Two exports plus one global.

`registerBuild(name, version)` records a build number on a global registry;
`readBuild(name)` reads it back and returns `number | undefined`.

The registry lives at `globalThis.__d22BuildRegistry`, typed
`Record<string, number> | undefined`, and it has to be **declared** so that
every module in the program can see the type - which is what a `.d.ts` file in
a real project would do for a polyfill, a test helper or a bundler-injected
constant.

- `readBuild("nothing")` -> `undefined` before anything is registered
- registering the same name twice overwrites

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex3
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex4 - a namespace of types and values

`Api` is a namespace holding all three kinds of declaration at once:

- `Api.Row` - an interface, `{ id: string; amount: number }`
- `Api.Id` - a type alias equal to `Row["id"]`, so `string`
- `Api.VERSION` - a value, the `number` `2`

`makeRow(id, amount)` takes an `Api.Id` and a `number` and returns an `Api.Row`.

Namespaced types are written `Api.Row`, with a dot, in type position.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A namespace can export interfaces, type aliases and values side by side. Only
the values survive to runtime; the types are erased, which is why a namespace of
pure types costs nothing.

## Hint 2

`Api.Id` should be derived rather than repeated: an indexed access into `Row`
means the two cannot drift when the row's id type changes.

Left to you: whether a namespace is the right container at all. Plain module
exports do the same job in modern code; namespaces earn their place in
declaration files, where there is no module to export from.

exercises.prompt:
## ex6 - an enum with helpers

`Level` is a numeric enum - `Debug = 10`, `Info = 20`, `Error = 40` - merged
with a namespace of the same name that adds two functions:

- `Level.isAtLeast(value, minimum)` - inclusive, so `isAtLeast(Info, Info)` is
  `true`
- `Level.parse(name)` - `Level | undefined`; `parse("Error")` is `40`,
  `parse("Fatal")` is `undefined`, and `parse("20")` is `undefined` too

That last case is the trap: a numeric enum object has entries in both
directions, so `Level["20"]` is the string `"Error"`, and a string is not a
level.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex6
```

A namespace merges with an enum of the same name, exactly as it merges with a
function - and, as with a function, the enum has to be declared first.

## Hint 2

For `parse`, look the name up on the enum object itself. The object is indexed
by both the member names and their numeric values, so the result may be a
number, a string, or `undefined` - and only the number is a level.

Left to you: whether to index the enum object or to hand-write a lookup table.

not need a cast.

exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - a registry other files can extend

`CommandRegistry` is an interface declared **empty** and then extended by two
further declarations - one adding `build: { target: string }`, one adding
`test: { pattern: string }`. That is the plugin-registry pattern: the base
declares the extension point, and each feature adds its own entry.

From it:

- `CommandName` is `keyof CommandRegistry`, so `"build" | "test"`
- `dispatch(name, payload)` is generic over `K extends CommandName` and takes
  `CommandRegistry[K]` as its payload, so `dispatch("build", { pattern: "x" })`
  is a compile error

`dispatch("build", { target: "web" })` -> `"build:web"`, and
`dispatch("test", { pattern: "*.ts" })` -> `"test:*.ts"`.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

An index signature is the opposite of a registry: it says "any key, and I know
nothing about the value". Replace it with real members contributed by separate
declarations of the same interface.

## Hint 2

Once the registry has literal keys, `keyof` gives you the command names and
`CommandRegistry[K]` gives you the matching payload - so the generic parameter
does all the checking with no runtime code involved.

## Hint 3

The body needs one assertion. Indexing a handler table by `K` gives the union of
every handler type, and the compiler cannot see that the handler you got matches
the payload you were given - a correlated-union limitation, not a mistake on
your part.

Left to you: a handler table or a `switch`. The table keeps the registry and the
implementations next to each other; the switch narrows `name` but not `payload`,
which is worth trying so you can see why.

## Hint 1

An index signature is the opposite of a registry: it says "any key, and I know
nothing about the value". Replace it with real members contributed by separate
declarations of the same interface.

## Hint 2

Once the registry has literal keys, `keyof` gives you the command names and
`CommandRegistry[K]` gives you the matching payload - so the generic parameter
does all the checking with no runtime code involved.

## Hint 3

The body needs one assertion. Indexing a handler table by `K` gives the union of
every handler type, and the compiler cannot see that the handler you got matches
the payload you were given - a correlated-union limitation, not a mistake on
your part.

Left to you: a handler table or a `switch`. The table keeps the registry and the
implementations next to each other; the switch narrows `name` but not `payload`,
which is worth trying so you can see why.

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - a class, a type and a namespace

`Money` is one name in three declaration spaces at once - the capstone of this
set.

The class: `new Money(amount, currency)` with `readonly amount: number` and
`readonly currency: Money.Currency`.

- `plus` is overloaded: `plus(other: Money): Money` and `plus(amount: number): Money`.
  Adding two different currencies throws, and the message contains `currency`.
- `toString()` is the symbol followed by the amount to two decimal places, so
  `new Money(3, "USD").toString()` is `"$3.00"`

The namespace, merged onto the class:

- `Money.Currency` - the type `"USD" | "EUR"`
- `Money.SYMBOLS` - `Record<Currency, string>`, mapping `USD` to `$` and `EUR`
  to `E`
- `Money.zero(currency)` - a `Money` with an amount of `0`

`Money.zero("GBP")` is a compile error.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d22_declaration_files ex8
```

lessons.briefing:
# d23 - Real-world API shapes (drill set)

Eight problems from the boundary layer: result types, an HTTP wrapper that
tells a bad status from a bad payload, query strings, DTO mapping, a cache with
a clock, a signature whose arity depends on the method, a route matcher and a
small typed client. They draw on the whole track - narrowing, generics, mapped
and template literal types, `satisfies` and async - because that is what this
layer actually needs.

Both gates run, and every exercise is self-contained: each file defines the
types it needs, even where a neighbour defines something similar. Nothing here
touches the network - every collaborator (the fetcher, the clock, the sender) is
injected, which is the only way this code is testable at all.

## ex1 - a result you have to look inside

`Result<T, E>` is the discriminated union
`{ ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }`, and three functions go with
it:

- `ok(value)` -> `Result<T, never>`
- `err(error)` -> `Result<never, E>`
- `unwrapOr(result, fallback)` -> the value if `ok`, the fallback otherwise

- `unwrapOr(ok(0), 99)` -> `0`, and `unwrapOr(ok(undefined), 5)` -> `undefined`

Those last two are the point: the decision is made by the discriminant, never by
the truthiness of the value.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex1
```

## ex2 - bad status against bad payload

`getJson(fetcher, url, guard)` calls `fetcher(url)`, which resolves with
`{ status: number; body: unknown }`, and resolves with

```ts
{ ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; reason: "http" | "shape"; status: number }
```

- a status in the 2xx range **and** a body the guard accepts -> `{ ok: true, data }`
- a status outside 2xx -> `{ ok: false, reason: "http", status }`
- a 2xx whose body fails the guard -> `{ ok: false, reason: "shape", status }`

201 is a success: the check is a range, not an equality. `T` comes from the
guard, so the caller never writes it.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex2
```

## ex3 - build the query string

`buildQuery(params)` turns
`Record<string, string | number | boolean | undefined>` into a query string.

- keys are sorted alphabetically, joined with `&`, and there is **no** leading
  `?`
- an `undefined` value drops the key entirely
- keys and values are both percent-encoded
- `false` and `0` are values, not absences

Examples:

- `buildQuery({ b: 1, a: "x y", d: true })` -> `"a=x%20y&b=1&d=true"`
- `buildQuery({ a: 1, c: undefined })` -> `"a=1"`
- `buildQuery({})` -> `""`
- `buildQuery({ "a b": "c&d" })` -> `"a%20b=c%26d"`

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex3
```

## ex4 - dto in, domain model out

Three exports.

`UserDto` is the wire shape: `{ user_id: string; display_name: string; created_at: string }`.

`CamelKeys<T>` is a mapped type that renames every `snake_case` key to
`camelCase`, leaving the value types alone:

- `CamelKeys<UserDto>` -> `{ userId: string; displayName: string; createdAt: string }`
- `CamelKeys<{ a_b_c: number }>` -> `{ aBC: number }`

`User` is the domain shape - the camel-cased keys, except that `createdAt` is a
`Date`. `toUser(dto)` builds one.

- `toUser({ user_id: "u1", display_name: "Ada", created_at: "2024-03-01T10:00:00.000Z" })`
  -> a `User` whose `createdAt` is a real `Date`

`User` and `CamelKeys` are given in the stub; the renaming type and the mapper
are yours.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex4
```

## ex5 - a cache that can tell the time

`createTtlCache<T>(ttlMs, now)` returns
`{ set(key, value): void; get(key): T | undefined; size(): number }`.

`now` is an injected clock returning milliseconds - there is no `Date.now()`
anywhere in the implementation.

- an entry is live while `now() - writtenAt < ttlMs`
- at exactly `ttlMs` it has expired: the comparison is inclusive
- reading an expired entry returns `undefined` **and drops it**, so `size()`
  falls
- the age is measured from the write, and a rewrite restarts it

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex5
```

## ex6 - the method decides the arity

`describeRequest(method, url, ...rest)` is generic over
`M extends "GET" | "POST"`, and its **rest parameter type is a conditional**:
no body for a `GET`, exactly one for a `POST`.

- `describeRequest("GET", "/users")` -> `"GET /users"`
- `describeRequest("POST", "/users", "{}")` -> `"POST /users {}"`
- `describeRequest("GET", "/users", "{}")` is a compile error
- `describeRequest("POST", "/users")` is a compile error

An empty body string is still a body: `describeRequest("POST", "/x", "")` is
`"POST /x "`.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex6
```

## ex7 - a route that types its own params

`defineRoute(path, handler)` returns `{ path; run(url) }`.

The handler's parameter type is derived from the path: every `:name` segment
becomes a `string` member.

- `defineRoute("/users/:userId/posts/:postId", handler)` gives the handler
  `{ userId: string; postId: string }`
- `defineRoute("/health", handler)` gives it an object with no members
- `route.path` keeps the literal path type it was built with

`run(url)` returns the handler's result, or `undefined` when the url does not
match:

- `"/users/7/posts/9"` -> the handler runs with `{ userId: "7", postId: "9" }`
- `"/users/7/posts"` -> `undefined` (wrong number of segments)
- `"/teams/7/posts/9"` -> `undefined` (a literal segment must match exactly)

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex7
```

## ex8 - a client built from an endpoint table

`ENDPOINTS` is the single source of truth:

```
getUser:     { method: "GET",  path: "/users/:id" }
createOrder: { method: "POST", path: "/orders" }
getPost:     { method: "GET",  path: "/users/:userId/posts/:postId" }
```

frozen and checked against `Record<string, { method: "GET" | "POST"; path: string }>`.

`createClient(send)` returns `{ call(name, params) }`:

- `name` is constrained to the endpoint names, so `call("deleteUser", {})` is a
  compile error
- `params` is derived from that endpoint's path, so `call("getUser", {})` is a
  compile error and `call("createOrder", {})` is fine
- `call` substitutes the params into the path and calls
  `send(method, url)`, resolving with whatever `send` resolved with

`call("getPost", { userId: "u1", postId: "p9" })` sends
`("GET", "/users/u1/posts/p9")`.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex8
```
