# Reading - typescript/d23_realworld_apis

The debrief. Per problem: what the boundary was really being asked to guarantee,
the shortcut that works until a particular value arrives, and one sentence on
the model answer.

## Notes

**This set is about the layer where the types stop being true.** Everything
inside your program is checked; everything arriving from outside it - a
response body, a query string, a url, a clock - is a promise somebody else made.
The job of a boundary function is to turn that promise into something the
compiler can rely on, and to be honest about what happens when it cannot.

**Model failure as data, not as an exception, when the caller has a decision to
make.** `Result` (ex1) and the tagged failure in `getJson` (ex2) exist because
"the server said 404" and "the server sent nonsense" want different handling,
and an exception flattens them into one. The discriminant is what makes the
handling checkable.

**Derive types from the one place the fact is written.** The endpoint table
(ex8), the route path (ex7) and the DTO shape (ex4) are each a single source of
truth with types read out of them - by `keyof typeof`, by a template-literal
recursion, by a key remap. The alternative is writing the same fact twice and
finding out later that only one copy was updated.

**Inject every collaborator.** The fetcher, the clock and the sender are all
parameters here, which is why the whole set runs in milliseconds with no
network, no timers and no mocking framework. It is also better design
independently of testing: a cache that takes a clock can be driven by a test, by
a simulation, or by a monotonic timer, and none of that is the cache's business.

**And read the edge cases as requirements, not as trivia.** `0` and `""` and
`false` are values (ex1, ex3). `201` is a success (ex2). Exactly at the ttl the
entry has gone (ex5). An empty body is a body (ex6). A path's last parameter has
no trailing slash (ex7). Each of these is one character in the implementation
and one incident in production.

## ex1 - a result you have to look inside

What this was testing: the discriminated union as an error-handling shape, and
`never` as the "this branch is impossible" type in a constructor's signature.
The narrowing is the whole ergonomics of the pattern - `if (result.ok)` gives
you `value` and nothing else, and the `else` gives you `error` and nothing else.

The classic mistake is `result.value ?? fallback`, which is correct until the
value is legitimately `undefined`, and `result.value || fallback`, which is
wrong for `0`, `""` and `false` as well. Both compile only if `value` is read
without narrowing, which is a second smell.

The model answer returns object literals from `ok` and `err` with `never` on the
unused side, and `unwrapOr` is a single ternary on the discriminant.

## ex2 - bad status against bad payload

What this was testing: an async boundary function whose success type comes from
an injected guard, and the discipline of distinguishing failures that mean
different things. "The server said no" and "the server said yes and sent
something unexpected" have different fixes and different owners.

The classic mistake is `if (response.status === 200)`, which rejects every 201,
204 and 202 the API is entitled to send. The second is trusting the body because
the status was fine, which is how `undefined is not a function` ends up three
layers away from the request that caused it.

The model answer checks the range, then the guard, then returns the narrowed
body - and the fact that `data` is typed `T` at the call site with no cast is
entirely the guard's doing.

## ex3 - build the query string

What this was testing: a small pure function with a long tail of edge cases,
which is what most boundary code turns out to be. Nothing here is difficult; all
of it is easy to get subtly wrong, and each mistake is invisible until a
particular value shows up.

The classic mistake is `if (!params[key]) continue`, which silently drops
`flag=false` and `n=0`. The second is `encodeURIComponent` applied to the whole
string at the end, which escapes the `&` and `=` that were supposed to be
structural.

The model answer sorts, filters on `undefined`, encodes each half separately and
joins - four steps in a chain, each of which is one of the requirements written
out.

## ex4 - dto in, domain model out

What this was testing: the anti-corruption layer - a wire shape, a domain shape,
and an explicit function between them - plus the mapped type that describes the
mechanical half of the difference. The type-level renaming is satisfying; the
lesson is that it stops exactly where the semantics begin.

The classic mistake is shipping the DTO into the application and letting
`user.created_at` spread through the codebase as a string, at which point every
consumer parses it (or forgets to). The second is trying to make `CamelKeys`
convert the date too, which no key-remapping type can do.

The model answer renames with a key remap over a recursive template literal, and
converts with three plain assignments - and `new Date(...)` sits in exactly one
place.

## ex5 - a cache that can tell the time

What this was testing: injecting the clock. Every property this cache has is
time-dependent, and with `Date.now()` inside there is no way to test any of them
without sleeping - so the parameter is not ceremony, it is the difference
between a testable component and a flaky one.

The classic mistake is `>` rather than `>=` on the age comparison, which leaves
the entry alive for one extra millisecond at exactly the boundary; the gate sets
the clock to precisely `ttlMs` after the write to catch it. The second is
returning `undefined` without deleting, so a cache of expired entries grows
forever.

The model answer keeps the write time per entry, deletes on the expired read,
and reports `entries.size` - and `now` is called, never captured, so a clock
that moves is seen.

## ex6 - the method decides the arity

What this was testing: a conditional type in a rest-parameter position, which is
how a single function can have argument lists that depend on an earlier
argument. It is the lighter-weight cousin of overloads, and it composes with
generics in a way overloads do not.

The classic mistake is an optional parameter, which accepts both wrong calls and
pushes the check to runtime - the stub is that version. The second is checking
`if (body)` inside, which treats an empty body as absent.

The model answer puts the conditional on the rest tuple and asserts once when
destructuring it, because the implementation genuinely cannot know which branch
the caller resolved to.

## ex7 - a route that types its own params

What this was testing: template literal types earning their keep. The whole
value of this function is that `params.userId` is checked and `params.slug` is
an error, and that both facts come from the string the caller typed - no schema,
no duplication, no code generation.

The classic mistake is a single recursive pattern requiring a trailing slash,
which drops the last parameter of every path; `"/users/:id"` then hands the
handler an empty object. The second is annotating `path: string`, which throws
away the literal and makes the whole derivation produce `never`.

The model answer collects names with two patterns, maps them once into an
object of strings, and matches segment by segment at runtime - with exactly one
cast, at the boundary where a loop-built object meets a derived type.

## ex8 - a client built from an endpoint table

What this was testing: the set as a whole, and most of the track with it. A
frozen table checked with `satisfies` (d20), `keyof typeof` to name the
endpoints (d11), a template-literal recursion to read each path's parameters
(d17), a mapped type to turn them into an object (d14), and a generic that ties
the two arguments together so that a wrong pair does not compile.

The classic mistake is the annotation on `ENDPOINTS`. It looks like
documentation and it is a demolition: `EndpointName` becomes `string`, every
path becomes `string`, `PathParams` produces an index signature, and the client
accepts any name with any params - which is precisely the client you were trying
not to write.

The model answer keeps one source of truth and derives everything from it, so
adding a fourth endpoint is one line and the type errors appear at exactly the
call sites that need updating.

## Further reading

- [MDN: encodeURIComponent](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/encodeURIComponent) - what it escapes and why it goes around each key and value separately (ex3).
- [MDN: HTTP response status codes](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status) - the 2xx range ex2 has to accept in full.
- [Handbook: Template Literal Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/template-literal-types.html) - the path-parameter extraction in ex7 and ex8.
- [Handbook: Mapped Types - key remapping](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/mapped-types.html#key-remapping-via-as) - the `as` clause that renames the DTO keys in ex4.
- [Handbook: Narrowing - discriminated unions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#discriminated-unions) - the shape behind `Result` in ex1 and the tagged failures in ex2.

exercises.prompt:
## ex1 - a result you have to look inside

`Result<T, E>` is the discriminated union
`{ ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }`, and three functions go with
it:

- `ok(value)` -> `Result<T, never>`
- `err(error)` -> `Result<never, E>`
- `unwrapOr(result, fallback)` -> the value if `ok`, the fallback otherwise

- `unwrapOr(ok(0), 99)` -> `0`, and `unwrapOr(ok(undefined), 5)` -> `undefined`

Those last two are the point: the decision is made by the discriminant, never by
the truthiness of the value.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex1
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - bad status against bad payload

`getJson(fetcher, url, guard)` calls `fetcher(url)`, which resolves with
`{ status: number; body: unknown }`, and resolves with

```ts
{ ok: true; data: T } | { ok: false; reason: "http" | "shape"; status: number }
```

- a status in the 2xx range **and** a body the guard accepts -> `{ ok: true, data }`
- a status outside 2xx -> `{ ok: false, reason: "http", status }`
- a 2xx whose body fails the guard -> `{ ok: false, reason: "shape", status }`

201 is a success: the check is a range, not an equality. `T` comes from the
guard, so the caller never writes it.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex2
```

## Hint 1

The guard is what makes `T` appear: `(value: unknown) => value is T` is the only
place `T` occurs in the parameters, so the caller supplying `isUser` decides the
success type.

## Hint 2

Two checks in order: the status range first, then the guard. Reversing them
would report a 404 with an empty body as a shape problem, which sends whoever
reads the log to the wrong place.

Left to you: whether to include the body in the shape failure. The prompt does
not; think about what you would want in the log at three in the morning.

exercises.prompt:
## ex3 - build the query string

`buildQuery(params)` turns
`Record<string, string | number | boolean | undefined>` into a query string.

- keys are sorted alphabetically, joined with `&`, and there is **no** leading
  `?`
- an `undefined` value drops the key entirely
- keys and values are both percent-encoded
- `false` and `0` are values, not absences

Examples:

- `buildQuery({ b: 1, a: "x y", d: true })` -> `"a=x%20y&b=1&d=true"`
- `buildQuery({ a: 1, c: undefined })` -> `"a=1"`
- `buildQuery({})` -> `""`
- `buildQuery({ "a b": "c&d" })` -> `"a%20b=c%26d"`

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Sorting makes the output stable, which is what lets a cache key or a test
compare two query strings for equality. `Object.keys` has no guaranteed order
for you to rely on instead.

## Hint 2

Skip on `=== undefined`, not on falsiness: `0`, `""` and `false` all have to
survive, and the gate checks two of the three.

`encodeURIComponent` is the right encoder for a single component; it escapes
`&` and `=`, which is exactly why it goes around each key and each value
separately rather than around the joined result.

Left to you: what an array value should do. The prompt does not allow one -
decide what you would want (`a=1&a=2`, or `a=1,2`) before someone widens the
parameter type for you.

exercises.prompt:
## ex5 - a cache that can tell the time

`createTtlCache<T>(ttlMs, now)` returns
`{ set(key, value): void; get(key): T | undefined; size(): number }`.

`now` is an injected clock returning milliseconds - there is no `Date.now()`
anywhere in the implementation.

- an entry is live while `now() - writtenAt < ttlMs`
- at exactly `ttlMs` it has expired: the comparison is inclusive
- reading an expired entry returns `undefined` **and drops it**, so `size()`
  falls
- the age is measured from the write, and a rewrite restarts it

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Store the write time next to the value. A `Map<string, { value: T; writtenAt:
number }>` is the whole data structure, and `now()` is called once per operation.

## Hint 2

Expiring on read - delete the entry, then return `undefined` - is what makes
`size()` fall without a background timer. A cache that only checks on read is
called lazy expiry, and it is what almost every in-process cache does.

Left to you: whether `get` should also expire *other* keys while it is there.
Doing so bounds the memory; doing it on every read costs a scan. Neither is
wrong, and the gate does not care.

## Hint 1

Store the write time next to the value. A `Map<string, { value: T; writtenAt:
number }>` is the whole data structure, and `now()` is called once per operation.

## Hint 2

Expiring on read - delete the entry, then return `undefined` - is what makes
`size()` fall without a background timer. A cache that only checks on read is
called lazy expiry, and it is what almost every in-process cache does.

Left to you: whether `get` should also expire *other* keys while it is there.
Doing so bounds the memory; doing it on every read costs a scan. Neither is
wrong, and the gate does not care.

## ex6 - the method decides the arity

`describeRequest(method, url, ...rest)` is generic over
`M extends "GET" | "POST"`, and its **rest parameter type is a conditional**:
no body for a `GET`, exactly one for a `POST`.

- `describeRequest("GET", "/users")` -> `"GET /users"`
- `describeRequest("POST", "/users", "{}")` -> `"POST /users {}"`
- `describeRequest("GET", "/users", "{}")` is a compile error
- `describeRequest("POST", "/users")` is a compile error

An empty body string is still a body: `describeRequest("POST", "/x", "")` is
`"POST /x "`.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A rest parameter's type is a tuple, and a tuple can be produced by a conditional
type. `...rest: M extends "GET" ? [] : [body: string]` is a legal parameter
list, and the empty tuple means "no more arguments".

## Hint 2

`M` is inferred from the first argument, so the conditional is resolved before
the rest parameter is checked - which is why passing `"GET"` makes the third
argument an error rather than a mismatch.

## Hint 3

Inside the body, `rest` is still the unresolved conditional as far as the
compiler is concerned, so destructuring it needs one assertion. That is a known
limit: the implementation cannot see the branch the caller took.

Left to you: whether to distinguish a missing body from an empty one. The gate
requires `""` to be treated as present, so `body === undefined` is the check,
not `body`.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - a route that types its own params

`defineRoute(path, handler)` returns `{ path; run(url) }`.

The handler's parameter type is derived from the path: every `:name` segment
becomes a `string` member.

- `defineRoute("/users/:userId/posts/:postId", handler)` gives the handler
  `{ userId: string; postId: string }`
- `defineRoute("/health", handler)` gives it an object with no members
- `route.path` keeps the literal path type it was built with

`run(url)` returns the handler's result, or `undefined` when the url does not
match:

- `"/users/7/posts/9"` -> the handler runs with `{ userId: "7", postId: "9" }`
- `"/users/7/posts"` -> `undefined` (wrong number of segments)
- `"/teams/7/posts/9"` -> `undefined` (a literal segment must match exactly)

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex7
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - a client built from an endpoint table

`ENDPOINTS` is the single source of truth:

```
getUser:     { method: "GET",  path: "/users/:id" }
createOrder: { method: "POST", path: "/orders" }
getPost:     { method: "GET",  path: "/users/:userId/posts/:postId" }
```

frozen and checked against `Record<string, { method: "GET" | "POST"; path: string }>`.

`createClient(send)` returns `{ call(name, params) }`:

- `name` is constrained to the endpoint names, so `call("deleteUser", {})` is a
  compile error
- `params` is derived from that endpoint's path, so `call("getUser", {})` is a
  compile error and `call("createOrder", {})` is fine
- `call` substitutes the params into the path and calls
  `send(method, url)`, resolving with whatever `send` resolved with

`call("getPost", { userId: "u1", postId: "p9" })` sends
`("GET", "/users/u1/posts/p9")`.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d23_realworld_apis ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The table has to be frozen *and* checked - `as const satisfies ...` - or the
paths widen to `string` and every derived type collapses. That is d20 ex4 and
ex8, applied to an endpoint list.

## Hint 2

`(typeof ENDPOINTS)[K]["path"]` is the literal path for the endpoint `K`.
Feeding that into the same `PathParams` machinery as ex7 gives the params
object, and the generic `K` is what connects the two arguments to each other.

## Hint 3

Building the url is a `split`, a `map` and a `join`: a segment starting with `:`
is replaced by its value, everything else is kept. One cast to
`Record<string, string>` is needed to index the params object by a name the
compiler cannot see.

Left to you: whether the values should be `encodeURIComponent`d. They should -
and the gate does not check it, which is a reasonable illustration of what a
gate is and is not.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

The table has to be frozen *and* checked - `as const satisfies ...` - or the
paths widen to `string` and every derived type collapses. That is d20 ex4 and
ex8, applied to an endpoint list.

## Hint 2

`(typeof ENDPOINTS)[K]["path"]` is the literal path for the endpoint `K`.
Feeding that into the same `PathParams` machinery as ex7 gives the params
object, and the generic `K` is what connects the two arguments to each other.

## Hint 3

Building the url is a `split`, a `map` and a `join`: a segment starting with `:`
is replaced by its value, everything else is kept. One cast to
`Record<string, string>` is needed to index the params object by a name the
compiler cannot see.

Left to you: whether the values should be `encodeURIComponent`d. They should -
and the gate does not check it, which is a reasonable illustration of what a
gate is and is not.

lessons.briefing:
# d24 - Mixed gauntlet (drill set)

The last set, and the cumulative one: every exercise combines two or three
topics from across the track, and none of them tells you which. Guards with
generics, a frozen table with indexed access, mapped types with conditionals,
template literals with `infer`, `unknown` with a discriminated union, async with
generics, exhaustiveness with immutability - and a recursive variadic pipeline to
finish.

Both gates run. If a problem here feels like guessing, the topic it is testing is
named in `reading.md` for that exercise, and the drill set that covers it is
named there too - go back to it rather than pushing through.

## ex1 - guards plus generics

`firstMatching(values, guard)` returns the first element the guard accepts, or
`undefined`, and its return type is the **narrowed** type - `S | undefined`,
not `T | undefined`.

- `firstMatching([1, 2, "target", 3, "other"], isString)` -> `"target"`
- no match, or an empty list -> `undefined`
- it stops at the first match: for the list above the guard runs three times

Two type parameters, `T` and `S extends T`, and the guard is
`(value: T) => value is S`.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex1
```

## ex2 - a frozen table, read three ways

`RANKS` is `{ bronze: 1, silver: 2, gold: 3 }`, frozen and checked against
`Record<string, number>`. Three things come out of it:

- `RankName` -> `"bronze" | "silver" | "gold"`
- `RankValue` -> `1 | 2 | 3`
- `isHigher(a, b)` -> whether `a` outranks `b`, strictly: `isHigher("gold", "gold")`
  is `false`
- `namesAbove(name)` -> every rank above it, **ascending by value**

`namesAbove("bronze")` is `["silver", "gold"]`, and `namesAbove("gold")` is
`[]`. `isHigher("platinum", "gold")` is a compile error.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex2
```

## ex3 - a mapped type with a condition in it

`Stringified<T>` rewrites every member whose type is `number` to `string`, and
leaves everything else alone:

- `Stringified<{ a: number; b: boolean }>` -> `{ a: string; b: boolean }`
- `Stringified<{ nested: { a: number } }>` -> unchanged; only the top level is
  rewritten

`stringifyNumbers(value)` does the same at runtime and returns
`Stringified<T>`.

- `stringifyNumbers({ a: 1, b: "x", c: true })` -> `{ a: "1", b: "x", c: true }`
- `stringifyNumbers({ n: 0 })` -> `{ n: "0" }` - zero is a number like any other

The type is already applied to the function's return; making it do something is
the exercise.

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex3
```

## ex4 - split a literal, at both levels

`EventOf<S>` splits an event name at its **first** colon:

- `EventOf<"user:created">` -> `{ scope: "user"; name: "created" }`
- `EventOf<"a:b:c">` -> `{ scope: "a"; name: "b:c" }`
- `EventOf<"plain">` -> `never`

`splitEvent(event)` does the same at runtime and returns `EventOf<S>`, so
`splitEvent("order:paid")` is typed `{ scope: "order"; name: "paid" }`. A string
with no colon throws, and the message contains the word `colon`.

The argument has to be a string *literal* for any of this to be worth anything -
`EventOf<string>` is `never`, because `string` does not match the pattern.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex4
```

## ex5 - unknown in, a union out

`Command` is the union

```ts
{ type: "add"; item: string } | { type: "remove"; id: number } | { type: "clear" }
```

`parseCommand(input: unknown)` returns a `Command` when the input is one, and
`null` otherwise.

- `{ type: "add", item: "milk" }` -> the add command
- `{ type: "add" }` -> `null`, `{ type: "remove", id: "3" }` -> `null`
- `{ type: "reset" }` -> `null`
- `null`, `[]` and `"clear"` -> `null`

The returned object is rebuilt, not passed through, so nothing extra rides along
with it.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex5
```

## ex6 - async plus generics

`firstSuccess(tasks)` calls the task factories **in order** and resolves with
the first one that succeeds.

- `[fail, win, win]` -> the second task's value, and the third is never called
- when every task rejects, the **last** rejection is what comes out
- an empty list rejects with an error whose message contains `no tasks`

The return type is `Promise<T>`, where `T` comes from the tasks.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex6
```

## ex7 - an exhaustive, immutable reducer

`CartState` is `{ readonly lines: readonly { readonly sku: string; readonly qty: number }[] }`,
and `CartEvent` is

```ts
{ type: "added"; sku: string; qty: number }
  | { type: "removed"; sku: string }
  | { type: "quantity"; sku: string; qty: number }
  | { type: "cleared" }
```

`reduceCart(state, event)` returns a **new** state:

- `added` with a new sku appends `{ sku, qty }`; with an existing sku it adds to
  that line's quantity, **in place** in the list
- `removed` drops the line with that sku; an absent sku is a no-op
- `quantity` sets the quantity; a quantity of `0` or less **removes** the line;
  an unknown sku is a no-op
- `cleared` empties the list

The input state is never modified. `assertNever(value: never): never` throws
with the value in its message, and the `default` branch of the switch calls it.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex7
```

## ex8 - the pipeline, typed all the way through

The finale.

`PipeResult<T, Fns>` walks a tuple of step functions and reports the type the
last one produces, awaiting each result along the way:

- `PipeResult<number, [(value: number) => string]>` -> `string`
- `PipeResult<number, [(value: number) => string, (value: string) => boolean]>` -> `boolean`
- `PipeResult<number, [(value: number) => Promise<string>]>` -> `string`

`pipeAsync(input, ...steps)` runs the steps in order, awaiting each one, and
resolves with `PipeResult<T, Fns>`:

- `pipeAsync(2, (n: number) => n + 1, async (n: number) => String(n), (s: string) => s + "!")`
  resolves with `"3!"`, and the three steps run in order
- `pipeAsync("untouched")` resolves with `"untouched"` - no steps, no change
- a step that throws rejects the pipeline

The steps are a rest parameter constrained to `readonly ((arg: never) => unknown)[]`,
which accepts a function of any parameter type.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex8
```

# Reading - typescript/d24_mixed_gauntlet

The debrief. Each section names the topics the problem was mixing, then the
usual three: what it was really testing, the version that looks right, and one
sentence on the model answer.

## Notes

**This set has no theme, which is the theme.** Everything up to here announced
its topic in the title, so you arrived at each problem knowing which tool to
reach for. Real code does not do that, and neither does an interview - the first
and hardest step is recognising which of the things you know applies.

**The recurring pair is "a type derived from data" and "a runtime that agrees
with it".** A frozen rank table and two functions that read it (ex2). A mapped
type with a conditional and a loop that asks the same question (ex3). A
template-literal split and an `indexOf` that cuts at the same place (ex4). A
recursive fold over a tuple and a `for` loop over an array (ex8). In every case
the type and the code are two statements of one fact, and the bug is always that
they drifted.

**The recurring discipline is claiming exactly what you proved.** `S | undefined`
rather than `T | undefined` (ex1). `Command | null` rather than `unknown`
(ex5). `never` for a literal that does not contain a colon (ex4). A `readonly`
state and an `assertNever` default (ex7). None of these change what the code
does; all of them change what the next person can rely on.

**And the recurring shape at the boundary is: check the container, then the
discriminant, then the payload, then rebuild.** ex5 is that pattern written out,
and ex2, ex3 and ex7 are it in miniature. Skipping a step is what turns a type
error into a production incident three modules away.

**Where to go from here.** The drill sets are done; the interview lessons
(`i1`-`i3`) are the timed version of the same material, and the numbered lessons
00-11 are the reference. If any exercise in this set needed more than one hint,
the topic line at the top of its section names the drill to redo - and redoing
one set is a better use of an hour than reading three chapters.

## ex1 - guards plus generics

Topics: type guards (d18) and generic constraints (d10).

What this was testing: that a guard's narrowing can travel out of a function
through its return type. The body is four lines; the exercise is the `S` in
`S | undefined`, which is what turns "I looked for a string" into "I have a
string".

The classic mistake is returning `T | undefined`, which compiles, runs
correctly, and makes every call site narrow again - usually with a cast. The
second is `values.filter(guard)[0]`, which examines every element and allocates
an array to throw away.

The model answer loops and returns on the first acceptance, with `S extends T`
on the signature so the compiler agrees that the narrower type is a legal thing
to promise.

## ex2 - a frozen table, read three ways

Topics: `as const` and `satisfies` (d20), `keyof` and indexed access (d11).

What this was testing: one frozen table producing a name union, a value union,
and two functions that compare through it. The point is that all four artefacts
have a single source of truth, so adding `platinum: 4` is one line and every
type follows.

The classic mistake is the annotation on `RANKS`, and its damage is total here:
`RankName` becomes `string`, `RankValue` becomes `number`, and both functions
accept anything. The second is sorting by name rather than by value, which is
right for this table by accident and wrong for the next one.

The model answer freezes and checks the table, then reads it three times -
twice at the type level and twice at runtime - with exactly one assertion, at
`Object.keys`, where the standard library is deliberately conservative.

## ex3 - a mapped type with a condition in it

Topics: mapped types (d14) and conditional types (d15).

What this was testing: a conditional in a mapped type's value position - the
combination that expresses "change these members, leave those alone" without
listing either group. It is also the first place people meet the rule that a
mapped type is shallow: `nested` keeps its `number` because the map does not
recurse.

The classic mistake is a runtime that converts more than the type says, usually
by testing `!isNaN(Number(entry))` and turning numeric strings into strings
again. The type and the implementation have to ask the same question.

The model answer puts one conditional in the mapped type, one `typeof` in the
loop, and a single assertion where the loop-built object meets the derived type -
which is the only place the compiler cannot follow.

## ex4 - split a literal, at both levels

Topics: template literal types (d17), `infer` (d16).

What this was testing: a type and a function that split the same string the same
way, and the fact that the type-level split is non-greedy for the same reason
`indexOf` is - both stop at the first occurrence. The `"a:b:c"` case in the gate
exists to prove the two agree.

The classic mistake is `event.split(":")` with destructuring, which produces
`["a", "b", "c"]` for the three-part case and quietly loses `"c"`. The second is
a false branch of `{ scope: string; name: string }` instead of `never`, which
lets a string with no colon typecheck as an event.

The model answer captures both halves in one pattern, returns `never` when the
pattern does not match, and uses `indexOf` plus two `slice` calls at runtime so
that the first colon is the separator in both worlds.

## ex5 - unknown in, a union out

Topics: `unknown` (d19), discriminated unions (d07), narrowing (d06).

What this was testing: turning an untrusted value into a type the rest of the
program can narrow on. Everything downstream of this function gets to write
`switch (command.type)` and be told when it forgot a case; that is what the
validation buys.

The classic mistake is returning the input after checking it - `return input as
Command` - which passes every gate here and carries whatever else the payload
had along with it. The second is checking the payload before the discriminant,
which produces confusing behaviour for `{ item: "milk" }` with no type at all.

The model answer rejects the containers that are not objects, casts once, and
then checks discriminant and payload together per branch - returning a fresh
literal each time.

## ex6 - async plus generics

Topics: async typing (d21), generic higher-order functions (d09).

What this was testing: sequential fallback with the type carried through
unchanged, and the difference between a promise and a function that makes one. A
`Promise<T>[]` has already started; a `(() => Promise<T>)[]` has not, and only
the second can be tried in order.

The classic mistake is `return task()` inside the `try`, which returns before the
promise settles so the `catch` never fires and the first failure reaches the
caller. The second is inventing a new error when everything fails, which
discards the only diagnostic information the function had.

The model answer rejects the empty list up front, awaits each task inside a
`try`, remembers the last error as `unknown`, and rethrows it - so the failure
the caller sees is the last one that actually happened.

## ex7 - an exhaustive, immutable reducer

Topics: discriminated unions (d07), `never` and exhaustiveness (d19), readonly
types (d20).

What this was testing: the reducer shape, with the two guarantees that make it
worth using. `readonly` on the state means an accidental `push` does not
compile; `assertNever` in the `default` means an unhandled event type does not
compile either. Neither costs anything at runtime.

The classic mistake is a `quantity` of zero leaving a line with `qty: 0` in the
cart, which is invisible in tests and eventually gets printed on an invoice. The
second is mutating `state.lines` - easy to do, impossible once the type is
`readonly`, which is the argument for making it readonly first.

The model answer branches on the discriminant, rebuilds the lines with `map`,
`filter` or a spread depending on the event, returns the original state
unchanged for the two no-ops, and hands the narrowed-to-`never` event to
`assertNever` in the default.

## ex8 - the pipeline, typed all the way through

Topics: variadic tuples and recursive conditional types (d16), `Awaited` and
async sequencing (d21), rest parameters (d02).

What this was testing: a type that walks a tuple the same way the function walks
an array, one element per step, with `Awaited` normalising each result so a sync
step and an async step are indistinguishable to the next one. It is the same
recursion as `Curried` in d16 ex8, pointed at the result rather than the
parameters.

The classic mistake is unwrapping the promise with a hand-written conditional -
`R extends Promise<infer U> ? U : R` - which is right for one level and wrong for
a step that returns a promise of a promise. The second is forgetting the base
case, so `pipeAsync(x)` with no steps returns `never`.

The model answer recurses on the tail with `Awaited<R>`, falls through to `T`
when the tuple is empty, and runs a plain `for` loop with one `await` at runtime -
and the two casts in the body mark the exact places where a value-level loop
cannot be checked against a type-level fold.

And that is the set, and the track. If ex8 read as a sequence of familiar moves
rather than a puzzle, the twenty-four drill sets did what they were for.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Narrowing](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html) - type predicates, discriminated unions and exhaustiveness, which between them cover ex1, ex5 and ex7.
- [Handbook: Conditional Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html) - including `infer` and the recursion ex3, ex4 and ex8 are built on.
- [Handbook: Mapped Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/mapped-types.html) - the loop in ex3, and the modifiers that make ex7 immutable.
- [TypeScript 4.9: the satisfies operator](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-9.html#the-satisfies-operator) - the declaration in ex2 that makes the whole exercise work.
- [MDN: Promise.any](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/any) - the standard library's answer to ex6, and how it differs.

again. The type and the implementation have to ask the same question.

The model answer puts one conditional in the mapped type, one `typeof` in the
loop, and a single assertion where the loop-built object meets the derived type -
which is the only place the compiler cannot follow.

## ex4 - split a literal, at both levels

Topics: template literal types (d17), `infer` (d16).

What this was testing: a type and a function that split the same string the same
way, and the fact that the type-level split is non-greedy for the same reason
`indexOf` is - both stop at the first occurrence. The `"a:b:c"` case in the gate
exists to prove the two agree.

The classic mistake is `event.split(":")` with destructuring, which produces
`["a", "b", "c"]` for the three-part case and quietly loses `"c"`. The second is
a false branch of `{ scope: string; name: string }` instead of `never`, which
lets a string with no colon typecheck as an event.

The model answer captures both halves in one pattern, returns `never` when the
pattern does not match, and uses `indexOf` plus two `slice` calls at runtime so
that the first colon is the separator in both worlds.

## ex5 - unknown in, a union out

Topics: `unknown` (d19), discriminated unions (d07), narrowing (d06).

What this was testing: turning an untrusted value into a type the rest of the
program can narrow on. Everything downstream of this function gets to write
`switch (command.type)` and be told when it forgot a case; that is what the
validation buys.

The classic mistake is returning the input after checking it - `return input as
Command` - which passes every gate here and carries whatever else the payload
had along with it. The second is checking the payload before the discriminant,
which produces confusing behaviour for `{ item: "milk" }` with no type at all.

The model answer rejects the containers that are not objects, casts once, and
then checks discriminant and payload together per branch - returning a fresh
literal each time.

## ex6 - async plus generics

Topics: async typing (d21), generic higher-order functions (d09).

What this was testing: sequential fallback with the type carried through
unchanged, and the difference between a promise and a function that makes one. A
`Promise<T>[]` has already started; a `(() => Promise<T>)[]` has not, and only
the second can be tried in order.

The classic mistake is `return task()` inside the `try`, which returns before the
promise settles so the `catch` never fires and the first failure reaches the
caller. The second is inventing a new error when everything fails, which
discards the only diagnostic information the function had.

The model answer rejects the empty list up front, awaits each task inside a
`try`, remembers the last error as `unknown`, and rethrows it - so the failure
the caller sees is the last one that actually happened.

## ex7 - an exhaustive, immutable reducer

Topics: discriminated unions (d07), `never` and exhaustiveness (d19), readonly
types (d20).

What this was testing: the reducer shape, with the two guarantees that make it
worth using. `readonly` on the state means an accidental `push` does not
compile; `assertNever` in the `default` means an unhandled event type does not
compile either. Neither costs anything at runtime.

The classic mistake is a `quantity` of zero leaving a line with `qty: 0` in the
cart, which is invisible in tests and eventually gets printed on an invoice. The
second is mutating `state.lines` - easy to do, impossible once the type is
`readonly`, which is the argument for making it readonly first.

The model answer branches on the discriminant, rebuilds the lines with `map`,
`filter` or a spread depending on the event, returns the original state
unchanged for the two no-ops, and hands the narrowed-to-`never` event to
`assertNever` in the default.

## ex8 - the pipeline, typed all the way through

Topics: variadic tuples and recursive conditional types (d16), `Awaited` and
async sequencing (d21), rest parameters (d02).

What this was testing: a type that walks a tuple the same way the function walks
an array, one element per step, with `Awaited` normalising each result so a sync
step and an async step are indistinguishable to the next one. It is the same
recursion as `Curried` in d16 ex8, pointed at the result rather than the
parameters.

The classic mistake is unwrapping the promise with a hand-written conditional -
`R extends Promise<infer U> ? U : R` - which is right for one level and wrong for
a step that returns a promise of a promise. The second is forgetting the base
case, so `pipeAsync(x)` with no steps returns `never`.

The model answer recurses on the tail with `Awaited<R>`, falls through to `T`
when the tuple is empty, and runs a plain `for` loop with one `await` at runtime -
and the two casts in the body mark the exact places where a value-level loop
cannot be checked against a type-level fold.

And that is the set, and the track. If ex8 read as a sequence of familiar moves
rather than a puzzle, the twenty-four drill sets did what they were for.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Narrowing](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html) - type predicates, discriminated unions and exhaustiveness, which between them cover ex1, ex5 and ex7.
- [Handbook: Conditional Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html) - including `infer` and the recursion ex3, ex4 and ex8 are built on.
- [Handbook: Mapped Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/mapped-types.html) - the loop in ex3, and the modifiers that make ex7 immutable.
- [TypeScript 4.9: the satisfies operator](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-9.html#the-satisfies-operator) - the declaration in ex2 that makes the whole exercise work.
- [MDN: Promise.any](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise/any) - the standard library's answer to ex6, and how it differs.

## ex1 - guards plus generics

`firstMatching(values, guard)` returns the first element the guard accepts, or
`undefined`, and its return type is the **narrowed** type - `S | undefined`,
not `T | undefined`.

- `firstMatching([1, 2, "target", 3, "other"], isString)` -> `"target"`
- no match, or an empty list -> `undefined`
- it stops at the first match: for the list above the guard runs three times

Two type parameters, `T` and `S extends T`, and the guard is
`(value: T) => value is S`.

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex1
```

## Hint 1

Two topics: type predicates (d18) and a constrained second type parameter (d10).
`S extends T` is what lets the return type be narrower than the element type.

## Hint 2

`Array.prototype.find` has a predicate overload that would do this - and
returning early from a loop makes the "stops at the first match" requirement
visible, which the gate counts.

Left to you: `find` with the guard, or the explicit loop. Both narrow correctly;
only one of them shows the reader why the answer is `S` and not `T`.

## Hint 1

Two topics: type predicates (d18) and a constrained second type parameter (d10).
`S extends T` is what lets the return type be narrower than the element type.

## Hint 2

`Array.prototype.find` has a predicate overload that would do this - and
returning early from a loop makes the "stops at the first match" requirement
visible, which the gate counts.

Left to you: `find` with the guard, or the explicit loop. Both narrow correctly;
only one of them shows the reader why the answer is `S` and not `T`.

exercises.prompt:
## ex2 - a frozen table, read three ways

`RANKS` is `{ bronze: 1, silver: 2, gold: 3 }`, frozen and checked against
`Record<string, number>`. Three things come out of it:

- `RankName` -> `"bronze" | "silver" | "gold"`
- `RankValue` -> `1 | 2 | 3`
- `isHigher(a, b)` -> whether `a` outranks `b`, strictly: `isHigher("gold", "gold")`
  is `false`
- `namesAbove(name)` -> every rank above it, **ascending by value**

`namesAbove("bronze")` is `["silver", "gold"]`, and `namesAbove("gold")` is
`[]`. `isHigher("platinum", "gold")` is a compile error.

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three topics: `as const satisfies` (d20), `keyof typeof` and indexed access
(d11). The two derived types are already written; the declaration is what makes
them mean something.

## Hint 2

`Object.keys` returns `string[]` no matter how precisely the object is typed -
that is deliberate, because an object may have more keys at runtime than its
type admits. One assertion at that line is the accepted cost.

Left to you: whether to sort explicitly. The insertion order of the object
happens to be ascending here; relying on that is the kind of decision that
survives until someone reorders the table.

exercises.prompt:
## ex3 - a mapped type with a condition in it

`Stringified<T>` rewrites every member whose type is `number` to `string`, and
leaves everything else alone:

- `Stringified<{ a: number; b: boolean }>` -> `{ a: string; b: boolean }`
- `Stringified<{ nested: { a: number } }>` -> unchanged; only the top level is
  rewritten

`stringifyNumbers(value)` does the same at runtime and returns
`Stringified<T>`.

- `stringifyNumbers({ a: 1, b: "x", c: true })` -> `{ a: "1", b: "x", c: true }`
- `stringifyNumbers({ n: 0 })` -> `{ n: "0" }` - zero is a number like any other

The type is already applied to the function's return; making it do something is
the exercise.

exercises.prompt:
## ex4 - split a literal, at both levels

`EventOf<S>` splits an event name at its **first** colon:

- `EventOf<"user:created">` -> `{ scope: "user"; name: "created" }`
- `EventOf<"a:b:c">` -> `{ scope: "a"; name: "b:c" }`
- `EventOf<"plain">` -> `never`

`splitEvent(event)` does the same at runtime and returns `EventOf<S>`, so
`splitEvent("order:paid")` is typed `{ scope: "order"; name: "paid" }`. A string
with no colon throws, and the message contains the word `colon`.

The argument has to be a string *literal* for any of this to be worth anything -
`EventOf<string>` is `never`, because `string` does not match the pattern.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex4
```

exercises.prompt:
## ex5 - unknown in, a union out

`Command` is the union

```ts
{ type: "add"; item: string } | { type: "remove"; id: number } | { type: "clear" }
```

`parseCommand(input: unknown)` returns a `Command` when the input is one, and
`null` otherwise.

- `{ type: "add", item: "milk" }` -> the add command
- `{ type: "add" }` -> `null`, `{ type: "remove", id: "3" }` -> `null`
- `{ type: "reset" }` -> `null`
- `null`, `[]` and `"clear"` -> `null`

The returned object is rebuilt, not passed through, so nothing extra rides along
with it.

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex5
```

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## ex6 - async plus generics

`firstSuccess(tasks)` calls the task factories **in order** and resolves with
the first one that succeeds.

- `[fail, win, win]` -> the second task's value, and the third is never called
- when every task rejects, the **last** rejection is what comes out
- an empty list rejects with an error whose message contains `no tasks`

The return type is `Promise<T>`, where `T` comes from the tasks.

Edit `ex6/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two topics: async typing (d21) and generic wrappers (d09). The tasks are
*factories* - `() => Promise<T>` - which is what makes "the third is never
called" possible; an array of promises would already be running.

## Hint 2

`return await task()` inside the `try`, so a rejection is caught here rather
than at the caller. Without the `await` the promise escapes the `try` and the
loop ends after one iteration.

*factories* - `() => Promise<T>` - which is what makes "the third is never

exercises.prompt:
## ex7 - an exhaustive, immutable reducer

`CartState` is `{ readonly lines: readonly { readonly sku: string; readonly qty: number }[] }`,
and `CartEvent` is

```ts
{ type: "added"; sku: string; qty: number }
  | { type: "removed"; sku: string }
  | { type: "quantity"; sku: string; qty: number }
  | { type: "cleared" }
```

`reduceCart(state, event)` returns a **new** state:

- `added` with a new sku appends `{ sku, qty }`; with an existing sku it adds to
  that line's quantity, **in place** in the list
- `removed` drops the line with that sku; an absent sku is a no-op
- `quantity` sets the quantity; a quantity of `0` or less **removes** the line;
  an unknown sku is a no-op
- `cleared` empties the list

The input state is never modified. `assertNever(value: never): never` throws
with the value in its message, and the `default` branch of the switch calls it.

Edit `ex7/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three topics: discriminated unions (d07), `never` as an exhaustiveness check
(d19) and `readonly` types (d20). Make the state readonly first - it will tell
you every place you were about to mutate.

## Hint 2

Every branch returns a new object. `map` for a change in place, `filter` for a
removal, a spread for an append - and `return state` unchanged is a legitimate
answer for the two no-op cases.

## Hint 3

`assertNever` takes `never` and returns `never`. Returning its result from the
`default` branch is what tells the compiler the switch is total; if you later
add a fifth event type, that line is where the build breaks.

Left to you: whether `quantity` on an unknown sku should insert instead of doing
nothing. The prompt says do nothing; the other reading is defensible and is a
different event.

(d19) and `readonly` types (d20). Make the state readonly first - it will tell

`assertNever` takes `never` and returns `never`. Returning its result from the

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## ex8 - the pipeline, typed all the way through

The finale.

`PipeResult<T, Fns>` walks a tuple of step functions and reports the type the
last one produces, awaiting each result along the way:

- `PipeResult<number, [(value: number) => string]>` -> `string`
- `PipeResult<number, [(value: number) => string, (value: string) => boolean]>` -> `boolean`
- `PipeResult<number, [(value: number) => Promise<string>]>` -> `string`

`pipeAsync(input, ...steps)` runs the steps in order, awaiting each one, and
resolves with `PipeResult<T, Fns>`:

- `pipeAsync(2, (n: number) => n + 1, async (n: number) => String(n), (s: string) => s + "!")`
  resolves with `"3!"`, and the three steps run in order
- `pipeAsync("untouched")` resolves with `"untouched"` - no steps, no change
- a step that throws rejects the pipeline

The steps are a rest parameter constrained to `readonly ((arg: never) => unknown)[]`,
which accepts a function of any parameter type.

Edit `ex8/solution.ts`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript d24_mixed_gauntlet ex8
```

lessons.briefing:
# i1 — Interview concepts

You can write TypeScript now. This part of the track is about *saying* it out
loud, under time pressure, to someone who is deciding whether to hire you.

Those are different skills. In an interview nobody watches you narrow a union
in an editor — they ask "what is the difference between `any` and `unknown`?"
and listen to thirty seconds of speech. The candidates who do well are not the
ones who know more; they are the ones who have said the answer before, have a
concrete example ready, and can name the follow-up question themselves.

So this lesson has two halves. `reading.md` is a bank of **60 questions with
model answers**, grouped by topic and tagged by how often they actually come up
(⭐ occasionally, ⭐⭐ regularly, ⭐⭐⭐ expect it). Each answer is written the way
a strong candidate would say it — three to six sentences, one example, and the
follow-up named — and each is cross-referenced to the lesson to redo if it does
not feel solid. The four exercises here spot-check the concepts that can be
checked in code, because knowing an answer and being able to write it are not
the same thing either.

## How to use the question bank

Open it with:

```
uv run dojo read typescript i1_interview_concepts
```

Then work like this, out loud:

1. Read the question. **Cover the answer.**
2. Say your answer to the wall, in full sentences, including an example. Aim for
   thirty seconds — long enough to show depth, short enough that the interviewer
   can steer.
3. Uncover and compare. Not word by word: check that you named the same
   *mechanism*, gave a concrete example, and did not say anything wrong.
4. If a question needed a second attempt, note the lesson it points at and redo
   that lesson's review exercise.

Do the ⭐⭐⭐ questions until they are boring. Those are the ones that will be
asked, and a hesitant answer to a ⭐⭐⭐ question costs you more than a blank on
a ⭐ one — because the interviewer reads it as "has not thought about this".

Two habits worth building while you practise. Say **"it depends, and here is
what it depends on"** when that is the truth: "`interface` or `type`? For an
object shape they are nearly the same; I use `interface` when it might be
extended or merged, `type` for unions and anything computed." And volunteer the
trade-off — "the cost of a string enum is that data from `JSON.parse` needs a
cast at every boundary". Interviewers are listening for judgement, not recall.

## Exercise 1 — `any` versus `unknown`, in code

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. `lengthOf` currently takes `any`. Change it to
`unknown` and implement it so the body earns its way to an answer:

- `lengthOf("hello")` → `5`, `lengthOf([1, 2, 3])` → `3`
- `lengthOf({ a: 1, b: 2 })` → `2` (its key count)
- `lengthOf(null)` → `0`, `lengthOf(42)` → `0`, `lengthOf(undefined)` → `0`

The type gate checks the parameter is exactly `unknown`. Being able to *say* why
that matters is the point: `any` disables checking and spreads, `unknown` keeps
it and forces one narrowing step.

```
uv run dojo test typescript i1_interview_concepts ex1
```

## Exercise 2 — make the union exhaustive

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. A fourth state (`failed`) was added to `JobState` and
`describeJob` was never updated — and nothing complained, because of a
catch-all `default`. Fix both halves:

- add the missing branch: `{ status: "failed", message: "gate red" }` →
  `"failed: gate red"`
- replace the `default` with an `assertNever` call so the *next* variant is a
  compile error instead of a wrong string

The other three renderings must keep working: `"queued"`, `"running (40%)"`,
`"done in 120ms"`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript i1_interview_concepts ex2
```

## Exercise 3 — declaration merging

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Add a **second** `interface DojoEvents` declaration —
do not edit the first — carrying a `fail` event with `exercise` and `message`,
then implement `describeEvent`:

- `describeEvent("pass", { exercise: "ex1" })` → `"pass ex1"`
- `describeEvent("fail", { exercise: "ex2", message: "wrong shape" })` →
  `"fail ex2: wrong shape"`

This is the answer to "what can an `interface` do that a `type` alias cannot?",
written as code. The type gate checks `keyof DojoEvents` is `"pass" | "fail"`.

```
uv run dojo test typescript i1_interview_concepts ex3
```

## Exercise 4 — what a `catch` actually gives you

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. `errorMessage` claims its parameter is an `Error`. It
is not — `throw` accepts any value. Change the parameter to `unknown` and
implement it:

- `new Error("boom")` → `"boom"`, `new TypeError("bad type")` → `"bad type"`
- `"just a string"` → `"just a string"`
- `42` and `null` → `"unknown error"`

```
uv run dojo test typescript i1_interview_concepts ex4
```

## Review — safeGet

Edit `review1/solution.ts`. Both `any`s have to go. Implement
`safeGet(source, key)` taking `unknown` and returning `unknown`:

- `safeGet({ title: "Unions" }, "title")` → `"Unions"`
- `safeGet({ count: 0 }, "count")` → `0`
- `safeGet({}, "title")`, `safeGet(null, "title")`, `safeGet("a string", "title")`
  → `undefined`

```
uv run dojo test typescript i1_interview_concepts review1
```

# Reading - typescript/i1_interview_concepts

The question bank. Sixty questions with model answers, grouped by topic, tagged
⭐ (occasionally asked) / ⭐⭐ (regularly) / ⭐⭐⭐ (expect it), each pointing at
the lesson to redo if the answer does not come easily.

## Notes

**How the answers are written.** Each one is what a strong mid-level candidate
would actually say: three to six sentences, one concrete example, and the
follow-up question named so you can head it off. They are deliberately not
exhaustive — an interview answer that runs three minutes is a worse answer than
one that runs thirty seconds and invites a follow-up. Cover the answer, say
yours out loud, then compare the *mechanism* you named rather than the words.

**How to prioritise.** Do every ⭐⭐⭐ until it is boring; they are the questions
that decide screens. Then the ⭐⭐, which are where a good candidate separates
from an adequate one. The ⭐ questions are for depth — you will not be rejected
for missing one, but landing one well is memorable.

**A rule for every answer:** name the mechanism, give the example, state the
trade-off. "Types are erased at compile time, so a `Lesson` interface cannot be
checked at runtime — that is why `JSON.parse` results need a guard; the cost is
one validation step per boundary." That shape works for almost every question
in this file.

## Fundamentals — what TypeScript is

**1. What is TypeScript, in one paragraph?** ⭐⭐⭐
TypeScript is JavaScript plus a static type checker that runs at build time
only. Every annotation is erased before the code runs — `tsc` emits plain
JavaScript — so types can prove that the pieces of your program fit together but
cannot validate anything at runtime. For example, an `interface User` gives you
autocomplete and compile errors, and does nothing whatsoever to a malformed API
response. That erasure is the single fact that explains most of the language's
design.
*Follow-up: "so what do you do about untrusted data?" · Weak here → redo 00_hello_dojo and 10_guards_assertions.*

**2. What does TypeScript compile to, and what disappears?** ⭐⭐⭐
It compiles to JavaScript at whatever target you configure, and everything
type-level disappears: annotations, interfaces, type aliases, generics, `as`
casts, `satisfies`. Three constructs are the exception because they emit real
code — `enum`, `namespace`, and parameter properties in constructors
(`constructor(private id: string)`). A good way to say it: "if I can delete it
and the JavaScript still runs, it was erased."
*Follow-up: "why is that a reason to prefer unions over enums?" · Weak here → redo 05_literals_enums.*

**3. What does `strict` actually turn on?** ⭐⭐
It is a bundle, not one flag: `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`,
`strictFunctionTypes`, `strictBindCallApply`, `strictPropertyInitialization`,
`noImplicitThis`, `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, and `alwaysStrict`. The two that
change how you write code every day are `noImplicitAny` (parameters must be
typed) and `strictNullChecks` (`null` and `undefined` are tracked as real
members of a type rather than being assignable to everything). Learning
TypeScript with `strict` off is learning a weaker, different language.
*Follow-up: "how would you turn it on in a large legacy codebase?" · Weak here → redo 00_hello_dojo.*

**4. Type inference — when should you annotate?** ⭐⭐
Annotate the boundaries and let inference do the middle: function parameters
(required under `noImplicitAny`), exported function return types, and empty
containers like `const rows: Row[] = []`. Skip annotations on locals initialised
from an expression, and on callbacks where contextual typing already knows the
parameter types. The reason to annotate exported *return* types specifically is
that an inferred public contract can be changed by an innocent edit to a body,
and nobody notices until a build breaks elsewhere.
*Follow-up: "show me a case where inference gives the wrong thing." · Weak here → redo 01_primitives_and_inference.*

**5. What is type widening?** ⭐⭐
When TypeScript infers a type for a mutable binding it widens the literal to its
base type: `let x = "a"` is `string`, `const x = "a"` is `"a"`, and object
properties widen too, so `{ mode: "dark" }` gives `mode: string`. This is why
passing `let mode = "dark"` to something expecting `"dark" | "light"` fails while
the `const` version succeeds. The three fixes are `const`, an explicit
annotation, or `as const`.
*Follow-up: "what does `as const` do to an array?" · Weak here → redo 05_literals_enums.*

**6. `tsc` vs Babel vs esbuild vs `--isolatedModules`?** ⭐
`tsc` is the only one that typechecks; the others strip types file by file and
are much faster, which is why most modern setups typecheck with `tsc --noEmit`
in CI and transpile with esbuild/SWC in the build. `isolatedModules` tells
`tsc` to reject constructs a single-file transpiler cannot handle safely —
re-exporting a type without `export type`, `const enum`, and similar. If a build
tool cannot see other files, anything requiring cross-file knowledge has to go.
*Follow-up: "why is `import type` needed then?" · Weak here → redo 11_async_and_modules.*

## `any`, `unknown`, `never`, `void`

**7. `any` vs `unknown`?** ⭐⭐⭐
Both accept every value; the difference is what you may do next. `any` switches
checking off for that value and everything derived from it, so
`value.a.b.c()` compiles and explodes at runtime. `unknown` keeps checking on:
you can hold it and pass it around, but you must narrow before you use it, which
forces exactly one honest check at the boundary. `JSON.parse` returns `any`, and
wrapping it to return `unknown` is a one-line improvement almost every codebase
should make.
*Follow-up: "where is `any` still the right answer?" · Weak here → redo 10_guards_assertions.*

**8. What is `never`, and where does it show up?** ⭐⭐⭐
`never` is the empty type — no value has it — so it is assignable to everything
and nothing is assignable to it. You see it as the return type of a function
that never finishes normally (`function fail(m: string): never { throw ... }`),
as the result of narrowing that has eliminated every member of a union, and as
the element type of an unannotated empty array in some positions. The practical
use is exhaustiveness: `assertNever(value: never)` in a `switch` default turns a
forgotten union member into a compile error.
*Follow-up: "what happens to `never` inside a union?" (it disappears) · Weak here → redo 04_unions_narrowing.*

**9. `void` vs `undefined`?** ⭐⭐
`void` as a return type means "I will ignore whatever you return", and a
function type returning `void` accepts an implementation returning anything —
which is why `items.forEach(x => list.push(x))` compiles even though `push`
returns a number. `undefined` is a real value with a real type. The rule: a
function *declaration* annotated `: void` may not return a value, but a function
*type* with a `void` return accepts one and discards it.
*Follow-up: "why does that special case exist?" · Weak here → redo 02_functions.*

**10. When is `any` acceptable?** ⭐⭐
In a constraint position where you are only saying "some function" —
`<F extends (...args: any[]) => any>` — because `unknown[]` breaks
contravariant parameter matching and the real types are recovered immediately by
`Parameters<F>` and `ReturnType<F>`. Also during a migration, behind a `// TODO`
and ideally behind a lint rule that counts them. Everywhere else, `unknown` plus
a narrowing step says the same thing honestly.
*Follow-up: "how do you stop `any` spreading?" (`noImplicitAny`, `no-explicit-any`, code review) · Weak here → redo 08_utility_types.*

**11. What type is the variable in a `catch` block?** ⭐⭐
`unknown`, since TypeScript 4.4 with `useUnknownInCatchVariables` (part of
`strict`) — because `throw` accepts any value and real libraries throw strings
and plain objects. So `error.message` does not compile until you narrow, and the
standard shape is
`error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)`. Before 4.4 it was
`any`, which is why old codebases are full of unchecked `err.message`.
*Follow-up: "what breaks `instanceof Error`?" (cross-realm values) · Weak here → redo i1 ex4.*

## Structural typing and assignability

**12. Structural vs nominal typing?** ⭐⭐⭐
TypeScript compares types by shape, not by name: any object with a
`name: string` satisfies `{ name: string }`, whoever declared it. Java and C# are
nominal — the declared name is the identity — which is why the same code feels
different in each. The consequence to name: `type UserId = string` and
`type OrderId = string` are the *same type*, so aliases give you no protection
against mixing them up.
*Follow-up: "how would you get nominal typing when you need it?" · Weak here → redo 03_objects_interfaces.*

**13. How do you fake nominal typing?** ⭐⭐
With a branded (or "opaque") type: intersect the primitive with something nobody
can produce accidentally, such as
`type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: unique symbol }`. You then create
values through a single factory that casts once, and everywhere else the
compiler refuses to mix `UserId` with a plain `string`. The cost is that one
cast plus a little ceremony at the boundary; the benefit is a whole class of
argument-order bugs becoming impossible.
*Follow-up: "what does that compile to?" (nothing — it is erased) · Weak here → redo 03_objects_interfaces.*

**14. What is excess property checking?** ⭐⭐
Structural typing says extra properties are fine, but a *fresh object literal*
assigned directly to a typed target gets an extra check that rejects unknown
members — because a literal with a member the target has never heard of is
almost always a typo. Assign the literal to a variable first and the check
disappears, which looks inconsistent until you know it is deliberate. It is what
catches `{ retires: 2 }` when you meant `retries`.
*Follow-up: "how do you allow extra properties on purpose?" (an index signature, or a widening variable) · Weak here → redo 03_objects_interfaces.*

**15. Are function parameters checked covariantly or contravariantly?** ⭐
Contravariantly, in principle: a function accepting a *wider* parameter is
assignable where a narrower one is expected. TypeScript enforces that for
function-typed properties under `strictFunctionTypes`, but *method* declarations
stay bivariant for historical and ergonomic reasons — largely so that arrays and
DOM event handlers keep working. The honest one-liner: "parameters are
contravariant, except methods, which are bivariant on purpose."
*Follow-up: "give me an unsound example." (an `Array<Dog>` where `Array<Animal>` is expected) · Weak here → redo 07_generics_2.*

**16. Why does `{ a: 1, b: 2 }` satisfy `{ a: number }` but `Dog[]` also satisfy `Animal[]`?** ⭐
The first is plain structural assignability: extra members are ignored. The
second is array covariance, which is unsound and known to be — you could push a
`Cat` into the `Animal[]` and corrupt the `Dog[]`. TypeScript accepts it because
the sound alternative makes everyday code miserable, and this pragmatism is a
recurring theme in the language.
*Follow-up: "what does `readonly T[]` change about that?" · Weak here → redo 01_primitives_and_inference.*

## `interface` vs `type`

**17. `interface` vs `type` — which and why?** ⭐⭐⭐
For describing an object shape they are almost interchangeable. `interface`
supports declaration merging (declare it twice and members combine — how you
augment `Window` or a library's types) and produces friendlier error messages;
`type` can express what an interface cannot: unions, tuples, primitives, mapped
and conditional types. My default is `interface` for object shapes that might be
extended or merged, `type` for everything else — and consistency inside a module
matters more than the choice.
*Follow-up: "show me something only a type alias can do." (`type Level = "a" | "b"`) · Weak here → redo 03_objects_interfaces.*

**18. What is declaration merging?** ⭐⭐
Two declarations of the same interface in the same scope combine into one type;
namespaces merge the same way, and an interface can merge with a class or a
function declaration. It is the mechanism behind module augmentation —
`declare global { interface Window { myThing: X } }` — and behind libraries that
let you extend their types from your own code. Type aliases cannot do it:
declaring the same alias twice is "Duplicate identifier".
*Follow-up: "when is that a footgun?" (silent merges across files) · Weak here → redo i1 ex3.*

**19. `extends` vs `&` (intersection)?** ⭐⭐
`interface B extends A` checks compatibility at declaration time and reports a
conflict; `type B = A & { ... }` produces an intersection, and conflicting
members silently become `never` rather than erroring. Intersections also compose
with unions and other computed types, which `extends` cannot. Performance-wise,
long intersection chains are slower for the checker than interface extension.
*Follow-up: "what does `{ a: string } & { a: number }` give you?" (`a: never`) · Weak here → redo 03_objects_interfaces.*

**20. What is an index signature, and what does it not protect you from?** ⭐⭐
`{ [key: string]: number }` says every string key yields a number, so
`tally.typo` typechecks and is `undefined` at runtime — the type is a promise
you made, not one the compiler verified. When the key set is actually closed,
`Record<"a" | "b", number>` is far safer because a missing member is a compile
error. `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is the flag that makes every indexed read
`T | undefined`.
*Follow-up: "how does that interact with `Object.keys`?" (it returns `string[]`, not `keyof T`) · Weak here → redo 03_objects_interfaces and 08_utility_types.*

## Unions, narrowing, exhaustiveness

**21. What is a union type, and what can you do with one before narrowing?** ⭐⭐⭐
`A | B` is a value that is one of several types, and before you narrow it you
may only touch members that *every* constituent has — so `string | number` gives
you `toString()` but not `toUpperCase()`. That refusal is the feature: in plain
JavaScript calling `toUpperCase` on a number is a runtime crash. Narrowing with
`typeof`, `instanceof`, `in` or a discriminant opens up the full type.
*Follow-up: "what about intersections?" (opposite: more capability, fewer values) · Weak here → redo 04_unions_narrowing.*

**22. What is a discriminated union and why is it the most useful pattern in TypeScript?** ⭐⭐⭐
It is several object types unioned together, each with a shared property pinned
to a distinct *literal* — `{ kind: "circle"; radius: number } | { kind: "square";
side: number }`. Comparing that property is proof for the compiler, so
`switch (shape.kind)` narrows each branch to exactly one variant. It makes
illegal states unrepresentable, which beats one interface with five optional
members and defensive checks everywhere.
*Follow-up: "how do you keep the switch exhaustive?" · Weak here → redo 04_unions_narrowing.*

**23. How do you get exhaustiveness checking?** ⭐⭐⭐
Put a `default` branch that calls a helper typed `assertNever(value: never):
never`. In an exhaustive switch the value is narrowed to `never` there, so the
call compiles; miss a variant and the value is not `never` any more and you get
a compile error naming exactly what you forgot. Return the call
(`return assertNever(x)`) so the compiler also knows the function always
returns.
*Follow-up: "why does it also throw?" (types are erased; bad data really arrives) · Weak here → redo 04_unions_narrowing and i1 ex2.*

**24. What narrowing mechanisms does TypeScript have?** ⭐⭐
`typeof` for primitives, `instanceof` for class instances, `in` for property
presence, `===`/`switch` against literals for discriminated unions, truthiness
and `!= null` for nullability, `Array.isArray`, and user-defined type predicates
for anything else. Control flow analysis threads all of them through your
function, including early `return`s and `throw`s. The one to volunteer is that
narrowing is lost inside closures that may run later, and for mutable object
properties.
*Follow-up: "how do you narrow across a function boundary?" (a type predicate) · Weak here → redo 04_unions_narrowing.*

**25. What is a user-defined type guard?** ⭐⭐⭐
A function whose return type is a predicate — `function isLesson(value:
unknown): value is Lesson` — so callers who write `if (isLesson(x))` get `x`
narrowed inside the block. TypeScript does not verify that the body establishes
the claim, so a guard that returns `true` unconditionally compiles and lies;
guards deserve their own unit tests. Since 5.5, simple predicates can be
inferred automatically.
*Follow-up: "how do you use one with `filter`?" (`items.filter((i): i is T => ...)`) · Weak here → redo 10_guards_assertions.*

**26. What is an assertion function?** ⭐⭐
A function typed `asserts value is T` that throws when the claim is false;
after the call the value is narrowed for the rest of the scope with no `if`. Two
rules bite people: TypeScript will not *infer* an assertion signature, so the
declaration needs an explicit type, and the function must throw — returning
normally makes the narrowing a lie. Use guards when both outcomes are ordinary
and assertions for invariants.
*Follow-up: "why can't `const f = (v) => ...` be an assertion?" · Weak here → redo 10_guards_assertions.*

**27. How does `strictNullChecks` change your code?** ⭐⭐
It makes `null` and `undefined` ordinary union members instead of values
assignable to everything, so `string | null` must be narrowed before use. In
practice you write more `if (x)` and `x ?? fallback`, and you stop shipping
"cannot read properties of undefined". Optional chaining `?.` and the non-null
assertion `!` are the ergonomic tools — and every `!` is a claim you should be
able to justify.
*Follow-up: "when is `!` acceptable?" · Weak here → redo 04_unions_narrowing.*

**28. `??` vs `||`?** ⭐⭐⭐
`||` falls back on every falsy value — `0`, `""`, `false`, `NaN` — while `??`
falls back only on `null` and `undefined`. So `options.retries || 1` turns an
explicit zero into one, and `options.verbose || true` produces a flag nobody can
switch off. Use `??` for defaults on values where a falsy value is meaningful,
which is most of them.
*Follow-up: "what does `?.` return when it short-circuits?" (`undefined`) · Weak here → redo 03_objects_interfaces.*

## Literals, enums, `as const`

**29. What is a literal type?** ⭐⭐
A type whose only value is one specific value: `"circle"`, `42`, `true`. Unioned
together they model a closed set — `type Level = "beginner" | "advanced"` — which
gives autocomplete, catches typos, and lets a `switch` be checked for
exhaustiveness. This is why `status: string` is almost always the wrong
annotation for a status.
*Follow-up: "why does a `let` lose the literal type?" (widening) · Weak here → redo 05_literals_enums.*

**30. What does `as const` do?** ⭐⭐⭐
It is a const assertion: every property becomes `readonly` and every literal
keeps its literal type instead of widening, and array literals become readonly
tuples. It emits nothing — the JavaScript is identical — so it is purely a
compile-time description, unlike `Object.freeze`, which is a runtime call. The
usual pairing is `as const` on a config object plus `keyof typeof` to derive a
union of its keys.
*Follow-up: "how do you get a union of the *values*?" (`typeof obj[keyof typeof obj]`) · Weak here → redo 05_literals_enums.*

**31. Enums or union of string literals?** ⭐⭐⭐
Union of literals by default: it is erased, so nothing ships to the client, and
a plain string from `JSON.parse` is assignable without a cast. A string enum
gives you nominal typing (a raw string is *not* assignable), one import
carrying both values and type, and something to iterate with `Object.values` —
at the cost of an emitted runtime object and a cast at every boundary. Numeric
enums have unsound assignability and reverse mappings; avoid them.
*Follow-up: "what is `const enum` and why is it discouraged?" · Weak here → redo 05_literals_enums.*

**32. What are template literal types?** ⭐
Types the compiler can compute from string literals:
`` type Route = `/api/${"users" | "orders"}` `` produces two literal types. They
distribute over unions and combine with the intrinsic helpers `Uppercase`,
`Lowercase`, `Capitalize` and `Uncapitalize`. Real uses are typed event names
(`` `on${Capitalize<E>}` ``), route parameters, and CSS-in-JS variant props.
*Follow-up: "how would you parse a path into params?" (recursive conditional types) · Weak here → redo 09_mapped_conditional.*

**33. What does `satisfies` do that an annotation does not?** ⭐⭐⭐
It checks the value against a type without replacing the value's inferred type.
`const config: Record<string, string | number> = {...}` widens every member to
the union and adds an index signature that hides typos; `const config = {...}
satisfies Record<string, string | number>` validates the same constraint while
`config.host` stays `string` and `config.hsot` is an error. It is the right
default for configuration objects, palettes and route tables.
*Follow-up: "how does it combine with `as const`?" (`as const satisfies T`) · Weak here → redo 10_guards_assertions.*

## Generics

**34. What problem do generics solve?** ⭐⭐⭐
They let one implementation serve many types while *remembering* which one each
caller used. Without them your options are duplication (`firstString`,
`firstNumber`) or `any`/`unknown`, which throws away what the caller knew:
`first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined` gives `string | undefined` for a string
array with no annotation at the call site. The rule of thumb is that a type
parameter should appear at least twice in a signature — otherwise it is doing
nothing.
*Follow-up: "show me a needless generic." (`function log<T>(x: T): void`) · Weak here → redo 06_generics_1.*

**35. How does TypeScript infer type arguments?** ⭐⭐
It collects candidates from the arguments, picks a best common type, and then
uses that to contextually type the rest — which is why a callback's parameters
need no annotations once the array is known. Conflicting candidates in the same
position widen to a union or error, and when nothing determines a parameter it
falls back to `unknown` (or a declared default). If inference gives you
something odd, the fix is usually an explicit type argument or reordering the
parameters.
*Follow-up: "why does an empty array infer `never[]`?" · Weak here → redo 06_generics_1.*

**36. What is a generic constraint?** ⭐⭐⭐
`<T extends { length: number }>` says every `T` must be at least that shape:
inside the function you may use `.length`, and outside, arguments without it are
rejected. Crucially `T` is still inferred as the caller's specific type, so
`longest("abc", "de")` returns `string`, not `{ length: number }`. Constrain to
the shape you actually use and no more.
*Follow-up: "what does `T extends unknown` mean?" (nothing useful — except to trigger distribution) · Weak here → redo 07_generics_2.*

**37. What do `keyof` and `T[K]` do?** ⭐⭐⭐
`keyof T` is the union of `T`'s property names; `T[K]` is an indexed access type
— the type stored at that key. Together they give the most reusable signature in
the language: `function get<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`, which
makes `get(user, "streak")` a `number` and `get(user, "nope")` a compile error.
Every typed `pick`, `orderBy` or ORM `select` is that signature with more
decoration.
