# Reading - typescript/i2_interview_drills

The debrief. For each drill: what the interviewer was actually marking, the
mistake most candidates make, and the sentence that would have earned the point.

## Notes

**What a live-coding round measures.** Not whether you finish — most
interviewers have seen their own question take longer than they expected. They
are marking process: did you ask about the edge cases first, did you write the
signature before the body, did you narrate, did you catch your own bug. A
candidate who says "before I start — what should happen when two items have the
same key?" has already scored, whatever the code looks like ten minutes later.

**Type the signature first, out loud.** Every drill here is easier once the
signature exists, and saying it aloud gives the interviewer a chance to correct
your understanding before you spend eight minutes on the wrong function. It also
demonstrates the thing they most want to see: that you think in types rather
than adding them afterwards.

**Name your trade-offs as you make them.** "First occurrence wins — I would
document that", "this is a trailing-edge debounce; lodash also offers leading",
"I compare with `Object.is` so setting the same value does not notify". Each of
those is one sentence and each one converts a coding decision into visible
judgement.

**Finish with what you would do next.** "With more time I would add `cancel` to
the debounce, catch throwing listeners in the store, and write a type test for
the emitter." That closes the round on your terms and shows you know the
difference between a drill and production code.

## ex1 — groupBy

What is being marked: whether you reach for a generic without being asked, and
whether the accumulator's type is written down. `Record<string, T[]>` in the
signature is what makes `groups[k].push(item)` typecheck; the version that
starts with `const groups = {}` gets `{}` and then fights the compiler.

The mistake to avoid is calling the key function more than once per item — cheap
here, expensive when the key involves a hash or a date parse. Compute it once
into a local.

Two sentences worth saying out loud. First, the ordering guarantee: items stay
in input order within each bucket, which falls out of a single forward pass and
is the behaviour callers assume. Second, the object-versus-`Map` trade: an
object serialises to JSON and takes string keys, a `Map` preserves insertion
order of keys and takes any key type. Interviewers ask "why an object?" and a
candidate with an answer stands out.

## ex2 — a typed event emitter

This is the canonical TypeScript design question, and the marking scheme is
almost always the same: `interface EventMap`, then
`on<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, handler: (payload: EventMap[K]) => void)`.
If you produce that signature in the first two minutes you have passed; the
bodies are ordinary JavaScript.

The internal storage is where honest candidates get uncomfortable, and it is
worth pre-empting: a single map cannot hold handlers for different events with
precise types, because each key's handlers have a different parameter type. Every
real implementation stores them loosely and casts at the two edges. Saying "the
public API is precise and there is one deliberate cast inside" is the
professional answer; silently reaching for `any` on the public signature is not.

Three details separate a good answer from an adequate one. Returning an
unsubscribe function rather than requiring an `off(event, handler)` — because
the caller then cannot get the handler reference wrong. Iterating a *copy* of
the handler set when emitting, so a handler that unsubscribes during dispatch
cannot corrupt the iteration. And having an opinion about a throwing handler:
Node's `EventEmitter` lets it propagate, most application emitters should catch
and continue.

## ex3 — promisify

Two skills in one small drill. The runtime half is the error-first convention —
`(error, value)` where the value is only meaningful when `error` is null — and
the `value as T` cast is forced by the callback type's optional `value?`. That
cast is defensible and worth narrating: "the convention guarantees a value when
the error is null; the type cannot express that, so I assert it here."

The type half is the one people freeze on. `Promisified<F>` is a conditional
type with `infer` pulling the payload out of the callback's parameter:

```ts
type Promisified<F> = F extends (callback: Callback<infer T>) => void ? () => Promise<T> : never;
```

If you have seen `ReturnType` and `Awaited`'s implementations, this is the same
move. If you froze, that is the signal to redo `09_mapped_conditional`.

The follow-up they will ask: what if the callback fires twice? A promise ignores
every settle after the first, so a double-calling callback silently loses data —
which is either fine or a bug worth logging, and knowing that it happens at all
is the point.

## ex4 — debounce

Debounce is asked because it is a closure question wearing a utility's clothes.
The two mistakes are storing the timer *inside* the returned function (so it is
recreated every call and nothing is ever cancelled) and forgetting to pass the
arguments through, which the gate catches by asserting the call happened with
`"c"`.

`Parameters<F>` is what makes the wrapper's signature honest, and
`ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>` is the spelling that works in both Node and the
browser — `number` in one, a `Timeout` object in the other. Reaching for
`NodeJS.Timeout` in a browser project is a small tell.

Be ready for two follow-ups. "How would you add leading-edge behaviour?" — call
immediately if there is no pending timer, then suppress until the window
closes. "What is the difference from throttle?" — debounce waits for quiet;
throttle guarantees at most one call per interval regardless of quiet. Search
inputs want debounce; scroll handlers want throttle.

## ex5 — flatten a comment tree

The marking is on the traversal order and the optional `children`. Pre-order
depth-first is what a rendered comment thread needs, and saying "parent before
children, subtree before next sibling" before you write proves you understood
the requirement rather than guessing.

`node.children ?? []` is the small elegance: it turns the optional property into
"nothing to recurse into" and removes an `if`. The alternative,
`if (node.children) walk(node.children, depth + 1)`, is equally correct and one
line longer.

The follow-up is always depth. Recursion is limited by the call stack — around
ten thousand frames in Node — so a pathologically deep tree overflows. The
iterative version pushes `[node, depth]` pairs onto an explicit stack, and
because a stack is LIFO you push children in reverse to keep the same order.
Knowing that conversion exists is usually enough; being able to write it is a
bonus.

## ex6 — type a `pipe`

This drill tests whether you know what overloads are *for*: one runtime
function, several compile-time contracts, where the result type depends on the
arguments. A single generic signature cannot do it, and candidates who try
usually end up with `unknown` and a cast at every call site.

The implementation signature (`(value: unknown, ...fns: ((input: unknown) =>
unknown)[]) => unknown`) is invisible to callers, so it can be as loose as it
needs to be — and TypeScript checks it only loosely against the overloads, which
means the overloads are a promise you own. That sentence is the one that earns
the point.

Two things worth mentioning. Real libraries write eight or ten overloads by
hand for exactly this reason; variadic tuple types can express it generically
but with worse error messages. And `reduce` is the natural body: threading a
value through a list of functions *is* a fold.

## challenge — the typed store

A take-home is marked on API design, not on line count. The four members here
are the smallest interesting state container, and each carries a decision worth
narrating.

`setState` accepting `S | ((current: S) => S)` is React's shape, and it exists
because callers who derive the next state from the current one otherwise race
with each other. The typing wrinkle is real: `typeof updater === "function"`
cannot narrow a generic `S` that might itself be a function type, so one cast is
the accepted answer — say so rather than hiding it.

The `Object.is` no-op is the detail that separates people who have used a store
from people who have read about one. Without it, every `setState` notifies, and
in a React app that means a render per call whether anything changed or not.
`Object.is` rather than `===` because it treats `NaN` as equal to itself, which
`===` does not.

Iterating a copy of the listener set is the same defensive move as in the
emitter, and it matters more here: a listener that unsubscribes itself on first
call is a normal pattern. And `select<R>(selector: (state: S) => R): R` is
`Box.map` from lesson 06 wearing a different name — a method-level type
parameter on a type-level generic.

If the interviewer asks what is missing before this is production-ready: batching
(so several `setState` calls in one tick notify once), reference-equality
selectors with memoisation, and something to catch a throwing listener.

## review1 — mapValues

The drill that looks trivial and is not, because `Object.keys` is typed
`string[]` rather than `(keyof T)[]`. That is deliberate and sound: structural
typing means a value can always have more properties than its type declares, so
the compiler cannot promise the key list matches the type. Every implementation
therefore contains one cast, and being able to explain *why* — rather than
apologising for it — is exactly what this review is training.

`{} as Record<keyof T, U>` for the accumulator is the same "object under
construction" problem as `pickKeys` in lesson 08. The `Object.fromEntries`
alternative trades the loop for a different cast and loses the key literals,
which is a fair trade to describe out loud.

Bringing this back through `dojo review` is deliberate: `keyof`, indexed access
and one honest cast are the three things this whole track has been circling, and
they are what a mid-level TypeScript interview is most likely to poke at.

## Further reading

- [Handbook: More on Functions — overloads](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#function-overloads) — the mechanism behind the `pipe` drill.
- [Handbook: `keyof` and Indexed Access Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/keyof-types.html) — the pair behind the emitter, `mapValues` and half of every typed library API.
- [MDN: closures](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Closures) — the JavaScript half of `debounce`, `once` and the store.
- [Vitest: fake timers](https://vitest.dev/guide/mocking#timers) — how the debounce gate advances time without waiting for it.
- [Zustand source](https://github.com/pmndrs/zustand/blob/main/src/vanilla.ts) — the challenge, as shipped: about forty lines, and every decision in this drill appears in it.

exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — the 45-minute take-home: a typed store (hard)

> "Build me a tiny state container — the kind a small app would use instead of
> Redux. `getState`, `setState`, `subscribe`, `select`. Generic in the state
> type. Take your time; I care more about the API than about how much you
> finish."

Edit `challenge/solution.ts`. Finish the `Store<S>` interface and implement
`createStore`:

1. `getState()` returns the current state.
2. `setState(next)` accepts either a new state **or** an updater function
   `(current) => next`.
3. `subscribe(listener)` registers a listener called with the new state on every
   change, and returns an unsubscribe function.
4. Setting the state to the value it already holds notifies **nobody** — compare
   with `Object.is`.
5. `select(selector)` applies a selector to the current state and returns its
   result, typed.

Honest difficulty note: the `setState` overload is where the typing gets
awkward, because `typeof updater === "function"` cannot narrow a generic `S`
that might itself be a function. One documented cast is the accepted answer.

```
uv run dojo test typescript i2_interview_drills challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is the take-home version: a small state container with four members, and
every one of them is a typing decision as much as a coding one. Finish the
`Store<S>` interface first - `getState`, `setState`, `subscribe`, `select` - and
notice that `select` needs its own type parameter, like `Box.map` back in lesson
06.

Read the four behaviour rules in the README before you write any of it.

## Hint 2

`setState` accepting `S | ((current: S) => S)` is the React-style API, and it
brings one wrinkle: `typeof updater === "function"` cannot narrow a generic `S`
that might itself be a function type, so you will need a cast in that branch.

`subscribe` returns an unsubscribe closure. Notify by iterating a *copy* of the
listener set, so a listener that unsubscribes during a notification cannot
disturb the loop.

The no-op rule is what stops render storms: if the next state is the same value,
do not notify at all. `Object.is` is the comparison to reach for.

## Hint 3

Close over `let state` and a `Set` of listeners, then return an object literal
implementing the four members: `getState` returns `state`; `setState` computes
the next value, compares with `Object.is`, assigns and notifies; `subscribe`
adds and returns a deleter; `select` applies the selector to the current state.

Left to you: whether `setState` should merge a partial state instead of
replacing it. Redux replaces, React's `useState` replaces, `setState` in class
components merged - and an interviewer will absolutely ask which one you built.

## Hint 1

This is the take-home version: a small state container with four members, and
every one of them is a typing decision as much as a coding one. Finish the
`Store<S>` interface first - `getState`, `setState`, `subscribe`, `select` - and
notice that `select` needs its own type parameter, like `Box.map` back in lesson
06.

Read the four behaviour rules in the README before you write any of it.

## Hint 2

`setState` accepting `S | ((current: S) => S)` is the React-style API, and it
brings one wrinkle: `typeof updater === "function"` cannot narrow a generic `S`
that might itself be a function type, so you will need a cast in that branch.

`subscribe` returns an unsubscribe closure. Notify by iterating a *copy* of the
listener set, so a listener that unsubscribes during a notification cannot
disturb the loop.

The no-op rule is what stops render storms: if the next state is the same value,
do not notify at all. `Object.is` is the comparison to reach for.

## Hint 3

Close over `let state` and a `Set` of listeners, then return an object literal
implementing the four members: `getState` returns `state`; `setState` computes
the next value, compares with `Object.is`, assigns and notifies; `subscribe`
adds and returns a deleter; `select` applies the selector to the current state.

Left to you: whether `setState` should merge a partial state instead of
replacing it. Redux replaces, React's `useState` replaces, `setState` in class
components merged - and an interviewer will absolutely ask which one you built.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

This is the most-asked TypeScript design question there is, and the answer is
always the same shape: an interface mapping event names to payload types, then
`keyof` and an indexed access type to tie `on` and `emit` together.

Get the two signatures right before you write a line of the bodies.

## Hint 2

```ts
on<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, handler: (payload: EventMap[K]) => void): () => void;
emit<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, payload: EventMap[K]): void;
```

Storage is a `Map` from event name to a set of handlers. The types inside that
map cannot be precise - handlers for different events have different parameter
types - so store them loosely and cast at the two edges, which is what every
real implementation does.

`on` returns an unsubscribe function; closing over the set and the handler is
all it takes.

## Hint 3

Give the class a `private readonly handlers = new Map<keyof EventMap, Set<...>>()`,
create the set lazily in `on`, add the handler, and return an arrow that deletes
it. In `emit`, look the set up, return early when it is missing, and call each
handler with the payload - iterating a copy, so a handler that unsubscribes
during dispatch cannot break the loop.

Left to you: whether `emit` should catch a throwing handler. Node's EventEmitter
does not; most application-level emitters should. Say which you chose and why.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

This is the most-asked TypeScript design question there is, and the answer is
always the same shape: an interface mapping event names to payload types, then
`keyof` and an indexed access type to tie `on` and `emit` together.

Get the two signatures right before you write a line of the bodies.

## Hint 2

```ts
on<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, handler: (payload: EventMap[K]) => void): () => void;
emit<K extends keyof EventMap>(event: K, payload: EventMap[K]): void;
```

Storage is a `Map` from event name to a set of handlers. The types inside that
map cannot be precise - handlers for different events have different parameter
types - so store them loosely and cast at the two edges, which is what every
real implementation does.

`on` returns an unsubscribe function; closing over the set and the handler is
all it takes.

## Hint 3

Give the class a `private readonly handlers = new Map<keyof EventMap, Set<...>>()`,
create the set lazily in `on`, add the handler, and return an arrow that deletes
it. In `emit`, look the set up, return early when it is missing, and call each
handler with the payload - iterating a copy, so a handler that unsubscribes
during dispatch cannot break the loop.

Left to you: whether `emit` should catch a throwing handler. Node's EventEmitter
does not; most application-level emitters should. Say which you chose and why.

## Drill 3 — promisify (5 minutes)

> "Old error-first callback API. Give me a `promisify` that wraps it — and while
> you are there, write the *type* that converts the callback signature into the
> promise one."

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`.

- `promisify(succeed)()` resolves with the callback's value
- `promisify(fail)()` rejects with the callback's error
- `Promisified<(callback: Callback<number>) => void>` is `() => Promise<number>`

The type half needs a conditional type with `infer`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two halves, and they are independent. `Promisified<F>` is a *type* that takes a
callback-style function type and produces the promise-returning version of it -
which means pattern-matching the callback's payload out of the signature.
`promisify` is the runtime wrapper.

Do the runtime half first if the type half stalls; the gate grades them
separately.

## Hint 2

For the type: a conditional with `infer` is how you pull `T` out of
`(callback: Callback<T>) => void`. The stub's `Promisified<T>` takes the wrong
thing - it should take the *function* type, not the payload.

For the function: return an arrow that returns `new Promise<T>((resolve,
reject) => ...)`, and inside, call `fn` with a callback that rejects on a
non-null error and resolves otherwise.

## Hint 3

```ts
export type Promisified<F> = F extends (callback: Callback<infer T>) => void
  ? () => Promise<T>
  : never;
```

The wrapper resolves with `value as T` - the error-first convention means the
value is only meaningful when the error is null, and the optional `value?` in
the callback type is what forces that cast.

Left to you: what to do when a buggy callback fires twice. A promise ignores the
second settle, which is either a feature or a silently swallowed bug - worth
saying out loud.

## Hint 1

Two halves, and they are independent. `Promisified<F>` is a *type* that takes a
callback-style function type and produces the promise-returning version of it -
which means pattern-matching the callback's payload out of the signature.
`promisify` is the runtime wrapper.

Do the runtime half first if the type half stalls; the gate grades them
separately.

## Hint 2

For the type: a conditional with `infer` is how you pull `T` out of
`(callback: Callback<T>) => void`. The stub's `Promisified<T>` takes the wrong
thing - it should take the *function* type, not the payload.

For the function: return an arrow that returns `new Promise<T>((resolve,
reject) => ...)`, and inside, call `fn` with a callback that rejects on a
non-null error and resolves otherwise.

## Hint 3

```ts
export type Promisified<F> = F extends (callback: Callback<infer T>) => void
  ? () => Promise<T>
  : never;
```

The wrapper resolves with `value as T` - the error-first convention means the
value is only meaningful when the error is null, and the optional `value?` in
the callback type is what forces that cast.

Left to you: what to do when a buggy callback fires twice. A promise ignores the
second settle, which is either a feature or a silently swallowed bug - worth
saying out loud.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Debounce is the interview classic: after a burst of calls, run the function
once, `waitMs` after the *last* one. Every earlier call's pending timer is
cancelled.

The typing half is `Parameters<F>` - the wrapper takes exactly what the wrapped
function takes, and the gate checks that a wrong argument type is rejected.

## Hint 2

```ts
function debounce<F extends (...args: any[]) => void>(
  fn: F,
  waitMs: number,
): (...args: Parameters<F>) => void { ... }
```

The body closes over one timer handle. On each call: clear the pending timer if
there is one, then set a new one that calls `fn(...args)`.

Use `ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>` for the handle's type - it is `number` in
the browser and a `Timeout` object in Node, and this spelling is right in both.

## Hint 3

Declare the timer outside the returned arrow, `clearTimeout` when it is set,
then assign a fresh `setTimeout` whose callback clears the handle and calls
`fn(...args)`.

Left to you: whether the *first* call should fire immediately (a "leading edge"
debounce) and whether the wrapper should expose a `cancel`. Lodash offers both;
mentioning them shows you know which variant you built.

## Drill 5 — flatten a comment tree (10 minutes)

> "We render comments as a flat list with indentation. Take the nested tree and
> give me a flat array, each item with its depth. Order matters — a parent before

Edit `ex5/solution.ts`.

```ts
flattenTree([
  { id: "a", children: [{ id: "a1", children: [{ id: "a1x" }] }, { id: "a2" }] },
  { id: "b" },
]);
// [ {id:"a",depth:0}, {id:"a1",depth:1}, {id:"a1x",depth:2}, {id:"a2",depth:1}, {id:"b",depth:0} ]
```

`children` is optional. An empty forest flattens to `[]`.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A recursive shape and a flat output, in *depth-first, pre-order* - a node
appears before its children, and a subtree is finished before the next sibling
starts. Say that ordering back to the interviewer before you start; half the
wrong answers are breadth-first by accident.

The `children` property is optional, which is the only fiddly part.

## Hint 2

An inner helper carrying the depth is the readable shape:

```ts
const walk = (nodes: readonly TreeNode[], depth: number): void => {
  for (const node of nodes) {
    // record, then recurse into node.children with depth + 1
  }
};
```

`node.children ?? []` turns the optional array into "nothing to recurse into",
which removes the `if` entirely.

## Hint 3

Declare a `FlatNode[]` accumulator, define `walk(nodes, depth)` that pushes
`{ id: node.id, depth }` and then calls itself with the children and
`depth + 1`, call it with the roots at depth `0`, and return the accumulator.

Left to you: what happens with a tree ten thousand levels deep. Recursion blows
the stack; an explicit stack of `[node, depth]` pairs does not - and knowing
that trade-off is often the follow-up question.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

A recursive shape and a flat output, in *depth-first, pre-order* - a node
appears before its children, and a subtree is finished before the next sibling
starts. Say that ordering back to the interviewer before you start; half the
wrong answers are breadth-first by accident.

The `children` property is optional, which is the only fiddly part.

## Hint 2

An inner helper carrying the depth is the readable shape:

```ts
const walk = (nodes: readonly TreeNode[], depth: number): void => {
  for (const node of nodes) {
    // record, then recurse into node.children with depth + 1
  }
};
```

`node.children ?? []` turns the optional array into "nothing to recurse into",
which removes the `if` entirely.

## Hint 3

Declare a `FlatNode[]` accumulator, define `walk(nodes, depth)` that pushes
`{ id: node.id, depth }` and then calls itself with the children and
`depth + 1`, call it with the roots at depth `0`, and return the accumulator.

Left to you: what happens with a tree ten thousand levels deep. Recursion blows
the stack; an explicit stack of `[node, depth]` pairs does not - and knowing
that trade-off is often the follow-up question.

> "Type this for me: `pipe(value, f, g, h)` applies the functions left to right,

- `pipe(2, double, label, shout)` → `"N=4"`

  `double` takes a number

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`pipe(2, double, toLabel)` should be typed by following the chain: the first
function's output is the second's input, and the last one's output is the
result. A single generic signature cannot express that, because the number of
steps varies.

The tool for "one function, several contracts" is the one from lesson 02.

## Hint 2

Write overload signatures for one, two and three functions:

```ts
export function pipe<A, B>(value: A, ab: (input: A) => B): B;
export function pipe<A, B, C>(value: A, ab: (input: A) => B, bc: (input: B) => C): C;
```

Each one threads the type parameters through, which is what makes the middle
callbacks contextually typed at the call site. Then one implementation
signature, loose enough to cover them all, with a `reduce` body.

## Hint 3

Three overloads (two, three and four arguments), then
`export function pipe(value: unknown, ...fns: ((input: unknown) => unknown)[]): unknown`
whose body is `fns.reduce((current, fn) => fn(current), value)`.

Left to you: the implementation signature is invisible to callers, and
TypeScript checks it only loosely against the overloads - so the overloads are a
promise you are making. Being able to say that is the point of the drill.

exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

`pipe(2, double, toLabel)` should be typed by following the chain: the first
function's output is the second's input, and the last one's output is the
result. A single generic signature cannot express that, because the number of
steps varies.

The tool for "one function, several contracts" is the one from lesson 02.

## Hint 2

Write overload signatures for one, two and three functions:

```ts
export function pipe<A, B>(value: A, ab: (input: A) => B): B;
export function pipe<A, B, C>(value: A, ab: (input: A) => B, bc: (input: B) => C): C;
```

Each one threads the type parameters through, which is what makes the middle
callbacks contextually typed at the call site. Then one implementation
signature, loose enough to cover them all, with a `reduce` body.

## Hint 3

Three overloads (two, three and four arguments), then
`export function pipe(value: unknown, ...fns: ((input: unknown) => unknown)[]): unknown`
whose body is `fns.reduce((current, fn) => fn(current), value)`.

Left to you: the implementation signature is invisible to callers, and
TypeScript checks it only loosely against the overloads - so the overloads are a
promise you are making. Being able to say that is the point of the drill.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Same keys, new values. Two type parameters: the source object type and whatever
the transform produces. `Record<keyof T, U>` is the return type, which says "the
same keys, all of them, holding `U`".

The transform receives the value and the key, in that order.

## Hint 2

```ts
function mapValues<T extends object, U>(
  source: T,
  transform: (value: T[keyof T], key: keyof T & string) => U,
): Record<keyof T, U> { ... }
```

`Object.keys` is typed `string[]` rather than `(keyof T)[]` - deliberately,
because a value can always have more properties than its type declares - so
iterating needs one cast. Keep it on the loop and nowhere else.

The accumulator needs `{} as Record<keyof T, U>` for the same reason
`pickKeys` did in lesson 08: an object under construction is not yet the type
it will be.

## Hint 3

Cast the key list, loop it, and assign `transform(source[key], key)` into the
accumulator.

Left to you: whether to reach for `Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(source)
.map(...))` instead. It is one line and it hands you back
`{ [k: string]: U }` - so you trade a loop for a cast, which is the kind of
trade worth being able to justify out loud.

lessons.briefing:
# i3 — Interview rapid-fire

Five short rounds over the five concepts that come up most often, in shapes you
have not seen before. Nothing here is new material — that is the point. This is
the last lesson of the track, and its job is to make the ⭐⭐⭐ answers automatic.

Then it keeps doing that job. Every exercise in this lesson is fresh phrasing of
something you already learned, and `review1` feeds the spaced-review scheduler,
so `dojo review` brings this material back at three days, a week, three weeks
and two months. The ladder is the mechanism; you just have to keep showing up.

Give each round the time box in its heading. If one takes longer, the note to
write down is *which* part cost the time — the type, the edge case, or the
JavaScript.

## Round 1 — `unknown` in, narrowed out (60 seconds)

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Change the `any` to `unknown` and implement
`toNumber(value)`:

- `toNumber(42)` → `42`; `toNumber("42")` → `42`; `toNumber("3.5")` → `3.5`
- `toNumber("")`, `toNumber("   ")`, `toNumber("abc")` → `null`
- `toNumber(NaN)` → `null` — `typeof NaN` is `"number"`, and it is not a usable one
- `toNumber(null)`, `toNumber({ value: 1 })` → `null`

`Number("")` is `0`, which is the trap this round is built around.

```
uv run dojo test typescript i3_interview_rapidfire ex1
```

## Round 2 — close the union (90 seconds)

Edit `ex2/solution.ts`. `Level` has four members and `levelBadge` handles two,
hidden by a catch-all `default`. Add the missing cases and replace the default
with an `assertNever` call:

- `"beginner"` → `"*"`, `"intermediate"` → `"**"`, `"advanced"` → `"***"`,
  `"master"` → `"****"`

```
uv run dojo test typescript i3_interview_rapidfire ex2
```

## Round 3 — constrain the key (90 seconds)

Edit `ex3/solution.ts`. Rewrite `sortByKey` with a generic element type and a
key constrained to that element's keys, sorting a **copy** ascending:

- `sortByKey(learners, "streak")` → Grace(3), Eli(7), Ada(12)
- `sortByKey(learners, "name")` → Ada, Eli, Grace
- the input array is unchanged afterwards

Five ⭐⭐⭐ concepts, one more time, with the traps that make each of them an
interview question rather than a triviality.

## Notes

**Why these five.** `unknown` at the boundary, exhaustiveness with `never`, a
constrained generic with `keyof`, a utility type written from scratch, and
`satisfies` on a config object. Across mid-level full-stack screens these are
the TypeScript topics that come up most, and each one has a short, sayable
answer that this track has now given you three times.

**Retrieval, not review.** Rereading a lesson feels productive and does very
little; being asked a question cold and having to produce the answer is what
moves it into long-term memory. That is why these exercises are freshly phrased
rather than repeats, and why the review ladder — 3 days, 7, 21, 60 — matters more
than any single sitting. `dojo review run` is the command; keeping the streak is
the work.

**Speak the shape before you type it.** Every round here has a signature that
gives away the solution: `(value: unknown) => number | null`,
`<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K) => T[]`,
`T extends null | undefined ? never : T`. In an interview, saying the signature
out loud is both the fastest way to the answer and the clearest demonstration
that you think in types.

**When you finish the track.** The honest last step is to be interviewed — by a
friend, a colleague, or an interviewer you do not mind losing. Nothing in a
course reproduces the specific pressure of explaining variance to a stranger
while your screen is shared.

## ex1 — `unknown` in, narrowed out

Three traps in one small function. `typeof NaN === "number"` is true, so a
`typeof` check alone lets `NaN` through — `Number.isFinite` is the guard, and it
is the *static* method deliberately, because the global `isFinite` coerces its
argument (`isFinite("42")` is `true`, which defeats the point). `Number("")` is
`0`, so an empty string silently becomes a valid number unless you check for it.
And `Number("   ")` is also `0`, which is why the check is on the *trimmed*
string.

The design question worth raising in an interview: which string formats count?
`Number()` accepts `"1e3"`, `"0x1f"`, `"Infinity"` and leading/trailing
whitespace; `parseFloat` accepts a numeric prefix and ignores the rest
(`parseFloat("42abc")` is `42`); `parseInt` needs a radix and truncates. Naming
that difference unprompted is the kind of detail that gets remembered.

*Weak here → redo `10_guards_assertions`.*

## ex2 — close the union

The shipped code is a realistic bug: two branches, a catch-all `default`, and a
union that grew. Nothing failed to compile, and the wrong answer (`"?"`) is
plausible enough to survive review. That is precisely why `assertNever` is worth
the five lines — it converts "somewhere in this codebase a string is now wrong"
into a compile error at the exact site.

The one-sentence explanation to have ready: "in an exhaustive switch the default
branch narrows the value to `never`, and nothing is assignable to `never`, so the
call only compiles when every case is handled." Follow it with the reason it
also throws: types are erased, so a bad value really can arrive at runtime from
`JSON.parse` or a JavaScript caller.

The final nudge in the hint — returning `"*" | "**" | "***" | "****"` instead of
`string` — is the habit this track keeps pushing: give callers the narrowest
useful type. It costs nothing and lets them `switch` exhaustively in turn.

*Weak here → redo `04_unions_narrowing` and `i1_interview_concepts` ex2.*

## ex3 — constrain the key

`<T, K extends keyof T>` for the third time, because it is the single most
common generic signature in real TypeScript. The stub's `(items: readonly any[],
key: string)` is what the same function looks like when nobody bothered: it
compiles, it runs, and it accepts `sortByKey(learners, "nickanme")` without a
murmur.

Two runtime details the gate checks. The copy — `sort` mutates, and a `readonly`
parameter makes the compiler enforce that you copied. And returning `0` for
equal values rather than a guess, which matters because `Array.prototype.sort`
has been required to be *stable* since ES2019: equal elements keep their input
order, so a stable sort by one key after another gives you a predictable
multi-key ordering.

The follow-up to expect: "what if the property is a `Date`, or a mixed
`string | number`?" `<` works on dates by coercion and on mixed types by
lexicographic accident, which is why a production version takes an optional
comparator. Saying that is better than pretending `<` is universal.

*Weak here → redo `07_generics_2`.*

## ex4 — write the utility type

`MyNonNullable<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T` is four things at
once: a conditional type, a naked type parameter (so it distributes over the
union), `never` as the "drop this" signal, and the fact that `never` disappears
from a union. Being able to unpack that sentence is a strong senior answer to
"how does `Exclude` work?".

`MyReturnType<F> = F extends (...args: never[]) => infer R ? R : never` is the
`infer` half. `never[]` in the parameter position is the trick that makes the
pattern match every function regardless of its parameters — parameters are
checked contravariantly, and `never` is assignable to everything, so it fits
them all. The standard library uses `any[]` for the same reason; both work, and
knowing *why* one of them is needed is the point.

The runtime half is the type-guard predicate:
`items.filter((item): item is MyNonNullable<T> => item !== null && item !==
undefined)`. Without the predicate, `filter` returns `T[]` and the `null` is
still in the type — a genuinely common frustration, and the reason
`array.filter(Boolean)` is such a poor idea in TypeScript (it also drops `0`,
`""` and `false`, which the gate checks for).

*Weak here → redo `08_utility_types` and `09_mapped_conditional`.*

## review1 — `satisfies`, one more time

The annotation `: Record<string, { method: Method; path: string }>` does three
damaging things at once: it widens each `path` to `string`, widens each `method`
to the `Method` union, and — worst — gives the object an index signature, so
`keyof typeof ROUTES` becomes `string` and `describeRoute("lisstLessons")`
typechecks. That last consequence is the one people miss, and it is the strongest
argument for `satisfies` in a single example.

`as const satisfies T` is the combination worth memorising for config: `as const`
keeps every literal and makes it read-only, `satisfies` still validates the whole
shape, and the object's own inferred type — with exactly its real keys — survives.
Route tables, feature flags, design tokens, and command registries all want it.

The open question in the hint is a real design point: `Record<string, ...>` as
the constraint checks the *values* but not the key set. If you want the key set
constrained too, name it — `Record<RouteName, RouteDefinition>` — and now a
missing route is a compile error as well.

*Weak here → redo `05_literals_enums` and `10_guards_assertions` ex4.*

## Further reading

- [Handbook: Narrowing](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html) — `unknown`, type guards and the exhaustiveness recipe, all in one page.
- [Handbook: Utility Types](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/utility-types.html) — `NonNullable`, `ReturnType` and the rest, with their definitions.
- [TypeScript 4.9: the `satisfies` operator](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-4-9.html#the-satisfies-operator) — the motivating example, one page.
- [MDN: `Array.prototype.sort` — stability](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/sort#sort_stability) — why returning `0` for equal elements is the right move.
- [MDN: `Number.isFinite` vs the global `isFinite`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Number/isFinite) — the coercion difference behind round 1.

## Round 1 — `unknown` in, narrowed out (60 seconds)

Edit `ex1/solution.ts`. Change the `any` to `unknown` and implement
`toNumber(value)`:

- `toNumber(42)` → `42`; `toNumber("42")` → `42`; `toNumber("3.5")` → `3.5`
- `toNumber("")`, `toNumber("   ")`, `toNumber("abc")` → `null`
- `toNumber(NaN)` → `null` — `typeof NaN` is `"number"`, and it is not a usable one
- `toNumber(null)`, `toNumber({ value: 1 })` → `null`

`Number("")` is `0`, which is the trap this round is built around.

exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two `any`s and a `string` key: every promise this signature could make, it has
declined to make. The version you want is the one from lesson 07 - an element
type and a key constrained to that element's keys.

And it returns a *new* array, because the input is `readonly`.

## Hint 2

```ts
function sortByKey<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K): T[] { ... }
```

The comparator receives two `T`s, reads `a[key]` and `b[key]`, and returns a
negative number, zero, or a positive one. `<` works for both strings and numbers,
which is why this can stay generic without a constraint on `T[K]`.

Copy before sorting - and note that with a `readonly` parameter the compiler
will not let you forget.

## Hint 3

Spread into a new array, `.sort()` with a comparator that returns `0` when the
values are equal and otherwise `-1` or `1` from a `<` comparison.

Left to you: `sort` is stable in modern JavaScript engines, so equal elements
keep their relative order - which is why returning `0` rather than guessing is
the right move. Being able to say "stable since ES2019" is a nice detail.

## Hint 1

Two `any`s and a `string` key: every promise this signature could make, it has
declined to make. The version you want is the one from lesson 07 - an element
type and a key constrained to that element's keys.

And it returns a *new* array, because the input is `readonly`.

## Hint 2

```ts
function sortByKey<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K): T[] { ... }
```

The comparator receives two `T`s, reads `a[key]` and `b[key]`, and returns a
negative number, zero, or a positive one. `<` works for both strings and numbers,
which is why this can stay generic without a constraint on `T[K]`.

Copy before sorting - and note that with a `readonly` parameter the compiler
will not let you forget.

## Hint 3

Spread into a new array, `.sort()` with a comparator that returns `0` when the
values are equal and otherwise `-1` or `1` from a `<` comparison.

Left to you: `sort` is stable in modern JavaScript engines, so equal elements
keep their relative order - which is why returning `0` rather than guessing is
the right move. Being able to say "stable since ES2019" is a nice detail.

Edit `ex4/solution.ts`. Implement two standard-library types from scratch and
one runtime helper:

  `compact([1, null, 2, undefined, 3])` → `[1, 2, 3]`, and

## Hint 1

Two one-line conditional types and one runtime filter. `MyNonNullable<T>` drops
`null` and `undefined` from a union; `MyReturnType<F>` pulls the result type out
of a function type.

## Hint 2

The first distributes over the union because the checked type is a naked type
parameter, and `never` disappears from a union:


The second needs `infer` in the return position of a function pattern.

## Hint 1

As written, `keyof typeof ROUTES` is `string` - the annotation gave the object
an index signature, so every route name in the world typechecks and typos are
invisible. The gate checks that `ROUTES` has exactly two known keys and that
each `path` keeps its literal type.

Two operators fix it, and you have met both.

## Hint 2

`as const satisfies Record<string, { method: Method; path: string }>` does the
whole job: `as const` freezes the values and keeps them literal, and `satisfies`
still checks every entry against the shape - so a route with
`method: "PATCH"` is a compile error.

The annotation has to go: an annotation and a `satisfies` clause on the same
declaration means the annotation wins.

## Hint 3

Drop the `: Record<...>` annotation, append
`as const satisfies Record<string, { method: Method; path: string }>`, and
implement the function as a lookup returning `` `${route.method} ${route.path}` ``.

Left to you: whether to keep `Record<string, ...>` as the constraint or narrow
it further. Ask what you are protecting against - a bad `method`, a missing
`path`, or a misspelled route name - and note which of the three each spelling
catches.

## Hint 1

As written, `keyof typeof ROUTES` is `string` - the annotation gave the object
an index signature, so every route name in the world typechecks and typos are
invisible. The gate checks that `ROUTES` has exactly two known keys and that
each `path` keeps its literal type.

Two operators fix it, and you have met both.

## Hint 2

`as const satisfies Record<string, { method: Method; path: string }>` does the
whole job: `as const` freezes the values and keeps them literal, and `satisfies`
still checks every entry against the shape - so a route with
`method: "PATCH"` is a compile error.

The annotation has to go: an annotation and a `satisfies` clause on the same
declaration means the annotation wins.

## Hint 3

Drop the `: Record<...>` annotation, append
`as const satisfies Record<string, { method: Method; path: string }>`, and
implement the function as a lookup returning `` `${route.method} ${route.path}` ``.

Left to you: whether to keep `Record<string, ...>` as the constraint or narrow
it further. Ask what you are protecting against - a bad `method`, a missing
`path`, or a misspelled route name - and note which of the three each spelling
catches.
